editorialDecl.p: New English translation produced by the Falsafa project (Thothica) using an in-house agentic AI translation system, rendered from the Perseus source edition and reviewed by the project. Contributed to provide a translation for a work that previously had no English translation in the corpus.

div.p: Whatever I have written against Marcion in the past may now be left aside. We are undertaking a new work out of an old one. My first little treatise I cancelled, as too hastily put together, in favour of a fuller composition made afterwards. This too, before I had supplied it with copies, I lost through the treachery of a man then a brother, afterwards an apostate, who had by chance transcribed some of it most inaccurately and made it public. The necessity of correction arose; and the occasion of this fresh revision persuaded me to add something. So this pen, now passing from a second draft to a third, and from the third again to a first, must of necessity preface this issue of its little work, lest the variety of it, found scattered abroad, confuse anyone. The Pontus which is called Euxine is denied its nature and mocked by its name. For the rest, do not judge the Pontus to be hospitable by its situation; so far has it withdrawn from our more civilized waters, as if out of some shame at its own barbarism. The fiercest tribes inhabit it, if indeed there is any inhabiting in a wagon. Their dwelling is unfixed, their life is raw, their lust promiscuous and for the most part open; and even when they conceal it, they hang their quivers on the yoke as a sign, so that no one may casually intrude. So not even of their weapons are they ashamed. They devour at their banquets the corpses of their parents cut up together with cattle. Those who have not died in such a way as to be fit for eating are reckoned to have met an accursed death. Nor are the women softened by their sex into any modesty: they bare their breasts, they do their spinning with axes, they would rather make war than marry. There is hardness in the sky too. The day is never open, the sun never willing, the whole air is one fog, the entire year is winter, and whatever blows is the north wind. Liquids return to their state only by fire; rivers are denied by ice; mountains are heaped high with frost. Everything is numb, everything is stiff; nothing there has any warmth except savagery — that savagery, of course, which gave the stage its fables of the sacrifices of the Tauri, the loves of the Colchians, and the crosses of the Caucasus. But there is nothing among the people of Pontus so barbarous and so dismal as that Marcion was born there: more foul than any Scythian, more unsettled than the wagon-dweller, more inhuman than the Massagetes, more audacious than an Amazon, darker than the fog, colder than winter, more brittle than the ice, more treacherous than the Danube, more precipitous than the Caucasus. How not? — when in his hands the true Prometheus, almighty God, is torn to pieces by blasphemies. And by now Marcion is more savage even than the beasts of that barbarous land. For what beaver is so great a self-mutilator of the flesh as the man who has abolished marriage? What Pontic mouse so great a gnawer as the man who has nibbled away the Gospels? Truly, O Euxine, you have brought forth a beast more acceptable to philosophers than to Christians. For that cynic Diogenes wanted to find a man, carrying his lantern about at midday; but Marcion, having put out the light of his own faith, lost the God he had found. His disciples will not deny that his first faith was with us, his own letters being witnesses, so that from this point on he can be marked out as a heretic — one who, abandoning what was first, afterwards chose for himself what previously was not. For just so far will a thing be reckoned heresy as it is brought in afterwards, just so far will it be held truth as it was handed down before and from the beginning. But another little book will sustain this argument against heretics — that they may be refuted even without examining their doctrines, on the ground that they are what they are by the very fact of their novelty. Now, in so far as the engagement is to be allowed — and that the brief plea of prescription, everywhere invoked, may not for once be reckoned to diffidence — I will first set out the rule of my adversary, that it may be plain to all in what the principal question is to be fought out.

The occasion of recasting this little work — what befell the first little book of it we have stated in the preface — has also conferred this upon us: that, in treating again of the two gods against Marcion, we should distinguish for each its own title and volume according to the division of the matter; defining the one god to be altogether non-existent, and defending the other to be worthily God; inasmuch as it so pleased the Pontic to bring in the one and exclude the other. For he could not build up a lie without the demolition of the truth. He had of necessity to undermine the one, that he might rear up what he wished. So builds he who lacks materials of his own. But it had been enough to dispute on this point only: that no god is that one who is brought in over the Creator; so that, the false god being driven off by sure rules which prescribe a single and perfect divinity, no further inquiry might now be made into the true God, who, just as it is established that He exists — even so, while it is not established that another exists — so ought of necessity to be held, of whatever kind, without controversy, to be adored rather than judged, and to be conciliated rather than canvassed, or rather than feared on account of His severity. For what is more necessary for man than care toward the true God, upon whom (so to speak) he had lighted, because there was no other god?

Following the track of my earlier work, which I am bent on restoring now that it has been lost, the argument here passes on to Christ — though this comes as an addition, after the defence already completed of the single Godhead. For it has been sufficiently established beforehand that Christ is to be understood as belonging to no other God than the Creator, since it was determined that no other God is to be believed in besides the Creator, whom indeed Christ proclaimed; and since the apostles in turn announced no other Christ than that of the very God whom Christ proclaimed, that is, the Creator — so that no mention of another God, and therefore none of another Christ, was ever raised before the scandal of Marcion. This is most easily proved by a review of the apostolic and the heretical churches: namely, that the perversion of the rule is to be pronounced wherever the later date is found. This too I wove into my first book. But even now this separate encounter, which is to examine the question of Christ on its own, will at least achieve this, that while we prove Christ to be the Creator's, the god of Marcion is thereby also excluded. It befits truth to use all its forces, not as one in difficulty. For the rest, in the shorthand of legal objections it wins outright. But it has been resolved to meet at every point an adversary so frantic with eagerness that he has more readily presumed that a Christ has come who was never announced than the one who was always proclaimed.

The whole position and the whole apparatus of the impious and sacrilegious Marcion we now summon to his very own gospel, which by interpolating he made his own. And in order to furnish it with credit, he devised a sort of dowry for it, a work entitled Antitheses from the oppositions of contraries, and forced into a separation of law and gospel — by which, dividing two gods, accordingly diverse, the one of one instrument, or, what is more usual to say, of one testament, and the other of the other, he might thereafter give patronage to the gospel too, believed in according to the Antitheses. But these I would have struck down by a direct hand-to-hand engagement, that is, through each separate thrust of the man of Pontus, had they not been far more conveniently beaten back in the gospel itself and along with the gospel for whose sake they are contrived; although it is so easy to meet them with a preliminary objection — and indeed in such a way that I accept them, that I ratify them, that I say they work with us, so that they may the more blush for the blindness of their own author — that now the Antitheses are ours against Marcion. And indeed I confess that one order ran its course in the old arrangement with the Creator, another in the new with Christ. I do not deny that the evidences of utterance differ, the precepts of virtue, the disciplines of the law, provided only that the whole diversity converges upon one and the same God — him, namely, by whom it is established to have been arranged just as it was also foretold. Long ago Isaiah proclaims that a law would go forth from Zion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem — another law, surely, and another word. In short, "He shall judge," he says, "among the nations, and shall convict a numerous people" — namely not of the single nation of the Jews, but of the nations, who through the new law of the gospel and the new word of the apostles are judged and convicted in themselves of their former error, as soon as they have believed, and thereupon "beat their swords into ploughshares, and their pikes" (which is a kind of hunting-spear) "into pruning-hooks" — that is, they convert their once fierce and savage spirits into upright senses and into workers of good fruit. And again: "Hear me, hear me, my people, and you kings, give ear to me; for a law shall go forth from me, and my judgement for a light of the nations" — by which he had judged and decreed that the nations too were to be illumined through the law and the word of the gospel. This will be the law also with David, "blameless," because perfect, "converting the soul" — surely from idols to God. This will be also the word concerning which the same Isaiah says: "For the Lord will make a shortened word upon the earth." For the new testament has been abridged and freed from the burdensome trappings of the law. But why say more, when novation is proclaimed by the Creator through the same prophet more plainly and more clearly than the light itself? "Remember not the former things, and consider not the things of old: the old things have passed away, new things arise: behold, I make new things, which shall now arise." Likewise through Jeremiah: "Make for yourselves a new freshness, and sow not among thorns, and be circumcised in the foreskin of your heart." And elsewhere: "Behold, the days shall come, says the Lord, and I will perfect for the house of Jacob and the house of Judah a new testament, not according to the testament which I arranged for their fathers in the day when I took hold of their arrangement to lead them out of the land of Egypt." So far does he signify the former testament to be temporary, while he shows it to be changeable, even while he promises an eternal one for the future. For through Isaiah, "Hear me and you shall live, and I will arrange for you an everlasting testament," adding "the holy and faithful things of David," that he might show that testament was to run its course in Christ. The same Christ, descended from the stock of David, according to the registration of Mary, he was also foretelling figuratively in the rod to come forth from the root of Jesse. Therefore, if he said that other laws and other words and new arrangements of the testaments were to come to be from the Creator — so that he even appointed other and preferable offices of the very sacrifices, and that indeed among the nations, Malachi saying, "I have no will in you, says the Lord, and your sacrifices I will not receive from your hands; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, even a clean sacrifice" — namely simple prayer from a pure conscience — it is of necessity that every change coming from innovation should incur a diversity with those things of which it is made, and a contrariety from the diversity. For just as nothing is changed which is not made diverse, so nothing is diverse which is not made contrary. Therefore the contrariety from diversity will be reckoned to belong to the same one whose was the change from innovation. He who arranged the change, the same instituted the diversity too; he who proclaimed the innovation, the same foretold the contrariety too. Why do you interpret the difference of things into a distance of powers? Why do you twist the Antitheses of examples against the Creator, which you can recognize even in his very feelings and affections? "I," he says, "will strike, and I will heal: I," he says, "will kill, and I will make alive" — making evil things, namely, and working peace; by which indeed you are wont to reproach him under the name even of mobility and inconstancy, as forbidding what he commands and commanding what he forbids. Why, then, did you not reckon the Antitheses too among the natural properties of a Creator always contrary to himself? You could not even have considered the world — unless I am mistaken, even among the Pontic peoples — except as built up out of diversities of mutually rival substances. First, then, you ought to have determined one god of light, another of darkness, that so you might be able to assert one of the law, another of the gospel. But it has been judged beforehand from manifest things, that of whom the works and characters are established through the Antitheses, of the same form are established his sacraments too.

Nothing is without an origin except God alone. And as far as origin precedes in the standing of all things, so far must it precede also in their re-examination, that the standing may be established; for you cannot discern what a thing is and of what kind, unless you are certain that it is, once you have learned whence it is. And so, having come down to this subject in the order of my little work, I demand of Marcion the origin of the apostle as well — a fresh sort of disciple, the pupil of no other, who for the present believe nothing except that nothing is to be believed rashly, and that whatever is believed without acknowledgement of its origin is believed rashly. And I shall most fittingly carry this inquiry to the point of anxiety, since the man is affirmed to me as an apostle whom I do not find in the roll of the apostles in the gospel. So then, hearing that he was afterwards taken on by the Lord, when the Lord was already at rest in the heavens, I judge it a kind of improvidence that Christ did not know beforehand that this man would be necessary to him, but, once the office of the apostolate had been arranged and dismissed upon its work, thought he must be added by sudden encounter and not by foresight — by necessity, so to speak, not by will. Therefore, shipmaster of Pontus, if you have never received stolen or contraband wares into your boats, if you have never diverted or adulterated any cargo whatever — being doubtless the more cautious and faithful in the things of God — I would have you publish to us by what token you have taken on the apostle Paul, who stamped him with the mark of a title, who consigned him to you, who put him on board, that you may be able to set him forth with assurance, lest he be proved to belong to that one who has produced all the documents of his apostleship. He professed himself an apostle, you say, and indeed not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ. Plainly anyone can profess himself; but his profession is made good by another's authority: one writes, another countersigns, another seals, another enters it in the records. No one is at once witness and professor on his own behalf. Besides this you have surely read that many would come who would say, I am Christ. If there is one to lie that he is Christ, how much more one to proclaim himself an apostle of Christ? Still I am moving in the character of a disciple and an inquirer, that even from here I may blunt your faith — you who have no means of proving it — and shame your effrontery — you who lay claim, and do not take up the means by which you might lay claim. Let there be a Christ, let there be an apostle, but of that other God, so long as they are not proved except out of the instrument of the Creator. For Genesis long ago promised me Paul as well. For among those figures and prophetic blessings of Jacob upon his sons, when he had said to Benjamin, Benjamin, he says, a ravening wolf shall feed in the morning, and at evening shall give food — for he foresaw that Paul would arise from the tribe of Benjamin, a ravening wolf feeding in the morning, that is, in his early age laying waste the flock of the Lord as a persecutor of the churches, and afterwards giving food at evening, that is, in his now declining age teaching the sheep of Christ as a doctor of the nations. For the harshness too of Saul's persecution of David at first, and afterwards his repentance and amends, receiving good for evil, portended nothing else than Paul in Saul according to the tribe, and Jesus in David according to the reckoning of the virgin. If these sacraments of the figures displease you, at least the Acts of the Apostles have handed down to me this order of Paul's career, not to be denied by you either. Thence I show the apostle to have been a persecutor, not from men nor through man; thence I am induced to believe him myself; thence I expel you from his defence, and I do not fear you saying, Do you then deny the apostle Paul? I do not blaspheme him whom I protect. I deny him in order to compel you to prove him; I deny him in order to convince you that he is mine. Or if you look to our faith, accept what makes it; if you appeal to your own, produce what underpins it. Either prove that what you believe is, or, if you do not prove it, how do you believe? Or what manner of believer are you against him by whom alone is proved to be that very thing which you believe? Have now both the apostle from my side, just as the Christ also, as much my apostle as my Christ. We shall fight on these same lines here too, we shall challenge on the very step of prescription — that the apostle, namely, who is denied to the Creator, who indeed is brought forward against the Creator, must teach nothing, hold nothing, will nothing according to the Creator, and above all must proclaim another God with as great constancy as that with which he broke off from the law of the Creator. For it is not likely that, turning men away from Judaism, he should not equally have shown into the faith of what God he was turning them, since no one could pass over from the Creator without knowing to whom he was to pass. For either Christ had already revealed another God — and then the apostle's testimony followed, that he might not be reckoned the apostle of a God whom Christ had revealed, and because what had already been revealed by Christ could not be hidden from the apostle — or else Christ had revealed nothing of the kind concerning God, and then it ought all the more to have been revealed by the apostle, since now it could not be by another, and is surely not to be believed if not revealed even by the apostle. This we have established beforehand, that from here we may profess that we shall prove no other God carried about by the apostle, just as we proved none by Christ, out of Paul's own epistles, which therefore — mutilated even in their number — the very shape of the heretic's gospel ought already to have prejudged.

The Pontic brings forward two gods, like the two Symplegades of his own shipwreck: the one he could not deny, that is, our Creator; and the one he will not be able to prove, that is, his own. He suffered, unhappy man, the prompting of this presumption from a simple clause of the Lord's pronouncement, which sets forth, with respect to men and not to gods, those examples of the good and the bad tree — that neither does the good tree bring forth bad fruits nor the bad good; that is, neither does a good mind or faith produce bad works, nor a bad one good. For sickening (as many do even now, and especially the heretics) over the question of evil — whence comes evil — and with his senses dulled by the very enormity of his curiosity, finding the Creator declaring, "I am he who creates evils," in proportion as he had already presumed the Creator to be the author of evil, both from this and from other arguments which so persuade every perverse mind, in the same proportion he interpreted the Creator to be the bad tree producing bad fruits, namely evils, and presumed that there must be another god to take the part of the good tree producing good fruits. And so, finding in Christ as it were another dispensation of mere and pure goodness, distinct from the Creator's, he readily argued for a new and alien divinity revealed in his Christ, and thereafter with a little leaven soured the whole mass of faith with a heretic's sourness. He had also a certain Cerdo as the deviser of this scandal, by whom these two blind men the more easily fancied they had perceived two gods. For they had not seen one whole. To bleared eyes even a single lamp looks many. The one god, then, whom he was compelled to confess, he pulled down by branding him with evil; the other, whom he was striving to invent, he built up by laying a foundation of goodness. By what articles he distributed these two natures we have shown in our own replies.

But now God Almighty, the Lord and Founder of the universe, is put to trouble. For this reason only, I suppose: because He has been known from the beginning, because He never lay hid, because He always shone forth — even before Romulus himself, much more before Tiberius. Except that to the heretics alone He is not known, who make trouble for Him, on this account thinking that another god must be presumed, because they can rather find fault with Him whom they grant to exist than deny Him — weighing God by the arbitration of their own sense; just as if a blind man, or one with swimming eyes, should for that reason wish to presume another sun, milder and more wholesome, because he does not see the one he looks at. There is one sun, O man, which tempers this world; and when you think it not, it is best and most useful; and even when to you it is too keen and hostile, or even too sordid and corrupt, it is yet equal to its own reason. If you cannot perceive that reason, then neither could you have borne the rays of any other sun, if there had been one — a greater one, of course. For you who are blind toward an inferior god — what of a loftier one? Nay rather, spare your own weakness, and do not stretch yourself into danger, having a God certain and undoubted, and on this very score sufficiently seen, since you have first beheld Him to be one whom you know not save in the part in which He Himself willed. But God you do not, as one who knows, deny; and as one who knows not, you canvass — nay, even accuse, as though you knew, Him whom, if you knew, you would not accuse, nay, would not even canvass. While you render Him His name, you deny the substance of the name, that is, of the greatness which is called God — not acknowledging it as great as, if man could have known it in every way, it would not be greatness. Isaiah, even then an apostle, foreseeing heretical hearts, says: "Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been His counsellor? Or whom has He consulted, or who has shown Him the way of understanding and knowledge?" To whom the apostle too agrees: "O the depth of the riches and the wisdom of God! how unsearchable are His judgments" — those of God the judge, of course — "and His ways past finding out" — those of understanding and knowledge, which no one showed Him, unless perchance these censors of divinity, saying, "God ought not to have so done," and, "He ought rather to have done thus" — as though anyone knew the things that are in God, save the Spirit of God. But having the spirit of the world, not acknowledging God through wisdom in the wisdom of God, they seem to themselves wiser in counsel than God; since, as the wisdom of the world is foolishness with God, so the wisdom of God is foolishness with the world. But we know the foolish thing of God wiser than men, and the weak thing of God stronger than men. And so God is then greatest, when to man He is little; and then best, when to man not good; and then most one, when to man He is two or more. But if from the beginning the animal man, not receiving the things that are of the Spirit, esteemed the law of God foolishness — which he therefore neglected to observe, and so, by not having faith, even what he seemed to have was taken from him: the grace of Paradise and the familiarity of God, through which he would have known all the things of God had he obeyed — what wonder, if, given back to his own matter and relegated to the workhouse of the earth that had to be laboured, in the very work bent down and stooping toward the earth, he handed on, to his whole race, the spirit of the world usurped from it — at least to the race that is animal and heretical, not receiving the things that are of God? Or who will doubt that that very transgression of Adam was a heresy, which he admitted by the choice of his own rather than of the divine sentence? Except that Adam never said to his potter, "You did not fashion me prudently." He confessed his seduction. He did not hide his seductress. He was a very raw heretic. He did not obey, yet he did not blaspheme the Creator, nor reproach the Author, whom from his very beginning he had found good and best, and whom — if at all — he had himself made his judge from the beginning.

Here, then, I join the first step of the argument: whether he ought to have come so suddenly. First, because he too is the son of his own god. For this was the proper order: that the Father should profess the Son before the Son the Father, and that the Father should bear witness concerning the Son before the Son concerning the Father. Next, because he was sent, over and above the name of son. For the patronage of the sender ought likewise to have preceded as testimony to the one sent, since no one who comes on the authority of another vindicates that authority for himself by his own assertion, but rather looks for his defence from that other, with the prior recommendation of him who supplies the authority. For the rest, neither will he be acknowledged as a son whom the father never named, nor believed to be sent whom the commissioner never designated — though the father would have named him and the commissioner designated him, had there been one. Everything will be held suspect that has strayed from the rule, and the primary order of things does not allow the father to be acknowledged after the son, the commissioner after the commission, and God after Christ. Nothing is prior to its own origin in being acknowledged, just as nothing is prior to it in being arranged. Suddenly a son, suddenly sent, suddenly Christ. And yet I should think nothing sudden with God, since nothing is unarranged by God. But if it was arranged, why was it not also proclaimed, so that it might be proved both arranged from the proclamation and divine from the arrangement? And surely a work so great — one prepared, namely, for the salvation of mankind — would not, even on this account, have been sudden, in that it was to profit through faith. For just as it had to be believed in order to profit, so it required preparation in order to be capable of being believed, built upon the foundations of arrangement and proclamation. By this order faith was rightly to be shaped, both shown to man by God and presented to God by man — bound to believe from acknowledgement that the thing was possible, having learned to believe it, that is, from the proclamation.

You have now the answer we have made ready to the Antitheses. I pass now to the demonstration of the gospel — not, to be sure, a Jewish one, but a Pontic, and for the present adulterated — which is to furnish beforehand the order I am approaching. We lay it down first of all that the evangelic instrument has the apostles for its authors, on whom this charge of promulgating the gospel was imposed by the Lord himself. If it has also apostolic men, yet not them alone, but with the apostles and after the apostles — since the preaching of disciples might be made suspect of a passion for glory, if there did not stand by it the authority of their masters, nay of Christ, who made the apostles masters. In short, John and Matthew instil faith into us from the apostles, Luke and Mark renew it from the apostolic men — beginning from the same rules, so far as concerns the one God the Creator, and his Christ, born of a virgin, the supplement of the law and the prophets. For let it be his own concern if the arrangement of the narratives has varied, provided there is agreement on the head of the faith, on which there is no agreement with Marcion. On the contrary, Marcion ascribes to his gospel, namely, no author — as though it had not been lawful for him to fix on it a title too, for whom it was no wickedness to overturn the very body. And here I might already plant my foot, contending that a work is not to be acknowledged which does not raise its forehead, which presents no constancy, which promises no faith from the fullness of a title and the due profession of an author. But we prefer to engage at every point, nor do we conceal what can be understood from what is ours. For out of those compilers whom we have, Marcion seems to have chosen Luke as the one to mangle. Now Luke was not an apostle but an apostolic man, not a master but a disciple, certainly lesser than his master, surely as much later as the follower of a later apostle, of Paul without doubt — so that, even if Marcion had brought in his gospel under the very name of Paul, that single instrument, destitute of the patronage of predecessors, would not suffice for faith. For there would be demanded that gospel too which Paul found, to which he gave credence, with which he soon strove to make his own agree — seeing that for that very reason he went up to Jerusalem to become acquainted with the apostles and to consult them, lest perchance he had run in vain, that is, lest he should not have believed according to them and should not evangelize according to them. In short, when he conferred with the authors and agreed upon the rule of faith, they joined right hands, and thereupon distinguished their offices of preaching, that they should go to the Jews, Paul to the Jews and to the nations. Therefore if the very illuminator of Luke desired the authority of predecessors for his own faith and preaching, how much more shall I demand for Luke's gospel that authority which was necessary to the gospel of his master?

ON THE EPISTLE TO THE GALATIANS. The epistle that teaches the Galatians we too confess to be foremost against Judaism. For we embrace that whole abolition of the old law, as itself coming from the Creator's arrangement, just as we have already often argued in this work concerning the renewal foretold by the prophets of our God. But if the Creator promised that old things should pass away, with new things, namely, about to arise, and Christ, fixing the boundary of that distinction (the law and the prophets were until John) by setting John as the terminus between either order — of the old thereafter ceasing and the new beginning — then of necessity the apostle too, in Christ revealed after John, weakens the old and confirms the new, and so concerns himself with no other faith than the Creator's, with whom the passing away of the old was also being preached. Therefore both the destruction of the law and the building up of the gospel work for me in this epistle also, belonging to that presumption of the Galatians by which they presumed that Christ was to be believed as the Creator's, with the Creator's law preserved — for it still seemed incredible that the law should be laid aside by its own author. Moreover, if they had heard at all of another God from the apostle, they would assuredly have known of their own accord that they must withdraw from the law of that God whom they had left in following another. For who would wait any longer to learn that he ought to follow a new discipline, when he had received a new God? Rather, because the same divinity was being preached in the gospel which had always been known in the law, but the discipline was not the same, this was the whole state of the question: whether the Creator's law ought to be excluded by the gospel in the Creator's Christ. Take away this state of the case, and the question is void. And the question being void, all of their own accord recognising that they must withdraw from the order of the Creator through the faith of another God, no matter would have been left for the apostle to teach this so pressingly, which the very faith would of itself have dictated. Therefore the whole intent of this epistle teaches nothing else than the withdrawal of the law coming from the Creator's arrangement, as we shall still go on to urge. If likewise he brings forward no mention of any new God — which he would nowhere have done more readily than in this matter, so as to set forth the reason for dismissing the law by this single and most sufficient definition of a new divinity — it appears how he writes: I marvel that you are so quickly transferred from him who called you into grace to another gospel: another in conduct, not in religion; in discipline, not in divinity; since the gospel of Christ ought to call them away from the law to grace, not from the Creator to another God. For no one had moved them from the Creator, so as to seem to be transferred to another gospel as while they are transferred to the Creator. For also, by adding that there was no other gospel at all, he confirms that which he maintains to be. But the Creator too promises a gospel, saying through Isaiah, Go up onto the high mountain, you who bring good tidings to Sion; lift up your voice in strength, you who bring good tidings to Jerusalem; likewise of the person of the apostles, How timely are the feet of those bringing good tidings of peace, of those bringing good tidings of good things — to the nations also, surely; since, In his name, he says, shall the nations hope — Christ's name, to whom he says, I have set you for a light of the nations. But there is also a gospel of the new God, you say, then defended by the apostle. Then there are two gospels with two gods, and the apostle will have lied in saying that there is no other at all, when there is another, since he could so have defended his own gospel as rather to show it the one than to determine it the only one. But perhaps, to escape this point, you will say he therefore subjoined, Though an angel from heaven should preach otherwise, let him be anathema, because he knew the Creator too would preach a gospel. So again you entangle yourself. For this is what you are bound by: to confirm two gospels is not the part of one who has already denied that there is another. Yet the sense of him who set his own person first shines out: But even if we or an angel from heaven should preach otherwise. For it was said by way of illustration. For the rest, if not even he himself was to preach otherwise, then surely no angel either. Thus he named an angel for this purpose, that much more should men not be believed when even an angel was not to be, nor an apostle, lest he should refer the angel to the Creator's gospel. Thereupon, running through the order of his own conversion from persecutor into apostle, he confirms the scripture of the Acts of the Apostles, in which the very subject of this epistle is also recognised: that certain men had intervened who said that men ought to be circumcised and to keep the law of Moses, and that the apostles, then consulted on this question, declared on the authority of the Spirit that burdens ought not to be imposed on men which the fathers themselves had not been able to bear. But if from this too the Acts of the Apostles agree with Paul, why you reject them already appears, namely because they preach no other God than the Creator, nor a Christ of any other than the Creator's — since not even the promise of the Holy Spirit is proved to have been exhibited from any source but the instrument of the Acts. And it is surely not likely that they should agree with the apostle in part, when they show his order according to his own testimony, but disagree in part, when they announce the divinity of the Creator in Christ — so that Paul should not have followed the preaching of the apostles, from whom he received the form for unteaching the law.

The principal question, then — and from it the whole engagement — is one of number: whether two gods may be introduced; or, by poetic and pictorial licence, even three; and now, by heretical licence, a third kind. But Christian truth has pronounced strictly: If God is not one, He is not at all — for we more worthily believe that whatever is not such as it ought to be does not exist. That you may know God ought to be one, ask what God is, and you will find no otherwise. As far as the human condition can define concerning God, I define what the conscience of all men also acknowledges: that God is the supreme great One, established in eternity, unborn, unmade, without beginning, without end. For this state must be reckoned to eternity, which makes God the supreme great One — since this is itself in God — and likewise the other attributes, so that God is the supreme great One in form and in reason and in might and in power. Since concerning this all men agree (for no one will deny that God is something supremely great, unless he be able to pronounce God on the contrary to be something lowest and slight, so as to deny God by taking away what belongs to God), what then will be the condition of this very supreme great One? Surely this: that nothing be made equal to Him — that is, that there be no other supreme great one; because if there were, it would be made equal, and if made equal, it would no longer be the supreme great One, the condition being overturned and (so to speak) the law which allows nothing to be made equal to the supreme great One. Therefore it must be the one and only thing that is the supreme great One, having no peer, lest it be not the supreme great One. Therefore it will not be otherwise than by that through which it has its being, that is, absolutely one and only. Accordingly, since God is the supreme great One, our truth has rightly pronounced: If God is not one, He is not at all. Not as if we doubted that God exists, in saying "If not one, He is not at all," but because the One we are confident exists, Him we define to be that which, if it is not, God is not — namely, the supreme great One. Further, the supreme great One must of necessity be one and only. Therefore God too will be one and only; not God otherwise than as the supreme great One, nor the supreme great One otherwise than as having no peer, nor having no peer otherwise than by being one and only. Certainly, whatever other god you bring in, you will not be able to maintain him a god under any other form than by ascribing to him also that which is proper to divinity — as eternity, so also supreme greatness. How then will two supreme great ones subsist, when this is the supreme great One, to have no peer; but to have no peer belongs to one alone and can in no way exist in two?

It will be fitting, then, for those entering upon the examination of the known God — if it be asked in what condition He is known — to begin from His works, which are prior to man; so that His goodness, discovered at once together with Himself, and thence established and prescribed, may suggest to us some sense of understanding how the subsequent ordering of things turned out. But the disciples of Marcion, recognizing the goodness of our God, are able to acknowledge it as worthy of God by the very same titles by which we have shown it unworthy in their god. For this very thing — that there is matter for His being recognized — He found not with another, but made of His own for Himself. The first goodness of the Creator, finally, is that whereby God willed not to lie hid for ever, that is, that there should be something to which God might be known. For what is so good as the knowledge and the fruit of God? For even though it did not yet appear that this was good, since there was not yet anything to which it might appear, yet God foreknew what good was going to appear, and therefore committed it to His own supreme goodness, the negotiatress of the good that was to appear — a goodness by no means sudden, nor of a goodness that comes upon Him from outside, nor of a roused emotion, as though to be reckoned from the point at which it began to operate. For if goodness itself constituted the beginning from the point at which it began to operate, it had no beginning itself when it made. But the beginning being made by it, the reckoning of times too was born — those times for distinguishing and marking which the stars and the heavenly luminaries were set in order. "For they shall be," He says, "for seasons and for months and for years." Therefore it had no time before time, which made time; just as it had no beginning before the beginning, which constituted the beginning. And thus, lacking both the order of a beginning and the measure of a time, it will be reckoned of an immense and unending age; nor can it be reputed sudden or come from outside or roused, having nothing from which it could be so reputed — that is, any kind of time — but is to be presumed both eternal and inborn in God and perpetual, and on this score worthy of God; suffusing already herewith the goodness of Marcion's god, which I say is later not only in beginnings and times, but even than the very malice of the Creator — if indeed malice could have been committed by goodness.

There was no need, you say, of any such order, because he was about to prove himself at once both son and sent and the Christ of God by the very facts, through the evidences of his powers. But I shall deny that this appearance alone availed for his testimony — an appearance which he himself afterward discredited, seeing that, in declaring that many would come and work signs and produce great powers, even to the turning aside of the elect, and yet were not on that account to be admitted, he showed how rash is faith placed in signs and powers, since these are most readily produced even among false Christs. Or what kind of thing is it, if he wished himself to be proved and understood and received from this source — I mean from powers — by which he refused that the rest should equally be received, men who likewise were to come as suddenly as they were proclaimed by no author? If it is because he came before them and was the first to seal the evidence of powers that he thus occupied faith, as one occupies a place at the baths, and snatched it away from any who came later — see that he too is not caught in the condition of those who come later, found later than the Creator already known beforehand, and accordingly already having worked powers before, and already having declared that none other was to be believed except after him, the Creator namely. Therefore if to have come first and to have pronounced first concerning those who come later is to shut out their faith, then he too will already stand condemned beforehand by the very fact that he is acknowledged as later; and the authority to lay this down upon those who come later will belong to the Creator alone, who could be later than none. Even now, since I am about to prove that the Creator gave forth those same powers — which alone you claim for your Christ's credit — sometimes of old through his servants, and at other times appointed them to be given forth through his Christ, I can on this very ground rightly object that Christ was all the more not to be believed on the strength of powers alone, in proportion as men could not but interpret him as belonging to none other than the Creator, since they answered to the Creator's own powers, both those given forth through his servants and those promised in his Christ. And yet, even if other evidences — new ones, namely — were found in your Christ, we should more readily believe that the new things too belonged to him whose the old also are, than to one whose are only the new, lacking the trials of a victorious faith founded on antiquity. So that even thus he ought to have come as one proclaimed, with both his own proclamations building up faith in him and his powers doing the same — especially against the Christ of the Creator who is to come, fortified with his own signs and prophets — so that the rival of Christ might shine forth through every species of difference. But how could the Christ of a god never proclaimed himself be proclaimed? This, then, is what the case requires: that neither your god nor your Christ be believed, since the god ought not to have remained unknown, and Christ ought to have been acknowledged through the god.

It is another matter if with Marcion the mystery of the Christian religion took its beginning from the discipleship of Luke. But if it ran its course also from of old, it surely had an authentic apparatus, through which it came down even to Luke, by whose attendant testimony Luke too can be admitted. But Marcion, having got hold of Paul's epistle to the Galatians — in which he rebukes even the apostles themselves for not walking with a straight foot toward the truth of the gospel, and at the same time accuses certain false apostles of perverting the gospel of Christ — strives to demolish the standing of those gospels which are published as their own and under the name of the apostles, or even of apostolic men, so that he may, namely, confer upon his own the credit which he takes from them. Now even if Peter and John and James, who were thought to be pillars, were reprehended, the cause is manifest. For with respect to persons they seemed to vary their conduct. And yet, since Paul himself became all things to all men that he might gain all, Peter too may have had this in his counsel, to act somewhat otherwise than he taught. Likewise, if false apostles too had crept in, their character also is published — claiming circumcision and the Jewish calendar. So far were they marked out by Paul not on account of preaching but of conduct — Paul being equally about to mark them out, had they erred in anything concerning God the Creator or his Christ. Therefore the several points will have to be distinguished. If Marcion complains that the apostles are held suspect of prevarication and dissimulation, even to the depraving of the gospel, he now accuses Christ, by accusing those whom Christ chose. But if the apostles did indeed transmit an entire gospel, reprehended only for an inequality of conduct, while the false apostles interpolated their truth, and our writings are derived thence — which then will be that genuine instrument of the apostles, which has suffered adulterers? the one that illumined Paul, and from him Luke? Or, if it has been so utterly destroyed as to have been obliterated, as by a kind of deluge, so by an inundation of falsifiers, then Marcion too has nothing true. Or if that will be the true one, that is, the apostles', which Marcion alone has — then how does that agree with ours which is referred not to the apostles but to Luke? Or if what Marcion uses is not at once to be assigned to Luke because it agrees with ours — adulterated, namely, even as to the title — but is the apostles': then ours too, which agrees with his, is equally the apostles', but adulterated as to the title also.

Lastly, he writes that he went up to Jerusalem, to the patronage of Peter and of the other apostles, after fourteen years, to confer with them about the rule of his gospel, lest he should have run, or be running, in vain for so many years — that is, if he were preaching anything outside their form. So far did he desire to be approved and established by those whom, if ever, you wish to be understood as the more closely akin to Judaism. But when he says that not even Titus was circumcised, he begins to show that the question of circumcision alone was being shaken from the defence still made of the law by those whom for that reason he calls false and surreptitiously introduced brethren, men proceeding to establish nothing else than the continuance of the law, out of a faith in the Creator no doubt still intact, and so perverting the gospel — not by interpolation of the scripture, by which they would have fashioned a Christ of the Creator, but by retention of the old discipline, that they might not exclude the Creator's law. Therefore, he says, because of the false surreptitious brethren, who had crept in to spy out our liberty, which we have in Christ, that they might bring us into bondage, we did not yield to subjection even for an hour. Let us attend both to the very sense and to its cause, and the corruption of the scripture will appear. When he sends before, But not even Titus, who was with me, being a Greek, was compelled to be circumcised, and then subjoins, Because of the surreptitious false brethren, and the rest, he is beginning, surely, to give the reason for a contrary act, showing on what account he did what he would neither have done nor disclosed, had not that on account of which he did it occurred. In short, I would have you say: had not those false brethren crept in to spy out their liberty, would they have yielded to subjection? I think not. Therefore they yielded, because there were those for whose sake it might be believed. For this was fitting for a faith still raw and still in suspense about the observance of the law, the apostle himself too being suspected of having run, or running, in vain. And so the false brethren had to be frustrated, as they spied out the Christian liberty, lest they should lead it into the bondage of Judaism before Paul knew that he had not run in vain, before his predecessors gave him their right hands, before from their reckoning he should take up the office of preaching among the nations. Necessarily, then, he yielded for a time; and so the reason holds for his circumcising Timothy and bringing in shaven men into the temple, which things are told in the Acts — so true that they agree with the apostle when he professes that he was made a Jew to the Jews, that he might gain the Jews, and lived under the law for the sake of those who were under the law, and so too for the sake of those surreptitiously introduced, and at last became all things to all, that he might gain all. If these things too require to be understood from this, then no one will doubt this either, that Paul was the preacher of that God and Christ whose law, though for the moment excluding it, he had yet admitted to suit the times — a law to be cast off at once, had he brought in a new God. Well, then, that Peter and James and John gave their right hands to Paul, and covenanted about the distribution of office, that Paul should go to the nations and they to the circumcision, only that they should remember the poor — and this according to the law of the Creator, who cherishes the poor and needy, as was proved in the review of your gospel. So clear is it that the question was about the law alone, while it is shown what ought to be kept out of the law. But he reproves Peter for not walking with a straight foot toward the truth of the gospel. He reproves him plainly, yet for no other reason than for the inconstancy of diet, which he varied according to the quality of persons, fearing those who were of the circumcision — not for any perversion of divinity, on account of which he would have withstood others too to their faces, he who for the lesser cause of doubtful conduct did not spare Peter himself. But how would the Marcionites have it believed? For the rest, let the apostle proceed, denying that a man is justified by works of the law, but by faith. Yet the faith of the same God whose also is the law. For he would not have laboured to distinguish faith from the law, when the diversity of the divinity itself would of its own accord have distinguished it, had there been any. With reason he did not rebuild what he had destroyed. But the law had to be destroyed from the time the voice of John cried in the wilderness, Prepare the ways of the Lord, that the rivers and hills and mountains might be filled and brought low, and the crooked and rough ways made into straightness and into plains — that is, the difficulties of the law into the facilities of the gospel. He remembered too that it was already the psalm's time: Let us break their bonds from us, and cast away their yoke from us — from the time the nations raged and the peoples imagined vain things; the kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ; so that now a man should be justified out of the liberty of faith, not out of the bondage of the law, because the just lives by faith. But if the prophet Habakkuk announced this beforehand, you have the apostle too confirming the prophets, just as Christ does. His, then, will be the faith in which the just shall live, whose also is the law, in which the worker is not justified. Accordingly, if in the law there is a curse, but in faith a blessing, you have both set forth by the Creator: Behold, he says, I have set before you a curse and a blessing. You cannot claim a distinction which, though it be of things, is therefore not of authors, since it is set forth by one author. But why Christ was made a curse for us is made plain by the very teaching of the apostle: how it agrees with us, that is, according to the faith of the Creator. For not because the Creator pronounced, Cursed is everyone hanged on a tree, will Christ therefore seem to belong to another God, and to have been on that account already then cursed in the law by the Creator. And how could the Creator have fore-cursed him whom he does not know? But why should it not rather befit the Creator to have given his own Son to his own curse, than to have subjected him to that God of yours — and that for a stranger man? In short, if this seems savage in the Creator regarding his Son, so it is in your God too; but if it is rational even in yours, so it is in mine too, and more in mine. For it would more easily be believed to be his — to have looked through the curse of Christ to a blessing for man — who had at some time set both a curse and a blessing before man, than his who has never with you professed either. We have received, then, a spiritual blessing through faith, he says — by which, namely, the just shall live, according to the Creator. This, then, is what I say, that the faith is of that God whose is the pattern of the grace of faith. But also, when he adds, For you are all sons of faith, it is shown what here above the heretic's industry has erased: the mention of Abraham, namely, by which the apostle affirms us to be sons of Abraham through faith, according to which mention he here too noted us sons of faith. For otherwise, how sons of faith? and of whose faith, if not Abraham's? For if Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him for righteousness, and thereafter he deserved to be named the father of many nations, while we too by believing God are likewise the more justified, like Abraham, and likewise obtain life, since the just lives by faith — so it comes about that he both above pronounced us sons of Abraham, as of the father of faith, and here sons of faith, through which Abraham had been promised the father of nations. The very point that he was recalling faith from circumcision — was he not seeking to constitute sons of Abraham, who had believed in the integrity of the flesh? In short, the faith of another God cannot be admitted to the pattern of another God, so as to reckon believers unto righteousness, to make the just live, to call the nations sons of faith. This whole thing is his with whom it is already known beforehand under the same mention of Abraham, while by the very sense he is convicted.

But someone will argue that two supreme great ones can subsist, distinct and disjoined within their own bounds; and will of course call in the example of the kingdoms of the earth, so many in number and yet supremely great each in its own region; and will think that human things are everywhere to be compared with divine. Now if room be given to this argument, what prevents the introduction — I do not say of a third and a fourth god, but of as many in number as there are kings of the nations? The matter concerns God, whose principal property this is, to admit comparison with no example. This nature itself, if no Isaiah, then God Himself through Isaiah, will proclaim: "To whom will you liken me?" Perhaps human things may be compared with divine, but God not so. For God is one thing, the things of God another. Lastly, you who use the example of a king as of a supreme great one — beware lest you may no longer use it. For a king, though he be the supreme great one on his throne, up to God, is yet beneath God; and being compared to God, he will fall away from being the supreme great one, that title being transferred to God. If this be so, how will you use the example of a thing which, when it comes to the comparison, is lost? What now, if even among kings the supreme great one cannot be seen as manifold, but as one and singular — namely in him who, by reason of the height of his greatness and the subjection of all the other ranks, is received as the king of kings, the very summit, as it were, of dominion? But also kings of another form, who singly preside over a united empire, if they be everywhere compared with petty kingdoms (so to speak) in an examination to settle which of them excels in the substance and forces of his kingdom, the summit of greatness must of necessity be distilled into one, all the rest being by gradual comparison drawn off and excluded from the supreme greatness. So even though, when dispersed, the supreme great one seems manifold, yet in its own forces and its own nature and its own state it is one and only. Accordingly, when two gods are compared, as two kings and two supreme great ones, the unity of the supreme greatness must of necessity concede to one of them by the verdict of the comparison; for the supreme stands by its own victory, the rival, who is also great but not supreme, being overcome; and by the falling away of the rival it possesses a certain solitude out of the singularity of its own pre-eminence, and is one and only. This inescapable grip binds the verdict to this conclusion: either we must deny that God is the supreme great One, which no wise man will allow, or we must allow it to be shared with no other. Or what reason composed two supreme great ones? For first I will demand: why not more, if two — since the substance of divinity ought to be believed the more abundant, if number suited it? More honest and more generous was Valentinus, who at one stroke dared to conceive two, Bythos and Sige, until he poured forth the swarm of his divinity in a brood of thirty Aeons, like the sow of Aeneas. Whatever reason does not allow more supreme great ones to be admitted, the same allows neither two — since these are themselves "more" after one. For after one comes number. The reason that could admit two, the same could admit more. For after two comes multitude, once unity has been exceeded. In fine, with us the force of that reasoning does not, by its very limit, permit more gods to be believed — nor does that rule which establishes one God permit two; the rule by which God must be that to which nothing is made equal, as to the supreme great One, but which is one and only, to which nothing is made equal. Now then, two supreme great ones, two equals — to what use, to what profit would they be reckoned? What did number profit, when two equals differ not from one? For it is one thing that is the same in two. Even if there were more equals, all would have been as much one, differing in nothing among themselves, in so far as equal. Further, if neither of the two differs from the other, then since both are supreme great ones, both as gods, neither excels the other; they show no reason for their number, since they have no pre-eminence. But the number of divinity ought to stand on the supremest reason — if only because its worship too would be brought into a difficulty. For lo, beholding two gods as equal as two supreme great ones, what should I do if I worshipped both? I should fear lest, by an abundance of service, it should be thought superstition rather than religion; for two so equal, and both in either, I could oblige in one, by this very thing bearing testimony to their parity and unity, while I venerated the one in the other, while in one I had two for me. If I worshipped the one, I should likewise reflect that I might seem to confess the vanity of the number, superfluous because without difference; that is, I should reckon it safer to worship neither than to worship the one with scruple or both in vain.

Therefore, when the goodness of God Himself had looked forward to man, that he should know God, it added this also to its own heralding: that it first contrived a dwelling for man — a certain vast mass afterwards, and afterwards a greater one too — that in the great, as in the lesser, he might first try himself and make progress, and so be advanced from the good of God, that is, from the great, to His best also, that is, to the greater habitation. To the good work He applies the best minister too, His own Word. "My heart," He says, "has belched forth a good Word." Let Marcion acknowledge from this first that the fruit is best — the best fruit, of course, of the best tree. A most unskilled countryman indeed has grafted good upon a bad stock. But the slip of blasphemy will not avail; it will wither with its own grafter, and so the nature of the good tree will bear witness to itself. Look to the sum: what things the Word brought forth as fruit. "And God said, Let it be, and it was made; and God saw that it was good" — not as though, ignorant of the good, He should not have seen it; but because it was good, therefore, seeing it, He honoured and sealed and discharged the goodness of His works by the dignity of His regard. So too He blessed the things He did well, that the whole God might be commended to you, good both to say and to do. The Word knew not yet how to curse, because not yet how to do ill. We shall see the causes which exacted this too from God. Meanwhile the world consisted of all good things, sufficiently showing beforehand how great a good was being prepared for him for whom this whole was being prepared. Who, finally, was worthy to inhabit the works of God but His own image and likeness? That too goodness wrought — and a more operative goodness — not with an imperial word, but with a familiar hand, with even a coaxing word sent before: "Let us make man after our image and likeness." Goodness spoke, goodness formed man of slime into so great a substance of flesh, built up out of one matter into so many qualities. Goodness breathed in a soul, not dead but living. Goodness set him over all things to be enjoyed and ruled, and even named by him. Goodness yet further added delights to man, that, though possessing the whole world, he might dwell in the more pleasant places, transferred into Paradise, even then from the world into the Church. The same goodness provided a helper too, lest anything should not be good. "For it is not good," He says, "that man be alone." It knew that the sex of Mary, and thereafter of the Church, would profit him. But even the law which you accuse, which you twist into controversies, goodness dispensed, taking thought for man, that he might cleave to God, lest he should seem not so much free as cast off, to be levelled with His servants, the other animals, loosed from God and free out of His disdain; but that man alone might glory, because he alone had been worthy to receive a law from God, and that, as a rational animal, capable of understanding and knowledge, he might be held in by that very rational liberty, subject to Him who had subjected all things to him. To the observing of which law goodness likewise attached counsel: "But on the day on which you eat, you shall die the death." For most kindly did it demonstrate the outcome of transgression, lest ignorance of the danger should aid negligence of obedience. Further, if the reason of imposing the law preceded, there followed also the reason of observing it, so that punishment should be assigned to transgression — which yet He willed not to come to pass who had foretold it beforehand. Acknowledge, then, the goodness of our God, at least thus far, from His good works, from His good blessings, from His indulgences, from His providences, from His laws and forewarnings, good and kind.

He disdained, I suppose, to imitate the order of our God — as displeased with him, and that precisely when he was to refute him. Being new, he wished to come in a new way: a son before the Father's profession, and sent before the authority of the commissioner — so that he might himself bring in a faith of the most monstrous kind, by which it should be believed that Christ had come before it was known that he existed. It is also fitting for me to take up this point: why he did not come after Christ. For when I consider that his lord was so very long-suffering toward a most harsh Creator who in the meantime was announcing his own Christ to men — by whatever reason he did this, deferring both his own revelation and his intervention — by that same reason I say that he ought to have shown patience toward the Creator in respect of his Christ also, who was to carry out his own arrangements, so that, once every operation of the rival god and the rival Christ had been completed and fulfilled, he might then at last bring on his own arrangements over them. But repentance of so great a patience produced this, that he did not persevere to the end of the Creator's affairs. To no purpose did he endure that the Christ should be proclaimed of one whom he did not endure to be displayed. Either he broke into the course of another's time without cause, or without cause he did not break into it so long. What detained him, or what disturbed him? And yet he transgressed in both directions: revealed too late after the Creator, but too early before his Christ. The one he ought long since to have done away with, the other not yet. Not to have endured the one raging so long, but to have disquieted the other while he was still at rest! In regard to both he falls away from the title of the supremely good god — certainly himself variable and uncertain, lukewarm, that is, toward the Creator and hot against Christ, and to no purpose in both. For he no more held the Creator in check than he stood in the way of Christ. The Creator remains, just as he is altogether; and Christ will come, just as he is described. Why did he come after the Creator, whom he could not amend? Why was he revealed before his Christ, whom he could not recall? Or if he amended the Creator, he was revealed after him so that the things to be amended might come first: therefore he ought likewise to have waited for his Christ, intending to amend him too, and so likewise to be the later amender of him, just as of the Creator. It is another matter if he too is to come again after him — so that at his first coming he advanced against the Creator, destroying his law and prophets, but at his second he should advance against Christ, refuting his kingdom. Then, therefore, when he has completed his own order, then, if at all, is he to be believed; or else, if his work is already perfect from this point, then he is to come to no purpose, accomplishing nothing.

The rope of the contention, then, must be drawn, swaying with equal effort on either side. I call mine true, Marcion his. I affirm Marcion's to be adulterated, Marcion mine. Who shall decide between us, except the reasoning of time — assigning authority to that which shall be found the more ancient, and prejudging vitiation against that which shall later be convicted? For inasmuch as the false is a corruption of the true, by so much must the truth precede the false. A thing will be prior to its undergoing, and the matter prior to its rivalry. Otherwise, how absurd it is, that if we prove ours the more ancient, and Marcion's the later, ours should be thought false before it had its matter from the truth, and Marcion's be believed to have suffered rivalry from ours before it was even published, and finally that should be reckoned the truer which is the later — after so many and so great works and evidences of the Christian religion already published to the world, which surely could not have been published without the truth of the gospel, that is, before the truth of the gospel. As regards, then, the gospel of Luke for the present — inasmuch as its communion between us and Marcion is disputed about the truth — so much more ancient than Marcion is that which is according to us, that Marcion himself once believed in it, when in the first heat of faith he contributed money to the catholic Church, money soon flung out along with himself, after he revolted into his heresy from our truth. What now, if the Marcionites should deny his first faith among us, against his own epistle too? What, if they should not even acknowledge his epistle? Certainly the Antitheses they not only confess to be Marcion's, but even put forward. From these the proof suffices me. For if that gospel which is referred to Luke is among us the very one (let us see whether it be among Marcion too) which Marcion through his Antitheses arraigns as interpolated by the protectors of Judaism toward the embodiment of the law and the prophets — by which they fashioned Christ thence too — surely he could not have arraigned but that which he had found. No one reprehends after the fact things which he is ignorant are to come to be. An emendation does not precede the fault. As an emendator of the gospel overturned from the times of Tiberius even to those of the Antonines, Marcion alone and first turned up, awaited so long by Christ, who now repented that he had hastened to send forth the apostles without the aid of Marcion. Save that heresy is the business of human rashness, not of divine authority, which thus always emends the gospels while it vitiates them — since, even if Marcion is a disciple, he is yet not above his master; and if Marcion is an apostle — "Whether I," says Paul, "or they, so we preach" — and if Marcion is a prophet, "the spirits of the prophets too shall be subject to the prophets: for they are not of subversion, but of peace"; even if Marcion is an angel, he is rather to be called anathema than evangelist, because he evangelized otherwise. And so, while he emends, he confirms both — both ours as the earlier, by emending what he found, and his own as the later, by constituting as new and his own what he established out of the emendation of ours.

Still, he says, I speak after the manner of man: While we were children, we were placed under the elements of the world, to be in bondage to them. But this is not said in a merely human way. For it is not an illustration, but the truth. For what child — in sense, that is, such as the nations are — is not subject to the elements of the world, which it looks up to in place of God? But the human way lay in this, that, though he had said After the manner of man, yet a man's testament no one despises or overrides. For by the example of a human testament that endures, he was protecting the divine. The promises were spoken to Abraham and to his seed. He did not say, To seeds, as of many, but, To his seed, as of one, which is Christ. Let Marcion's sponge blush! Unless that I review out of abundance what he has taken away, since it is the stronger thing to convict him out of what he has kept. But when it came to pass that the time was fulfilled, God sent his Son — surely he who is the God also of those very times of which the age consists, who ordained too the signs of the times, suns and moons and constellations and stars, who lastly both arranged and foretold the revelation of his Son at the extremity of the times. In the last days the mountain of the Lord shall be made manifest; and, In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, according to Joel. It was for him to have waited for the time to be fulfilled, whose was also the end of time, as the beginning. But that idle God, of no operation and of no preaching, and so of no time either — what did he do at all to bring it about that the time should be fulfilled and the fulfilment awaited? If nothing, it is empty enough that he should have awaited the Creator's times, serving the Creator. And for what purpose did he send his Son? That he might redeem those who were under the law; that is, that he might make the crooked into a straight way and the rough into smooth ways, according to Isaiah, that the old should pass and the new arise, a new law out of Sion and the word of the Lord out of Jerusalem, and that we might receive the adoption of sons — the nations, namely, who were not sons. For he himself shall be a light of the nations, and in his name the nations shall hope. And so, that it might be certain that we are sons of God, he sent his Spirit into our hearts, crying, Abba, Father. For in the last days, he says, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. Whose grace, except his whose is also the promise of grace? What father, except him who is also the maker? After these riches, then, there was no returning to the weak and beggarly elements. But elements, among the Romans too, the first letters are wont to be called. Not, therefore, by disparagement of the world's elements did he wish to turn them away from the God of those elements, even though by saying above, If, then, you serve those who by nature are not gods, he brands the error of natural — that is, physical — superstition, which holds the elements in place of God; yet not even so does he tax the God of the elements. But what elements he wishes understood — the first letters, namely, of the law — he himself declares. You observe days and months and seasons and years and sabbaths, I suppose, and pure suppers and fasts and great days. For to cease from these too, as from circumcision, was required by the decrees of the Creator, who also says through Isaiah, Your new moons and sabbaths and the great day I will not endure; the fast and the holidays and your ceremonies my soul hates. And through Amos, I hate, I have rejected your ceremonies, and I will not smell in your assemblies; likewise through Hosea, I will turn away all her joys and her ceremonies and her sabbaths and her new moons and all her assemblies. What he himself had appointed, you say, did he erase? Rather he than another; or if another, then that one assisted the sentence of the Creator, taking away what the Creator too had condemned. But it is not for this place to ask why the Creator broke his own laws. It is enough that we have proved that he would break them, so that it may be confirmed that the apostle determined nothing against the Creator, since the very removal of the law is from the Creator. But as something of the booty is wont to slip from thieves as evidence, so I believe Marcion too left behind the last mention of Abraham, none more to be taken away, though he turned it in part. For if Abraham had two sons, one of the handmaid, the other of the freewoman, but he who was of the handmaid was born after the flesh, while he who was of the freewoman by promise (which things are allegorical, that is, portending something else; for these are two testaments, or two displays, as we find it interpreted: one from Mount Sinai, generating into the bondage of the synagogue of the Jews according to the law, the other generating above every principality, might, dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age but in that to come, which is our mother, into which we have promised the holy church; and therefore he adds, Wherefore, brethren, we are not the sons of the handmaid, but of the freewoman) — assuredly he made plain that the nobility of Christianity, in the son of Abraham born of the freewoman, has the sacrament of an allegory, just as the legal bondage of Judaism in the son of the handmaid, and that so both arrangements belong to that God with whom we find the delineation of both arrangements. The very word he uses, By that liberty wherewith Christ has set us free, does it not constitute him the emancipator who had been lord? For not even Galba emancipated other men's slaves, though he would more easily set free the free. By him, therefore, will liberty be provided, with whom was the bondage of the law. And with reason. It did not befit the emancipated to be bound again by the yoke of bondage, that is, of the law, the psalm being now fulfilled: Let us break their bonds, and cast away their yoke from us, after the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ. The emancipated from bondage, then, he persisted in erasing the very mark of bondage, circumcision — out of the authority, namely, of the prophetic preaching, mindful of what was said through Jeremiah, And circumcise the foreskins of your heart; for Moses too said, You shall circumcise your hardness of heart, that is, not the flesh. In short, if, coming from another God, he excluded circumcision, why does he also deny that uncircumcision avails anything in Christ, just as circumcision? For he ought to have preferred its rival, which he was assailing, had it been of a God who was circumcision's rival. But since both circumcision and uncircumcision were reckoned to one God, therefore both were of no avail in Christ, on account of the precedence of faith — that faith of which it was written, And in his name the nations shall believe; that faith which, by saying that it is perfected through love, he likewise showed to be the Creator's. For whether he means the love which is toward God — and this too is the Creator's, You shall love God with your whole heart, and with your whole soul, and with all your strength — or the love toward one's neighbour, And your neighbour as yourself, it is the Creator's. But he that troubles you shall bear judgement. From what God? From the good one? But he does not judge. From the Creator? But neither will he condemn the asserter of circumcision. But if there shall be no other to judge but the Creator, then he will not condemn the defenders of the law except he himself who appointed that it should cease. What now, if he even confirms it in the part in which he ought? For the whole law, he says, is fulfilled in you: You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Now if he wishes it understood as, It is fulfilled, as though now not to be fulfilled, then he does not wish me to love my neighbour as myself, so that this too should have ceased with the law. But we must persevere always in this precept. Therefore the law of the Creator has been approved even by the adversary, and has obtained from him not loss but compendium, its sum reduced into one precept now. But neither does this befit another more than the author.
