And so, when he says, Bear one another's burdens, and so you shall fulfil the law of Christ — if this cannot be done unless one love his neighbour as himself, it appears that, You shall love your neighbour as yourself, through which is heard, Bear one another's burdens, is the law of Christ, which is the Creator's, and that so Christ is the Creator's, while the law of Christ is the Creator's. You are mistaken: God is not mocked. But the God of Marcion can be mocked, who knows neither to be angry nor to avenge. For what a man sows, that also shall he reap. Therefore he holds out a God of retribution and judgement. But in doing good let us not grow weary, and while we have time, let us work good. Deny that the Creator commanded good to be done, and let the contrary doctrine be of a contrary divinity. But if he preaches retribution, from the same will come both the harvest of corruption and of life. And in his own time we shall reap, because Ecclesiastes too says, There will be a time for everything. But to me also, the servant of the Creator, the world is crucified, yet not the God of the world, and I to the world, yet not to the God of the world. For he set down the world as regards its conduct, in renouncing which we are mutually transfixed and die to one another. Persecutors he calls them of Christ. But when he adds that he bears the marks of Christ in his body (which surely are bodily things), he has now professed not a putative but a true and solid flesh of Christ, whose bodily marks he displays.

From this point, now, to all the questions, O you dogs whom the apostle thrusts out of doors, barking at the God of truth! These are the bones of your argumentations, which you gnaw at. If God is good, and foreknowing of the future, and powerful to avert evil, why did He suffer man — His very image and likeness, nay even His substance (by reason, that is, of the soul's census) — to fall away from obedience to the law into death, encompassed by the devil? For if He is both good, who would not have such a thing come to pass; and foreknowing, who was not ignorant that it would come to pass; and powerful, who was able to drive it off — then by no means would that have come to pass which under these three conditions of the divine majesty could not have come to pass. But if it did come to pass, then on the contrary it is settled that God is to be believed neither good nor foreknowing nor powerful; since, in proportion as no such thing would have come to pass had God been such — that is, good and foreknowing and powerful — in that same proportion it came to pass because God is not such. To these things, the first task is to defend in the Creator those attributes which are called into doubt — goodness, I mean, and foreknowledge and power. And I will not linger over this article, the definition even of Christ Himself going before. The proofs are to be entered upon from works. The works of the Creator testify to both: both His goodness, whereby they are good, as we have shown, and His power, whereby they are so great, and indeed out of nothing. For even if out of some matter, as certain ones will have it, yet by this very fact out of nothing, since they were not that which they are. Finally, even so they are great, since good; even so God is powerful, since all things are His, whence also Almighty. But of foreknowledge what shall I say, which has as many witnesses as it has made prophets? And yet what title to foreknowledge is there in the Author of all, who, in ordering all things, of course foreknew them, and in foreknowing them ordered them? — certainly that very transgression, which, unless He had foreknown, He would not have entrusted the guarding against it under the fear of death. Therefore, if these faculties were in God, before which no evil could or ought to have come upon man, and yet it nonetheless came to pass, let us examine also the condition of man, lest it came to pass rather through him which could not come to pass through God. I find man instituted by God as free and of his own arbitration and of his own power, observing in him no image and likeness of God more than the form of this kind of state. For not by his face and bodily lineaments, so various in the human race, was he expressed after the one God, but in that substance which he drew from God Himself, that is, of a soul answering to the form of God, and he was sealed by the liberty and power of his own arbitration. This state of his the very law also confirmed, then laid down by God. For a law would not be laid down for one who had not in his own power the obedience due to the law; nor again would the threat of death be assigned to transgression, if the contempt of the law were not imputed to man's freedom of arbitration. So too in the later laws of the Creator you will find Him setting before man good and evil, life and death; but also, not otherwise, the whole order of discipline arranged through precepts — God calling away, and threatening, and exhorting — only on the supposition of a man free and voluntary both to obedience and to contempt.

Let me have made these preliminary thrusts as it were from the first step still, and as it were from a distance. But seeing that from here I am now to fight in close combat for a fixed conclusion, I see that certain lines must even now be drawn first, lines along which the fight must be conducted — the Scriptures of the Creator, namely. For since it is by these that I am about to prove that Christ belonged to the Creator, as fulfilled afterward in his Christ, I must of necessity first lay down the form and, so to speak, the nature of these very Scriptures, lest, when they are brought into the dispute and applied to the cases, their defence both of themselves and of the cases be confused and blunt the reader's attention. Two properties, then, of prophetic utterance I allege as henceforth to be acknowledged by our adversaries. One, by which future things are sometimes announced as already past. For it befits Divinity to reckon whatever it has decreed as already accomplished, since with it there is no difference of time, with whom eternity itself directs the uniform state of the seasons. And it is more proper to prophetic divination to display what it foresees, while it foresees it, as already seen and thus already discharged — that is, in every way future — as through Isaiah: "I have set my back for scourges, but my cheeks for blows, and my face I turned not away from spittings." For whether even then Christ was pronouncing this concerning himself, as we hold, or the prophet was pronouncing concerning himself, as the Jews hold, what was not yet done was nonetheless uttered as already past. The other species will be that by which very many things are foreshown figuratively, through riddles and allegories and parables, to be understood otherwise than as they are written. For we read that the mountains shall drop sweetness — yet not so that you should expect must from the rocks or new wine from the cliffs; and we hear of a land flowing with milk and honey — yet not so that you should believe you will ever press cakes and cheeses from the clods; since neither did God promise himself to be at once a waterworks-engineer and a husbandman, when he says, "I will set rivers in a thirsting region, and in the wilderness the box-tree and the cedar." Likewise, when he proclaims concerning the conversion of the nations, "The beasts of the field shall bless me, the sirens and the daughters of the sparrows," he is certainly not going to derive favourable omens from the young of swallows and from little foxes and from those monstrous and fabulous songstresses. And why should I say more of this kind? — when even the apostle of the heretics interprets that very law which grants a free mouth to the oxen that tread out the grain, not of oxen but of us; and alleges that the rock which supplied drink was a companion, Christ; teaching likewise that the two pleas concerning the sons of Abraham ran their course allegorically among the Galatians; and suggesting to the Ephesians that what was proclaimed at the beginning concerning the man who would leave father and mother, the two to become one flesh, this he recognizes in Christ and the Church.

In sum, if that is the truer which is the prior, that the prior which is also from the beginning, that from the beginning which is from the apostles — it will likewise be established that that has been handed down from the apostles which has been held sacrosanct among the churches of the apostles. Let us see what milk the Corinthians drew from Paul, to what rule the Galatians were brought back, what the Philippians read, the Thessalonians, the Ephesians, what too the Romans of our neighbourhood resound — to whom both Peter and Paul left the gospel sealed even with their own blood. We have the churches that are John's nurslings too. For even though Marcion rejects his Apocalypse, yet the order of bishops, traced back to its origin, will stand upon John as author. So too the high birth of the rest is recognized. I say therefore that among them — and now not only among the apostolic churches, but among all that are confederated with them by the fellowship of the mystery — that gospel of Luke has stood from the beginning of its publication which we most of all defend, whereas Marcion's is to most unknown, and to none known but that it is, by the same fact, condemned. That gospel too has churches, plainly, but its own — as much later as adulterous; whose lineage if you inquire, you will more easily find it apostatic than apostolic, with Marcion, namely, for founder, or some one of Marcion's swarm. Wasps too make combs; Marcionites too make churches. The same authority of the apostolic churches will give patronage to the other gospels too, which we likewise have through them and according to them — John's, I mean, and Matthew's — although that which Mark published is affirmed to be Peter's, whose interpreter Mark was. For Luke's digest too men are wont to ascribe to Paul. It is allowable that what the disciples have promulgated should be regarded as their masters'. And so for these too Marcion is to be pressed — that, omitting them, he rather fastened upon Luke, as though these too had not been among the churches from the beginning, just as Luke also. Nay, it is more credible that these were from the beginning, as prior, since apostolic, since dedicated together with the churches themselves. For the rest, what kind of thing is it, that if the apostles published nothing, the disciples rather published — who could not even have existed as disciples without any teaching of masters? Therefore, since it is established that these too were among the churches, why did Marcion not touch these too — either to be emended, if adulterated, or to be acknowledged, if entire? For it is also fitting that, if any were perverting the gospel, they should rather take care to pervert those whose authority they knew to be the more received. Hence the false apostles too, in that through falsehood they imitated the apostles. Therefore, in so far as he would have emended things which would have had to be emended, if they had been corrupted, by so much he confirmed that those were not corrupted which he thought needed no emendation. In short, he emended what he reckoned corrupted. But neither this with reason, because it was not corrupted. For if the apostolic writings ran their course entire, while Luke's, which is according to us, agrees so with their rule that it abides with them among the churches, then it is established that Luke's too ran its course entire, even to the sacrilege of Marcion. In short, where Marcion laid hands upon it, then it was made diverse from and rival to the apostolic ones. Therefore I will give counsel to his disciples, that either they convert those writings — though late — to the form of his, that they may seem to agree with the apostolic ones (for they do daily reform it, in proportion as they are daily refuted by us), or that they blush for their master, exposed on both sides, since now from conscience he transmits the truth of the gospel, now from shamelessness overturns it. These compendious methods, more or less, we use when we are extricating ourselves against the heretics concerning the faith of the gospel — pleading both the order of times that prescribes against the lateness of falsifiers, and the authority of the churches that gives patronage to the tradition of the apostles, because the truth must precede the false, and must proceed from those by whom it was handed down.

ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. The forestructure of the former epistle so led me that I have not gone back over its heading, being certain that it can be reviewed elsewhere too — common, namely, and the same in all the epistles, in that he does not prescribe salvation to those to whom he writes, but grace and peace. I do not say what he, the destroyer of Judaism, has to do with the still Jewish custom. For even today the Jews address one another in the name of peace, and of old in the scriptures they so saluted. But I understand that he defended by his own office the preaching of the Creator: How timely the feet of those bringing good tidings of good things, of those bringing good tidings of peace. For as the evangelist of good things, that is, of the grace of God, he knew that peace was to be preferred. When, announcing these from God our Father and the Lord Jesus, he uses common names, suitable to our sacrament too, I do not think it can be discerned what God is Father, and what Lord is preached as Jesus, except from what is added, to whom they more befit. First, indeed, I prescribe that the Lord Father is to be acknowledged as no other than the Creator and founder both of man and of the universe; and further, that to the Father the name of Lord too is added on account of power, which the Son too receives through the Father; and then, that grace and peace belong not only to him from whom they were preached, but to him who had been offended. For grace is not made except after an offence, nor peace except after war. And the people, by transgression of discipline, and the whole race of man, by dissimulation of nature, had both sinned and rebelled against the Creator. But the God of Marcion, both because he is unknown could not be offended, and because he knows not to be angry. What grace, then, from one not offended? what peace from one not rebelled against? He says that the cross of Christ is foolishness to those who perish, but the power and wisdom of God to those who are to obtain salvation; and to show whence this came, he adds: For it is written, I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and bring to nought the prudence of the prudent. If these are the Creator's, and he reckons among foolishness the things which pertain to the cause of the cross, then both the cross and, through the cross, Christ will pertain to the Creator, by whom was preached that which pertains to the cross. Or if the Creator, as a rival, on that account took away wisdom, that the cross of Christ his adversary might be reckoned foolishness, how can the Creator have pronounced anything pertaining to the cross of a Christ not his own, whom he did not know when he preached it? But also, why with the Lord who is supremely good and of lavish mercy do some refer salvation, believing the cross to be the power and wisdom of God, others perdition, to whom the cross of Christ is reputed foolishness — if it is not the Creator's part to have punished some offence both of the people and of the human race by the loss of wisdom and prudence? This the sequel will confirm, when he says, Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world? and when here too he adds why: Since in the wisdom of God the world did not by wisdom know the Lord, God thought good to save the believers by the foolishness of preaching. But first I will dispute about the world, since the most subtle heretics here especially interpret world as the God of the world, while we understand the man who is in the world, from the simple form of human speech, by which we very often put that which contains for that which is contained. The circus cried out, and the forum spoke, and the basilica roared — that is, those who transacted business in those places. Therefore, because man, not God, in the world's wisdom did not know God, whom he ought to have known — both the Jew in the wisdom of the scriptures and every nation in the wisdom of works — therefore the same God, who was not acknowledged in his own wisdom, determined to beat back the wisdom of men with foolishness, by saving the believers, namely, in the foolish preaching of the cross. Since the Jews desire signs, who ought already to have been certain of God, and the Greeks seek wisdom, who set up their own, namely, not God's wisdom. For the rest, if a new God were being preached, in what had the Jews sinned in desiring signs by which to believe, or the Greeks in following the wisdom they should the rather believe? Thus the very recompense upon Jews and Greeks confirms both a zealous and a judging God, who from emulous retribution and as judge made foolish the wisdom of the world. But if the causes are his whose scriptures are adduced, then the apostle, treating of the Creator unknown, surely teaches that the Creator is to be known. Also, that he preaches Christ a stumbling-block to the Jews, he seals the Creator's prophecy concerning him, who says through Isaiah, Behold, I have set in Sion a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence; and the rock was Christ. This Marcion too keeps. But what is the foolish thing of God wiser than men, except the cross and death of Christ? What is the weak thing of God stronger than man, except the nativity and flesh of God? But if Christ was neither born of a virgin nor framed of flesh, and through this neither truly suffered the cross nor death, there was nothing foolish and weak in him; nor did God then choose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise, nor the weak things of the world to confound the strong, nor the base and least and contemptible things, which are not — that is, which are not truly — to confound the things which are, that is, which truly are. For nothing arranged by God is truly small and ignoble and contemptible, but what is by man. But with the Creator even the old things can be reckoned to foolishness and weakness and baseness and littleness and contempt. What more foolish, what weaker, than the exaction by God of bloody sacrifices and reeking holocausts? What weaker than the cleansing of little vessels and pallets? What more base than another dishonouring of the flesh already blushing? What so lowly as the prescription of retaliation? What so contemptible as the abstaining from foods? The whole Old Testament, so far as I know, every heretic derides. For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound wisdom. The God of Marcion has nothing of the kind, because he does not even emulously confute contraries with contraries, that no flesh should glory; that, as it is written, He that glories, let him glory in the Lord. In whom? Surely in him who commanded this. Unless the Creator of the precept, that one may glory in the God of Marcion.

So far we seem to dispute as though Marcion set up two equal gods. For while we defend that the supreme great God must be believed one and only, excluding parity from Him, we have, as it were, treated of these two as of two equals; nonetheless, in teaching that they cannot be equal according to the form of the supreme great One, we have sufficiently confirmed that there cannot be two — although it is certain that Marcion sets up gods unequal: the one a judge, fierce, mighty in war; the other mild, peaceable, and merely good and best. Let us examine this side too: whether diversity at least admits of two, if parity could not admit them. Yet here also the same rule of the supreme great One will plead for us, inasmuch as it claims the whole estate of divinity. For fittingly, and as it were laying hold of the adversary's mind with a detaining hand — since he does not deny the Creator to be God — I most justly lay it down as a prescription that there is no room for that diversity among those whom, having confessed gods on equal terms, he cannot make diverse: not because men too may not be most diverse under the same appellation, but because that One will not be called God, since neither will He be believed, unless as the supreme great One. Since, then, he is forced to acknowledge as the supreme great One Him whom he does not deny to be God, it cannot be allowed that he should ascribe to the supreme great One any diminution by which He would be made subject to another supreme great one. For He ceases to be such, if He be made subject. But it is not for God to cease from His own state, that is, from being the supreme great One. For in that more powerful god also the supreme greatness will be able to be imperilled, if it begins to be cheapened in the Creator. So when two gods are pronounced two supreme great ones, neither must of necessity be greater or less than the other, neither more sublime nor more abased than the other. Deny to be God the one you call worse; deny to be the supreme great One the one you believe lesser. But having confessed both to be God, you have confessed two supreme great ones. You will take nothing from the one or add nothing to the other. Acknowledging the divinity, you have denied the diversity.

But since from this we are now understood to be building toward this — that man's free power of arbitration is such that what befell him is to be charged not to God but to himself — lest you should from this object that he ought not to have been so instituted, if liberty and the power of arbitration was to prove destructive, this too I will first defend: that he ought to have been so instituted; whereby I may the more strongly commend that he was both so instituted and worthily of God so instituted, the better cause being shown which made him so instituted. The goodness of God and His reason will be patrons of this institution too, conspiring in all things with our God. For neither is reason without goodness reason, nor goodness without reason goodness — unless perchance with Marcion's god there be an irrationally good, as we have shown. It behoved that God be known: this surely is good and rational. It behoved that there be something worthy that should know God: what so worthy could be looked to as the image and likeness of God? And this is good without doubt, and rational. It behoved, therefore, that the image and likeness of God be instituted as of free arbitration and of its own power, in which this very thing should be reckoned the image and likeness of God — the liberty, namely, and power of arbitration; for which thing that substance was fitted to man which should be of this state — the breath, namely, of a God of course free and of His own power. But also, otherwise, what sort of thing was it that man, possessing the whole world, should not in the first place reign by the possession of his own mind — lord of others, slave of himself? You have, then, the goodness of God to acknowledge from His regard, and the reason from His disposition. Let goodness alone now be reckoned, which bestowed so much upon man, that is, liberty of arbitration. Let reason claim something else for itself in this kind of institution. For God alone is good by nature. For He who has what He is without beginning, has it not by institution, but by nature. But man, who is wholly of institution, having a beginning, with the beginning was allotted the form whereby he should be; and so was disposed toward good not by nature, but by institution, not having it of his own to be good — because he was disposed toward good not by nature, but by institution — according to the Institutor of the good, namely the Founder of good things. That man might then have a good now his own, made over to him by God, and that there might be now a property of the good in man and in a manner a nature, liberty and power of arbitration was assigned to him out of institution as a kind of balance-holder of the good made over by God — liberty which should effect the good, as his own, to be now spontaneously rendered by man; since this too the reason of goodness exacted, that it be exercised voluntarily, that is, out of liberty of arbitration, not favouring the institution, not serving it, so that man might at last stand good — if according to institution indeed, yet of his own will, he were now found good, as of a property of nature; and so that, against evil too (for that also of course God foresaw), the man might hold out the stronger, being free, of course, and of his own power; because, if he lacked this right of going to meet the good too not by will but by necessity, he would have been seizable by evil also out of the weakness of servitude, accordingly a slave to evil as to good. Wholly, then, the liberty of arbitration toward either part was granted him, that, as lord of himself, he might steadily go to meet both the good by spontaneously keeping it and the evil by spontaneously shunning it; since otherwise too, man being set under the judgment of God, it behoved to make that judgment just out of the deserts of his arbitration, free, of course. For neither the wage of good nor of evil would be rightly weighed out to him who had been found either good or evil by necessity, not by will. To this end also the law was constituted, not excluding but proving liberty, by obedience spontaneously rendered or transgression spontaneously committed; thus toward either outcome lay open the liberty of arbitration. Therefore, if both the goodness and the reason of God are found about the liberty of arbitration granted to man, it is not fitting, the first definition of goodness and reason being omitted — which must be settled before all treatment — afterward to prejudge from the deeds that God ought not so to have instituted, because the issue turned out otherwise than became God; but, this being discerned, that He ought so to have instituted, the other matters are to be explored, saving what has been discerned. For the rest, it is easy for those who stumble straightway upon man's ruin, before they have inspected his condition, to refer to the Author what happened, because neither has the reason of the Author been examined. In short, both the goodness of God, perceived from the beginning of His works, will persuade that nothing evil could have come from God, and the liberty of man, reconsidered, will show itself rather guilty of what it itself committed.

If it is now sufficiently settled concerning these two properties, in the meantime, of Jewish literature, remember, reader, that it has been settled — so that, when we have brought forward something of this kind, the question may not be reopened about the form of the Scripture, but only about the state of the case. Since, then, heretical madness presumed that a Christ had come who had never been announced, it followed that it should contend that the Christ had not yet come who was always proclaimed; and thus it was compelled to ally itself with Jewish error and to build its argument out of it — as though the Jews, themselves also assured that the one who came was another, had not only rejected him as a stranger but even killed him as an adversary, whereas they would certainly have acknowledged him and attended him with every office of religion, had he been their own. No doubt it was not the Rhodian law but the Pontic that provided for that skipper, that the Jews might not be allowed to err concerning their own Christ — when, even if nothing of the kind were found proclaimed against them, the merely human condition, liable to deception, would surely have persuaded that the Jews could have erred, inasmuch as they are men; nor is any prejudgment at once to be drawn about the verdict of those whom it was credible to have erred. Moreover, since it was also proclaimed that they would not acknowledge Christ and would therefore even kill him, then he himself will be the one both unknown to them and slain by them, against whom they were thus marked out beforehand as bound to offend. If you demand that this be proved, I will not unroll those Scriptures which, declaring Christ liable to be slain, certainly affirm him also to be liable to be unrecognized — for unless he had been unrecognized, he could clearly have suffered nothing; but reserving these for the question of the passion, it will suffice for the present to bring forward those proclamations which meanwhile prove Christ liable to be unrecognized, and this briefly, while they show that all force of understanding was taken away from the people by the Creator. "I will take away," he says, "the wisdom of their wise men, and the prudence of their prudent men I will hide"; and, "With the ear you shall hear, and shall not hear; and with the eyes you shall see, and shall not see: for the heart of this people is waxed gross, and with their ears they have heard heavily, and they have closed their eyes; lest at any time they should hear with their ears and see with their eyes and understand with the heart and be converted, and I should heal them." For they had deserved this dulling of their saving senses, loving God with their lips but standing far off from him with their heart. Therefore, if Christ indeed was being announced by the Creator — who consolidates the thunder, and shuts up the spirit, and announces his Christ to men, according to the prophet Joel — if all the hope of the Jews, not to say of the Gentiles too, was set upon the revelation of Christ, then without doubt they were shown to be such as would not acknowledge and not understand him, the powers of acknowledgement and understanding being taken away, wisdom and prudence; so that he who was announced — that is, Christ — their chief wise men, that is the scribes, and their prudent men, that is the Pharisees, were to err concerning him; and likewise the people, who with the ears were to hear and not hear — namely Christ teaching — and with the eyes to see and not see — namely Christ working signs — according to what is said elsewhere too: "And who is blind, but my children? and who is deaf, but those who rule them?" But also when he reproaches through the same Isaiah: "I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have rejected me; the ox knew his owner and the ass his master's crib, but Israel has not known me, and the people has not understood me." We indeed, certain that Christ always spoke in the prophets — the Spirit, namely, of the Creator, as the prophet testifies, "The person of our spirit, Christ the Lord," who from the beginning, the vicar of the Father, was both heard and seen in God's name — we know that those very utterances were his, reproaching Israel even then with the things they were foretold to commit against him: "You have forsaken the Lord, and have provoked to anger the Holy One of Israel." But if you should prefer to refer the whole reckoning of Jewish ignorance, from of old, not to Christ but rather to God himself — unwilling that even the Word and the Spirit of the past, that is, the Christ of the Creator, should be despised and unrecognized by them — even thus you are refuted. For, not denying that the Christ of the Creator is his Son and Spirit and substance, you must of necessity grant that those who did not acknowledge the Father could not acknowledge the Son either, through the condition of the same substance: for if the fullness was not understood, much more the portion — certainly inasmuch as it shares in the fullness. These things being so discerned, it now appears how the Jews both rejected and killed Christ, not understanding him as a strange Christ, but failing to acknowledge their own. For how could they have understood as a stranger one of whom nothing had ever been announced, when they could not understand one of whom it had always been proclaimed? For that admits of being understood or not understood which, having the substance of proclamation, will have also the matter either of acknowledgement or of error; whereas that which lacks matter does not admit of any outcome of wisdom. And so far is it from being the case that they rejected and persecuted Christ as belonging to another god — rather, only as a man whom they considered an impostor in signs and a rival in doctrines — that they brought even the man himself, as their own, that is, as a Jew, but a transgressor and destroyer of Judaism, to trial, and punished him by their own right, since they would surely not have judged a stranger. So far is it from appearing that they understood Christ to be an alien, who did not even judge his manhood to be that of an alien.

But we now enter from here upon another step, summoning, as we have professed, Marcion's gospel itself, intending even so to prove it adulterated. For certainly all that he laboured at — even by building up the Antitheses beforehand — he forces to this end: that he may establish a diversity of the old and new testament, accordingly a Christ of his own separated from the Creator, as of another god, as alien to the law and the prophets. Certainly it was for this that he erased whatever was contrary to his opinion and conspiring with the Creator, as if interwoven by his champions; but whatever was suited to his opinion he reserved. These we will examine, these we will embrace, if they be more for us, if they strike at Marcion's presumption. Then those others too will stand established as erased by the same vice of heretical blindness by which these others were reserved. Thus the intention and form of our little work will hold, under that condition surely which has been agreed upon from either side. Marcion lays it down that there is one Christ who, in the times of Tiberius, was revealed by a hitherto unknown god for the salvation of all nations, another who was destined by the Creator-god for the restitution of the Jewish state, one day to come. Between these he splits a great — nay, a total — difference, as great as between the just and the good, as great as between the law and the gospel, as great as between Judaism and Christianity. Hence will be our objection too, by which we fix it that nothing of the Christ of another god ought to be in common with the Creator; but he is to be pronounced the Creator's if he has administered his arrangements, if he has fulfilled his prophecies, if he has assisted his laws, if he has represented his promises, if he has restored his powers, if he has reformed his opinions, his manners, if he has expressed his properties. Of this compact and this objection, I beg you, reader, be everywhere mindful, and begin to recognize either Marcion's Christ or the Creator's. In the fifteenth year of the principate of Tiberius he sets forth that he came down into the city of Galilee, Capernaum — surely out of the Creator's heaven, into which he had before come down out of his own. Was there, then, any order in this, that he should be described as descending first out of his own heaven into the Creator's? For why should I not reprehend even these things, which do not fulfil the faith of an orderly narrative, ever failing in falsehood? Plainly let these be said once for all, by which we have already elsewhere discussed whether one descending through the Creator, and indeed against the Creator himself, could have been admitted by him, and thence transmitted to an earth equally his own. But now I demand also the rest of the order of the descent, holding that he descended. For let it be his concern, if it is anywhere set down that he appeared. To appear savours of a sudden, unexpected sight — of one who has once dashed his eyes upon that which appeared without delay. But to have descended, while it is being done, is both seen and steals upon the eyes. From the fact itself too it makes an order, and so compels one to ask, in what state, with what bearing, with what onset or tempering, even at what time of day or night, he descended. Moreover, who saw him descending, who reported it, who asseverated a thing surely not to be easily believed even to one asseverating it? It is unworthy, in short, that Romulus should have had a Proculus to affirm his ascent into heaven, but that Christ, a god, should have found no announcer of his descent from his own heaven — as though that other did not ascend by the same ladders of falsehood as this one descended. But what had he to do with Galilee, if he were not the Creator's, to whom that region was destined as he entered upon his preaching? — Isaiah saying, "Drink this first, do it quickly, region of Zabulon and land of Nephthalim, and the rest who are by the sea and the Jordan, Galilee of the nations, people who sit in darkness, behold a great light: you who inhabit the land, sitting in the shadow of death, a light has arisen upon you." Well, however, that even the god of Marcion is claimed as the illuminator of the nations — by which he ought the rather to have descended even from heaven, and, if at all, to have descended into Pontus rather than into Galilee. For the rest, by both the place and the work of illumination meeting Christ according to the prophecy, we begin already to acknowledge him foretold — showing that at his first entry he came not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfil them. For this Marcion erased as added. But in vain will he deny that Christ said what he straightway did in part. For the prophecy he meanwhile fulfilled as to place. From heaven straight to the synagogue. As the saying goes, "To the matter we have come for, set thy hand, Marcion": take away also that from the gospel, "I am not sent but to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and, "It is not to take the bread from the children and give it to the dogs" — namely lest Christ should seem to be Israel's. The deeds suffice me in place of the words. Take away the voices of my Christ — the facts will speak. Behold he comes into the synagogue; certainly to the lost sheep of the house of Israel. Behold he offers the bread of his teaching first to the Israelites; certainly he prefers them as children. Behold he does not yet impart it to others; certainly he passes them by as dogs. But to whom should he have imparted it more than to the strangers of the Creator, if he had not himself first of all been the Creator's? And yet how could he have been admitted into the synagogue, so sudden, so unknown — of whose tribe, people, house, and lastly of whose registration under Augustus no one was as yet certain, that registration which the Roman archives guard as the most faithful witness of the Lord's nativity? They would surely have remembered, unless they knew him circumcised, that he was not to be admitted into the holy of holies. But even if the synagogue were entered at large, yet not to teach, save by one well known and tried and approved, long since commended for this very thing, or from elsewhere, with this function. But they were all astonished at his teaching. Plainly. "Because," it says, "his word was in power" — not because he taught against the law and the prophets. For surely the divine utterance furnished both force and grace, building up rather than destroying the substance of the law and the prophets. Otherwise they would not have been astonished, but would have shuddered. Nor would they have marvelled, but would straightway have turned away from a destroyer of the law and the prophets, and surely above all from a preacher of another god — since he could not even have taught against the law and the prophets, and under this title against the Creator, without a profession sent before of a diverse and rival divinity. Since, then, the Scripture signifies nothing of the kind, but only that the force and power of his word were a marvel, it more easily shows that he taught according to the Creator, because it did not deny it, than against the Creator, because it did not signify it. And so either he is to be acknowledged as belonging to him according to whom he taught, or to be judged a prevaricator, if he taught according to him against whom he had come. In the same place the spirit of a demon cries out: "What is there to us and to thee, Jesus? Thou hast come to destroy us. I know who thou art, the Holy One of God." Here I will not discuss whether this surname too suited him whom it would not have been right to call even Christ, were he not the Creator's. Concerning the names the demand has already been made elsewhere. But now I dispute how the demon came to know him called by this name, no preaching ever having been sent forth before concerning him by a god unknown and at that time mute — of whom he could not even attest that he was holy, as one unknown even to his own Creator. But what had he as yet put forth of a new divinity by which he could be understood to be the Holy One of another god? Only that he had entered the synagogue, and had not even by a word done anything against the Creator? As, then, he in no way could have acknowledged as Jesus and the Holy One of God him whom he did not know, so him whom he knew he acknowledged. For he remembered that the prophet had proclaimed the Holy One of God, and that Jesus was the name of God in the son of Nun. These things he had also received from the angel, according to our gospel: "Therefore that which shall be born in thee shall be called holy, the Son of God, and thou shalt call his name Jesus." But he had also surely some sense of the Lord's arrangement (though a demon, yet), rather than of one alien and not yet sufficiently known. For he premised, "What is there to us and to thee?" — not as toward a stranger, this Jesus, to whom the spirits of the Creator pertain. For he did not say, "What is there to thee and to us?" but, "What is there to us and to thee?" — bewailing himself and reproaching himself with his lot; which already seeing he adds, "Thou hast come to destroy us." So far had he acknowledged Jesus to be the Son of a judging and avenging and, so to say, a fierce god, not of that best god who knows neither how to destroy nor to punish. To what end have we premised this passage? That we may teach that Jesus was acknowledged by the demon as none other, and confirmed by himself as none other, than the Creator's. "And yet," you say, "Jesus rebuked him." Plainly, as one invidious, and in his very confession petulant and ill-flattering — as though this were the supreme glory of Christ, if he had come for the destruction of demons and not rather for the salvation of men, who would not have even his disciples glory in the subjection of spirits, but in the white robe of salvation. Or why did he rebuke him? If as one lying altogether, then he was not Jesus, nor the Holy One of God at all; if as one lying in part — in that he had reckoned him indeed Jesus and the Holy One of God, but of the Creator — most unjustly did he rebuke one who thought what he knew ought to be thought, and did not reckon what he was ignorant ought to be reckoned, namely another Jesus and the Holy One of another god. But if the rebuke has no more probable footing than that which we interpret, then the demon too lied in nothing, was not rebuked for a lie; for he himself was Jesus, beside whom the demon could have acknowledged no other, and Jesus confirmed him whom the demon had acknowledged, while he rebukes the demon not for a lie.

By all these things, then, he shows of what God he speaks the wisdom among the perfect: of him, namely, who took away the wisdom of the wise and made void the prudence of the prudent, who made foolish the wisdom of the world, choosing its foolish things and arranging them for salvation. This wisdom he says was in secret — the wisdom which was in foolish and little and base things, which lay hidden too under figures, allegories, and riddles, to be revealed afterwards in Christ, set for a light of the nations by the Creator, who promised through the voice of Isaiah that he would lay open invisible and hidden treasures. For that the God who did nothing at all in which anything could be supposed to have been hidden should have hidden anything, is incredible enough. If he himself existed, he could not lie hidden, much less any of his sacraments. But the Creator is as well known as his sacraments, openly running their course, namely, among Israel, but overshadowed by significations, in which the wisdom of God lay concealed, to be narrated among the perfect in its own time, but set forth in the purpose of God before the ages. Whose are the ages, except the Creator's? For if the ages are built of times, and times are joined together of days and months and years, and days and months and years are marked by the suns and moons and constellations of the Creator, set by him for this (And they shall be, he says, for signs of months and years), it appears that both the ages are the Creator's, and that all that is said to have been purposed before the ages is of no other than him whose are the ages. Or let Marcion prove the ages of his God; let him show the very world too in which the ages are reckoned — a kind of vessel of times — and some signs or order of them. If he demonstrates nothing, I return to say this too: But why did he purpose our glory before the ages? It might seem that he purposed it before the ages, which he would reveal by the introduction of the age. But when he does this with almost all the ages of the Creator now run forth, he purposed it before the ages in vain, and not rather within the ages, since he was about to reveal it almost after the ages. For it is not his to have hastened in purposing whose it was also to have delayed in revealing. But to the Creator both befit: both to have purposed before the ages and to have revealed at the end of the ages, because both what he purposed and revealed he furnished beforehand, in the middle space of the ages, in figures and riddles and allegories. But because he subjoins of our glory that none of the princes of this age knew it — for if they had known it, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory — the heretic argues that the princes of this age crucified the Lord, the Christ, namely, of another God, that this too may fall back upon the Creator. But for him to whom we showed above in what ways our glory is to be reckoned of the Creator, it ought to be foreshown that the glory which was in secret with the Creator was rightly unknown even to all the virtues and powers of the Creator, because not even servants are permitted to know the counsels of their lords, much less those apostate angels and the very prince of transgression, the devil — whom I would contend to have been the more strangers, on account of their fault, from all consciousness of the Creator's arrangements. But now it does not even befit me to interpret the princes of this age as the virtues and powers of the Creator, because the apostle ascribes ignorance to them, whereas Jesus, even according to our gospel, the devil too knew in the temptation, and according to the common instrument the unclean spirit knew that he was the Holy One of God and was called Jesus and had come for their destruction. The parable too of the strong armed man, whom another stronger overpowered and seized his goods, if it be taken of the Creator according to Marcion, then the Creator could no longer have been ignorant of the God of glory, while he is overpowered by him, nor have nailed to the cross him against whom he could not prevail; and it remains that, according to me at least, it is credible that the virtues and powers of the Creator, knowing the God of glory, crucified him their own Christ — by that desperation and overflow of malice with which the most wicked servants too do not hesitate to slay their lords. For it is written with me that Satan entered into Judas. But according to Marcion, not even the apostle in this place suffers ignorance to be ascribed to the virtues of the Creator concerning the Lord of glory, because, namely, he does not wish them understood as the princes of this age. But if he seems not to have spoken of spiritual princes, then he spoke of secular ones — of the chief people, surely not among the nations — of its very rulers, of King Herod, of Pilate too, and of the Roman dignity, by which the greater principality of this age presided. Thus, while the argumentations of the opposite party are destroyed, our expositions are built up. But you wish further that our glory be of your God, and that it was with him in secret. And why does God and the apostle still both rely on the same instrument? What has he everywhere to do with the sentences of the prophets? For who has known the mind of the Lord, and who was his counsellor? It is Isaiah. What has he even to do with examples of our God? For when he affirms himself a prudent architect, we find this signified by the proclaimer of the divine discipline, the Creator, through Isaiah. For I will take away, he says, from Judaea, among the rest, also the wise architect. And was not Paul himself then destined — to be taken from Judaea, that is, from Judaism, unto the building of Christianity, about to lay the one foundation which is Christ? For of this too the Creator says through the same prophet, Behold, I lay in the foundations of Sion a precious stone, honourable, and he that believes in him shall not be confounded. Unless God professed himself the builder of an earthly work, so as not to signify of his own Christ, who was to be the foundation of believers in him, upon which, according as each shall have built up doctrine worthy or unworthy, if his work shall be proved by fire, if a reward shall be paid him by fire, it is the Creator's, because by fire your superstructure is judged — upon his own foundation, namely, that is, his own Christ. Do you not know that you are the temple of God, and that the Spirit of God dwells in you? If man — both substance and work and image and likeness, both flesh through earth and soul through the breath of the Creator — then the whole God of Marcion dwells in another's property, if we are not the temple of the Creator. But if anyone shall defile the temple of God, he shall be defiled — surely by the God of the temple. By threatening an avenger you will be threatening the Creator. Be foolish, that you may be wise. Why? For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God. With what God? If our former arguments have decided nothing for us toward this sense too, well that he here too builds up: For it is written, He that takes the wise in their craftiness; and again, The Lord knows the thoughts of the wise, that they are vain. For it will in sum have been prescribed by us that the apostle could use no sentence of that God whom he ought to destroy, if he were not teaching him. Therefore, he says, let no one glory in man. And this according to the Creator's discipline: Wretched is the man who has hope in man! and, It is good to trust in God rather than to trust in men; and so, to glory likewise.

Against this you will attempt to shake my treatment by means of the name of God, as though it were passive and granted to others also, because it is written: "The God of gods stood in the assembly of gods, and in the midst He shall judge the gods," and, "I have said, You are gods." Yet it does not for that reason belong to them to possess the supreme greatness because they are called gods; so neither to the Creator. I will answer even the fool, who has not even reflected on this — that just as much may be hurled back against Marcion's god, that he too is called a god, yet for all that not proved the supreme great One, just as neither are the angels or men of the Creator. If community of names prejudges conditions, how many worthless slaves insult the names of kings — Alexander and Darius and Holofernes? Yet not for that reason will what they are be taken from the kings. For even the idols of the nations are commonly "gods," but none is a god by that thing whereby it is called a god. So I do not, for the name of God nor for the sound nor for the mark of this name, defend the supreme greatness in the Creator, but for the very substance to which this name has fallen — finding this alone unborn, unmade, alone eternal and founder of the universe — and it is not to the name but to the state, not to the appellation but to His condition, that I both ascribe and vindicate the supreme greatness. And therefore, because the substance to which I ascribe it has now obtained to be called God, you think I ascribe it to the name, since I must of necessity through the name point out to what substance I ascribe it — namely, to that whereby He consists who is called God; and the supreme great One is reckoned from substance, not from name. Lastly, Marcion too, vindicating this for his own god, vindicates it according to state, not according to title. That supreme greatness, then, which we ascribe to God by the law of substance, not by the lot of name, we contend ought to belong equally to two who consist of that substance whereby God is named; because in so far as they are called gods, that is, supreme great ones — namely by merit of a substance unborn and eternal and thereby great and supreme — in so far the supreme great One cannot be held lesser and worse than another supreme great one. If the felicity and sublimity and integrity of the supreme great One will stand in Marcion's god, it will stand equally in ours too; if not in ours, equally not in Marcion's. Therefore the two supreme great ones will be neither equal — since the rule already laid down of the supreme great One, which does not sustain comparison, forbids it — nor unequal, since another rule of the supreme great One meets us, which admits no diminution. You are stuck, Marcion, in the midst of your own Pontic surge. On either side the waves of truth enfold you. You can establish gods neither equal nor unequal. For there are not two — and this belongs properly to the treatment of number. Although the whole matter is fought out concerning two gods, with these lines for the moment we have closed it in, within which we shall now engage concerning their individual properties.

By this definition all things are saved to God: both the nature of goodness and the reason of disposition and the abundance of foreknowledge and power. Yet you ought to exact of God both supreme gravity and especial fidelity in every institution of His, that you may cease to ask whether anything could have come to pass against God's will. For holding fast the gravity and fidelity of the good God — but a gravity and fidelity to be vindicated by His rational institutions — you will not wonder at this either, that God did not intervene against the things He willed not to come to pass, in order to preserve the things He willed. For if He had once granted man liberty and power of arbitration, and worthily had granted them, as we have shown, surely He had granted them to be enjoyed by the very authority of the institution — to be enjoyed, however, as far as on His own part, according to Himself, that is, according to God, that is, unto good (for who will permit anything against himself?); but, as far as on man's part, according to the motions of man's own liberty (for who does not grant this to him to whom he has once granted the enjoyment of anything — that he enjoy it according to his own mind and arbitration?). It was consequent, therefore, that God should withdraw from the liberty once granted to man, that is, should hold within Himself both His foreknowledge and His foremost power, through which He could have intervened, that man should not fall into danger by undertaking to enjoy his liberty ill. For if He had intervened, He would have rescinded the liberty of arbitration which He had permitted by reason and goodness. Suppose, finally, He had intervened; suppose He had rescinded the liberty of arbitration, while He recalls man from the tree, while He keeps the very circumventing serpent from his meeting with the woman — would not Marcion cry out, "O futile lord, unstable, faithless, rescinding what He instituted! Why had He permitted free arbitration, if He intervenes? Why does He intervene, if He permitted?" Let him choose where he should mark Him with error: in the institution, or in the rescinding. Would He not then rather have seemed deceived out of unforeknowledge of the future, when He had withstood it? And that He had indulged, as though ignorant how it would turn out — who would not say it? But even though He had foreknown that man would use His institution ill, what is so worthy of God as gravity, as fidelity to His institutions, of whatever sort? Man would have seen to it, if he had not well discharged what he had well received, so that he himself should be guilty toward the law which he had been unwilling to obey — not that the Lawgiver Himself should do fraud to His own law, by not allowing what He prescribed to be fulfilled. These things you were most worthily about to plead against the Creator, had He withstood man's free arbitration out of that providence and power which you demand; but now whisper to yourself, on the Creator's behalf, both gravity and patience and fidelity, He having discharged His institutions as both rational and good.

Let the heretic now learn over and above — since it is permitted, along with the Jew himself — the very reason of his errors, by which, having borrowed his lead from him in this argument, blind from blind, he has fallen into the same pit. We say that two states of Christ, demonstrated by the prophets, marked beforehand just so many comings of his: one in lowliness — the first, surely — when he was to be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb dumb before the shearer, so not opening his mouth, not comely even in look. "For we announced concerning him," he says, "as a little child, as a root in a thirsting earth; and he has no comeliness nor glory, and we saw him, and he had no comeliness nor beauty; but his appearance was without honour, failing beyond the sons of men, a man under stroke, and knowing how to bear infirmity" — so that he was set by the Father for a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence, made a little less than the angels by him, pronouncing himself a worm and not a man, the shame of man and the outcast of the people. These tokens of ignobility befit the first coming, just as those of loftiness befit the second, when he will become no longer a stone of stumbling nor a rock of offence, but the chief corner-stone, taken up after rejection and exalted to the completion of the temple — the Church, namely; and surely that rock in Daniel, cut out of the mountain, which shall break and grind to powder the image of the worldly kingdoms. Concerning which coming the same prophet says: "And behold, with the clouds of heaven, as the son of man, coming, he came even to the Ancient of days, and was present in his sight; and they that stood by brought him forward, and there was given to him royal power, and all the nations of the earth according to their kinds, and all glory serving him; and his power is unto everlasting, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom, which shall not be corrupted" — then, namely, when he is to have both an honourable appearance and an unfailing beauty beyond the sons of men. "For seasonable," he says, "in beauty beyond the sons of men, grace is poured out upon thy lips; therefore God has blessed thee for ever. Gird thy sword upon thy thigh, mighty one, in thy seasonableness and thy beauty" — when the Father, too, after he has diminished him somewhat below the angels, "will crown him with glory and honour, and will put all things under his feet." Then also "they who pierced him will know him," and will smite their breasts, tribe against tribe — surely because formerly they did not acknowledge him in the lowliness of the human condition. "And he is man," says Jeremiah, "and who shall know him?" Because also, "His generation," says Isaiah, "who shall declare?" So too in Zechariah, in the person of Jesus — nay, even in the very mystery of the name, the true high priest of the Father, Christ Jesus — he is delineated in a twofold state for the two comings: first clothed in filthy garments, that is, in the indignity of passible and mortal flesh, when the devil also opposed him, the author, namely, of Judas the betrayer — not to say also the tempter after baptism — and then, stripped of his former filth, adorned with the long robe and the mitre and the clean turban, that is, with the glory and honour of the second coming. For if I should also expound the two goats that were offered at the fast, do not these too figure the twofold order of Christ? Alike indeed and very similar, on account of the same Lord beheld — since he is to come in no other form, as one who is to be recognized by those by whom he was wounded. But one of them, surrounded with scarlet, cursed and spat upon and torn and pricked, was thrust by the people outside the city into destruction, marked with the plain insignia of the Lord's passion. The other, however, offered for sins and given to the priests of the temple for food, signed the proofs of the second manifestation, by which, all sins being expiated, the priests of the spiritual temple — that is, of the Church — should enjoy as it were a certain banquet of the Lord's grace, while the rest fast from salvation. Therefore, since the first coming was sung both for the most part overshadowed by figures and prostrated in every dishonour, but the second both manifest and worthy of God — for this reason, looking to the one they could easily both understand and believe, that is, the second, they were not without cause deceived concerning the more obscure, certainly the less worthy, that is, the first. And so to this day they deny that their Christ has come, because he came not in loftiness — while they are ignorant that he was to come also in lowliness.

And the hidden things of darkness he himself will illuminate — surely through Christ, who promised Christ as illumination, who declared himself also a lamp, searching hearts and reins. From him too shall be praise to each one, from whom too the contrary of praise, as from a judge. Surely, you say, here at least he interprets world as the God of the world, by saying, We have been made a spectacle to the world and to angels and to men. For if by world he had meant the men of the world, he would not afterwards have named men also. Nay, lest you should argue thus, the providence of the Holy Spirit showed how he had said, We have been made a spectacle to the world — namely, to the angels who minister to the world, and to the men whom they serve. For the force of so great a constancy, not to say the Holy Spirit, feared — writing especially to sons whom he had begotten in the gospel — to name freely the God of the world, against whom he could not seem to preach except expressly. I do not defend, according to the law of the Creator, that he who had his father's wife was displeasing to him. He followed the discipline of the common and public religion. But when he condemns the same man to be delivered to Satan, he is the herald of a condemning God. Let it be seen too how he said, Unto the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved in the day of the Lord, since he judged both of the destruction of the flesh and of the salvation of the spirit, and, in bidding evil to be taken away from the midst, recalled a most frequent sentence of the Creator. Purge out the old leaven, that you may be a new lump, as you are unleavened. Therefore the unleavened bread were figures of ourselves with the Creator. So too our Passover, Christ, has been sacrificed. Why is Christ the Passover, if the Passover were not a figure of Christ, by the likeness of the saving blood and of the flock of Christ? Why does he clothe us and Christ with the images of the Creator's solemnities, if they were not ours? But, turning us from fornication, he makes manifest the resurrection of the flesh. The body, he says, is not for fornication, but for the Lord, and the Lord for the body — as the temple for God, and God for the temple. The temple, then, for God shall perish, and God for the temple. But you see, He that raised up the Lord will raise us up also — and will raise us up in the body too, because the body is for the Lord, and the Lord for the body. And well that he heaps up, Do you not know that your bodies are the members of Christ? What will the heretic say? Shall the members of Christ not rise again, which are now no longer ours? For we were bought with a great price. With none at all, surely, if Christ was a phantasm and had no substance of body which he might pay for our bodies. Therefore Christ both had wherewith to redeem us, and if with something great he redeemed these bodies — into which the same fornication shall not be committed, since they are now Christ's members and not ours — surely he will keep safe for himself what he purchased at a great price. How now shall we honour, how take up, God in a body that is to perish? Then follows his engaging upon marriage, which Marcion, more constant than the apostle, forbids. For the apostle, though he prefers the good of continence, yet permits marriage both to be contracted and to be in use, and advises rather to keep it than to put it asunder. Plainly Christ forbids divorce, but Moses permits it. Marcion, taking away all conjugal intercourse from the faithful (let his catechumens see to it), ordering repudiation before marriage — whose sentence does he follow, Moses' or Christ's? But Christ too, when he commands that a woman should not depart from her husband, or, if she has departed, should remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband, both permitted repudiation, which he did not wholly forbid, and confirmed marriage, which he first forbade to be put asunder, and, if perchance put asunder, willed to be reformed. But what causes does he give for continence too? Because the time is contracted. I had thought it because another God is in Christ; and yet, from him by whom is the contraction of time, will come also that which suits the contraction of time. No one takes thought for another's time. You affirm your God to be petty, Marcion, whom in anything the Creator's time straitens. Surely, when he prescribes that one must marry only in the Lord, lest a faithful man contract a heathen marriage, he upholds the law of the Creator, who everywhere forbids marriages with men of other tribes. But, Even if there are those who are called gods, whether in the heavens or on earth, it appears how he said it: not as though they truly were, but because there are those who are called so, when they are not. For he had begun, about to dispute of things offered to idols: We know that an idol is nothing. But the Creator even Marcion does not deny to be God; therefore the apostle cannot seem to have placed the Creator too among those who are called gods and yet are not — since, even if they were, yet to us there would be one God the Father. From whom are all things to us, except him whose are all things? Which things are these? You have in what precedes, All things are yours, whether Paul, or Apollos, or Cephas, or the world, or life, or death, or things present, or things to come. So fully does he make the Creator the God of all, from whom are both the world and life and death, which cannot be of another God. From him, therefore, among all things, is Christ too. Teaching that each ought to live by his own labour, he had set before enough examples of soldiers, shepherds, husbandmen; but divine authority was wanting to him. He therefore opposes to the ungrateful the law of the Creator, which he was destroying; for of his own God he had no such law. You shall not muzzle, he says, the ox that treads out the corn; and he adds, Does it concern the Lord about oxen? — yes, even about oxen kind, for men's sake? For it is written for our sakes, he says. Therefore he both approved the allegorical law according to us, and as advocating for those who live of the gospel, and on this account that the evangelists are of no other than him whose is the law that looked forward to them, when he says, For it is written for our sakes. But he was unwilling to use the power of the law, because he preferred to labour for nothing. This he referred to his own glory, which he denied that anyone would make void — not to the destruction of the law, which he proved another would use. For behold, blind Marcion stumbles even upon the rock from which our fathers drank in the wilderness. For if that rock was Christ, surely it was the Creator's, whose also was the people. Of what is he interpreting a figure of a stranger sacrament? Or is it that he might teach this very thing, that the old things were figured unto a Christ to be reviewed out of them? For, about to run through the rest of the people's outcome too, he sends before, But these things were made examples to us. Tell me: were examples made to men by the Creator of another and unknown God, or does one God borrow examples from another — and that a rival? It frightens me about him from whom he transfers my faith to himself. Will the adversary make me better toward him? Now if I sin in the same things as the people, am I to suffer the same things, or not? But if not the same, in vain does he set before me to be feared what I am not to suffer. But from whom shall I suffer? If from the Creator, what is it his to inflict? And what manner of thing will it be that a zealous God should punish the sinner of his rival rather than, on the contrary, cherish him? If from that God of yours? But he knows not to punish. Thus this whole proposition of the apostle stands by no reason, if it is not the Creator's discipline. In short, even in the close he answers his preface. But these things, as they happened to them, were written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the ages have come. O Creator, both foreknowing now and admonishing the Christians of another! I pass over, when sometimes there are things equal to those already reviewed, certain of which I also briefly dismiss. A great argument of another God: the permission of all victuals against the law. As though we too did not confess that the burdens of the law were dismissed — but by him who imposed them, who promised renewal. So too he gave back the foods he took away, which he had furnished from the beginning. But if any other God had been the destroyer of our God, he would have forbidden his own nothing more than to live off the supplies of the adversary.

First, with a lifted eyebrow the Marcionites build up their amazement, that they bring forward a new god, as though we were ashamed of an old one. Even children are puffed up by new shoes; but shod by an old schoolmaster, they shall soon be whipped for their empty boasting. Hearing, then, of a new god in an old world and in an old age and under an old god, unknown, unheard of, whom for so many past ages no one knew, and ancient by that very ignorance — one Jesus Christ, and he new under old names, who is said to have revealed Him, and no other before — I give thanks for this their boast, since by it I have a very great help here, being about to prove this heresy, namely the profession of a new divinity. This will be the novelty that has begotten gods even for the heathen, always with a new and new title of each consecration. What new god, except a false one? Not even Saturn will so great an antiquity today prove a god, since novelty once produced even him, when first it consecrated him. But living and genuine divinity is reckoned neither from novelty nor from antiquity, but from its own truth. Eternity has no time. For it is itself all time. What it makes, it cannot suffer. That is free of age which cannot be born. If God is old, He will not exist; if He is new, He has not existed. Novelty testifies a beginning; antiquity threatens an end. But God is as alien from beginning and end as from time, the arbiter and measurer of beginning and end.

For He had not produced man only that he should live, but not also that he should live rightly — in regard, that is, to God and His law. Therefore He had Himself bestowed on him living indeed, in that He made him into a living soul; but living rightly He had commanded by admonition unto obedience to the law. So He proves man not instituted unto death, who now desires him restored unto life, preferring the sinner's repentance to his death. Therefore, as God led man into the state of life, so man drew upon himself the state of death; and this not through weakness, just as not through ignorance, lest anything be imputed to the Author. For although it was an angel that seduced him, yet he that was seduced was free and of his own power; and the image and likeness of God is stronger than an angel; and the breath of God is nobler than the material spirit of which the angels were composed. "Who makes," He says, "His angels spirits, and His attendants a flame of fire." For He would neither have subjected the universe to man if he were weak, and unfit to have dominion, and not mightier than the angels, to whom He subjected no such thing; so neither would He have imposed the weight of the law, if the law were grievous for a weak man to sustain; nor would He have met with the sentence of death one whom He knew excusable on the score of feebleness; finally, He would not have made man weak by liberty and power of arbitration, but rather by the lack of them. And, what is more, the same man, the same substance of soul, the same state of Adam, is by the same liberty and power of arbitration made today a conqueror over the same devil, when he is administered according to obedience to His laws.

Let the heretic now cease — an asp, as the saying goes, borrowing venom from a viper, from the Jew — let him now vomit out the poison of his own genius, claiming Christ to be a phantom. Save that even this opinion will have other authors: the half-baked and as it were abortive Marcionites, whom the apostle John pronounced antichrists, denying that Christ came in the flesh — yet not so as to establish the right of another god, for on that score too they would have been censured, but because they had presumed it incredible that God should be flesh. The more did the antichrist Marcion seize that presumption for himself, the more apt, namely, to deny the bodily substance of Christ, seeing that he had introduced his very god as neither the author nor the raiser-up of flesh — the best, no doubt, in this point too, and most utterly different from the lies and deceits of the Creator. And therefore his Christ, lest he should lie, lest he should deceive, and in this way perhaps be reckoned the Creator's, was not what he appeared, and lied as to what he was: flesh and not flesh, man and not man, and accordingly God a Christ, and not God. For why should he not have also carried about a phantom of deity? Or shall I believe him concerning his inner substance, who has cheated me concerning the outer? How shall he be held truthful in what is hidden, found so deceptive in what is open? But how, confusing in himself the truth of the spirit by the deceit of the flesh, did he commit that communion, denied by the apostle, of light — that is, of truth — and of deceit — that is, of darkness? Even now, when Christ-as-flesh is detected as a lie, it follows that all the things too which were done through the flesh of Christ were done in lie: encounters, contacts, eatings-together, the very powers as well. For if by touching someone he freed him from a defect, or was touched by someone, what was done bodily cannot be believed to have been truly done without the truth of the body itself. Nothing solid could be accomplished by what is empty, nothing full by what is void. A seeming state, a seeming act: an imaginary worker, imaginary works. So neither will the passions of his Christ deserve belief. For he suffered nothing who did not truly suffer; and a phantom could not truly suffer. The whole work of God, therefore, is overturned. The whole weight and fruit of the Christian name, the death of Christ, is denied — which the apostle so emphatically enjoins as true, making it the supreme foundation of the gospel and of our salvation and of his own preaching: "For I delivered to you first of all," he says, "that Christ died for our sins, and that he was buried, and that he rose again on the third day." But if his flesh is denied, how is his death asserted, which is the proper passion of the flesh, of one passing through death into the earth from which it was taken, according to the law of its own author? And his death being denied, since the flesh is denied, neither will his resurrection stand. For he did not rise for the same reason that he did not die: namely, not having the substance of the flesh, whose, just as death, so also resurrection is. Accordingly, the resurrection of Christ being invalidated, ours too is overthrown. For that will not avail for which Christ came, if his own will not avail. For just as those who said there is no resurrection of the dead are refuted by the apostle from the resurrection of Christ, so, the resurrection of Christ not standing, the resurrection of the dead too is taken away. And thus our faith is vain, and the preaching of the apostles is vain. They are found, moreover, even false witnesses of God, in that they bore witness, as it were, that God raised up Christ, whom he did not raise. And we are still in our sins. And those who have fallen asleep in Christ have perished — destined indeed to rise again, but as a phantom perhaps, like Christ himself.

He was to be called a Nazarene according to the prophecy, the Christ of the Creator. Hence even by that very name we Jews call them Nazarenes after him. For we too are they of whom it is written: "The Nazarites have been made whiter than snow" — they, namely, who formerly were sallow with the stains of delinquency and blackened with the darkness of ignorance. But the appellation of Nazarene was to befit Christ from the hiding-places of his infancy, to which he came down at Nazareth, avoiding Archelaus, son of Herod. This I have not omitted for this reason, that the Christ of Marcion ought to have foresworn all commerce even with the familiar places of the Christ of the Creator — having so many towns of Judea not so emancipated to the Christ of the Creator through the prophets. For the rest, he will be the Christ of the prophets wherever he is found according to the prophets. And yet at Nazareth too nothing new is noted that he preached, while he is reported to have been cast out elsewhere, deservedly on account of a single proverb. Here, observing the hands first laid upon him, I find it necessary now to determine beforehand concerning his bodily substance — that he cannot be believed a phantom who admitted a touch, and that indeed full of violence, being held and seized and dragged even to a precipice. For even though he escaped through their midst, yet he had first experienced force, and was afterward let go — the tumult, namely, being broken up, as is wont, or even burst through, yet not eluded by means of a mist, which would have given way to no touch at all, had it existed. For to touch and to be touched belongs to nothing but a body — even secular wisdom is worthy of the verdict.
