In short, he himself soon touched others, on whom laying hands (hands surely to be felt), he conferred the benefits of his medicines, as true and as un-imaginary as were the hands through which he conferred them. He, therefore, is the Christ of Isaiah, the remedier of infirmities. "He," it says, "takes away our weaknesses and bears our languors." Now the Greeks are wont to put "to bear" for what is "to take away." Meanwhile the general promise suffices me. Whatever Jesus has cured is mine. We will come, however, to the species of cures too. For the rest, to free from demons too is a cure of infirmity. And so the wicked spirits, as it were from the form of the former example already, went out with testimony, crying out, "Thou art the Son of God." Of what god, let it appear even here. But they were likewise rebuked and bidden to be silent. For accordingly Christ wished to be acknowledged the Son of God by men, not by unclean spirits — that Christ, at least, to whom this befitted, because he had sent before those by whom he could be acknowledged, and surely worthier preachers. To reject the proclamation of an unclean spirit was the part of him who abounded in holy ones. But he who had never been announced — if indeed he wished to be acknowledged, and had come in vain if he did not — would not have spurned the testimony of an alien and any substance whatever, who had none of his own, who had descended into another's. And even now, in so far as he was the destroyer of the Creator, he would have desired nothing more than to be acknowledged and divulged by the very spirits, out of fear; save that Marcion denies that his god is feared, defending that the good is not feared but the judge, with whom are the matters for fear — anger, savagery, judgements, vengeance, condemnation. But the demons too gave way surely out of fear. Therefore they were confessing the Son of a god to be feared — they who would have had occasion not to give way, had they not had to fear. And he, expelling them by command and rebuke, not by persuasion (as the good), showed himself one to be feared. Or did he perhaps rebuke them for this reason, that he was feared, being unwilling to be feared? And how did he wish them to go out, which they would not do but out of fear? He fell, then, into a necessity by which he behaved unlike his own nature, when he could, as the good, have spared them once for all. He fell also into another mark of prevarication, when he allowed himself to be feared by the demons as the Son of the Creator — so that now not by his own power did he expel the demons, but through the authority of the Creator. He goes forth into the wilderness. Solemn, and of this kind, is the region of the Creator. It behoved the Word to be seen there too in body, where he had once acted even in cloud. The state of the place too suited the gospel, which had pleased the law. Let the wilderness, then, take up joyfulness — this Isaiah had promised. Detained by the crowds, "It behoves me," he says, "to announce the kingdom of God to other cities also." Had he already anywhere shown his god? I think not yet. But was he speaking to those who knew another god too? Neither do I believe this. Therefore, if neither he had published another god nor they knew any besides the Creator, he was portending the kingdom of the same god whom alone he knew to be known to those who heard.

The head of the man is Christ. What Christ, who is not the author of man? For he set down head as authority, and authority will be of no other than the author. Of what man, then, is he the head? Surely of him concerning whom he subjoins, For a man ought not to veil his head, since he is the image of God. Therefore, if he is the image of the Creator (for the Creator, looking upon his Word, Christ, as the man to be, said, Let us make man after our image and likeness), how can I have another as my head, not him whose image I am? For since I am the image of the Creator, there is no room in me for another head. But also, why ought the woman to have power over her head? If it is because she is of the man and made for the man's sake, according to the institution of the Creator, then here too the apostle has taken care of his discipline, of whose institution he interprets the reasons of the discipline. He adds also, On account of the angels. What angels? that is, of whom? If apostates of the Creator, with reason — that, by that very countenance which gave them offence, she might carry a certain mark of the humility of her dress and the obscuring of her comeliness. But if on account of the angels of another God, what does he fear, if not even the Marcionites themselves desire women? We have often already shown that heresies are set among evils as an evil with the apostle, and that those are to be understood as approved who flee heresies as an evil. So likewise, in the sacrament of the bread and cup, we have already proved in the gospel the truth of the Lord's body and blood against the phantasm of Marcion. But also that every mention of judgement befits the Creator, as the God who judges, has been treated through almost the whole work. Now I speak of spiritual gifts, that these too were promised in Christ by the Creator, under that most just prescription, I think, by which the exhibition is to be believed of no other than him whose promise has been proved. Isaiah pronounced, A rod shall come forth from the root of Jesse, and a flower shall ascend from the root, and the Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him. Then he enumerates its kinds: the Spirit of wisdom and understanding, the Spirit of counsel and might, and the Spirit of knowledge and of godliness; the Spirit of the fear of God shall fill him. For he showed that Christ should arise in the figure of a flower from a rod that issued from the root of Jesse — that is, the virgin of the lineage of David, the son of Jesse — in which Christ the whole substance of the Spirit was to consist, not as though to come upon him afterwards who was always the Spirit of God, even before the flesh — lest from this you argue that the prophecy pertains to that Christ who, as a mere man, only out of the reckoning of David, should afterwards obtain the Spirit of his God — but because from the time he flowered in the flesh, taken from the stock of David, all working of spiritual grace had to rest in him, and to leave off and make an end, as far as concerns the Jews; as the very fact testifies, that thenceforth nothing of the Creator's Spirit breathes among them, the wise and prudent architect and counsellor and prophet having been taken away from Judaea, so that this is the meaning of, The law and the prophets were until John. Now receive how, after Christ's reception into heaven, he pronounced that gifts of grace would come. He ascended on high, that is, into heaven; he led captivity captive, that is, death or human bondage; he gave gifts to the sons of men, that is, donatives, which we call charismata. Elegantly he says to the sons of men, not at random to men, showing us the sons of men, that is, of true men, namely of the apostles. For in the gospel, he says, I have begotten you; and, My sons, of whom I am again in travail. Now too that promise of the Spirit made absolutely through Joel: In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh, and their sons and daughters shall prophesy, and upon my menservants and maidservants of my Spirit will I pour out. And surely, if in the last days the Creator promised the grace of the Spirit, and Christ the dispenser of spiritual things appeared in the last days — the apostle saying, But when the time was fulfilled, God sent his Son, and again, Because the time is now contracted — it appears, from the preaching of the last times too, that this grace of the Spirit pertains to the Christ of the Creator who preached it. Compare, then, the kinds in the apostle and in Isaiah. To one, he says, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom: at once Isaiah too set down the Spirit of wisdom. To another the word of knowledge: this will be the Spirit of understanding and counsel. To another faith in the same Spirit: this will be the Spirit of godliness and the fear of God. To another the gift of healings, to another of mighty works: this will be the Spirit of might. To another prophecy, to another the discerning of spirits, to another kinds of tongues, to another the interpretation of tongues: this will be the Spirit of knowledge. See the apostle, both in making the distribution of the one Spirit and in interpreting its particularity, conspiring with the prophet. I can say that the very one who fitted the unity of the various charismata to the framework of our body through many and diverse members showed the same to be Lord both of the human body and of the Holy Spirit, who would not have the merit of the charismata be in the body of the spirit, which he placed not even in the human body; who too, concerning love which is to be set before all charismata, instructed the apostle by the chief precept, which Christ also approved: You shall love the Lord with your whole heart and with all your strength and with all your soul, and your neighbour as yourself. And though this was written in the law, he recalls that the Creator would speak in other tongues and in other lips; and with this commemoration he confirms the gift of tongues, nor can he here be seen to have confirmed a strange gift by the preaching of the Creator. Likewise, in prescribing silence to women in the church, that they should not speak even for the sake of learning (for the right of prophesying he has already shown that they too have, when he imposes a veil on a woman even when prophesying), he takes from the law the authority for the subjection of the woman — which, to say it once for all, he ought not to have known except for its destruction. But that we may now withdraw from spiritual matters, the very facts ought to prove which of us rashly claims his God, and whether these things can be opposed to our side; and whether, if the Creator promised in his own Christ not yet revealed — destined, namely, for the Jews only — operations to be had in their own time, in his own Christ, and among his own people. Let Marcion, therefore, exhibit the gifts of his God: some prophets, who yet have spoken not from human sense but from the Spirit of God, who have both foretold things to come and laid bare the secrets of the heart; let him put forth some psalm, some vision, some prayer, only let it be spiritual, in ecstasy, that is, in rapture, if any interpretation of a tongue has come in; let him prove to me too that some woman among him has prophesied, of those holier women of his that he boasts of: if all these things are more readily produced by me — and surely conspiring with the rules and arrangements and disciplines of the Creator — without doubt both the Christ and the Spirit and the apostle will be my God's. He has my profession, whoever shall wish to demand it. Meanwhile the Marcionite will exhibit nothing of this kind, who already fears to pronounce whose his Christ is, not yet revealed. Just as mine is to be awaited, who has been preached from the beginning, his on that account is not, because he is not from the beginning. Better that we believe in a Christ to come than the heretic in none. How some at that time denied the resurrection of the dead must first be looked into. Surely in the same way as now too; since the resurrection of the flesh is always denied. For the soul most even of the wise, claiming it divine, promise that it is saved; and the very common folk venerate their dead with that presumption by which they trust that their souls remain. But that bodies, whether by fires at once, or by wild beasts, or even most carefully preserved, are yet abolished in time, is manifest. If, therefore, the apostle rebuts those who deny the resurrection of the flesh, surely against them he upholds what they denied, namely the resurrection of the flesh. You have the answer in compendium; the rest now out of abundance. For the very thing that it is called the resurrection of the dead requires the properties of the words to be defended. Thus a thing is not dead except what has lost the soul by whose faculty it lived. The body is what loses the soul, and by losing it becomes dead; so the term dead befits the body. Further, if the resurrection is of the dead, and the dead is nothing else than the body, the resurrection will be of the body. So too the term resurrection claims no other thing than what fell. For rising can be said even of what did not fall at all, what always lay before. But to rise again is only of what fell; for, by rising again, because it fell, it is said to rise again. For the syllable RE is always applied to repetition. We say, then, that the body falls into the earth through death, as the very fact testifies, by the law of God. For to the body it was said, You are earth, and into earth you shall go. Thus what is of earth shall go into earth. This falls, which goes into earth; this rises again, which falls. Because through a man came death, through a man too the resurrection. Here too Christ's body is shown to me in the name of man, who consists of a body, as we have often already taught. But if in Christ we are all made alive even as we are killed in Adam — since in Adam we are killed in body, so of necessity in Christ we are made alive in body. For the rest, the likeness does not hold if the making-alive in Christ does not concur in the same substance of the killing in Adam. But he interposed something further about Christ, not to be omitted on account of the present dispute. For the resurrection of the flesh will be the more proved, the more I show Christ to be of that God with whom the resurrection of the flesh is believed. When he says, For he must reign till he puts his enemies under his feet, even from this already he proclaims an avenging God, and thereupon him who promised this to Christ: Sit at my right hand, till I make your enemies the footstool of your feet: the Lord shall send forth the rod of your strength out of Sion, and you shall rule in the midst of your enemies. But it is necessary that I defend, as belonging to my sense, those scriptures which the Jews too try to take away from us. They say, then, that this psalm sang of Hezekiah, because he sat at the right hand of the temple, and God turned away and consumed his enemies; and that therefore the rest too, Before the morning-star from the womb I begot you, agrees with Hezekiah and with Hezekiah's birth. We bring forth the gospels (of whose credit we ought surely already in so great a work to have confirmed these men in something), declaring the Lord by a nocturnal nativity — so that this is, before the morning-star — and rather from the star understood, and from the testimony of the angel who by night announced to the shepherds that Christ was just then born, and from the place of the birth, for it is to an inn that men gather at night. Perhaps it was mystically done that Christ should be born by night, who was to be the light of truth in the darkness of ignorance. But neither would God have said, I begot you, except to a true son. For though of the whole people he says, I have begotten sons, yet he did not add, From the womb. But why did he add, From the womb, so vainly, as though it could be doubted of any man that he was born from the womb, unless because he wished it more curiously understood concerning Christ: From the womb I begot you, that is, from the womb alone, without the seed of man, ascribing to the flesh out of the womb what is of the spirit? This too befits him here: You are a priest for ever. But Hezekiah was neither a priest, nor for ever, even had he been one. After the order, he says, of Melchizedek. What has Hezekiah to do with Melchizedek, the priest of the Most High, and that uncircumcised, who blessed Abraham already circumcised after receiving the oblation of tithes? But the order of Melchizedek will agree with Christ, since indeed Christ is the proper and lawful high priest of God, the pontiff of an uncircumcised priesthood, then established among the nations, by whom he was rather to be received — about at some time to acknowledge both circumcision and the race of Abraham, when at last he comes, and will deem them worthy of acceptance and blessing. There is also another psalm beginning thus: God, give your judgement to the king — that is, to the Christ who is to reign — and your righteousness to the king's son — that is, to the people of Christ. For his sons are they who are reborn in him. But this psalm too will be said to sing of Solomon. Yet, since the things that befit Christ alone cannot teach that the rest too pertain not to Solomon but to Christ? He came down, he says, like rain upon the fleece, and like drops distilling upon the earth — describing his placid and imperceptible descent from heaven into flesh. But Solomon, even if he came down from somewhere, yet not like rain, because not from heaven. But I will propose simpler things. He shall have dominion, he says, from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth. This is given to Christ alone; for the rest, Solomon ruled over the one and small Judaea. All kings shall adore him. Which all, except Christ? And all nations shall serve him. To which all, except Christ? Let his name be for ever. Whose name is for ever, except Christ's? Before the sun shall his name endure. For before the sun is the Word of God, that is, Christ. And in him shall all the peoples be blessed. In Solomon no nation is blessed, but in Christ every one. What now, if this psalm shows him to be God too? And they shall call him blessed; because, Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders: blessed be the name of his glory, and the whole earth shall be filled with his glory. Against this, Solomon — I dare to say — lost even the glory he had in God, dragged through a woman even into idolatry. And so, since in the midst of the psalm this too is set, His enemies shall lick the dust, subjected, namely, to his feet, it will pertain to that on account of which I both brought in this psalm and defended it to my sense, that I might confirm both the glory of the kingdom and the subjection of the enemies according to the arrangement of the Creator, about to obtain it, to be believed of no other than the Creator's.

I know indeed in what sense they vaunt a new god — in the sense of being recognized. But I wished to strike back at that very recognition of novelty, which strikes raw minds, and at that natural charm of novelty itself, and thence now to challenge them concerning an unknown god. For of course, the one they set up as new by recognition, they show to have been unknown before recognition. Come then, back to the lines and to the contest. Persuade me that a god could have been unknown. I do indeed find altars set out to unknown gods — but that is Attic idolatry. Likewise to uncertain gods — but that is Roman superstition. Further, uncertain gods are less known, as being less certain, and therefore unknown, in so far as less certain. Which title shall we cut for Marcion's god out of the two? Both, I think — now uncertain and formerly unknown. For just as the known Creator-God made him unknown, so the certain God made him uncertain. But I will not wander off, so as to say: If God was unknown and lay hid, the region of His hiding-places overshadowed Him — new, of course, and itself unknown too, and likewise now also uncertain, certainly some immense one and undoubtedly greater than Him whom it conceals. But I will briefly set it forth and most fully follow it out, laying it down by prescription that God could not have been unknown by reason of His greatness nor ought to have been by reason of His goodness, especially being in both more pre-eminent than our Creator. But since I observe that with some it is held necessary to challenge every proof of a new and formerly unknown god to the form of the Creator, I ought first to commend that this very thing is done by us with reason, that I may the more steadfastly use the patronage of the reason set forth. Before all, indeed, what sort of thing is it that you, who acknowledge God the Creator and confess Him prior in being known, should not test another by the same methods by which you have already learned to know God in another? Every prior thing has furnished the standard for the one that follows. Two gods now are set before us, the unknown and the known. Concerning the known there is no question. It is established that He exists, since He would not have been known unless He existed. Concerning the unknown the dispute presses. For he may even not exist, since if he existed he would have been known. What therefore is sought, so long as it is unknown, is uncertain so long as it is sought, and may not exist so long as it is in uncertainty. You have a god certain, in so far as known, and uncertain, in so far as unknown. If this is so, does it seem to you to be defended by just reason, that uncertain things be proved by the standard and form and rule of certain things? For the rest, if for this case, itself still uncertain, arguments drawn from uncertain things be also applied, a series of questions will be entangled out of the treatment of those arguments — themselves likewise uncertain — endangering faith through the uncertain; and we shall go off into those undeterminable questions which the apostle does not love. But if, out of the certain and undoubted and absolute parts of the rule, they will prejudge the uncertain and doubtful and unsettled parts — plainly in those points wherein a diversity of state is found — perhaps these are not to be challenged to the form of the certain, being freed from the rest of the comparison's challenge by the diversity of their principal state. But when two gods are set forth, their principal state is common to them. For in that they are God, both are unborn, unmade, eternal. This will be the principal state. The rest let Marcion see to, if he has arranged them in diversity. For those are matters that come later in the treatment — nay, will not even be admitted, if the principal state be settled. And it is settled that both are gods; and so, since concerning their state it is settled to be common, when under it they are called to proof, if they be uncertain, they will have to be challenged to the form of those certain ones with whom they are reckoned to share the principal state, so that accordingly they may share the proof too. Hence therefore I will most steadfastly direct that he is not God who is today uncertain because formerly unknown; since He whom it is settled exists, by this very fact it is settled that He never was unknown, and therefore not uncertain.

"Yet in some way," you say, "the substance of the Creator is found capable of sin, since the breath of God, that is, the soul, sinned in man; nor can the corruption of the part fail to be referred to the original sum." Toward this the quality of the soul will have to be interpreted. First of all it must be held what the Greek scripture marked, naming a breath, not a spirit. For certain ones, translating from the Greek, not reconsidering the difference nor caring for the propriety of the words, put "spirit" for "breath," and give the heretics occasion of darkening the Spirit of God with sin, that is, God Himself. And the question has now been usurped. Understand therefore that the breath is lesser than the Spirit, even though it comes of the Spirit — like a little breeze of it, yet not the Spirit. For the breeze too is rarer than the wind; and if the breeze be of the wind, yet the wind is not the breeze. The breath may even be called the image of the Spirit. For man too is on that account the image of God, that is, of the Spirit; for God is Spirit. The breath, then, is the image of the Spirit. Further, the image will not in every respect be made equal to the truth. For it is one thing to be according to the truth, another to be the truth itself. So too the breath, since it is the image of the Spirit, cannot so match the image of God that, because the truth — that is, the Spirit, that is, God — is without sin, therefore the breath too — that is, the image — ought not to have admitted sin. In this the image will be less than the truth, and the breath inferior to the Spirit, having those lineaments of God, of course, in that the soul is immortal, in that it is free and of its own arbitration, in that for the most part it is foreknowing, in that it is rational, capable of understanding and knowledge; yet even in these it is the image, and not up to the very force of divinity, so neither up to integrity from sin — because this is yielded to God alone, that is, to the truth, and this alone is not permitted to the image. For just as the image, though it express all the lineaments of the truth, yet lacks the very force, not having motion, so too the soul, the image of the Spirit, could not express its single force, that is, the felicity of not sinning. Otherwise it would not be a soul, but a spirit; nor man, who was allotted a soul, but God. And in other respects too, not everything that shall be of God will be held to be God, that you should demand God and the breath, that is, void of sin, because the breath is of God. For neither, if you blow into a pipe, will you have made the pipe a man, though you blew of your own soul — as God too of His own Spirit. Finally, when the scripture manifestly says that God breathed into the face of man, and that man was made into a living soul, not into a quickening spirit, it separated the soul from the condition of its maker. For the work must of necessity be other than the workman, that is, inferior to the workman. For neither will the jug made by the potter be itself the potter; so neither will the breath made by the Spirit be on that account the Spirit. The very fact that the breath was named "soul" — see whether it has not passed from the condition of a breath into some lower quality. "Therefore," you say, "you have given the soul the weakness denied above." Plainly, when you exact it as equal to God, that is, immune from sin, I call it weak. But when it is challenged to the angel, I must of necessity defend it as stronger — the lord of the universe, whom angels now administer, who is even to judge angels, if he stand fast in the law of God, which at the beginning he willed not. This very thing, then, the breath of God could admit; it could, but ought not. For it had the power, by the slenderness of its substance, in that it is breath, not Spirit; but ought not, by the power of arbitration, in that it is free, not a slave — there standing by, moreover, the demonstration of not sinning, under the threat of dying, by which the slenderness of the substance should be propped, and the liberty of the sentence governed. And so the soul cannot now be seen to have sinned through that which is akin to it with God, that is, through the breath, but through that which was added to the substance, that is, through free arbitration — given indeed by God rationally, but by man driven whither he willed. But if these things are so, all the disposition of God is now cleared from the reproach of evil. For the liberty of arbitration will not throw back its own fault upon Him by whom it was given, but upon him by whom it was not administered as it ought. What evil, then, will you ascribe to the Creator? If man's sin, that will not be God's which is man's; nor is He to be held the author of the sin who is found its forbidder, nay, even its condemner. If death be the evil, death will make odious not its threatener, but its despiser, as its author. For by despising it he wrought it, which surely would not have come to be had he not despised it.

In this question, you who think that the angels of the Creator are to be set against us — as though they too acted in phantom, of seeming flesh, no doubt, with Abraham and Lot, and yet truly both met and were fed and did what had been commanded them — in the first place, you are not admitted to the examples of that God whom you are demolishing. For the better and more perfect a god you bring in, the more his examples are unfit for that god of yours, who, unless he is wholly different, will not at all be better and more perfect. Next, know that not even this is conceded to you, that the flesh in the angels was seeming, but rather of a true and solid human substance. For if it was no hard matter for that god to exhibit true sensations and acts of a seeming flesh, much more easily had he, to true sensations and acts, given a true substance of flesh — at least inasmuch as he is its proper author and craftsman. But your god, in that he has produced no flesh at all, may perhaps with reason have brought in a phantom of that whose truth he could not command. My God, however, who reformed that flesh, taken from the slime, into this quality, not yet from conjugal seed and yet flesh — was equally able, from whatever material, to have built up flesh for angels too, who also built the world out of nothing into so many and such bodies, and that by a word. And surely, if your god at some time promises men the true substance of angels — "For they shall be," he says, "as the angels" — why should not my God have fitted angels with the true substance of men, taken from wherever? For since you yourself will not answer me whence that angelic substance is taken among you, it suffices me to define this much, what is fitting for God: namely, the truth of that very thing which he set before three witnessing senses — sight, touch, hearing. It is harder for God to lie than to produce, from wherever, the truth of flesh, though not born. As for the rest, even to other heretics, who define that that flesh in the angels ought to have been born of flesh if it had truly been human, we answer with a sure reasoning, by which it both was truly human and unborn: truly human, on account of God's truthfulness as against the lie and deceit of the stranger-god, and because they could not be dealt with humanly by men except in a human substance; but unborn, because Christ alone was to be born into flesh out of flesh, that he might reform our nativity by his nativity, and so might dissolve our death too by his death, rising again in the flesh in which he was born, that he might also be able to die. Therefore he himself too, then, with the angels at Abraham's, appeared indeed in the truth of flesh, but not yet born, because not yet about to die — and as one already learning to converse among men. The more, then, the angels, neither appointed to die for us, ought not to have taken that brief loan of flesh by being born, since they were not, by dying, to lay it aside; but, taken from wherever and dismissed altogether in whatever way, they yet did not lie as to it. If the Creator makes his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire — as truly spirits as also fire — the same truly made them flesh too, that we may now recall and announce to the heretics that it is his promise to reform men at some time into angels, who once formed angels into men.

Out of so many kinds of works, why did he look especially to fishing, that from it he should take into the apostolate Simon and the sons of Zebedee (for it cannot seem a simple deed, from which an argument was to proceed), saying to Peter, trembling at the copious haul of fish, "Fear not, for henceforth thou shalt be catching men"? For by this saying he was suggesting to them an understanding of the prophecy fulfilled — that he was the one who had pronounced through Jeremiah, "Behold, I will send many fishers, and they shall fish them," men namely. In short, leaving their little boats they followed him, understanding him to be the very one who had begun to do what he had foretold. It is another matter if he affected to choose out of the guild of boatmen, intending one day to have for his apostle the skipper Marcion. We have indeed shown beforehand, against the Antitheses, that nothing avails to Marcion's design what he thinks a diversity of law and gospel — since this too was arranged by the Creator, and in short foretold in the promise of a new law and a new word and a new testament. But since he argues rather attentively, with that I-know-not-what fellow-sufferer of his and co-hateful one, concerning the cleansing of the leper, it will not irk me to meet him and first to show the force of the figurative law, which in the example of the leper not to be touched — nay, to be removed from all commerce — forbade communion with a man stained by sins; with such as these the apostle too forbids even to take food; for the brands of sins are shared, as by contagion, if anyone has mingled himself with a sinner. And so the Lord, wishing the law to be understood more deeply as signifying spiritual things through carnal — and on this account not destroying but rather building up — wishing to be acknowledged in a more pertinent sense, touched the leper, by whom even if a man could have been defiled, God surely would not be defiled, being incontaminable. Thus it will not be objected to him that he ought to have observed the law and not touched the unclean, whom the touch of the unclean was not going to defile. That this rather suits my Christ I teach thus, while I demonstrate that it does not suit yours. For if as the rival of the law he touched the leper, making nothing of the precept of the law through contempt of defilement, how could he be defiled who had no body to be defiled? For a phantom could not be defiled. He therefore who could not be defiled, as a phantom, will now be incontaminable not by divine power, but by the emptiness of a phantom; nor can he seem to have despised defilement, of which he had no matter; nor so to have destroyed the law, who had escaped defilement from the occasion of being a phantom, not from the display of power. But if Elisha, the prophet of the Creator, cleansed the single leper Naaman the Syrian out of so many Israelite lepers, neither does this make for a diversity of Christ, as though in this way the better — in that a stranger cleanses an Israelite leper whom his own lord could not cleanse — the Syrian the more easily cleansed signifying, through the nations, of those who bristled with the seven stains of capital delinquencies — idolatry, blasphemy, homicide, adultery, fornication, false testimony, fraud — the cleansing in Christ, the light of those nations. Wherefore seven times, as though through each several head, he washed in the Jordan — at once that he might sing the expiation of the whole week, and because the force and fullness of a single washing was consecrated to Christ alone, who was to make on earth, as a shortened word, so a shortened washing. For this too Marcion objects, that Elisha needed matter, employed water, and that seven times, whereas Christ, by a word alone, and that once, performed and represented the cure forthwith. As though I should not dare to claim the very word too for the substance of the Creator. Of no thing is he not the more powerful author who is the prior. It is plainly incredible that the power of the Creator should have wrought by a word the remedy of a single defect, who by a word brought forth at once so great a mass of the world. Whence is the Christ of the Creator the more discerned than from the power of his word? But for this reason another Christ, because otherwise than Elisha, because more powerful than his own servant! What do you establish, Marcion — that things are done in the same way by servants as by the very masters? Are you not afraid lest it turn to your disgrace, if you deny Christ to be the Creator's because he was more powerful than the Creator's servant — who is acknowledged greater compared to the littleness of Elisha, if indeed greater? For the cure is equal, though the operation differ. What more did your Christ furnish than my Elisha? Nay, what great thing did the word of your Christ furnish, when it furnished what the river of the Creator did? According to these, the rest too occur. For inasmuch as it pertained to the aversion of human glory, he forbade him to divulge it; but inasmuch as it pertained to the safeguarding of the law, he bade the order be fulfilled. "Go, show thyself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded." For the figurative arguments, as of the prophesied law, he still protected in their own images — which signified that a man once a sinner, presently cleansed by the word of God, ought to offer a gift to God at the temple, namely prayer and thanksgiving at the church through Christ Jesus, the catholic priest of the Father. And so he added, "That it may be to you for a testimony" — without doubt that by which he testified that he did not dissolve the law but fulfil it; by which he testified that he himself was the one announced as about to take up their diseases and infirmities. This so congruent and due interpretation of the testimony, the flatterer of his own Christ, Marcion, under pretext of mildness and gentleness, seeks to exclude. For "as good too," he says, "knowing besides that everyone freed from leprosy would carry out the solemnities of the law, for that reason he so commanded." What then? Did he persevere in goodness, that is, in the permission of the law, or not? For if he persevered as good, he will never be the destroyer of the law, nor be held to be of another god, the destruction of the law ceasing through which he is claimed for another god. If he did not persevere as good, by destroying the law afterward, then he placed a false testimony afterward among them in the cure of the leper; for he deserted goodness while he destroys the law. He is now evil, when overturner of the law, if good, when indulger of the law. But also, in that he indulged obedience to the law, he confirmed the law to be good. For no one suffers obedience to be paid to an evil thing. Therefore even so he is evil, if he indulged obedience to an evil law, and so worse, if he came as the destroyer of a good law. Accordingly, if he commanded the gift to be offered because he knew everyone freed from leprosy would so do, he could also not have commanded what he knew would be done spontaneously. In vain, then, did he come down, as though to destroy the law, when he yields to the obeyers of the law. And yet, as knowing their disposition, he ought rather to have anticipated, to avert them the more from it, if for this he had come. Why, then, did he not keep silent, that a man should obey the law by his own choice alone? — for then at least he might somewhat seem to have stood by his patience. But he even adds his own authority, magnified by the weight of testimony. Of what testimony now, except of the law asserted? Certainly it makes no difference in what way he confirmed the law — whether as good, or as superfluous, or as patient, or as inconstant — provided I drive you, Marcion, from your footing. Behold, he commanded the law to be fulfilled. In whatever way he commanded, in the same he could also have premised that opinion, "I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil." What, then, was it to you to have erased from the gospel what is safe? For you confessed that he did out of goodness what you deny he said. It is established, then, that he said it, because he also did it, and that you rather have erased the Lord's voice from the gospel than that our people have inserted it.

For from the very beginning of things their Founder was discovered together with them, since they were brought forth for this very purpose, that God might be known. For even though Moses, somewhat later, seems the first to have dedicated the God of the world in the temple of his own writings, the birthdays of His recognition are not therefore to be reckoned from the Pentateuch — since the whole pen of Moses does not establish the knowledge of the Creator, but, beginning from the very origin, recounts that He is to be reckoned from Paradise and Adam, not from Egypt and Moses. Indeed, the greater mass of the human race, possessed not even of the name of Moses, much less of his instrument, yet know the God of Moses; and even with idolatry overshadowing so great a dominion, they nevertheless set Him apart, as by His own proper name, as God and God of gods, and say, "If God grant it," and "What pleases God," and "I commend it to God." See whether they do not know Him whom they testify to be able to do all things. And this they owe to no books of Moses. The soul is before prophecy. For from the beginning the conscience of God is the dowry of the soul; the same and no other in Egyptians and in Syrians and in the people of Pontus. For they call Him the God of the Jews — the God of the soul. Do not, barbarous heretic, set Abraham before the world. Even if the Creator had been the God of one family only, yet He was not later than yours, being known even to the Pontians before him. Receive, then, from the predecessor the form: the uncertain from the certain, the unknown from the known. Never will God lie hid, never will God be wanting. He will always be understood, always be heard, even be seen, in whatever way He will. God has His witnesses — all this that we are and that we are in. Thus is proved both that God exists and that He is one, since He is not unknown, while the other still labours to be proved.

But even if you should transcribe the indictment of evil from man to the devil, as to the instigator of the sin, so as in this way too to direct the fault upon the Creator, as upon the author of the devil — He who makes His angels spirits — then, what was made by God, that is, the angel, will be His who made it; but what was not made by God, that is, the devil, that is, the accuser, it remains that he made himself such, by accusing concerning God, and that falsely: first, that God had forbidden them to eat of every tree; next, as though they would not die if they ate; thirdly, as though God had begrudged them divinity. Whence, then, came the malice of lying and of deceit toward men, and of defamation toward God? From God surely not, who instituted even the angel good out of the form of His good works. Finally, he is published as the wisest of all, before he was the devil — unless wisdom be an evil. And if you unroll the prophecy of Ezekiel, you will easily observe that that angel was as much good by institution as corrupt of his own will. For under the person of the prince of Tyre it is pronounced against the devil: "And the word of the Lord came to me, saying: Son of man, take up a lament over the prince of Tyre, and you shall say, Thus says the Lord: You are the seal of the likeness" — you who, of course, unsealed the integrity of the image and likeness — "the crown of comeliness" (this as to the most eminent of angels, as to the archangel, as to the wisest of all); "you were born in the delights of the Paradise of your God" — there, namely, where God had made the angels in the second formation of the figure of living creatures. "You were clad with the best stone: sardius, topaz, emerald, carbuncle, sapphire, jasper, ligure, agate, amethyst, chrysolite, beryl, onyx; and you filled your storehouses and your treasuries with gold. From the day you were created, when I set you with the Cherub on the holy mountain of God, you were in the midst of the fiery stones; you were without blame in your days, from the day you were created, until your hurts were found; out of the multitude of your trafficking you filled your store-rooms, and you sinned" — and the rest, which it is manifest pertain properly to the impeachment of the angel, not of that prince; in that no man was born in the Paradise of God, not even Adam himself, who was rather transferred thither; nor set with the Cherub on the holy mountain of God, that is, in the celestial sublimity, from which the Lord too testifies that Satan fell; nor abode among the fiery stones, among the gemming rays of the burning stars, whence Satan too, like lightning, was cast down. But the very author of sin was denoted under the person of a sinful man: blameless, indeed, in time past, from the day of his creation — created by God unto good, as by a good Creator of blameless creations, and adorned with all angelic glory, and set with God, as one good with the Good; but afterward transferred by himself into evil. "For from the time," he says, "that your hurts appeared" — reckoning to him those hurts whereby, namely, he hurt man cast out of obedience to God — and from that time he sinned from which he sowed the sin; and so thenceforth he plied the multitude of his trafficking, that is, of his malice, namely the census of sins, being himself no less than man instituted of free arbitration, as a spirit. For nothing nigh to Himself would God have ordained otherwise than by liberty of this kind. Yet by even predamning him He testified that he had of his own will gone out of bounds from the form of his institution, by a malice of his own desire conceived; and by measuring out a passage to his operations He carried out the reason of His own goodness, deferring by the same counsel the extinction of the devil as the restitution of man. For to the contest He gave space, that man too, by the same liberty of arbitration by which he had fallen to him, might crush the enemy — proving his own fault, not God's — and so worthily recover salvation through victory; and that the devil might be more bitterly punished by him whom he had crushed, being himself first vanquished; and that God might be found so much the more good, in upholding man, more glorious in Paradise, now about to return from death to the licence of plucking the tree of life.

Since, then, I am not admitted to the partnership of the Creator's examples — as belonging to a stranger and having their own reasons — I would have you yourself publish the counsel of your god, by which he displayed his Christ not in the truth of flesh. If he spurned that flesh as earthy and, as you say, stuffed with dung, why did he not likewise despise the likeness of it? For the image of no thing to be disdained is to be deemed worthy. The likeness follows the state. But how was he to converse among men except through an image of the human substance? Why, then, not rather through the truth, so that he might truly converse, if he had need to converse? How much more worthily would necessity have administered faith than a trick! You set up a sufficiently wretched god by this very thing, that he could not exhibit his Christ except in the effigy of a thing unworthy, and that, too, of a stranger's. For it will suit somewhat to use things unworthy if they are one's own, just as it will not be fitting to use a stranger's things, even though worthy. For why did he not come in some other, worthier substance, and above all in his own, lest he should seem to have stood in need both of what was unworthy and of what was a stranger's? If my Creator met with man both through the bush and the fire, and the same afterward through the cloud and the column, and used the bodies of the elements in representations of himself, these examples sufficiently show that God needed the preparation of neither a false nor even a true flesh. For the rest, if we look to the truth, no substance is worthy that God should put it on. Whatever he puts on, he himself makes worthy — without a lie, however. And therefore what kind of thing is it that he reckoned the truth of flesh more a disgrace than the lie of flesh? And yet he honoured that flesh by counterfeiting it. How great, then, is the flesh whose phantom was necessary to a superior god!

The paralytic too is cured, and that in a gathering, the people looking on. "For the people," says Isaiah, "shall see the loftiness of the Lord and the glory of God." What loftiness, and what glory? "Be strong, you hands let down, and you knees dissolved" — this will be the paralysis. "Be strong, and fear not." Not idly repeating "Be strong," nor in vain subjoining "Fear not," since with the reintegration of the limbs he was also promising a representation of strength: "Arise, and take up thy bed" — at once a vigour of mind too, toward not fearing those who were to say, "Who shall forgive sins but God alone?" You have, then, already both the discharged prophecy of a special medicine, and of the things which followed the medicine. Likewise recognize Christ the remitter of delinquencies in the same prophet. "For," it says, "in many he shall remit their delinquencies, and our delinquencies he himself takes away." For also in the former passage, from the person of the Lord himself: "Though your delinquencies be as scarlet, I will whiten them as snow; though as crimson, I will whiten them as wool" — in the scarlet showing the blood of the prophets, in the crimson that of the Lord, as the brighter. Micah too concerning the pardon of delinquencies: "What god is like thee, taking away iniquities and passing over injustices to the remnant of thine inheritance? And he held not his anger for a testimony, because he willed to be merciful; he will turn, and have mercy upon us; he will sink our delinquencies, and he will sink our sins into the depth of the sea." But even if nothing of the kind had been foretold concerning Christ, I should have examples of this benignity in the Creator, promising me the Father's affections in the Son too. I see the Ninevites obtain pardon of their crimes from the Creator — not to say, then too from Christ, because from the beginning he acted in the Father's name. I read too that Nathan the prophet said to David, acknowledging his delinquency in the matter of Uriah, "And the Lord has put away thy delinquency, and thou shalt not die"; likewise that king Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, guilty of idolatry and of the blood of Naboth, earned pardon under the name of penitence; that Jonathan, son of Saul, by entreaty blotted out the fault of an unsealed fast. Why should I weave again about the people itself, so often restored by indulgence of delinquencies? — by that god, namely, who prefers mercy to sacrifice, and the penitence of the sinner to his death. It is prior, then, that you deny that the Creator ever indulged delinquencies; the consequence is that you show that he foretold no such thing concerning his Christ either; and so you will prove this new benignity of the new Christ, if you have proved it neither equal to the Creator's nor foretold by the Creator. But whether to remit sins can belong to him who is denied to retain them, and whether it belongs to him to absolve whose it is not also to condemn, and whether it suits one to forgive against whom nothing has been committed — having engaged elsewhere already, we preferred to admonish rather than to discuss. Concerning "Son of man" our objection is twofold: that Christ could not lie, so as to pronounce himself Son of man if he were not truly so; nor be constituted Son of man who was not born of a man, either father or mother; and so it must be discussed of what man he ought to be taken as son, of father or of mother. If he is of God the Father, surely he is not of man; if not also of man, it remains that he is of a man for mother; if of a man, it now appears that he is of a virgin. For to whom a man is not given as father, neither will a husband be reckoned to his mother; and to whose mother a husband is not reckoned, she is a virgin. For the rest, two fathers will now be reckoned, God and man, if the mother be not a virgin. For she will have a husband, so as not to be a virgin, and by having a husband she will make two fathers, God and man, for him who should be the son both of God and of man. Such a nativity, if at all, the fables ascribe to Castor or Hercules. If these things are thus distinguished — that is, if he is the son of man from his mother because he is not from a father, but from a virgin mother because not from a human father — this will be the Christ of Isaiah, whom he proclaims a virgin should conceive. By what reasoning, then, you can admit "Son of man," Marcion, I cannot see all around. If of a human father, you deny him the Son of God; if of God too, you make Christ a Hercules out of the fable; if only of a human mother, you grant me mine; if neither of a human father, then he is the son of no man, and of necessity he must have admitted a lie, who said himself to be what he was not. One thing can come to the aid of your straits: if you dare either to surname even your god, the Father of Christ, a man too — which Valentinus did of his Aeon — or to deny the virgin a human being, which not even Valentinus did. What now, if by the very title of Son of man Christ is reckoned in Daniel? Does it not suffice for proof of the prophetic Christ? For when he calls himself that which was proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator, without doubt he offers himself to be understood as the very one concerning whom it was proclaimed. A community of names may, if at all, seem simple — and yet we maintain that he ought to be called neither Christ nor Jesus, holding the condition of diversity. But the appellation which is "Son of man," in so far as it comes by accident, by so much is it difficult that it too should concur over and above the community of name. For it is from a proper accident — especially since the same cause does not agree by which it comes into community. And indeed if Marcion's Christ too were said to be born of a man, then he too would take up a community of appellation, and there would be two sons of man, just as also two Christs and two Jesuses. Therefore, since the appellation is proper to him in whom it has its cause, if it be claimed also for another in whom there is a community of the name, not also of the appellation — the community of name too now becomes suspect in him for whom a community of appellation is claimed without a cause; and it follows that he is believed one and the same who is found more capable both of the name and of the appellation, while the other is excluded who has no community of appellation, lacking the cause. Nor will another be more capable of both than he who is prior, and both obtained the name of Christ and the appellation of Son of man — Jesus, namely, the Creator's. This was the one seen by the Babylonian king in the furnace with his martyrs, the fourth, as the Son of man. The same was revealed directly to Daniel himself, the Son of man coming with the clouds of heaven, a judge, as the Scripture also demonstrates. This I have said could have sufficed concerning the prophetic naming touching the Son of man. But the Scripture confers more upon me — by the interpretation, namely, of the Lord himself. For when the Jews, looking only at his manhood, and not yet certain of his Godhead, in that he was the Son of God too, rightly debated that a man could not remit delinquencies, but God alone — why did he not, according to their intention, answer them of a man, that he had power to remit delinquencies, since by naming Son of man he would name a man? — unless because by the very appellation of Son of man, from the instrument of Daniel, he willed to strike them back, that he might show a God and a man who remits delinquencies; namely that sole Son of man in the prophecy of Daniel, who obtained the power of judging, and through it surely of remitting delinquencies too (for he who judges, also absolves) — so that, this scandal being discussed through the recollection of Scripture, they might the more easily acknowledge him to be the very Son of man from the very remission of sins. In short, nowhere yet had he professed himself the Son of man before that passage, the first in which he first remitted sins, that is, in which he first judged, while he absolved. To these, whatever the opposite party shall have argued, consider what it is. For of necessity it tends to that madness, that it both defends the Son of man, lest it make him a liar, and denies that he was born of man, lest it grant the Son of a virgin. But if both divine authority and the nature of things and common wisdom do not admit the heretical insanity, there is occasion here too of interposing most briefly concerning the substance of the body, against the phantoms of Marcion. If he is born of a man, as Son of man, his body is from a body. Plainly you may more easily find a man born without a heart or brain, like Marcion himself, than without a body, like Marcion's Christ. And so look into the heart, or brain, of the man of Pontus.

Let us return now to the resurrection, which we have indeed satisfied elsewhere too in a proper volume, resisting all heretics; but here too we are not wanting, on account of those who do not know that little work. What, he says, shall they do who are baptised for the dead, if the dead rise not? See to it, this institution. The Kalends of February, perchance, will answer to that of asking for the dead. Do not, then, straightway brand the apostle as a new author or confirmer of it, since it was the more to establish the resurrection of the flesh, in that those who were vainly baptised for the dead did this in faith of the resurrection. We have him somewhere as the definer of one baptism. Therefore to be baptised for the dead too is to be baptised for bodies; for we have shown the dead to be the body. What shall they do who are baptised for bodies, if bodies rise not? And so rightly do we fix this step, that the apostle introduced his second disputation likewise concerning the body. But some will say, How do the dead rise? and with what body do they come? For the resurrection being defended, which was denied, it was consequent to treat of the quality of the body, which was not seen. But of that it is fitting to engage with others. For Marcion, in no wise admitting the resurrection of the flesh, and promising salvation to the soul alone, makes a question not of quality but of substance. But even from these things he is most manifestly hedged in, which the apostle treats concerning the quality of the body, on account of those who say, How shall the dead rise? and with what body do they come? For he has now preached that the body shall rise, if he treated of the body's quality. In short, if he proposes examples of a grain of wheat or of any such thing, or to which God shall give a body as he will; if he says that to each of the seeds there is its own body, so that there is one flesh of men, another of cattle and birds, and bodies celestial and terrestrial, and one glory of the sun, another of the moon, another of the stars — does he not hold out a carnal and corporeal resurrection, which he commends by carnal and corporeal examples? does he not also pledge it from that God whose are the examples too? So too the resurrection, he says. How? Just as the grain is sown a body, it rises a body. He called the sowing, then, the dissolution of the body into the earth, because it is sown in corruption, in dishonour, in weakness. That same order which is in the dissolution is here too in the resurrection of the body, namely, as in the grain. For the rest, if you take away from the resurrection the body which you gave to the dissolution, where will the difference of the outcome stand? Likewise too, if it is sown an animal body, it rises a spiritual body. And if the soul or the spirit has some proper body, so that the animal body can be seen to signify the soul, and the spiritual body the spirit, not on that account does he say that the soul shall be spirit in the resurrection, but the body, which, born with the soul and living through the soul, takes the name of animal, shall be spiritual, while it rises through the spirit into eternity. In short, if not the soul but the flesh is sown in corruption, while it is dissolved into the earth, then no longer will the soul be the animal body, but the flesh which was the animal body, since out of the animal is made the spiritual, as he also says below, Not first that which is spiritual. For to this end he forestructures even concerning Christ himself: The first man Adam was made into a living soul, the last Adam into a quickening spirit; though the most foolish heretic would not have it so, for he set down Lord instead of last Adam, fearing, namely, lest, if he had Lord as the last Adam, we should defend Christ also of the same one in the last Adam whose he is in the first. But the falsehood shines out. For why first Adam, except because there is also a last Adam? They have no order between them except things equal and of the same name or substance or author. For though there can in diverse things too be one first, another last, yet of one author. For the rest, if the author too is another, even he himself can indeed be called last. Yet what he introduced is first; but last only if it be equal to the first. But it is not equal to the first, because it is not of the same author. In the same way too he is convicted in the name of man. The first man, he says, of the dust earthy, the second Lord from heaven. Why second, if not a man, which the first too is? Or is the first too Lord, if the second is? But it is enough if in the gospel he applies to Christ Son of man and man, and in man Adam he cannot deny him. The sequel too presses him. For when the apostle says, As is the earthy — man, namely — such are the earthy also — men, surely — then also, As is the heavenly — man — such are the heavenly also — men. For he could not but have set heavenly men over against earthy men, that he might the more studiously distinguish their state and hope in the fellowship of the appellation. For he calls them earthy and heavenly men in state and hope, yet on a par, who according to their outcome are reckoned either in Adam or in Christ. And therefore now, to the exhortation of heavenly hope, As we have borne, he says, the image of the earthy, let us bear also the image of the heavenly — referring it not to any substance of the resurrection, but to the discipline of the present time. For, Let us bear, he says, not, We shall bear — preceptively, not promissively — wishing that we, just as he himself walked, so should walk, and depart from the image of the earthy, that is, the old man, which is the carnal working. In short, what does he subjoin? For this I say, brethren, that flesh and blood shall not possess the kingdom of God — the works, namely, of flesh and blood, by which too, writing to the Galatians, he took away the kingdom of God; being wont elsewhere too to put the substance for the works of the substance, as when he says that those who are in the flesh cannot please God. For when shall we be able to please God, except while we are in this flesh? Of working there is, I think, no other time. But if, though placed in the flesh, we flee the works of the flesh, then we shall not be in the flesh, while we are not in the substance of the flesh, but in the fault of it. But if under the name of flesh we are bidden to lay aside the works, not the substance, of the flesh, then to the works of the flesh, not to the substance of the flesh, under the name of flesh, is the kingdom of God denied. For that is not condemned in which evil is done, but that which is done. To give poison is a crime, yet the cup in which it is given is not guilty. So too the body is the vessel of carnal works, but the soul is what, being in it, tempers the poison of some evil deed. But what manner of thing is it that, if the soul, the authoress of the works of the flesh, shall earn the kingdom of God through the expiation of those things which it committed in the body, the body — a mere minister — should remain in damnation? Shall the cup be punished, the poisoner being absolved? And yet we do not at all defend the kingdom of God for the flesh, but the resurrection of its own substance, as the door of the kingdom, by which entrance is made. For the rest, the resurrection is one thing, the kingdom another. For first the resurrection, then the kingdom. We say, then, that the flesh rises, but, changed, obtains the kingdom. For the dead shall rise incorrupt — those, namely, who had been corrupt, their bodies fallen into dissolution. And we shall be changed, in a moment, in the momentary motion of an eye. For this corruptible — holding, surely, his own flesh, the apostle was saying — must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality, that the substance, namely, may be made fit for the kingdom of God. For we shall be as the angels. This will be the transformation of the flesh, but of the flesh raised up. Or if there shall be none, how shall it put on incorruption and immortality? Made another, then, through transformation, it shall then obtain the kingdom of God — no longer flesh nor blood, but what God shall have given to it for a body. And therefore rightly the apostle: Flesh and blood shall not obtain the kingdom of God — ascribing it to the transformation which comes after the resurrection. But if then shall come to pass the word that is written with the Creator, Where, death, is your victory or your contention? Where, death, is your sting? (and this word is the Creator's through the prophet), his too will be the thing — that is, the kingdom — whose word shall come to pass in the kingdom. Nor does he give thanks to another God, in that he received for us, surely, victory over death and triumph.

"And rightly so," they say. "For who is not as well known to his own as to strangers?" No one. I hold this saying too. For what sort of thing is it that anything should be a stranger to God, to whom nothing would be a stranger, if there were any such — since this is God's property, that all things be His and all things pertain to Him? — or else He would at once hear from us, "What then has He to do with strangers?" — which He shall hear more fully in its place. But for now it is enough that none is proved of whom nothing is proved. For as the Creator is from this very fact God, and undoubted God, because all things are His and nothing is a stranger to Him, so the other is for that reason not God, because all things are not his and therefore are even strangers to him. In fine, if the universe is the Creator's, I see no room left for another god. All things are full and occupied by their own Author. If any room of any space lies vacant for divinity among the creatures, plainly it will lie vacant for a false one. Truth lies open by the falsehood. Why does not so great a force of idols somewhere admit Marcion's god? Therefore this too I demand of the form of the Creator: that a god ought to be known from the works of some proper world and man and age of his own — since even the error of the world has on this very account presumed gods, whom it sometimes confesses to have been men, because something was seen to have been provided by each one for the uses and conveniences of life. So this too, from the form of God, has been believed to be divine: to institute or to demonstrate what is fit and necessary for human affairs. So far did authority pass over to false divinity from the source whence it had preceded in the true. At least one little pea Marcion's god ought to have brought forth as his own, that he might be proclaimed as some new Triptolemus. Or else show a reason worthy of God why he made nothing, if he exists; for he would have made something, if he had existed — by that prejudgement, of course, by which our God too is not otherwise manifest to exist than because He made this whole. For once the prescription will stand, that they cannot both confess the Creator to be God and have the one they wish believed equally a god, without proving him to the form of Him whom both they and all men hold God; so that, since by this very fact no one doubts the Creator to be God because He made this whole, by this very fact no one ought to believe him too God who made nothing — unless perchance a reason be brought forward. This must seem twofold: that either he was unwilling to make anything, or unable. A third falls away. But to have been unable is unworthy of God. Whether to have been unwilling is worthy, I wish to inquire. Tell me, Marcion: did your god wish to be known at some time or other, or not? For with no other purpose did he descend and preach and suffer and rise again, than to be known. And without doubt, if he was known, he wished it. For nothing would have been done concerning him, unless he had wished it. Why then did he so greatly procure knowledge of himself, that he was exhibited in the dishonour of the flesh — and that the greater, if a false flesh? For this is the more disgraceful, if he even lied the substance of a body, who also admitted upon himself the Creator's curse by hanging on a tree. How much more honourably might he have prepared the knowledge of himself beforehand by some signs of his own contriving — especially as he had to be known against Him from whose works he had not been known from the beginning. For what sort of thing is it that the Creator, who (as the Marcionites would have it) was ignorant that there was another god above himself, who even with an oath asserted himself alone, should have armed the knowledge of himself with such great works, which he might not have so cared for, according to the presumption of his own singularity; but that the loftier one, knowing the inferior god so equipped, should have provided for himself no apparatus of being recognized? — when he ought to have made even more remarkable and more magnificent works, that the god too might be known from his works, after the manner of the Creator, and from the more honourable works might be the more powerful and the more noble than the Creator.

Therefore, up to man's sin, God was from the beginning only good; from then on, judge and severe, and — what the Marcionites will have — cruel. At once the woman is condemned to bring forth in pains and to serve her husband — she who before, without any saddening, had heard of the increase of the race through blessing: "Increase only, and multiply"; she who had been destined as a help to the male, not for servitude. At once the earth too is cursed — but before blessed. At once thistles and thorns — but before hay and herbs and the fruitful things of the trees. At once sweat and the labour of bread — but before, sustenance free out of every tree, and food secure. From then on man unto the earth — but before, of the earth; from then on unto death — but before, unto life; from then on in skin garments — but before, naked without scruple. Thus the prior goodness of God is according to nature, the later severity according to cause. The one inborn, the other accidental; the one His own, the other applied; the one put forth, the other brought to bear. For neither ought nature to have kept goodness unwrought, nor cause to have let severity escape dissembled. The one God showed to Himself, the other to the matter in hand. Begin now even to arraign the state of judge as akin to evil — you who therefore dreamed up another god, good only, because you cannot a judge; although Him too we have shown to be a judge. Or if not a judge, then certainly a perverse and vain constitutor of a discipline that is not to be vindicated, that is, not judged. But you do not reprobate God as judge, you who prove a god not a judge. Without doubt you will have to accuse justice itself, which furnishes the judge — or even reckon it among the kinds of evil, that is, ascribe injustice among the titles of goodness. For now justice will be an evil, if injustice be a good. Further, when you are forced to pronounce injustice among the worst of things, by the same yoke you are pressed to reckon justice among the best. For nothing is a rival of evil that is not good, just as nothing is a rival of good that is not evil. Therefore, by as much as injustice is evil, by so much is justice good. Nor is goodness only a kind, but the very guardianship of goodness, to be reckoned; because goodness, unless it be governed by justice so as to be just, will not be goodness, if it be unjust. For nothing is good that is unjust; but all is good that is just.

All these sleights-of-hand about a seeming corpulence in Christ Marcion took up with this intent: that the nativity of Christ might not, from the testimony of a human substance, also be defended, and so Christ be claimed for the Creator, as being announced one capable of being born and therefore fleshly. Most foolish here too is the man of Pontus; as though flesh in God should not more easily be believed unborn than false — especially when this very faith is built up beforehand by the angels of the Creator, who conversed in true flesh, yet not born. For that Philumene too rather persuaded Apelles and the rest of Marcion's deserters that Christ did indeed, in good faith, carry about flesh, but of no nativity — having, namely, borrowed it from the elements. But if Marcion was afraid that faith in flesh would bring in faith in nativity too, then doubtless one who appeared a man was at any rate believed born. For a certain woman had cried out, "Blessed is the womb that bore thee, and the breasts that thou hast sucked." And how were his mother and his brothers said to stand outside? But we shall see about these chapters in their place. Certainly, since he himself too proclaimed himself the son of man, he was professing himself born. Now, that I may put off all these things to the examination of the gospel — yet, as I laid down above, if in every way he had to be believed born who appeared a man, to no purpose did he think that faith in nativity should be cancelled by a design of imaginary flesh. For what did it profit that what was held as true was not truly so, both flesh and nativity? Human opinion may see to that: already you honour your god with the title of deceit, if he knew himself to be other than what he had made men think. Even then you might have fitted him also with a seeming nativity, so as not to have dashed against this question too. For even little women sometimes seem to themselves pregnant, swollen either by a tribute of blood or by some ailment. And surely he ought to have run through the whole scene of a phantom, so as not to have danced past the origin of the flesh, having acted the person of the substance itself. Plainly you refused the lie of nativity: for you have brought forth the very flesh as true. A most shameful thing, no doubt, even a true nativity for God! Come now, harangue against those most holy and reverend works of nature, inveigh against the whole of what you are: destroy the origin of flesh and soul; call the womb a sewer, the workshop, that is, for producing so great an animal, namely man; pursue with abuse the unclean and shameful torments of childbirth, and then the foul, anxious, ludicrous issues of the delivery itself. And yet, when you have destroyed all these things, to confirm them as unworthy of God, nativity will be no more unworthy than death, infancy than the cross, nature than punishment, the flesh than condemnation. If Christ truly suffered these things, it was a smaller thing to be born. If he suffered them in a lie, as a phantom, he could also have been born in a lie. These chief arguments of Marcion, by which he makes another Christ, we have, I think, sufficiently shown not to stand at all, while we teach that truth befits God rather than the lie of that state in which he displayed his Christ. If it was truth, it was flesh; if it was flesh, he was born. For those things which this heresy assaults are confirmed when those by which it assaults are destroyed. And so, if he is to be held fleshly because born, and born because fleshly, because he was no phantom, he himself will have to be acknowledged who was announced by the prophets of the Creator as to come in flesh and from nativity — the Christ of the Creator, that is.

He brings forward into argument the publican chosen by the Lord, as though chosen by an adversary of the law, a stranger to the law and profane to Judaism. It escaped him even concerning Peter, a man of the law, and yet not only chosen but having attained the testimony of an acknowledgement bestowed by the Father. Nowhere had he read that Christ was proclaimed the light and hope and expectation of the nations. And yet he rather approved the Jews by saying that a physician is not necessary for the sound, but for the sick. For if he wished the ethnics and publicans, whom he chose, to be understood as the sick, he was confirming the Jews to be sound, for whom he denied a physician necessary. If this is so, ill did he come down to destroy the law, as if to remedy bad health, in which those who walked were in good health, for whom a physician was not necessary. But what kind of thing is it that he should set forth the likeness of a physician and not fulfil it? For just as no one applies a physician to the sound, so neither to men so estranged as a man is from the god of Marcion, having both his author and his protector, and from him rather Christ for a physician. The likeness prejudges this — that a physician is rather furnished by him to whom belong those who languish. But whence did John too come into the midst? Suddenly Christ, suddenly John too. Such are all things with Marcion, which have their own and full order with the Creator. But of John the rest elsewhere. For we must answer each several joint as it presents itself. Now I will maintain this, to demonstrate that both John suits Christ and Christ John — both surely the prophet of the Creator, since the Christ of the Creator — and so let the heretic blush, having frustrated in vain the order of John. For if John had administered nothing at all — the crier, according to Isaiah, in the wilderness and the preparer of the Lord's ways through the denunciation and the laudation of penitence — if he had not also dipped him among the rest, no one would have provoked the disciples of Christ, eating and drinking, to the form of the disciples of John, assiduously fasting and praying; because, if any diversity stood between Christ and John and the flock of each, there would be no force in the comparison, the intention of the challenge would be void. For no one would marvel and no one would be tormented, if the preachings of a diverse and rival divinity did not agree with one another in their disciplines too, not first agreeing about the authorities of their disciplines. So far was Christ John's and John Christ's — both the Creator's, and both of the law and the prophets, preachers and masters. But Christ would also have rejected John's discipline, as of another god, and would have defended the disciples, as rightly walking otherwise — initiated, namely, into another and contrary divinity. But as it is, humbly rendering the reason that the sons of the bridegroom could not fast so long as the bridegroom was with them, but afterward promising that they would fast when the bridegroom should be taken from them, he neither defended the disciples but rather excused them, as reprehended not without reason, nor rejected John's discipline, but rather conceded it — assigning it to John's time, as destining it for his own time — though he would otherwise have rejected it and defended its rivals, had not what already was not already been his own. I hold my Christ even in the name of bridegroom, concerning whom the psalm: "He, like a bridegroom going forth from his chamber: from the height of heaven his going forth, and his return to the very height of it." Who also, through Isaiah, rejoicing toward the Father, says, "Let my soul exult in the Lord, for he has clothed me with the garment of salvation, and with the tunic of joyfulness as a bridegroom; he has set a mitre about me as about a bride."
