For in himself he reckons the Church too, concerning which the same spirit to him: "And thou shalt set them all about thee as the ornament of a bride." This bride Christ fetches for himself, even through Solomon, from the calling of the nations. Indeed you have read, "Come, bride, from Lebanon" — the mention of mount Lebanon being elegantly thrown in, which by the word for frankincense is among the Greeks; for out of idolatry he was espousing the Church to himself. Deny now that you are most insane, Marcion. Behold, you assail the law of your own god too. He does not join marriages, the joined he does not admit; he dips no one but the celibate or the eunuch; he reserves baptism for death or for divorce. Why, then, do you make his Christ a bridegroom? This is the name of him who joined male and female, not of him who separated. You have erred also in that pronouncement of the Lord by which he seems to discern new and old. You have been puffed up with the old skins and made brainless with the new wine, and so to the old, that is, the former gospel, you have sewed a patch of heretical novelty. In which point another Creator — I would learn — when through Jeremiah he commanded, "Make for yourselves a new freshness," did he not turn them away from the old? When through Isaiah he declares, "The old things have passed, and behold the new which I make," did he not convert them to the new? Long ago we laid it down that this destination of the former things, promised rather by the Creator, is exhibited by Christ, under the authority of one and the same god, whose are both the old and the new. For neither does he commit new wine into old skins who has not also had old skins, and no one puts a new addition upon an old garment but he to whom an old garment too is not wanting. He does not do a thing, if it is not to be done, who has whence to do it, if it were to be done. And so if in this he was directing the likeness, to show that he separated the novelty of the gospel from the oldness of the law, he was demonstrating that even that which he separated was his own, and was not to be marked off by the separation of things alien — because no one adds his own things to alien, that he may be able to separate them from the alien. Separation takes place through a conjunction from which it is made. Thus the things which he separated he also showed to have been in one, just as they would have been, had he not separated. And yet even so we grant this separation through reformation, through amplitude, through advance — just as fruit is separated from the seed, when it is yet fruit from the seed: so the gospel too is separated from the law, while it is brought forward out of the law, other than it, but not alien — diverse, but not contrary. Nor is the form of speech in Christ new. When he sets forth likenesses, when he refutes questions, it comes from the seventy-seventh psalm: "I will open," it says, "my mouth in a parable" — that is, a likeness; "I will utter problems" — that is, I will expound questions. If you had wished to prove him a man of another nation, surely you would prove it from a property of speech.

ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE CORINTHIANS. If the word God has become common through the fault of human error, in that many are called and believed gods in the world, yet the blessed God of our Lord Jesus Christ will be understood as no other than the Creator, who both blessed the universe (you have Genesis) and is blessed by the universe (you have Daniel). Likewise, if a father can be called the father of no God more than of the Creator, yet the Father of mercies will be the same who has been called merciful and compassionate and most rich in mercy. You have in Jonah the very example of mercy, which he furnished to the Ninevites entreating him; easy to be bent too by Hezekiah's weeping, and by Ahab, the husband of Jezebel, beseeching that the blood of Naboth be forgiven, and by David acknowledging his sin to indulge at once — preferring, namely, the repentance of the sinner to his death, out of the affection of mercy. If the God of Marcion has produced or pronounced anything of the kind, I will acknowledge the Father of mercies. But if from the time he was revealed he ascribes this title to him, as though from then he were the Father of mercies, from when he set about to free mankind — but we too from that time deny him, from which he is said to be revealed. He cannot, then, ascribe anything to him whom he then shows when he ascribes anything to him. For if he were first established to be, then something could be ascribed to him too. For what is ascribed is an accident, but accidents are preceded by the showing of the very thing to which they happen — especially when what is ascribed to him who has not first been shown is already another's. He will the more be denied to be, the more that by which he is affirmed to be is of him who has already been shown. So too the new testament will be of no other than him who promised it; and if not the letter, yet his spirit; this will be the newness. In short, he who had cut the letter on tablets of stone, the same had also pronounced concerning the spirit, I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh. And if the letter kills, but the spirit makes alive, both are his who says, I will kill and I will make alive, I will smite and I will heal. We have of old claimed the twofold power of the Creator, both of judge and of good: of the letter killing through the law, and of the spirit making alive through the gospel. Things which, though diverse, were first reviewed with one — these cannot make two gods. He commemorates too of the veil of Moses, by which he covered his face, incontemplable to the sons of Israel. If for this reason, that he might defend the greater splendour of the new testament, which abides in glory, than of the old, which had to be made void, this too suits my faith, which prefers the gospel to the law; and see whether it suits mine the more. For there will be a setting of something over a thing where there was also that over which it is set. But when he says, But the senses of the world were blunted — surely not of the Creator, but of the people, who is in the world. For of Israel he says, To this day that same veil is upon their heart. He shows that the veil of the face in Moses was a figure of the veil of the heart in the people, because not even now is Moses perceived among them by the heart, just as not then by the face. What is it, then, that is still veiled in Moses which pertains to Paul, if the Creator's Christ preached by Moses has not yet come? how are the hearts of the Jews still noted as covered and veiled, the preachings of Moses concerning Christ — in whom they ought to understand him — not yet exhibited? What has it to do with an apostle of another Christ, that the Jews did not understand the sacraments of their own God — except because the veil of their heart pertained to the blindness by which they had not perceived the Christ of Moses? In short, what follows, But when it shall be turned to God, the veil shall be taken away, this he says properly of the Jew, with whom is the veil of Moses, who, when he shall have passed into the faith of Christ, understands that Moses preached of Christ. But how shall the veil of the Creator be taken away in the Christ of another God, whose sacraments the Creator could not have veiled — unknown things, namely, of one unknown? He says, then, that we now, with open face — namely of the heart, which is veiled in the Jews — beholding Christ, are transfigured into the same image from glory, by which, namely, Moses too was transfigured from the glory of the Lord, into glory. Thus, setting forth the bodily illumination of Moses from his meeting with the Lord, and the bodily veil from the weakness of the people, and superinducing the spiritual revelation and spiritual splendour in Christ — as from the Lord, he says, of the spirits — he testifies that the whole order of Moses was a figure of a Christ ignored among the Jews, but acknowledged among us. We know that certain senses can suffer ambiguity from the sound of the pronunciation or the mode of the punctuation, when a doubleness of these intervenes. This Marcion seized, reading thus: In whom the God of this age — so as, by showing the Creator the God of this age, to suggest another God of another age. We, on the contrary, say it must be punctuated thus: In whom God, then: has blinded the minds of the unbelievers of this age; In whom, that is, in the unbelieving Jews, in whom the gospel was covered to some still under the veil of Moses. For God had threatened them — loving him with their lips, but in heart standing far off from him: With the ear you shall hear and not hear, with the eyes you shall see and not see; and, Unless you believe, neither shall you understand; and, I will take away the wisdom of the wise and make void the prudence of the prudent. But these things he was not threatening about hiding the gospel of an unknown God. So, even if he is the God of this age, yet of the unbelievers of this age he blinds the heart, because they did not of their own accord recognise his Christ, to be understood from the scriptures. And having treated thus far what is set in the ambiguity of punctuation, lest it profit the adversary — content with my victory, I can even pass over this whole contention altogether. For a simpler answer will be at hand: to interpret the lord of this age as the devil, who said, as the prophet reports, I will be like the Most High, I will set my throne in the clouds — as indeed the whole superstition of this age is enslaved to him who blinds the hearts of the unbelievers, and chiefly of the apostate Marcion. In short, he did not see the close of the sense meeting him: For God, who said out of darkness let light shine, has shone in our hearts, unto the illumination of the knowledge of himself in the person of Christ. Who said, Let there be light? And of the illumination of the world, who said to Christ, I have set you for a light of the nations — of those sitting, namely, in darkness and in the shadow of death? To whom the Spirit answers in the psalm, out of foresight of the future. The light of your countenance, he says, is signed upon us, Lord. But the countenance of God is Christ the Lord. Whence also the apostle above, Who is, he says, the image of God. Therefore, if Christ is the person of the Creator who says, Let there be light, then both Christ and the apostles and the gospel and the veil and Moses and the whole series, according to the testimony of the close, are of the Creator, the God of this age — certainly not of him who never said, Let there be light. I pass over here too about another epistle, which we have inscribed To the Ephesians, but the heretics To the Laodiceans. For he says that the nations should remember that at that time, when they were without Christ, aliens from Israel, without converse and testaments and the hope of promise, they were even without God — surely in the world, even if of the Creator. Therefore, if he said the nations were without God, but their God is the devil, not the Creator, it appears that by the lord of this age must be understood him whom the nations received in place of God, not the Creator, whom they do not know. But what manner of thing is it that the treasure should not be held to be of the same one whose are also the vessels in which it is — in our earthen vessels? For if it is the glory of God that so great a treasure should be held in earthen vessels, and the earthen vessels are the Creator's, then both the glory is the Creator's, whose vessels savour of the eminence of the power of God, and the very power; because for this reason it was committed into earthen vessels, that its eminence might be proved. For the rest, it will no longer be the glory of another God, and therefore not even his power, but rather a disgrace and weakness, whose eminence earthen and indeed alien vessels have received. But if these are the earthen vessels in which he says we suffer so much, in which too we carry about the mortification of God, the God is ungrateful and unjust enough, if he is not also to raise up this substance in which, for his faith, so much is endured, in which too the death of Christ is carried about, in which too the eminence of power is consecrated. For he proposes, That the life of Christ too may be made manifest in our body — namely, as his death too is carried about in the body. Of what life of Christ, then, does he speak? that by which we now live in him? And how in the sequel does he exhort, not to things visible nor temporal, but to things invisible and eternal — that is, not to things present, but to things future? But if he speaks of the future life of Christ, saying that it will appear in the body, he plainly preached the resurrection of the flesh — saying indeed that our outward man is corrupted, and not as though by eternal destruction after death, but by labours and discomforts, of which he sent before, adding, And we shall not fail. For in saying too that our inward man is renewed from day to day, here he shows both: both the corruption of the body from the vexation of temptations, and the renewal of the mind from the contemplation of the promises.

For the rest, even if we could confess that he exists, we should have to argue that he exists to no purpose. For he would be to no purpose who had no thing of his own — since every thing is a cause, namely that there be someone whose the thing is. Further, in so far as nothing ought to exist without cause, that is, without a thing — because if it exists without cause, it is just as if it did not exist, not having, by reason of having no thing, the cause of itself — in so far I shall more worthily believe God not to exist than to exist without cause. For he is without cause who, by not having a thing, has no cause. But God ought not to exist without cause, that is, without a thing. So as often as I show him to exist without cause, as though he existed, this I establish: that he does not exist; because if he had existed, he would by no means have existed without cause. So too I say that he captures from man even faith itself without cause — man being wont to believe God otherwise, namely God formed from the authority of His works — since he provided nothing of the kind whereby man might learn God. For even though very many believe in him, they do not straightway believe with reason, not having the pledge of God, His works worthy of God. So under this head of cessation and defect of works he is akin to impudence and malignity: to impudence, whereby he captures a faith not owed to him, for the preparing of which he provided nothing; to malignity, whereby he has made many guilty of unbelief by procuring nothing for faith.

So, if there is a fellowship and conspiracy of goodness and justice, you cannot guard against their separation. With what face will you constitute the diversity of two gods, in the separation reckoning apart a good god and apart a just god? There the good stands fast where also the just. From the beginning, finally, the Creator was as good as just. Both went forth alike. His goodness wrought the world, His justice modulated it — which even then judged that the world must be made of good things, because it judged with the counsel of goodness. It is the work of justice that a separation was pronounced between light and darkness, between day and night, between heaven and earth, between the upper water and the lower, between the gathering of the sea and the mass of the dry land, between the greater luminaries and the lesser, the diurnal and the nocturnal, between male and female, between the tree of the knowledge of death and of life, between the world and Paradise, between the water-born and the earth-born animals. All things, as goodness conceived them, so justice distinguished. This whole was disposed and ordered by a judgment. Every situation, condition of the elements, every effect, motion, state, rising, setting of each, are the judgments of the Creator. Do not think Him therefore to be defined a judge from the time evil began, and so cast a shadow over justice from the cause of evil. For by these means we have shown that it came forth together with the goodness that authored all things, so that it too is to be reckoned inborn in God and natural and not come from outside, being found in the Lord the arbitress of His works.

Appeal now, as you are wont, to that comparison of Christ in Isaiah, contending that it suits in nothing. For first, you say, the Christ of Isaiah is to be called Emmanuel; next, to take the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. But this one who came was neither published under such a name nor performed any warlike deed. But I will admonish you to recognize the coherence too of both passages. For there is subjoined also the interpretation of Emmanuel: "God with us"; that you may regard not only the sound of the name but also the sense. For the sound, which is Emmanuel, in Hebrew, belongs to its own nation; but its sense, which is "God with us," from the interpretation is common to all. Inquire, then, whether this utterance, "God with us," which is Emmanuel, has, ever since Christ shone forth, been bandied about in Christ. And I think you will not deny it, seeing that you yourself too say, "It is called God with us," that is, Emmanuel. Or if you are so empty that, because among you it is called "God with us," not Emmanuel, you on that account refuse that he has come whose own it is to be called Emmanuel — as though this were not also "God with us" — you will find among the Hebrew Christians, nay among the Marcionites too, that they name Emmanuel when they wish to say "God with us"; just as every nation, with whatever sound it has said "God with us," has pronounced Emmanuel in sense, cancelling the sound. But if Emmanuel is "God with us," and "God with us" is Christ, who is also in us — for as many of you as have been dipped into Christ have put on Christ — then Christ is as properly his in the signification of the name, which is "God with us," as in the sound of the name, which is Emmanuel. And so it stands that he has now come who was proclaimed Emmanuel, because what Emmanuel signifies has come, that is, "God with us."

Concerning the sabbath too I premise this, that this question could not have arisen if Christ did not carry about the Lord of the sabbath. For it would not be debated why he destroyed the sabbath, if he ought to destroy it. Now he ought to destroy it, if he were of another god, and no one would marvel at him doing what befitted that other. They marvelled, then, because it did not befit him to carry about the Creator-god and to assail his sabbath. And, that we may settle each first point — lest we everywhere renew the same against every argumentation of the adversary that rests on some new institution of Christ — this definition shall now stand: that there was debate about the novelty of any institution because about the novelty of divinity nothing had as yet been published, just as neither debated; nor can it be retorted from the very novelty of any institution that another divinity than the Creator's was sufficiently demonstrated by Christ, since the very novelty too, foretold by the Creator, has been established not to be marvelled at in Christ. And surely another god ought first to have been set forth, afterward his discipline brought in — because a god furnishes authority to a discipline, not a discipline to a god; unless indeed Marcion plainly did not learn letters so perverse through a master, but a master through letters. The rest concerning the sabbath I direct thus. If Christ broke into the sabbath, he did it according to the example of the Creator — seeing that, in the siege of the city of Jericho, the ark of the testament being carried about the walls for eight days, even on the sabbath, by the precept of the Creator, the sabbath was destroyed by working, as those think who reckon this even of Christ, being ignorant that neither Christ destroyed the sabbath nor the Creator, as we shall presently teach. And yet through Joshua then too the sabbath was shaken, that this also might be reported of Christ; even if he pursued with hatred the most solemn day of the Jews — that Christ, not of the Jews, professing the Creator even by his hatred of the sabbath, as the Christ of him, was following him who cries out by the mouth of Isaiah, "Your new moons and your sabbaths my soul hates." But however these things may be said, we know that even in this species an abrupt defence must be applied against an abrupt provocation. Now I will dispute even to the very matter, in which the discipline of Christ seemed to destroy the sabbath. The disciples had hungered; on that day they had rubbed out ears plucked with their hands; having worked a food, they had broken the holy-days. Christ excuses them, and is liable for the sabbath violated; the Pharisees accuse him; Marcion catches at the state of the controversy (that I may play a little with the truth of my Lord) of the letter and of the will. For from the Scripture of the Creator there is taken — and from the will of Christ a colour, as from the example of David entering the temple on the sabbath and boldly working a food, the loaves of proposition being broken. For he too remembered that this privilege had been granted to the sabbath from the beginning, from which the day itself was discovered — pardon of fasting, I mean. For when the Creator had forbidden the manna to be gathered for two days, he permitted it only on the preparation-day, that the previous provision of food might free the holy-days of the following sabbath from fasting. Well, then, that the Lord too followed the same cause in the destruction (if they wish it so called) of the sabbath; well that he expressed the affection of the Creator too in the honour of not fasting on the sabbath. In short, then at last would he have destroyed the sabbath — and the Creator himself — if he had commanded the disciples to fast on the sabbath against the standing of the letter and will of the Creator. But since he did not constantly protect the disciples, but excuses them; since he opposes human necessity as a kind of intercessor; since he keeps a preferable honour of the sabbath, of not saddening rather than of being idle; since he equates David and his companions with his own disciples in fault and in pardon; since it pleases him that the Creator indulged; since out of his example he too is so good — is he therefore alien to the Creator? Thereupon the Pharisees observed whether he would work cures on the sabbath, that they might accuse him — certainly as the destroyer of the sabbath, not as the professor of a new god; for perhaps I shall everywhere drive in this one point, that another Christ was nowhere proclaimed. But the Pharisees erred altogether about the law of the sabbath, not noticing that it indicated conditionally the holy-days of works, under a certain species of them. For when he says of the sabbath day, "Thou shalt not do in it any work of thine," by saying "thine" he defined it of human work, which each performs from his craft or business, not of the divine. But the work of salvation and of soundness is not man's but God's own. Just as again in the law, "Thou shalt not," it says, "do any work in it, except what shall be done for every soul" — that is, in the cause of freeing a soul: because the work of God can be done even through a man unto the salvation of a soul, yet from God; which Christ too, a man, was to do, because also God. Into this sense of the law, then, wishing to bring them through the restoration of the withered hand, he asks, "Is it lawful on the sabbaths to do well, or not? to free a soul, or to destroy it?" — that by permitting that work which he was to do for a soul, he might admonish them what works of the sabbath the law forbade, namely human, and what it enjoined, namely divine, which should be done for every soul. He is called Lord of the sabbath, because he protected the sabbath as his own thing. And even if he had destroyed it, with reason, as Lord — rather he who instituted it. But he did not destroy it at all, as Lord — so that from this it may now appear that not even then, in the carrying about of the ark at Jericho, was the sabbath destroyed by the Creator. For that too was a work of God which he himself had commanded, and which he had arranged for the souls of his own men set in the crisis of war. But even if he somewhere professed hatred of the sabbaths — by saying "Your sabbaths," reckoning them men's, not his, which a people full of delinquencies celebrates without fear of God, loving God with the lips, not the heart — for their sabbaths, that is, whatever was done by his discipline, he made another state, which through the same prophet he afterward pronounces true and dainty and not to be profaned. Thus neither does Christ rescind the sabbath at all, whose law he held both above in the cause of the disciples, working for a soul (for he indulged the comfort of food to the hungry), and now in curing the withered hand — everywhere driving in by his deeds, "I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil," if Marcion with this voice has stopped his mouth. For here too he fulfilled the law, while he interprets its condition, illumines the difference of works, while he does what the law excepts concerning the holy-days of the sabbath, while he makes the very sabbath day, holy from the beginning by the Father's blessing, holier by his own benefaction — on which, namely, he ministered divine helps, which an adversary would have furnished on other days, that he might not adorn the sabbath of the Creator, that he might not render to the sabbath its due works. On which day, if Elisha the prophet too restored to life the dead son of the Shunammite, you see, Pharisee, and you, Marcion, that it was of old the Creator's to do well on the sabbaths, to free a soul, not to destroy it — that Christ brought in nothing new which is not of the form, the gentleness, the mercy, the proclamation too of the Creator. For here too he represents the prophecy of a special medicine. The dissolved hands grow strong, just as the dissolved knees in the paralytic.

Of our earthly dwelling-place he does not say that we have a house eternal, not made with hands, in heaven, because what is made with hands of the Creator perishes wholly, dissolved after death. For, treating of these things to console the fear of death and the sadness of dissolution itself, he makes it more manifest too through the sequel, when he subjoins that we groan over this tabernacle of the earthly body, desiring to be clothed upon with that which is from heaven; since even, when despoiled, we shall not be found naked — that is, we shall receive what we were despoiled of, that is, the body. And again: For we who are in this tabernacle of the body groan, in that we are burdened, not wishing to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon. For here he expressed what in the first epistle he touched: And the dead shall rise incorrupt — those who have already died — and we shall be changed — we who shall be found by God in the flesh. For those too shall rise incorrupt, the body, namely, being recovered, and that entire, so that from this they may be incorrupt; and these, on account of the now last moment of time, and on account of the merits of the vexations of antichrist, by an abridgement of death, but changed, shall obtain rather to be clothed upon by that which is from heaven than to put off the body. So, if these put on over their body that heavenly thing, then surely the dead too shall receive a body over which they too may put on incorruption from heaven; because of them too he says, This corruptible must put on incorruption, and this mortal immortality. They put on, when they shall have received a body; these put on over, because they have not lost the body; and therefore not rashly did he say, not wishing to be unclothed of the body, but to be clothed upon — that is, not wishing to experience death, but to be anticipated by life, that this mortal may be swallowed up by life, while it is snatched from death through the over-garment of transformation. Therefore, because he shows this to be better, that we be not saddened by the anticipation of death, if it perchance come, he says too that we have from God an earnest of the Spirit, as though pledged unto the same hope of the over-garment; and that we are absent from the Lord so long as we are in the flesh, and on this account ought to count it good to be rather absent from the body and present with the Lord, that we may even gladly accept death. And so he says that we must all be manifested before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive the things he did through the body, whether good or evil. For if then is the retribution of merits, how can some already be reckoned with God? And by naming a tribunal, and the reckoning of good and evil work, he shows the judge of either sentence, and confirmed the representation of all bodies. For what was committed in the body cannot but be judged in the body. For God is unjust, if a man is not punished or aided through that by which he wrought. If, then, there is any new condition in Christ, the old things have passed, behold all things are made new — the prophecy of Isaiah is fulfilled. If too he bids us cleanse ourselves from the defilement of flesh and blood, the substance does not receive the kingdom of God; if he destines too the church a holy virgin to be assigned to Christ — surely as a bride to a bridegroom — the image cannot be joined to one hostile to the truth of the thing itself. If he calls the false apostles deceitful workers, transfigurers of themselves, by hypocrisy, namely, of conduct, not of adulterated preaching, he taxes them. So fully was the difference about discipline, not about divinity. If Satan is transfigured into an angel of light, this cannot be directed against the Creator. For the Creator is God, not an angel; he would have been said to transfigure himself into a God of light, not into an angel, had he not signified that Satan whom both we and Marcion know to be an angel. Of paradise his pen is its own to every question it suffers. Here perhaps I shall wonder, if God could have a paradise of his own who has no terrestrial arrangement — unless he used the Creator's paradise too on sufferance, as he did the world. And yet to take up a man into heaven is the Creator's example, in Elijah. But I shall rather wonder that the Lord supremely good — to whom smiting and raging are alien — should have applied to his apostle, to buffet him, an angel of Satan, not even his own at least, but the Creator's, and, when besought thrice, should not have granted it. The God of Marcion, then, also corrects, emulating the Creator who casts down the proud — putting down, namely, the mighty from their throne. Or is he himself perchance the one who also gave Satan power over the body of Job, that virtue might be approved in weakness? Why too does the chastiser of the Galatians still hold the form of the law, prefixing that every word should stand by three witnesses? Why does he threaten that he will not spare sinners, the preacher of a most gentle God? Nay, he affirms that the very power of acting more harshly in their presence was given him by the Lord. Deny now, heretic, that your God is to be feared, whose apostle was feared!

When at this stage we expel God — He for whom no condition so proper and worthy of God has marked the way as the witness of being Creator — the most impudent Marcionites, wrinkling their noses, turn to the demolition of the Creator's works. "No doubt," they say, "the world is a great work and worthy of God." Is the Creator, then, not at all God? Plainly He is God. Therefore the world too is not unworthy of God; for God has made nothing unworthy of Himself, even though He made the world for man, not for Himself, even though every work is inferior to its maker. And yet, if to have made anything of any kind is unworthy of God, how much more unworthy of God it is to have made nothing at all — even unworthy — by which He might be hoped the author even of worthier things. To say something, then, even of this "unworthy" world — which among the Greeks too has the name of ornament and adornment, not of filth — those very professors of wisdom, from whose talents every heresy draws its life, have pronounced its substances, supposedly unworthy, to be gods: as Thales water, Heraclitus fire, Anaximenes air, Anaximander all the heavenly bodies, Strato heaven and earth, Zeno air and aether, Plato the stars (which kind of gods he calls fiery) — when, considering of the world its greatness and force and power and honour and beauty, the resource, the constancy, the law of the several elements, which conspire to the begetting, nourishing, completing, and renewing of all things, very many of the natural philosophers shrank from holding that the world had a beginning and an end, lest its substances — so great, of course — should be reckoned less than gods, which both the Magi of the Persians and the hierophants of the Egyptians and the gymnosophists of the Indians worship. The very common superstition too of ordinary idolatry, when in its images it is ashamed of the names and fables of the dead of old, flees to an interpretation of natural things, and overshadows its disgrace with ingenuity, figuring Jupiter into a fiery substance and his Juno into an airy one — according to the sound of the Greek words — likewise Vesta into fire, and the Camenae into waters, and the Great Mother into the earth, reaped of its seed, ploughed by arms, watered by bathings. So too Osiris, who is forever buried and sought in what is living and found with joy, they make an argument for the recurrence of crops and the renewal of the elements of life and the returning year; just as the lions of Mithras philosophize the mysteries of the parched and burning nature. And those substances superior in situation or state it is enough to say have more easily been held gods than unworthy of God. Let me come down to lowly things. One little flower, I think, from the hedgerows — I do not say from the meadows — one shell of any sea — I do not say of the Red — one feather of a moorfowl — I say nothing of the peacock — will pronounce to you the Creator a sordid craftsman?

But indeed, when evil afterward broke out, and from then the goodness of God began to deal with an adversary, that same justice of God obtained another business too, namely the directing of goodness now according to a turning-against, so that, its own liberty being set aside, by which God is good even unprompted, it should be weighed according to the deserts of each — offered to the worthy, denied to the unworthy, taken from the ungrateful, accordingly vindicated against all rivals. So all this work of justice is a procuring of goodness; for what by judging it condemns, what by condemning it punishes, what (as you say) it rages against, surely profits the good, not the evil. In short, the fear of judgment confers toward good, not toward evil. For it did not suffice that good be commended of itself, now labouring under an adversary. For even if it be commendable of itself, yet not also conservable, since now assailable through an adversary, unless some force of fearing presided, which should compel even the unwilling to seek and guard the good. For the rest, with so many enticements of evil assailing the good, who would seek that which he might despise with impunity? Who would guard what he might lose without peril? Read the broad and much-more-frequented road of evil: would not all slide down it, if nothing were feared in it? We shudder at the terrible threats of the Creator, and are scarce torn from evil. What, if He threatened nothing? Will you call this justice an evil, which favours not evil? Will you deny this good, which provides for the good? What sort of God would you wish? — such as it would be expedient to prefer, under whom sins might rejoice, whom the devil might mock? Would you judge him a good God who could make man rather more evil by the security of sin? Who is an author of good, but he who is also its exactor? Accordingly, who is a stranger to evil, but he who is also its enemy? Who is its enemy, but he who is also its assailant? Who is its assailant, but he who is also its punisher? So God is wholly good, while He is all things on behalf of good. So, finally, He is almighty, because He is powerful both to help and to harm. It is the lesser thing only to profit, because there is nothing else He could do than profit. From such a god, with what confidence should I hope for good, if this alone he can do? How should I pursue the reward of innocence, if I do not also look for that of guilt? I must of necessity distrust, lest neither part be requited by one who could not avail toward both. So far is justice even the plenitude of divinity itself, exhibiting God perfect both as father and as lord — father by clemency, lord by discipline; father by a coaxing power, lord by a severe one; a father to be loved with piety, a lord to be feared of necessity; to be loved, because He prefers mercy to sacrifice, and to be feared, because He wills not sin; to be loved, because He prefers the sinner's repentance to his death, and to be feared, because He wills not His sinners who now repent no more. Therefore the law defines both: "You shall love God," and, "You shall fear God." The one it set before the obedient, the other before the transgressor.

Likewise too you are led by the sound of names, when you take "the strength of Damascus" and "the spoils of Samaria" and "the king of the Assyrians" as though they portended the Christ of the Creator a warrior, not noticing what the Scripture promises. "Since, before he knows to call father and mother, he shall receive the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians." For first you ought to look at the indication of age — whether it can exhibit Christ a man as yet, let alone a commander. No doubt the infant was about to call to arms by his wailing, and to give the signals of war not with a trumpet but with a rattle; and was about to mark out the enemy not from horse or from chariot or from a wall, but from the neck or back of his nurse or bearer; and so to subdue Damascus and Samaria in exchange for his pap. It is another matter if among the Pontic peoples, of a barbarous nation, the infants burst out into battle — anointed first, I suppose, in the sun, then armed with rags and provisioned with butter, who know how to handle a lance before they can mangle. But truly, if nature nowhere concedes this — to do military service before living, to take the strength of Damascus before knowing the word for father and mother — it follows that the pronouncement is seen to be figurative. "But that a virgin should bear," you say, "nature does not permit; and yet the prophet is believed." And rightly. For he built up faith in the incredible thing beforehand by giving the reason, namely that it would be for a sign. "Therefore," he says, "the Lord himself will give you a sign: behold, a virgin shall conceive in the womb and shall bear a son." Now a sign from God, unless it were some monstrous novelty, would not have been worthy of the name. In short, even the Jews, when at any time they dare to lie in order to cast us down — as though the Scripture contained not "a virgin," but "a young woman," who should conceive and bear — are refuted from this very point, that nothing could seem a sign which is an everyday matter, namely the pregnancy and childbirth of a young woman. So, the virgin-and-mother being appointed for a sign, she is rightly believed; but the infant-warrior is not equally so. For here the reason of a sign is not at work. But, the sign of the new nativity being assigned, then, after the sign, another order is declared, of the infant now about to eat honey and butter. Nor indeed is this a sign — of the malice he will not assent to; for this too belongs to infancy — but of his receiving the strength of Damascus and the spoils of Samaria against the king of the Assyrians. Keep the measure of his age, and seek the sense of the proclamation; nay, restore to the gospel the truth which, as a latecomer, you have detracted, and the prophecy is understood just as it is announced fulfilled. Now let those Magi of the East remain, honouring with gold and frankincense the new-born Christ in his infancy, and let the infant have received the strength of Damascus without battle and arms. For besides what is known to all — that the strength of the East, that is, its might and resources, is wont to abound in gold and perfumes — surely it belongs to the Creator to make even the gold of the other nations a strength, as through Zechariah: "And Judah shall set himself before Jerusalem and shall gather all the valour of the peoples round about, gold and silver." And concerning that gift of gold David then too: "And there shall be given to him of the gold of Arabia"; and again, "The kings of the Arabs and of Saba shall offer gifts to him." For the East had the Magi too for kings, well-nigh; and Damascus was formerly reckoned to Arabia, before it was transcribed into Syrophoenicia by the distinction of the Syrias — whose strength then Christ received, by receiving its insignia, namely gold and perfume. But the "spoils of Samaria" are the Magi themselves, who, when they had recognized him and honoured him with gifts and adored him on bended knee as god and king, under the testimony of the star their guide and leader, were made the spoils of Samaria, that is, of idolatry, believing, namely, in Christ. For he marked idolatry by the name of Samaria, as one infamous for idolatry, by which it had then revolted from God under king Jeroboam. Nor is this new to the Creator, to use figuratively a transference of names from a comparison of crimes. For he calls the rulers of the Jews rulers of the Sodomites, and the people itself he calls the people of Gomorrah. And the same elsewhere: "Thy father," he says, "was an Amorite, and thy mother a Hittite," on account of a like impiety — those whom at another time he had also called his own sons: "I have begotten and exalted sons." So too Egypt is sometimes understood, with him, as the whole world, under the description of superstition and malediction. So too Babylon, even in our John, is a figure of the city of Rome — likewise great, and proud in empire, and a warrior against the saints of God. By this usage, then, he entitled the Magi too, despoiled, by the appellation of Samaritans, because they had with the Samaritans, as we have said, idolatry. But "against the king of the Assyrians" understand against Herod, against whom the Magi at that time surely set themselves by not reporting concerning Christ, whom he was seeking to intercept.

Certainly he evangelizes to Zion and Jerusalem peace and all good things; certainly he ascends into the mountain and there passes the night in prayer, and surely is heard by the Father. Unroll, then, the prophets, and recognize the whole order. "Ascend into a high mountain," says Isaiah, "thou who evangelizest Zion; lift up thy voice with vigour, thou who evangelizest Jerusalem." Still in vigour they were astounded at his teaching; for he was teaching as one having power. And again: "Therefore the people shall know my name in that day." What name, but Christ's? "Because I am the very one who speaks." For then he himself it was who spoke in the prophets — the Word, the Son of the Creator. "I am present, while it is the hour, in the mountains, as one evangelizing the hearing of peace, as one evangelizing good things." Likewise Nahum of the twelve: "For behold, swift feet upon the mountain of one evangelizing peace." But of the voice of nocturnal prayer to the Father, manifestly the psalm: "My God, I will cry by day, and thou wilt hear, and by night, and not unto vanity for me." And elsewhere, of the same place and voice, the psalm: "With my voice I cried out to the Lord, and he heard me from his holy mountain." You have the representation of the name, you have the act of one evangelizing, you have the place of the mountain, and the time of night, and the sound of the voice, and the hearing of the Father; you have the Christ of the prophets. But why did he choose twelve apostles, and not some other number? Nay, from this too I could interpret my Christ, foretold not only by the voices of the prophets, but by the arguments of facts. For I detect figures of this number with the Creator: the twelve springs of Elim, and the twelve gems in the priestly tunic of Aaron, and the twelve stones chosen by Joshua out of the Jordan and laid up in the ark of the testament. For just so many apostles were portended — to water, like springs and rivers, the orb of the nations once arid and deserted of knowledge (as also through Isaiah: "I will set rivers in a waterless land"); like gems, to illumine the sacred vestment of the Church, which Christ the priest of the Father has put on; like stones too, solid in faith, whom the true Joshua chose out of the washing of the Jordan and received into the sanctuary of his testament. What of the kind suits Marcion's Christ, as concerns the defence of the number? A thing cannot seem done simply by him which can be seen not done simply by mine. The thing will belong to him with whom the preparation of the thing is found. He changes Peter's name too from Simon — because the Creator too reformed the names of Abraham and Sarah and Hoshea, calling this one Jesus, to those adding syllables. But why Peter? If on account of vigour of faith, many materials of solidity would have lent their name from their own. Or because Christ too is both a rock and a stone? Seeing that we also read him set as a stone of stumbling and a rock of offence. I pass over the rest. And so he affected to communicate to his dearest disciple a name peculiarly from his own figures — I think more nearly than from things not his own. There meet him from Tyre and from other regions a multitude, even from beyond the sea. To this the psalm looked: "And behold, foreigners and Tyre and the people of the Ethiopians, these were there. 'Mother Zion,' a man shall say, and a man was made in her" (since God was born a man), "and he built her by the will of the Father" — that you may know that the Gentiles then came together to him, because God was born a man, about to build the Church by the will of the Father, out of foreigners too. So too Isaiah: "Behold, these come from afar, and these from the north and the sea, and others from the land of the Persians." Concerning whom again: "Lift up thine eyes round about, and see, all are gathered together." Concerning whom too below: "Thou seest the unknown and the strangers, and thou shalt say to thy heart, Who has begotten these to me? and who has reared these for me? but where were these for me?" This will be the Christ not of the prophets? And who will be the Christ of the Marcionites? If perversity pleases — he who was not the prophets'.

ON THE EPISTLE TO THE ROMANS. When the work is being driven to a close, the things which recur must now be reviewed briefly, but some passed over which have recurred more often. It irks me to engage still about the law, who have so often proved that its concession furnishes no argument of a different God in Christ — being, namely, both preached and promised unto Christ with the Creator — inasmuch as this epistle too seems for the most part to exclude the law. But that God too is carried about by the apostle as judge we have often already shown, and in the judge an avenger, and the Creator in the avenger. So here too, when he says, For I am not ashamed of the gospel, for it is the power of God unto salvation to everyone that believes, to Jew and Greek, because the righteousness of God is revealed in it from faith to faith — without doubt he reckons both gospel and salvation to a just God, not to a good one, so to speak, according to the heretic's distinction — transferring from the faith of the law to the faith of the gospel, of his own law surely and his own gospel. Since too he says that wrath is revealed from heaven upon the impiety and injustice of men, who hold the truth in injustice. Of what God's wrath? Surely the Creator's. Therefore his truth too will be whose is also the wrath, which is to be revealed in vengeance for the truth. Adding too, But we know that the judgement of God is according to truth, he both proved the wrath itself, from which comes judgement for truth, and again confirmed the truth of the same God whose wrath he proved by proving the judgement. It is another matter, if the Creator, angry, avenges the truth of another God held in injustice. But how great pits Marcion has made in this epistle especially, by taking away what he would, will appear from the integrity of our instrument. It is enough for me to take as negligences and blindnesses of his those things which he likewise did not see to be erased. For if God shall judge the secrets of men, both of those who sinned in the law and of those without law — because these too do not know the law, and by nature do the things of the law — surely that God shall judge whose are both the law and nature itself, which is, as it were, a law to those ignorant of the law. But how shall he judge? According to the gospel, he says, through Christ. Therefore both the gospel and Christ are his whose are also the law and nature, which shall be vindicated through the gospel and Christ — by that judgement of God, surely, which above too was according to truth. Therefore, since the wrath which is to be revealed from heaven for the defence of that truth is of none but the God of wrath, so too here this sense, cohering with the former, in which the judgement of the Creator is proclaimed, cannot be referred to another God, who neither judges nor is angry, but to him whose, while these are — I mean the judgement and the wrath — these too of necessity are: the gospel and Christ, through whom these have to be transacted. And therefore he inveighs against transgressors of the law — teaching not to steal, and stealing — as a man of the law of God, not as touching the Creator himself in these ways, who, even while forbidding to steal, commanded a fraud upon the Egyptians of gold and silver — just as they twist the rest too against him. Forsooth the apostle feared to make plain a reproach to the God from whom he did not fear to have departed! And so much had he assailed the Jews, that he heaped up the prophetic rebuke: On your account the name of God is blasphemed. How perverse, then, that he himself should blaspheme him for whose sake of being blasphemed he upbraids the wicked! He prefers too the circumcision of the heart to uncircumcision; with the God of the law was made the circumcision of the heart, not of the flesh, in spirit, not in letter. But if this is the circumcision of Jeremiah, And circumcise the foreskins of your heart, as Moses too said, Circumcise your hardness of heart — then his will be the spirit circumcising the heart whose is also the letter reaping its flesh, and his the Jew who is in secret whose too is the Jew in the open, because the apostle would not even name a Jew who was not the servant of the God of the Jews. Then the law, now the righteousness of God through the faith of Christ. What is this distinction? Did your God serve the arrangement of the Creator, giving him his time and his law? or is his now whose it then was? His is the law whose too is the faith of Christ; it is a distinction of arrangements, not of gods. He admonishes those justified by the faith of Christ, not by the law, to have peace toward God. Toward what God? Of whom we were nowhere enemies, or against whose law and nature we rebelled? For if peace is fitting with him with whom there was war, by him too we shall be justified, and his will be Christ, by whose faith we shall be justified, to whose peace it is fitting that his enemies should at some time be reduced. But the law, he says, entered in, that sin might abound. Why? That grace might superabound, he says. Of what God the grace, if not whose too is the law? Unless the Creator on this account intercalated the law, to procure the business of the grace of another God — and that a rival, not to say an unknown one — that, as with him sin had reigned unto death, so too grace might reign in righteousness unto life through Jesus Christ, his adversary. For this the law of the Creator had concluded all under sin, and had brought the whole world into guilt, and stopped every mouth, that none should glory through it, so that grace might be reserved unto the glory of Christ — not the Creator's, but Marcion's. I can here too forestructure concerning the substance of Christ, from the prospect of the following question. For he says, We are dead to the law. Therefore the body of Christ can even be contended to be a body, not at once flesh. But also, of whatever substance it be, when he names the body of him whom he subjoins to have risen from the dead, no other body can be understood than of flesh, against which the law of death was pronounced. But behold he both bears witness to the law and excuses it from the cause of sin. What then shall we say? Is the law sin? God forbid. Blush, Marcion. God forbid. The apostle abominates the accusation of the law. But I do not know sin except through the law. O highest proclamation hence of the law, through which it was made plain that sin lay hidden! Not, then, did the law seduce, but sin through the occasion of the precept. Why do you impute to the God of the law what the apostle does not dare to impute to his law? Nay, he heaps up: The law is holy, and its precept just and good. If he so venerates the law of the Creator, how he destroys the Creator himself I do not know. Who distinguishes two gods, one just, another good, when he ought to be believed both whose precept is both good and just? But if he also confirms the law to be spiritual, surely it is prophetic too, surely figurative too. For I ought even from this to constitute Christ figuratively preached in the law, in such a way that he could not be acknowledged by all the Jews.

But while you mock even the smaller animals, which the supreme Craftsman has on purpose enlarged in talents or in strength — thus teaching that greatness is proved in smallness, just as virtue in weakness, according to the apostle — imitate, if you can, the buildings of the bee, the stables of the ant, the nets of the spider, the threads of the silkworm; endure, if you can, those very beasts of your couch and your bedding, the poisons of the blister-beetle, the stings of the fly, the trumpet and the lance of the gnat. What will the greater things be, when by such small ones you are either helped or hurt, so that not even in small things may you despise the Creator? Finally, turn yourself about upon yourself; consider man within and without: even this work of our God will please you, which your lord, that better god, fell in love with — for whose sake he laboured to descend from the third heaven into these poor elements; for whose cause he was even crucified in this cell of the Creator. But up to now he has neither rejected the Creator's water, with which he washes his own, nor the oil with which he anoints them, nor the union of honey and milk with which he gives his own their first nourishment, nor the bread by which he represents his very body — even in his own sacraments needing the beggarly things of the Creator. But you, a disciple above your master, and a slave above your lord, are wiser than he, demolishing what he desires. I wish to inspect whether it be at least out of faith, that you yourself do not also crave what you demolish. You oppose heaven, and yet in your dwellings you seek the freedom of heaven. You despise the earth — plainly already the enemy of your own flesh's matrix — and yet you wring out all its marrow for your sustenance. You reject the sea too, but only as far as its plenty, which you reckon a holier food. If I offer you a rose, you will not disdain the Creator. Hypocrite, that you may prove yourself a Marcionite by starving — that is, a repudiator of the Creator (for this ought to have been affected among you in place of martyrdom, if the world displeased you) — into whatever matter you may dissolve, you use the substance of the Creator. How great the obstinacy of your hardness! You cheapen the things in which you both live and die.

At all points God meets you: the same striking, but also healing; killing, but also making alive; humbling, but also exalting; creating evils, but also making peace — that from this too I may answer the heretics. For lo, they say, He Himself professes Himself the maker of evils, saying, "I am he who creates evils." For embracing the community of the word, which throws into ambiguity the two kinds of evils — since both sins are called evils and punishments — they will have Him everywhere understood to be the maker of evils, that He may be reported the author of malice. But we, applying a distinction of both forms, separating the evils of sin and the evils of punishment, the evils of fault and the evils of penalty, define for each part its own author: of the evils of sin and fault, the devil; but of the evils of punishment and penalty, God the Creator — so that the one part be reckoned to malice, this other to justice, which creates evil judgments against the evils of sin. Of these evils, then, the Creator professes Himself the author which suit a judge. These indeed are evils to those to whom they are repaid; but in their own name, good, in so far as just, and protective of the good and hostile to sins, and in this order worthy of God. Or prove them unjust, that you may prove them to be reckoned to malice, that is, evils of injustice; for if they belong to justice, they will now be not evils, but goods — evils only to the evil, to whom even goods outright are condemned in place of evils. Establish, then, that it was unjustly that man, the voluntary despiser of the divine law, was given back to that which he willed to lack; unjustly that the malice of that age was smitten by rains and then by fires; unjustly that Egypt — most foul, superstitious, and moreover the persecutor of its guest people — was struck with a tenfold chastisement. He hardened Pharaoh's heart: but he had deserved to be furnished unto destruction, who had already denied God, who had already so many times haughtily shaken off His envoys, who had already added the burden of labour to the people; finally, in that he was an Egyptian, he had long since been guilty before God of the idolatry of his nation, worshipping sooner the ibis and the crocodile than the living God. He spent the people itself too, but an ungrateful one. He sent the bears also against the boys, but disrespectful boys against the prophet.

This our interpretation will be helped, while elsewhere too, supposing Christ a warrior on account of certain names of arms and words of this kind, you are convicted by a comparison of the remaining senses as well. "Gird," says David, "thy sword upon thy thigh." But what do you read above concerning Christ? "Seasonable in beauty beyond the sons of men, grace is poured out upon thy lips." I laugh, if to him whom he was girding with a sword for war he was flattering about the seasonableness of beauty and the grace of lips. So likewise, subjoining, "And stretch forth, and prosper, and reign," he added, "for the sake of truth and gentleness and justice." For who will work these things with a sword, and not rather the contraries, deceit and harshness and injustice — the proper businesses, namely, of battles? Let us see, then, whether that sword be of another kind, whose act is of another kind. For the apostle John too, in the Apocalypse, describes a sword going forth from the mouth of God, twice-sharp, fore-sharpened — which we must understand to be the divine word; twice-sharp, by the two testaments of the law and the gospel; sharp with wisdom, hostile to the devil, arming us against the spiritual hosts of wickedness and of all concupiscence, cutting us off even from those dearest to us for the name of God. But if you will not have John acknowledged, you have our common master Paul, girding our loins with truth and the breastplate of justice, and shoeing us with the preparation of the gospel of peace, not of war, bidding us take the shield of faith, in which we may quench all the fiery darts of the devil, and the helmet of salvation, and the sword of the spirit, which is, he says, the word of God. This sword the Lord himself too came to send upon the earth, not peace. If your Christ is meant, then he too is a warrior. If he is not a warrior, brandishing an allegorical sword, then it was permitted to the Christ of the Creator also, in the psalm, to be girt without warlike matters with a figurative sword of the word — to whom the aforesaid seasonableness suits, and the grace of lips — with which he was then already girt upon his thigh, in David, intending one day to send it into the earth. For this is what he says: "And stretch forth, and prosper, and reign." Stretching forth the word into all the earth, to the calling of all nations; about to prosper by the success of the faith by which he was received; and reigning thenceforth, by which he conquered death by resurrection. "And thy right hand," he says, "shall lead thee wonderfully" — namely the power of spiritual grace, by which the acknowledgement of Christ is led on. "Thy arrows are sharp" — precepts flying everywhere, and threats and exposures of the heart, pricking and piercing every conscience. "The peoples shall fall under thee" — namely in adoration. So mighty in war and bearer of arms is the Christ of the Creator; so even now he receives spoils, not of Samaria alone but of all nations too. Recognize the spoils as figurative, whose arms you have learned to be allegorical. Since, then, the Lord speaks thus figuratively, and the apostle writes so, it is not rashly that we use his interpretations, the examples of which even our adversaries admit; and thus the Christ who has come will belong to Isaiah just in so far as he was no warrior, because no such one is proclaimed by Isaiah.

I come now to his ordinary opinions, through which he introduces the property of his teaching unto an edict, so to say, of Christ: "Blessed are the beggars" (for so the interpretation of the word that is in Greek requires) "for theirs is the kingdom of God." Now this very thing, that he began from benedictions, is the Creator's, who dedicated the universe, as he produced it, by no other voice than that of benediction. "For my heart," he says, "has belched forth an excellent word." This will be the excellent word, of benediction namely, which is acknowledged also as the initiator of the new testament from the old example. What wonder, then, if he entered also upon the affections of the Creator — through utterance of this kind ever loving the beggars and poor and lowly and widows and orphans, consoling, asserting, avenging them? — so that you may believe this as it were private benignity of Christ a rivulet from the fountains of the Saviour. In truth, where to direct myself I know not, in so great a frequency of utterances of this kind, as in a wood or in a meadow or in an orchard of apples. The thing must be sought at random, as it falls. The psalm cries out: "Judge the orphan and the beggar, and deal justly with the lowly and the poor; free the poor, and rescue the beggar from the hand of the sinner." Likewise the seventy-first psalm: "Justice shall judge the beggars of the people, and shall make safe the sons of the poor." And in what follows, concerning Christ: "All nations shall serve him." But David ruled over the one Jewish nation — lest anyone think it said of David, because he too had taken up the lowly and those labouring under necessities. "Because," it says, "he shall free the beggar from the strong, he shall spare the beggar and the poor, and the souls of the poor he shall make safe; from usury and injustice he shall redeem their souls, and honoured shall be their name in his sight." Likewise: "Let sinners be turned into the underworld, all the nations that forget God; because the beggar shall not be held in forgetfulness unto the end, the endurance of the poor shall not perish unto the end." Likewise: "Who is like our God, who dwells on high, and beholds lowly things in heaven and on earth, who raises up the beggar from the earth, and exalts the poor from the dung-heap, that he may make him sit with the princes of the people" — surely in his kingdom. So too of old in Kingdoms, Hannah, the mother of Samuel, rendering glory to God in spirit, "Who," she says, "raises the poor from the earth and the beggar, that he may make him sit with the chiefs of the people" — surely in his kingdom — "and on thrones of glory" — surely royal ones. But through Isaiah, how he inveighs against the harassers of the needy: "But you, to what end do you set fire to my vineyard, and the spoil of the beggar in your houses? Why do you injure my people, and confound the face of the beggars?" And again: "Woe to those who write wickedness, for in writing they write wickedness, avoiding the judgements of the beggars and seizing the things judged for the poor of my people." Which judgements he demands for orphans and widows too, as for the needy of comfort. "Judge the orphan, and deal justly with the widow, and come, let us be reconciled, says the Lord." Whose so great affection toward every condition of lowliness is the Creator's, his too will be the kingdom which is promised by Christ, to whose affection those have long since belonged to whom it is promised. For even if you think the Creator's promises were earthly, but Christ's heavenly — well that heaven appears, as yet, of no other god than him whose the earth too is; well that the Creator promised at least the lesser things, that I may the more easily believe him about the greater too, than him who never first built up the faith of his liberality concerning the lesser. "Blessed are they that hunger, for they shall be filled." I might have transmitted this title to the former, since the hungry are none other than the poor and beggars, were it not that the Creator had destined this promise too specially toward the prebuilding, namely, of his own gospel — seeing that through Isaiah, concerning those whom he was to call from the height of the earth, surely the nations: "Behold," he says, "swiftly, lightly they shall come" — swiftly, as hastening under the ends of the times; lightly, because without the burdens of the former law. "They shall not hunger, nor thirst." Therefore they shall be filled — which surely is not promised but to the hungry and thirsty. And again: "Behold," he says, "those who serve me shall be filled, but you shall hunger: behold, those who serve me shall drink, but you shall thirst." We shall see these contraries too, whether they are pre-ministered to Christ. Meanwhile, that he promises fullness to the hungry is the Creator-god's. "Blessed are they that weep, for they shall laugh." Run through the opinion of Isaiah: "Behold, those who serve me shall exult in joyfulness, but you shall be confounded: behold, those who serve me shall be delighted, but you shall cry out for sorrow of heart." Recognize these contraries too with Christ. Certainly delight and exultation in joyfulness are promised to those who are in the diverse condition, the sad and gloomy and anxious. And the psalm too, the 125th: "Those who sow," it says, "in tears, shall reap in exultation." Now to those exulting and taking joyfulness laughter accrues, as to the mourning and grieving weeping. Thus the Creator, proclaiming the matters of laughter and of weeping, said first that the weeping shall laugh. Therefore he who began from the consolation of the poor and lowly and hungry and weeping, straightway desired to represent that one whom he had demonstrated through Isaiah: "The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me to evangelize to the poor" — "Blessed are the beggars, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven"; "he has sent me to heal the broken in heart" — "Blessed are they that hunger, for they shall be filled"; "to call the languishing" — "Blessed are they that weep, for they shall laugh"; "to give to the mourners of Zion glory, and for ashes the joyfulness of ointment, and the garment of glory for the spirit of weariness." If Christ, admitted at once, administered these things, either he himself is the one who proclaimed that he would come to these things, or, if he has not yet come who proclaimed, ridiculously, but of necessity I might perhaps say, he commanded the Christ of Marcion: "Blessed shall you be, when men shall hold you in hatred, and shall reproach you, and shall cast out your name as evil, for the Son of man's sake." By this pronouncement, without doubt, he exhorts to endurance. What less does the Creator through Isaiah? "Fear not the ignominy from men, and by their nullification be not diminished." What ignominy, what nullification? That which was to be for the Son of man's sake. Who is this? He who is according to the Creator. Whence shall we prove it? By the destruction proclaimed against him too; as through Isaiah, to the Jews, the authors of the hatred: "Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations"; and elsewhere: "Sanctify him who circumscribes his own soul, who is held in spurning by the nations, by their servants and magistrates." For if the hatred was proclaimed against that Son of man who is according to the Creator, and the gospel attests that the name of Christians, surely derived from Christ, shall be hated for the Son of man's sake, which is Christ — then he constitutes as the cause of the hatred that Son of man who was according to the Creator, against whom the hatred was proclaimed. And surely if he had not yet come, the hatred of the name, which is carried on today, could not have preceded the person of the name. For both there is sanctifying among us, and one circumscribes his own soul, laying it down for us, and is held in spurning by the nations. And he who is born, he will be the Son of man, for whom our name too is refused.

If the Father sent him in the likeness of sinful flesh, not on that account shall the flesh which appeared in him be called a phantasm. For he ascribed sin above to the flesh, and made it the law of sin dwelling in his members and warring against the law of the mind. For this reason, then, the Son was sent in the likeness of sinful flesh, that he might redeem the flesh of sin by a like substance — that is, a fleshly one, which was like to the sinning flesh, while not itself sinning. For this too will be the power of God: in a like substance to perfect salvation. For it is no great thing if the Spirit of God should heal the flesh; but if flesh like to the sinning flesh, while it is flesh, but not of sin. Thus the likeness will pertain to the title of sin, not to a falsehood of substance. For he would not have added Of sin, if he wished a likeness of substance to be understood, so as to deny the truth; for he would have set down only Of flesh, not also Of sin. But when he so framed it, Of sinful flesh, he both confirmed the substance, that is, flesh, and referred the likeness to the vice of the substance, that is, to sin. Suppose now the likeness were said of substance — not on that account will the truth of substance be denied. Why, then, true, though like? Because true indeed, but not from seed, of a like state, but true of a reckoning not like, yet not unlike. For the rest, there is no likeness in contraries. Spirit would not be called the likeness of flesh, because flesh too would not take on a likeness of spirit; but it would be called a phantasm, if what was not appeared. But it is called a likeness when there is what appears. For it is, while it is the equal of another. But a phantasm, in that it only seems, is not a likeness. And here too, expounding how he would not have us be in the flesh, though we are in the flesh — that is, that we should not be in the works of the flesh — he shows that on this reasoning he wrote, Flesh and blood cannot obtain the kingdom of God: not condemning the substance, but its works; which, because they can not be admitted by us, though still placed in the flesh, will pertain not to the guilt of the substance, but of the conduct. Likewise, if the body indeed is dead because of sin — so that it is the death not of the soul but of the body — but the spirit is life because of righteousness, to which death came because of sin, that is, to the body. For nothing is restored except to him who lost it; and so there will be a resurrection of the dead, since it is of bodies. For he subjoins: He who raised Christ from the dead shall make alive your mortal bodies too. So fully did he both confirm the resurrection of the flesh — without which neither can a thing be called body nor anything else understood as mortal — and prove the bodily substance of Christ; since our mortal bodies too shall likewise be made alive, just as he too was raised up — not otherwise, namely, than because in the body. Here too I leap over a most ample chasm of intercepted scripture, but I lay hold of the apostle bearing witness to Israel that they have a zeal of God — their own, surely — yet not according to knowledge. For, being ignorant of God, he says, and seeking to set up their own righteousness, that is, of their own law, they did not submit themselves to the righteousness of God; for Christ is the end of the law unto righteousness to everyone that believes. Here will be the heretic's argument: that the Jews were ignorant of the superior God, against whom they set up their own righteousness, that is, of their own law, not receiving Christ, the end of the law. Why then does he bear witness of their zeal toward their own God, if he does not also upbraid them with ignorance toward the same God? — that they were indeed driven by zeal of God, but not according to knowledge, being ignorant of him, namely, while they are ignorant of his arrangements in Christ, the consummation that was to stand for the law, and so maintain their own righteousness against him. And so the Creator himself too attests their ignorance toward himself: Israel has not known me, and my people has not understood me; and that they would rather set up their own righteousness, teaching doctrines the precepts of men, and were also gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ — out of ignorance, namely. Nothing, therefore, can be expounded as of another God which befits the Creator, because otherwise the apostle would undeservedly have branded the Jews with ignorance toward an unknown God. For wherein had they sinned, if they set up the righteousness of their own God against him whom they were ignorant of? But behold he exclaims: O the depth of the riches and wisdom of God, and his ways past tracing out! Whence that outburst? Out of the remembrance, namely, of the scriptures which he had unrolled before, out of the contemplation of the sacraments which he had above expounded, of the faith of Christ coming out of the law. If Marcion erased these of set purpose, why does his apostle exclaim, beholding no riches of a God so poor and beggarly as one who founded nothing, preached nothing, lastly possessed nothing, as one who descends into another's property? But the wealth and riches of the Creator, once hidden, are now unlocked. For so he had promised: And I will give them hidden treasures, I will open the invisible to them. Thence, then, it was exclaimed: O the depth of the riches and wisdom of God! whose treasures now lay open. This is Isaiah's, and the sequel too is from the instrument of the same prophet: For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who was his counsellor? who has first given to him, and it shall be recompensed to him? You who took away so much from the scriptures, why did you keep these things, as though they too were not the Creator's? Plainly, let us see the precepts of the new God. Hating, he says, evil, and cleaving to good. Is it another thing with the Creator, Take away evil from you, and Turn away from evil and do good? Affectioned to one another in brotherly love; for it is not the very same as, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. Rejoicing in hope — of God, surely. For it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in magistrates. Enduring tribulation. For the Lord shall hear you in the day of tribulation. You have the psalm. Bless, and curse not. Who shall teach this but he who founded all things with blessings? Not minded on high things, but consenting to the lowly; be not wise in your own eyes. For they hear Woe through Isaiah. Render to no one evil for evil. And, Remember not the malice of your brother. Nor avenging yourselves. For vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord. Have peace with all men. Therefore the legal retaliation too did not permit the recompensing of injury, but checked its inception through fear of recompense. With reason, then, he concluded the whole discipline of the Creator in his chief precept, You shall love your neighbour as yourself. If this supplement of the law is from the law itself, what God is the God of the law I now do not know. I fear it is the God of Marcion. But if the gospel of Christ is fulfilled by this precept, and it is Christ's, not the Creator's, by which now we contend — did Christ say or not, I came not to dissolve the law, but to fulfil it? In vain did Pontus labour to deny that sentence. If the gospel did not fulfil the law, behold the law fulfilled the gospel. But well that in the close too he threatens the tribunal of Christ — surely of the judge and avenger, surely of the Creator — establishing him certainly as one to be propitiated whom he holds out as to be feared, even if he were preaching another.

After these things, or before these, when you have said that he too has his own creation and his own world and his own heaven — concerning that third heaven indeed we shall see, if we come also to the examination of your apostle — meanwhile, whatever substance it is, it ought certainly to have appeared together with its own god. But as it is, what sort of thing is it that the Lord was revealed in the twelfth year of Tiberius Caesar, while the substance, even up to the fifteenth year now of the emperor Severus, has not at all been discovered — which, surpassing the trifles of the Creator, would surely have ceased to lie hid, now that its lord and author lies hid no longer? And therefore, if it itself could not be manifested in this world, how did its lord appear in this world? If this world contained the lord, why could it not contain the substance, unless perchance it be greater than the lord? Now already there is a question of place, pertaining both to that higher world and to its very god. For lo, if he too has his own world beneath him, above the Creator, he made it of course in a place, the space of which lay vacant between his feet and the head of the Creator. Therefore the god himself too was in a place, and was making a world in a place; and that place will now be greater than both the god and the world. For there is nothing that is not greater — that which contains than that which is contained.
