And it must be seen whether some odd corners still lie vacant there, in which some third god too may pack himself together with his own world. Begin then now to count gods. For place too will be a god — not only in so far as greater than the god, but also in so far as unborn and unmade and thereby eternal and equal to the god, in which the god always was. Next, if he too contrived the world out of some underlying matter, unborn and unmade and coeternal with the god — as Marcion thinks concerning the Creator — you reduce this too to the majesty of place, which has enclosed both the god and the matter, two gods. For matter too is a god, according to the form of divinity, namely unborn and unmade and eternal. Or if he contrived the world out of nothing, he will be forced to think this of the Creator too, to whom he subjects matter in the substance of the world. But the other will have had to make out of matter too, the same reason meeting that god which was urged against the Creator, since he is equally a god. And thus reckon me for the moment three gods of Marcion: the maker, and place, and matter. Accordingly he sets the Creator too in a place, reckoning Him of course by the same condition, and subjects matter to Him — unborn, of course, and unmade, and on this score eternal, as the lord is. Further, reckoning evil also to matter — unborn to the unborn, unmade to the unmade, and eternal to the eternal — here he has now made a fourth god. You have therefore in the higher region three substances of divinity, in the lower four. When to these are added their Christs too — the one who appeared under Tiberius, the other who is promised by the Creator — Marcion now suffers a manifest fraud at the hands of those who presume to bring him in with two gods, when he assigns nine, though unwittingly.

Discern, then, first the justice of the judge, of which, if the reason be settled, then both the severity, and the things through which the severity runs its course, will be reckoned to reason and justice. And not to linger over many things — assert the rest of the causes too, that you may condemn the sentences; excuse the sins, that you may reprobate the judgments. Do not blame the judge, but convict the bad judge. For even if He exacted the sins of the fathers from the sons, the hardness of the people had compelled such remedies, that, providing even for their posterity, they might obey the divine law. For who does not care more for the salvation of his children than for his own? But also, if the blessing of the fathers was destined for their seed too, while as yet there was no merit of it, why should not the guilt of the fathers too overflow upon the sons? As grace, so also offence — that through the whole race both grace and offence might run on, saving what was afterward to be decreed: that they would not say the fathers had eaten the sour grape and the children's teeth been set on edge; that is, that the father should not take up the sin of the son, nor the son the sin of the father, but each be made guilty of his own sin; so that, after the hardness of the people, the hardness of the law being subdued, justice should now judge not the race, but the persons. Although, if you receive the gospel of truth, you will know to whom that sentence pertains, of Him who renders to the sons the sins of the fathers — namely to those who were of their own accord about to imprecate this sentence upon themselves: "His blood be upon our heads and upon our children's." This, therefore, all the providence of God determined, which it had already heard.

Concerning the question of the flesh, and through it of nativity, and of the one name Emmanuel, thus far. But concerning the other names, and chiefly that of "Christ," what will the opposite party reply? If the name of Christ is common among you in the same way as that of "God," so that, just as it suits to call the Son of each god Christ, so to call each father Lord — certainly reason will be against this argument. For the name of God, as being natural to deity, can be communicated to all to whom deity is claimed, just as also to idols, the apostle saying, "For there are also those who are called gods, whether in heaven or on earth." But the name of Christ, not coming from nature but from arrangement, becomes the proper name of him by whom it is found to have been arranged. Nor does it lie open to communication with another god — chiefly a rival, and one having his own arrangement, to whom he will also owe private names. For what kind of thing is it that, having invented diverse arrangements of two gods, they admit a community of names in discord of arrangements — when no proof would more strongly stand for two gods, and those rivals, than if in their arrangement a diversity of names too were found? For no state of differences is sealed except by the propriety of appellations. And when these are wanting, the Greek catachresis comes to the rescue, by abusing what belongs to another. But with God, I think, nothing ought to be wanting, nor should his arrangements be furnished out of another's. What god is this, who claims for his own son too names from the Creator? — I do not say a stranger's, but old and common ones, which even on that account would not suit a new and unknown god. How, in short, does he teach that a new patch is not to be sewn on an old garment, nor new wine entrusted to old skins, being himself sewn over and clothed in the old age of names? How did he cut off the gospel from the law, clad in the whole law? — in the name, namely, of Christ. Who forbade him to be called by one thing, while he preached another, while he came from elsewhere — since on this very account he did not even take the truth of a body, lest he should be believed the Christ of the Creator? But to no purpose did he refuse to seem the one he wished to be called; for even if he had truly been corporeal, he would the rather not seem the Christ of the Creator, if he were not so called. But as it is, he spurns the substance whose name he received — though he would have proved the substance from the name. For if Christ is "anointed," to be anointed is surely a passion of a body. He who had no body could not at all be anointed; he who could not at all be anointed could in no way be called Christ. It is another matter if he affected a phantom of the name too. "But how," he says, "could he creep into the faith of the Jews except by a name solemn and familiar among them?" You make God out inconstant or crafty; it is the counsel either of diffidence or of malice, to gain something by deceiving. Far more freely and simply did the false prophets act against the Creator, coming in the name of their own god. But neither do I find any effect of this counsel, since they more readily believed either their own Christ, or rather some impostor, than the Christ of another god — as the gospel will prove.

"After these things," it says, "did their fathers to the prophets." O versatile Christ — now the destroyer, now the asserter of the prophets! He destroyed as their rival, converting their disciples; he asserted them for himself as a friend, censuring their persecutors. Now in so far as the asserting of the prophets, to whose destruction he had come, would not suit the Christ of Marcion, by so much the censuring of the persecutors of the prophets, whom he fulfilled in all things, suits the Christ of the Creator — or because it is rather the Creator's to reproach the fathers' delinquencies to their sons than that god's who castigates not even each one's own. "But not at once," you say, "did he protect the prophets, if he wished the iniquity of the Jews to be affirmed, that they had not even dealt piously with their prophets." And yet no iniquity here was to be reproached to the Jews — rather they were to be praised and approved, if they censured those to whose destruction, after so great an age, the best god was moved. But, I think, now no longer best, now somewhat lingering even with the Creator, nor altogether the god of Epicurus. For behold he changes into a malediction, and shows himself one who knows how to be offended and to grow angry. For he says "Woe." But a question arises for us concerning the quality of that word, as though it were not so much of malediction as of admonition. And what is the difference, when even an admonition is not made without the sting of a threat, made especially the more bitter through the "Woe"? Both an admonition and a threat too will belong to him who knows how to be angry. For no one admonishes and no one threatens, that one may not do something, but he who will avenge it when done. No one would avenge but he who knows how to be angry. Others indeed acknowledge a word of malediction, but they would have Christ pronounce "Woe" thus, not as it were properly from his own opinion, but because the "Woe" is from the Creator, and that he wished to oppose to them the harshness of the Creator, that he might commend his own forbearance above in the benedictions. As though it did not befit the Creator, as furnishing both — both a good god and a judge — to subjoin in maledictions also severity, since he had premised benignity in benedictions, for the amplitude of either discipline to be furnished, both for following the benediction and for forestalling the malediction. For so too he had premised: "Behold, I have set before you a blessing and a curse." Which he portended also into this arrangement of the gospel. Otherwise, what kind of one is he who, to insinuate his own goodness, opposed the harshness of the Creator? Weak is the commendation which is propped on the destruction of another. And yet by opposing the harshness of the Creator he confirmed him one to be feared. If to be feared, surely the rather to be obeyed than neglected; and Marcion's Christ now begins to teach men toward the Creator. Then, if the "Woe" is the Creator's, which looks toward the rich, then Christ is not offended at the rich, but the Creator, and Christ holds ratified the cases of the rich — pride I mean, and glory, and worldly pursuits, and carelessness of God, through which they deserve a "Woe" from the Creator. But how should it not belong to the same one to reprobate the rich who above approved the beggars? Everyone reprobates the contrary of that which he has approved. And so if a malediction against the rich is to be reckoned to the Creator, the benediction of the same upon the beggars will be defended, and the whole work is now the Christ of the Creator's. If the benediction upon the beggars is ascribed to the god of Marcion, the malediction upon the rich too will be imposed upon the same, and he will now be the equal of the Creator, as good as he is judge; nor will there now be room for the distinction by which two gods are made, and, the distinction removed, it will remain to announce one god the Creator. Therefore, if "Woe" is the voice either of malediction or of some sterner outcry, and is directed by Christ against the rich, I must prove the Creator the spurner of the rich too, just as I have proved him the advocate of the beggars, so that I may show Christ in this opinion too the Creator's — who enriched Solomon. But because, leave being given him to choose, he rather asked for those things which he knew pleasing to God, wisdom, he had deserved to obtain riches too, which he willed no more than that. Although it is not unbefitting for God to furnish riches too, by which both the rich are helped with comfort and many works of justice and love are administered thence. But the accidental vices of riches assign that "Woe" upon the rich in your gospel too, "Because," it says, "you have received your consolation" — surely out of riches, from their glory and their secular fruits. And so in Deuteronomy Moses says, "Lest, when thou hast eaten and been filled and built great houses, thy cattle and oxen multiplied and thy money and gold, thy heart be lifted up, and thou forget the Lord thy God." Just as he assails Hezekiah too, a king puffed up with treasures and glorying in them rather than in God, before those who had come from Persia, through Isaiah: "Behold, days come, and all that is in thy house shall be taken away, and what thy fathers laid up shall be transferred to Babylon." So too through Jeremiah he published, "Let not the rich glory in his riches, and let him who glories" — namely in God — "glory." So too he inveighs against the daughters of Zion through Isaiah, puffed up with adornment and abundance of riches, threatening also elsewhere against the noble and proud: "Hell has enlarged its soul and opened its mouth, and the renowned and the great and the rich shall descend" (this will be Christ's "Woe" upon the rich), "and man shall be humbled" — surely exalted by riches — "and a man shall be dishonoured" — surely honourable on account of his substance. Concerning whom again: "Behold, the Lord of powers shall confound the glorious with might, and the lifted up shall be brought low, and the lofty shall fall by the sword." Who more than the rich? — because they have received their consolation, glory and honour, loftiness out of riches. From whom turning us away, in the 48th psalm too, "Fear not," he says, "when a man has been made rich, and when his glory abounds; because when he dies, he shall take nothing, nor shall his glory descend with him." Likewise in the 61st: "Desire not riches, and if they shine, set not your heart." This very word "Woe," lastly, was of old destined through Amos against the rich flowing in delights. "For woe," he says, "to those who sleep in ivory beds and flow in delights on their couches, who eat kids from the flocks of she-goats and suckling calves from the herds of oxen, applauding to the sound of instruments — they have reckoned these as things abiding and not as things fleeting — who drink strained wine and are anointed with the choicest ointments." Therefore, even if I should show the Creator only dehorting from riches, not also pre-condemning the rich — even by the very word with which Christ does — no one would doubt that the threatening upon the rich through Christ's "Woe" was added by the same one from whom the dehortation from the very matters, that is, from riches, had run before. For threatening is an accession to dehortation. He drives in a "Woe" upon the filled too, because they shall hunger; upon those who laugh now too, because they shall mourn. To these will answer those things which above were opposed to the benedictions with the Creator: "Behold, those who serve me shall be filled, but you shall hunger" — surely because you are filled; "and behold, those who serve me shall be delighted, but you shall be confounded" — surely about to weep, who now laugh. For just as in the psalm, "Those who sow in tears shall reap in gladness," so in the gospel, "Those who sow in laughter" — namely out of gladness — "shall reap in tears." These things the Creator of old set together; Christ, only by distinguishing, not by changing, renewed them. "Woe, when men shall bless you. For after these things did their fathers to the false prophets too." Equally the Creator accuses the followers of human benediction and praise through Isaiah: "My people, those who call you blessed seduce you and disturb the ways of your feet." He forbids elsewhere to trust at all in man, so also in the praise of man, as through Jeremiah: "Cursed is the man who has hope in man." For also in the 117th psalm: "It is good to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man, and it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in princes." Thus the Creator forswore all that is caught from man, much more benediction. But to reproach false prophets praised or blessed by their fathers is as much his as to reproach prophets harassed and refused: just as the injuries of the prophets would not have pertained to their god, so neither would the favours toward the false prophets have displeased any but the god of the prophets.

ON THE FIRST EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. It will not weary me to attend to the shorter epistles too. There is savour even in few things. The Jews had killed their own prophets. I can say, What has this to do with an apostle of another and indeed a supremely good God, who is said not even to condemn the offences of his own, and who too, by destroying those same prophets, in a manner slays them himself? For what evil did Israel commit with him, if it killed those whom he too reprobated, if he first pronounced a hostile sentence against them? But it sinned with their own God. He upbraided the iniquity to whom the injured one belongs; surely it is anyone rather than the adversary of the injured. But neither would he have loaded them by imputing the slaying of the Lord too, who both killed the Lord, by saying, and their own prophets — though Their own is the heretic's addition. For what so bitter, if they slew Christ the preacher of another God, who butchered the prophets of their own God? But the standing of the heightening is, that they had slain both the Lord and his servants. In short, if they slew the Christ of one God, the prophets of another, he equalled the impieties, he did not heighten them. But they were not to be equalled; therefore they could not be heightened, except the offences out of either title were committed against the same Lord. Therefore of the same God are both the Christ and the prophets. But what holiness he calls the will of God you would recognise from the contraries which he forbids. For he says, To abstain from fornication, not from marriage; that each should know how to treat his own vessel in honour. How? while not in lust, as the nations. But lust is not, even among the nations, ascribed to marriage, but to extraordinary and unnatural and monstrous things. The law of nature is contrary to luxury, and to baseness too and uncleanness, which excludes not marriage but lust, which would treat our vessel in the honour of marriage. But this passage I have treated with the precedence reserved for the other — that is, the fuller — holiness, preferring continence and virginity to marriage, but not to forbidden marriages. For I rebut the destroyers of the God of marriage, not the followers of chastity. He says that those who remain unto the coming of Christ, together with those who are dead in Christ, who shall first rise, shall be caught up in the clouds into the air, to meet the Lord. I recognise the heavenly substances themselves — even Jerusalem which is above — marvelling at these things already then foreseen, and announcing through Isaiah, Who are these that fly hither like clouds, and like doves with their young to me? If Christ has prepared this ascent for us, that will be the Christ of whom Amos says: Who builds his ascent into the heavens — surely for himself and his own. Thereafter from whom shall I now hope, except from him from whom I heard these things? Whose Spirit does he forbid to be quenched, and what prophecies does he forbid to be held as nothing? Surely not the Creator's Spirit, nor the Creator's prophecies, according to Marcion. For what he destroys, he has already quenched and made nothing, nor can he forbid that which he made nothing. Therefore it lies upon Marcion to exhibit today in his church the Spirit of his God, thenceforth, which is not to be quenched, and prophecies which are not to be held as nothing. And if he has exhibited what he thinks, let him know that we shall challenge whatever it be to the form of spiritual and prophetic grace and power, that it should both foretell things to come and reveal the secrets of the heart and expound mysteries. When he shall have produced and proved nothing of the kind, we shall produce both the Spirit and the prophecies of the Creator, foretelling according to himself. And so it will be established of whom the apostle spoke — namely, of those things which were to be in the church of that God who, while he is, his Spirit too works, and his promise is celebrated. Come now, you who deny the salvation of the flesh, and, whenever the body is named in such a context, interpret it as some other thing I know not what than the substance of the flesh — how did the apostle distinguish all in their new substances by definite names, and set all in the one matter of salvation, wishing that our spirit and body and soul be preserved without complaint at the coming of our Saviour Christ? For he set down both soul and body, as two things, so as two distinct ones. For though the soul too has a body of its own quality, as the spirit also, yet since both body and soul are distinctly named, the soul has its own proper term, not needing the common term of body; that is left to the flesh, which, not named by its own, must of necessity use the common one. For I see no other substance in man, after spirit and soul, to which the term body may be accommodated, except the flesh — understanding this so often under the name of body, as often as it is not named; much more here, since what is called body is named by its own name.

Since, then, no other world appears, any more than its god, it follows that they divide the two kinds of things, the visible and the invisible, between two author-gods, and so claim the invisible things for their own god. But who could persuade himself — except a heretical spirit — that the invisible things are his who has sent ahead nothing visible, rather than His who, having wrought the visible, has also made the invisible credible — since it is far juster to assent to some specimens than to none? We shall see also to which author the apostle reckons the invisible things, when we have examined him too. For now we are paving, by common senses for the most part and by just arguments, the way to faith for the appeal to the Scriptures that is to follow; confirming that this diversity of visible and invisible is so far to be reckoned to the Creator, just as His whole operation consists of diversities: of bodily and incorporeal, of animate and inanimate, of vocal and mute, of mobile and stationary, of fruitful and barren, of dry and moist, of hot and cold. So too has diversity tempered man himself, as well in body as in sense. Some limbs are strong, some weak; some honourable, some unhonourable; some twofold, some single; some matched, some unmatched. Likewise in sense: now gladness, now anxiety; now love, now hatred; now anger, now gentleness. But if it is so, that this whole universe is modulated of mutually rival conditions, then the invisible things too are owed to the visible, to be reckoned to no other author than Him to whom their rivals also are — things which mark the Creator Himself as diverse, commanding what He forbade and forbidding what He commanded, smiting and healing. Why in this one species alone do they take Him as uniform, the founder of visible things only — Him whom we ought accordingly to believe to have founded both the visible and the invisible, just as both life and death, and evils and peace? And surely, if those invisible things are greater than the visible creatures, which are great in their own place, in this way too it is fitting that the greater be His whose the great things also are, since not even the great, much less the greater, can belong to him whose lesser things do not even appear.

Good, then, is severity too, because it is just, if the judge is good, that is, just. Likewise good are the other things through which the good work of good severity runs on, whether anger or jealousy or fierceness. For all these are owed to severity, as severity is owed to justice. The forwardness of an age that owed reverence had to be vindicated. And so the things that accrue to the judge cannot be reproached to the judge, being themselves blameless, even as the judge. For what, if you say that there ought indeed to be a physician, but accuse his instruments because they cut and cauterize and amputate and bind, when without the instrument of his art the physician cannot be? But accuse the man who cuts ill, who amputates unseasonably, who cauterizes rashly, and so reprehend his instruments too as bad ministries. For it is just the same when you indeed admit God as judge, but destroy the motions and senses through which He judges. We are taught God by the prophets and by Christ, not by the philosophers nor by Epicurus. We who believe that God even acted on earth and took on the humility of human estate for the cause of man's salvation, are far from the opinion of those who will not have God care for anything. Thence comes to the heretics too a definition of this kind: if God is angry and jealous and exalted and exasperated, therefore He will also be corrupted, therefore He will also die. But well it is that it belongs to Christians even to believe God dead, and yet living unto the ages of ages. Most foolish are they who prejudge divine things from human, so that, because in man passions of this kind are held to be of a corruptible condition, therefore in God too they are esteemed of the same state. Discern the substances, and distribute to them their senses, as diverse as the substances exact, although they seem to share in the words. For we read both of the right hand and the eyes and the feet of God, nor yet for that reason will they be compared with human ones because they are partners in the appellation. As great as will be the diversity of the divine body and the human under the same names of members, so great will be the difference also between the divine mind and the human under the same words, albeit, of the senses — senses which corruptibility makes so corruptible in man, as incorruptibility makes them so incorruptible in God by the incorruptibility of the divine substance. Surely you confess God the Creator? "Surely," you say. How then do you esteem anything human in God, and not all divine? Him whom you deny not to be God, you confess not to be human; since by confessing Him God you have already prejudged Him surely diverse from every quality of human conditions. Further, since you equally acknowledge man breathed by God into a living soul, not God by man, it is perverse enough that you should set up human things in God rather than divine in man, and clothe God with the image of man rather than man with the image of God. And so this too is to be reckoned the image of God in man: that the human mind have the same motions and senses which God too has, although not such as God; for, according to the substance, both their state and their issue differ. Finally, their contrary senses — gentleness, I mean, patience, mercy, and the very matrix of these, goodness — why do you presume to be divine? Yet we do not perfectly attain them, because God alone is perfect. So too those other kinds, of anger I mean and exasperation, we do not so happily suffer, because God alone is happy of the property of incorruptibility. For He will be angry, but not be exasperated, but not be imperilled; He will be moved, but not be overturned. He must of necessity bring all to bear for the sake of all: as many senses as causes; both anger toward the wicked, and gall toward the ungrateful, and jealousy toward the proud, and whatever is not expedient for the evil. So too mercy toward the erring, and patience toward those who repent not, and pre-eminence toward the deserving, and whatever the good have need of. All these He suffers in His own manner, in which it becomes Him to suffer — He on whose account man suffers the same in his own manner likewise.

Now, if he caught at the name of Christ, as a sneak-thief at a dole-basket, why did he also wish to be called Jesus — a name not so awaited among the Jews? For even if we, having attained by the grace of God an understanding of his mysteries, acknowledge this name too as destined for Christ, it does not follow that to the Jews, from whom wisdom was taken away, the matter will be known. In short, to this day they look for a Christ, not a Jesus, and interpret Christ to be rather Elias than Jesus. He, then, who came also in that name in which the Christ was not presumed, could have come only in that name which alone was presumed. But, since he mixed with God — the awaited and the unawaited — both his counsels are confounded. For if for this reason Christ — that in the meantime he might creep in as it were the Creator's — Jesus stealthily attaches, because a Jesus was not expected in the Christ of the Creator: or if for this reason Jesus — that he might be held another's — Christ does not allow it, because no Christ of another was expected than the Creator's. Which of these can stand, I do not know. But both will stand in the Christ of the Creator, in whom Jesus too is found. "How?" you ask. Learn here too, along with the Jews, the partners of your error. When the successor of Moses was being appointed, Hoshea son of Nun, was he not certainly transferred from his former name and begin to be called Jesus? "Certainly," you say. We say this was first a figure of the future. For because Jesus Christ was to lead the second people — which we are, born in the deserts of the world — into the land of promise flowing with milk and honey, that is, the possession of eternal life, than which nothing is sweeter; and this not through Moses, that is, not through the discipline of the law, but through Jesus, through the grace of the gospel, when we have been circumcised with a knife of stone, that is, with the precepts of Christ — for Christ is a rock — therefore that man, who was being prepared in the images of this mystery, was inaugurated also with the figure of the Lord's name, surnamed Jesus. This name Christ himself testified to be his own even then, when he spoke to Moses. For who spoke, but the Spirit of the Creator, who is Christ? When, then, by command he said to the people, "Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall keep thee in the way and bring thee into the land which I have prepared for thee; attend to him and hearken to him, do not disobey him: for I have not hidden it from thee, since my name is upon him." He called him an angel indeed, on account of the greatness of the powers which he was to put forth, and on account of the office of a prophet, announcing, namely, the divine will; but Jesus, on account of the mystery of his future name. Again and again he confirmed his own name, which he himself had given him, since he had bidden him thenceforth be called not an angel, nor Hoshea, but Jesus. Therefore, if both names suit the Christ of the Creator, so much the more do both not suit the Christ of a non-Creator — just as neither does the rest of the order. There must, then, be made between us, henceforth, this fixed and just objection, necessary to both parties, by which it shall be determined that there ought to be nothing at all common to the Christ of another god with the Christ of the Creator. For the diversity must be defended by you, just as it must be fought against by us; since neither will you be able to prove that the Christ of another god has come, unless you have shown him far other than the Christ of the Creator, nor can we claim him for the Creator, unless we have shown him such as is determined by the Creator. Concerning the names we have now drawn our defences. I claim Christ for myself; I defend Jesus for myself.

"But I say to you," he says, "who hear" (showing this commanded of old by the Creator, "Speak in the ears of those who hear"), "love your enemies, and bless those who hate you, and pray for those who calumniate you." These the Creator shut up in one pronouncement through Isaiah: "Say, You are our brothers, to those who hate you." For if those who are enemies and hate and curse and calumniate are to be called brothers, surely he too commanded the haters to be blessed and the calumniators to be prayed for, who enjoined that they be reckoned brothers. Plainly Christ teaches a new patience, restraining even the requital of injury permitted by the Creator, who demands an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth; on the contrary he himself bids the other cheek besides be offered, and that the cloak too be yielded over the tunic. Plainly these things Christ added as supplements consonant with the discipline of the Creator. And so this is at once to be reported — whether the discipline of patience is proclaimed with the Creator. He commanded through Zechariah that no one should remember the malice of his brother, but not even of his neighbour. For again, "The malice of his neighbour," it says, "let no one reconsider." Much more did he indict patience under injury who indicted forgetfulness. But also when he says, "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay," he accordingly teaches a patience that awaits vengeance. Inasmuch, then, as it does not gain credit that the same one should seem both to demand a tooth for a tooth, an eye for an eye, in requital of injury, who not only forbids requital but even vengeance, even the recollection and reconsideration of injury — by so much is it opened to us how he ordained an eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth, not to permit a second injury of retaliation, which he had forbidden by interdicting vengeance, but to coerce the first, which he had forbidden by the retaliation set against it — so that each one, regarding the licence of a second injury, might contain himself from the first. For he knows that violence is more easily compressed by the representation of retaliation than by the promise of vengeance. But both had to be appointed for the nature and the faith of men, that he who believed God might await vengeance from God, while he who had less faith might fear the laws of retaliation. This will of the law, labouring under the understanding, the Lord both of the sabbath and of the law and of all the paternal arrangements, Christ, both revealed and made effective, commanding the offering of the other cheek too, that he might the more extinguish the requital of injury which the law too had wished to impede through retaliation — certainly which prophecy had manifestly coerced, both forbidding the memory of injury and reducing vengeance to God. Thus if Christ brought in anything, not by an adversary's but by a helper's precept, he did not destroy the disciplines of the Creator. In short, if I consider the very reason of this patience to be enjoined — and that so full and perfect — it will not stand, if he is not the Creator's who promises vengeance, who furnishes a judge. Otherwise, if so great a weight of patience — of not only not striking back but even offering the other cheek, and not only not cursing back but even blessing, and not only not retaining the tunic but even granting the cloak besides — is imposed on me by one who is not to defend me, he commanded patience to no purpose, not exhibiting to me the reward of the precept, the fruit of patience I mean, which is vengeance, which he ought to have permitted me, if he furnishes it not himself, or, if he did not permit it me, to furnish it himself; since it concerns discipline too that injury be avenged. For by fear of vengeance all iniquity is bridled. But, licence being sent forth at large, it will domineer, gouging out both eyes and rousing every tooth in the security of impunity. But this belongs to a best and only good god — to suffer injury to patience, to set open the door to violence, not to defend the upright, not to coerce the wicked. "Give to everyone that asks thee" — surely to the needy, or so much the more to the needy, even though to the abounding too. Lest, then, anyone be needy, you have for the giver a form commanded in Deuteronomy by the Creator. "There shall not be," it says, "in thee a needy man, that blessing he may bless thee, the Lord thy God" — the giver, namely, who shall have caused that there be no needy one. And more here. For he does not bid give to the asker. But "let there not be," he says, "a needy man in thee," that is, take care beforehand that there be not; whereby he the more prejudges that it must be given to the asker, even in what follows. "But if there be a needy man among thy brothers, thou shalt not turn away thy heart, nor close thy hand from a needy brother. Opening thou shalt open thy hand to him, lending thou shalt lend to him as much as he desires." For a loan is not wont to be given but to one who asks. But concerning the loan afterward. Now if anyone wish to argue that the Creator indeed bade give to brothers, but Christ to all who ask, so that this is new and diverse — nay, it will be one of those things through which the law of the Creator will be in Christ. For Christ commanded toward all no other thing than what the Creator did toward brothers. For even though the goodness is greater which works toward strangers, yet it is not prior to that which ought first toward neighbours. For who shall be able to love strangers? But if the second degree of goodness is toward strangers, which toward neighbours is the first, the second degree will belong to the same one whose is the first too, more easily than that the second should be his whose the first did not exist. Thus the Creator both, according to the order of nature, taught benignity first toward neighbours, intending to send it forth afterward toward strangers, and, according to the reason of his arrangement, first toward the Jews, afterward toward all the human race too. And therefore, so long as the mystery was within Israel, with reason he commanded mercy upon brothers alone; but when to Christ he gave the nations for an inheritance and the ends of the earth for a possession, and that began to be discharged which was said through Hosea, "Not my people, my people, and she that has not obtained mercy, having obtained mercy" — namely the nation — then Christ extended toward all the law of the paternal benignity, excepting no one in commiseration, as none in vocation. Thus even if he taught anything more, this too he received into the inheritance of the nations. "And as you wish men to do to you, so do you also to them." In this precept surely the other part of it is understood: "And as you do not wish men to do to you, so do you also not do to them." If a new and hitherto unknown god and not yet plainly published commanded this, who had formed me by no prior institution, by which I might first know what I ought to wish or not wish for myself, and so do to others what I should wish for myself, and not do what I should not wish for myself — he permitted my opinion to be promiscuous, and did not bind me to a conformity of will and deed, so that I should do to others what I should wish for myself and should not do to others what I should not wish for myself. For he did not define what I ought to wish or not wish for myself and for others, so that, to a law of will I might match my deed, and might both not furnish to another what I should wish furnished to me by another — love, obedience, comfort, protection, and such goods — and likewise do to another what I should not wish done to me by another — violence, injury, contumely, fraud, and such evils. In short, by this inconformity of will and deed act the ethnics, not yet instructed by God. For even if good and evil are known by nature, yet not the discipline of God, by which known, then at last a conformity of will and deed out of faith, as under the fear of God, is enacted. And so the god of Marcion, though most fully revealed, yet, revealed, could not have sent forth a compendium of this precept of which we treat, so strict and obscure and still blind and the more easily to be interpreted according to my own choice rather — of which he had built up beforehand no distinction. But my Creator both of old and everywhere commanded the needy, the poor and orphans and widows, to be protected, helped, refreshed; as also through Isaiah: "Break thy bread to the beggars, and those who are without a roof bring into thy house, and if thou see one naked, cover him." Likewise through Ezekiel, of the just man: "His bread he shall give to the hungry, and shall cover the naked." Sufficiently, then, even then he taught me to do to others those things which I should wish done to me. Accordingly, denouncing, "Thou shalt not kill, Thou shalt not commit adultery, Thou shalt not steal, Thou shalt not bear false witness," he taught me not to do to others what I should not wish done to me; and therefore the precept in the gospel will belong to him who both built it up beforehand and distinguished it and arranged it according to the choice of his discipline, and now with reason has bound it up in a compendium — since in other respects too the Lord, that is Christ, was proclaimed as one who would make a curtailed word upon the earth.

ON THE SECOND EPISTLE TO THE THESSALONIANS. We are compelled to repeat certain things again and again, that we may confirm by them what coheres. We say that here too the Lord, the recompenser of either merit, is carried about by the apostle — either the Creator, or, what Marcion would not have, the equal of the Creator — with whom it is just that to our afflicters affliction should be repaid, and to us, who are afflicted, rest, in the revelation of the Lord Jesus coming from heaven with the angels of his power and in a flame of fire. But the flame and fire which I defend the heretic has quenched, lest, namely, he should make the God ours. Yet the vanity of the erasure shines out. For when the apostle writes that the Lord will come to vengeance, to be exacted of those who know not God and who obey not the gospel — whom he says shall pay a penalty of destruction, eternal, from the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might — it follows that he introduces a flame of fire, namely, coming to punish. So here too, though Marcion be unwilling, Christ is of the burning God, and in that other it is the Creator's, that he avenges himself even on those who know not the Lord, that is, on the heathen. For he set apart, Those who obey not the gospel — whether Christian sinners or Jews. Further, to exact penalties of the heathen, who perchance do not know the gospel, is not the part of that God who is naturally unknown, and is nowhere revealed except in the gospel, not knowable to all. But to the Creator even a natural acknowledgement is owed, by understanding from his works and thence seeking unto fuller knowledge. His, therefore, it is to strike even those ignorant of God, whom it is not lawful to be ignorant of. The very thing he says, From the face of the Lord and from the glory of his might, using the words of Isaiah, savours from the very cause of the same Lord rising up to shatter the earth. But who is the man of sin, the son of perdition, who must first be revealed before the Lord's coming, exalting himself above all that is called God and above all religion, about to sit in the temple of God and to boast himself God? According to us, indeed, antichrist, as the old and new prophecies teach, as John the apostle, who says that already the antichrists have gone forth into the world, forerunners of the spirit of antichrist, denying that Christ has come in the flesh, and dissolving Jesus — namely, in God the Creator: but according to Marcion, I do not know whether he be the Christ of the Creator. He has not yet come, with him. But whichever of the two he is, I ask why he comes in all power and signs and lying wonders? Therefore, he says, because they received not the love of the truth, that they might be saved; and for this there shall be sent them a working of deceit, that all may be judged who believed not the truth, but consented to iniquity. Therefore, if it is antichrist — and according to the Creator — then the Creator will be God who sends him to thrust into error those who believed not the truth that they might be saved; his too will be the truth and salvation who avenges them by the suggestion of error — that is, the Creator's, to whom the very zeal belongs of deceiving by error those whom he did not take by truth. But if it is not antichrist, according to us, then it is the Christ of the Creator, according to Marcion. And what manner of thing will it be that, to avenge his own truth, he should send the Christ of the Creator? But if he agrees too about antichrist, I shall likewise say: What manner of thing is it that Satan, an angel of the Creator, should be necessary to him, and be slain by him, having to discharge the working of deceit for the Creator? In sum, if it is beyond doubt that the angel and the truth and the salvation are his whose are also the wrath and the emulation and the sending of deceits against the despisers and deserters, even against the ignorant (so that now Marcion too may come down a step, conceding his God too to be a zealous one) — who shall more worthily be angry? I think, he who from the beginning of things prepared nature by works, benefits, plagues, preachings, witnesses, unto the acknowledgement of himself, and yet was not acknowledged; or he who once, by the single instrument of the gospel — and that uncertain, surely not openly preaching another God — was brought forth? So, to whom vengeance befits, to him will befit the material of vengeance — I mean the gospel, and the truth and salvation. But that he should bid him work who would eat, is the discipline of him who ordered a free mouth for the ox treading out the corn.

Hemmed in by these things, they break out into saying: "It is enough for our god, this one work, that he set man free by his supreme and surpassing goodness, to be preferred to all the locusts." O greater god, whose so great a work could not be found greater than in the man of a lesser god! Indeed, the first thing is for you to prove that he exists by the means whereby a god must be proved — by works; and then secondly by benefits. For first it is asked whether he exists, and so, what sort he is. The one is discerned from works, the other from benefits. But not because he is said to have set man free is it thereby established that he exists; rather, if it shall be established that he exists, then it will also be said that he set free, so that it may be established even whether he set free — since he might both exist and not have set free. How then, because he will be said to have set free, will he also be believed to exist, when he might both exist and not have set free? Now in this article, drawn off from the question of the unknown god, it has been sufficiently established that he made nothing, just as he ought to have made, in order to be known from his works; because, if he had existed, he ought to have been known — and certainly from the beginning of things; for it did not become God to lie hid. I must of necessity go back to the origin of the question of the unknown god, to shake out its other little branches too. For first it will have to be asked: he who afterwards brought himself into knowledge — why afterwards, and not from the beginning of things? — for to those to whom he was surely necessary, in so far as a god, and indeed the more necessary the better he was, he ought not to have lain hid. For it cannot be said that there was no material or cause for knowing the god, since both man was from the beginning in the world, to whom he now comes to aid, and the malice of the Creator was there, against which, as a good god, he comes to aid. Therefore either he was ignorant both of the cause and the material of his necessary revelation, or he doubted, or he was unable, or he was unwilling. All these are unworthy of God, especially of a best god. But this point too we will fill out elsewhere with reproach of the late revelation, as now with mere demonstration.

These things, so discerned, show the whole order of God the judge to be the worker — and, that I may say it more worthily, the protector — of that catholic and supreme goodness which, set apart from judicial senses and pure in its own state, the Marcionites will not acknowledge in the same God, raining upon the good and the evil and making His sun to rise upon the just and the unjust — which the other god by no means bestows. For even though this testimony too of Christ against the Creator Marcion dared to erase from the gospel, yet the very world is inscribed with it and is read of by every conscience. And this very patience of the Creator will be unto Marcion's judgment — that patience which awaits the sinner's repentance rather than his death, and prefers mercy to sacrifice, already turning aside the destruction destined for the Ninevites, and lavishing space of life upon Hezekiah's tears, and restoring the state of his kingdom to the tyrant of Babylon feigning repentance: I mean that mercy which both granted to the people the son of Saul who was to die by a vow, and freed David, confessing his sins against the house of Uriah, by pardon, and so often restored Israel itself as often as it judged, so often washed it as often as it rebuked. Not therefore, looking only at the judge, turn aside — turn also to the examples of the best. While you note Him when He avenges, consider Him when He indulges. Weigh leniency against austerity. When you have met with both in the Creator, you will find in Him also that on account of which you believe in another god. Come, finally, to the inspection of His doctrines, disciplines, precepts, and counsels. You will say perhaps that these are determined also by human laws. But before all the Lycurguses and Solons, Moses and God. No posterity but receives from the beginnings. Yet it was not from your god that my Creator learned to prescribe, "You shall not kill, you shall not commit adultery, you shall not steal, you shall not bear false witness, you shall not covet another's, honour father and mother, and you shall love your neighbour as yourself." To these chief counsels of innocence, chastity, and justice and piety, there accrue also the prescriptions of humanity: when in every seventh year slaves are loosed into liberty; when at the same time the field is spared, yielding place to the needy; when even to the ox that treads out the corn the bonds of his mouth are loosed, unto the fruit of his present labour — that the more easily a humanity, premeditated in cattle, might be schooled toward the refreshment of men.

Let us compare the rest of his order with the Scriptures. Whatever that little body of his may be — since it both had a state and was beheld — if inglorious, if ignoble, if without honour, mine will be the Christ; for such was he announced in state and aspect. Isaiah is here again: "We announced," he says, "in his presence: as a little child, as a root in a thirsting earth; and he has no comeliness nor glory, and we saw him, and he had no comeliness nor beauty, but his appearance was without honour, failing beyond all men." Just as also the Father's voice above to the Son: "As many shall be astonished at thee, so shall thy form be without glory from men." For even if "seasonable in beauty beyond the sons of men," in David above — yet in that allegorical state of spiritual grace, when he is girt with the sword of the word, which is truly his comeliness and beauty and glory. Otherwise, in an incorporeal state, in the same prophet he is a worm even and not a man, the shame of man and the outcast of the people. Nor does he announce his inner quality to be of this sort. For if the fullness of the spirit settled in him, I acknowledge the rod from the root of Jesse. Its flower will be my Christ, upon whom, according to Isaiah, rested the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and might, the spirit of acknowledgement and piety, the spirit of the fear of God. For to no man could this diversity of spiritual evidences have belonged except in Christ — likened to a flower for the grace of the spirit, but reckoned from the stock of Jesse, to be counted thence through Mary. But I demand, of set purpose: if you grant him the whole bent of humility and patience and tranquillity, will he, on the strength of these, be the Christ of Isaiah? "A man under stroke, and knowing how to bear weakness, who was led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a lamb before the shearer opened not his mouth"; who neither strove nor cried, nor was his voice heard abroad; who did not break the bruised reed — that is, the shattered faith of the Jews; who did not quench the burning flax — that is, the momentary ardour of the Gentiles. He can be none other than the one foretold. His act must be recognized by the rule of the Scriptures, distinguished, unless I am mistaken, by a twofold operation: of preaching and of power. But concerning both titles I will so arrange it that — since it has been resolved to discuss Marcion's gospel too — we shall defer to that point, as to the matter actually in hand, the species of doctrines and signs. Here, however, let us in general work off the order we have begun, teaching that meanwhile Christ is announced a preacher through Isaiah: "For who," he says, "among you fears God, and will hearken to the voice of his Son?" Likewise a healer. "For he himself," he says, "took away our weaknesses, and bore our infirmities."

Here now, when he interposes concerning the loan, "And if you lend to those from whom you hope to receive, what grace is it to you?" run through what follows in Ezekiel concerning the same just man: "His money," it says, "he has not given for usury, and what abounds he will not take" — the redundancy of the loan, namely, which is interest. First, then, it was that he should root out the fruit of the loan, that he might the more easily accustom a man to lose even the very loan, if at all, whose fruit he had learned to forgo. For this we say was the work of the law, providing for the gospel. The faith of certain men then, little by little, toward the perfect lustre of Christian discipline, it was forming by those first precepts of a benignity still stammering. For above too, "And the pledge," it says, "thou shalt restore to the giver" — surely if he be not able to pay, since to a payer the pledge would in any case be restored without his writing it. Much more manifestly in Deuteronomy: "Thou shalt not sleep upon his pledge; restoring thou shalt restore to him his cloak about the setting of the sun, and he shall sleep in his cloak." More clearly still above: "Thou shalt remit every debt which thy neighbour owes thee, and thy brother thou shalt not demand back, because the remission of the Lord thy God has been invoked." Now when he bids the debt be remitted, surely to one not about to pay (for it is more, even if he be about to pay, when he forbids it to be demanded back), what else does he teach than that we should lend to one not about to pay, who indicted so great a loss upon the loan? "And you shall be sons of God." Nothing more shameless, if he shall make us sons to himself who did not permit us to make sons by taking away marriage. How will he draw his own into that name which he has already erased? I cannot be the son of a eunuch, especially when I have the same Father whom even the universe has. For he is as much the Father of all, being the founder of the universe, as a eunuch is the founder of no substance. And even if the Creator had not mingled male and female, even if he had not granted sons to all the animals too, this I was of his before paradise, before delinquency, before exile, before the two were one. Anew I was made a son, straightway when he brought me forth with his hands, when he moved me with his breath. He now again names me son, begetting me now not into a soul, but into a spirit. "Because he," it says, "is sweet toward the ungrateful and evil." Well done, Marcion; ingeniously enough you took from him the rains and suns, lest the Creator should appear. But who is this sweet one, who has not even hitherto been known? How sweet, from whom no benefits of this kind of sweetness, of suns and rains, had preceded, who had lent them? — one not about to receive again from the human race, like the Creator, who, for so great a liberality of the elements, still bears with men rendering the debt of gratitude more readily to idols than to himself. Truly sweet even in spiritual commodities. For "the utterances of the Lord are sweeter than honey and the honeycombs." He, then, censured the ungrateful too who deserved to find men grateful, whose sun and rains even you, Marcion, held in ingratitude. But yours could not now complain of the ungrateful, who had not prepared grateful ones. Commanding mercy too, "Be," he says, "merciful, as your Father has had mercy on you." This will be, "Break thy bread to the hungry, and those without a roof bring into thy house, and if thou see one naked, cover him," and, "Judge the orphan, and justify the widow." I acknowledge his old teaching, who prefers mercy to sacrifice. Or if another has now commanded mercy, because he himself too is merciful, why was he not merciful to me for so great an age? "Do not judge, lest you be judged. Do not condemn, lest you be condemned. Forgive, and you shall be forgiven. Give, and it shall be given to you — a good measure, pressed down and overflowing, they shall give into your bosom. With the same measure with which you have measured, it shall be measured back to you." As I think, these things sound a retribution provoked according to merits. From whom, then, the retribution? If from men only, then he teaches a human discipline and reward, and we shall obey men altogether: if from the Creator, as from a judge and assessor of merits, then he impels our obedience toward him with whom he has appointed the retribution to be caught at or feared, according as each shall have judged or condemned or forgiven or measured: if from himself, then he too now judges, which Marcion denies. Let the Marcionites therefore choose whether it be worth so much to fall away from the rule of their master as it is worth to have a Christ teaching either for men or for the Creator. But the blind leads the blind into the pit. Some believe Marcion. But the disciple is not above his master. This Apelles ought to have remembered, the emendator of the disciple Marcion. Let the heretic too take the beam out of his own eye, then let him censure, if any, the straw he thinks in the eye of the Christian. Accordingly the good tree too does not bring forth evil fruit, because neither does truth heresy, nor the evil good, because neither does heresy truth. So neither did Marcion bring forth anything good out of the evil treasure of Cerdo, nor Apelles out of Marcion's. For much more congruently shall we interpret of these men those things which Christ allegorized of men, not of two gods according to the scandal of Marcion. I think I am not rashly insisting thus far still upon this line, by which I define that nowhere at all was another god revealed by Christ. In this one adultery I marvel that the hand of Marcion grew numb. Unless that even robbers are afraid. No misdeed is without dread, because neither without consciousness of itself. So long, then, did the Jews too know no other god than him besides whom they knew none as yet, nor call any other god than him whom alone they knew. If it is so, who will seem to have said, "Why do you call me, Lord, Lord?" Either he who had never been so called, as one nowhere as yet published, or he who was always held to be Lord, as known from the beginning, the god of the Jews, namely? Who likewise could have added, "And do not do what I say?" Either he who at that moment was trying to teach, or he who from the beginning had committed to them the utterances both of the law and the prophets? Who could also reproach them with disobedience, even if he had never reproached them otherwise? Now he who before Christ harangued, "This people loves me with their lips, but their heart stands far off from me," surely imputed to them an old contumacy. Otherwise, how absurd, that a new god, a new Christ, the illuminator of a new and so great a religion, should pronounce contumacious and disobedient those whom he could not have tried.

ON THE EPISTLE TO THE LAODICEANS. By the truth of the church, we hold this epistle sent to the Ephesians, not to the Laodiceans; but Marcion at some time desired to interpolate its title, as though he too were a most diligent investigator in this matter. But nothing turns on the titles, since the apostle wrote to all when he wrote to some — yet certainly preaching in Christ that God to whom belong the things that are preached. To whom, then, will they belong, according to the good pleasure which he set forth in the sacrament of his will, unto a dispensation of the fulfilment of the times (so to speak, as that word sounds in the Greek) to recapitulate — that is, to bring back to the beginning, or to review from the beginning — all things in Christ which are in the heavens and which are on earth — except him whose are all things from the beginning, even the very beginning, from which are both the times and the dispensation of the fulfilment of the times, on account of which all things are reviewed unto the beginning in Christ? But of another God what is the beginning — that is, the whence — whose work is none? what times without a beginning? what fulfilment without times? what dispensation without fulfilment? In short, what did he do on earth already of old, that any long dispensation of the times to be fulfilled should be reckoned, unto the reviewing of all things in Christ, even of those which are in the heavens? Nor shall we suppose that the things in the heavens, whatever they are, were wrought by another than by him by whom it is established that the things on earth too were wrought, by all consent. But if it cannot be that all these things are reckoned of another God from the beginning than the Creator, who will believe that they are reviewed by another unto another Christ, and not by their own author and unto his own Christ? If they are the Creator's, of necessity they must be diverse, since of a diverse God; if diverse, surely contrary. How then are contraries reviewed unto him by whom in the end they are destroyed? For also, what Christ do the following words announce, when he says, That we should be unto the praise of his glory, who first hoped in Christ? For who could have first hoped, that is, hoped before he came, in God, except the Jews, to whom Christ was foretold from the beginning? He, then, who was foretold was also first hoped in. And so this he refers to himself, that is, to the Jews, that he may make a distinction, turning to the nations: In whom you too, when you had heard the word of truth, the gospel, in whom you believed and were sealed with the holy Spirit of his promise. Of what promise? made through Joel: In the last days I will pour out of my Spirit upon all flesh — that is, upon the nations too. So both the Spirit and the gospel will be in that Christ who was first hoped in, while he was being preached. But the Father of glory too is he whose Christ is sung the King of glory in the psalm, ascending: Who is this King of glory? the Lord of hosts, he is the King of glory. From him is the Spirit of wisdom desired, with whom this species too of spiritual things is enumerated among the seven spirits through Isaiah. He will give the enlightened eyes of the heart who enriched the outward eyes too with light, who is displeased with the blindness of the people. And who is blind but my children? you are blinded, the servants of God. With him too are the riches of the inheritance in the saints, who promised that inheritance out of the calling of the nations. Ask of me, and I will give you the nations for your inheritance. He wrought in Christ his might, by raising him from the dead, and placing him at his right hand, and subjecting all things — who also said, Sit at my right hand, till I make your enemies the footstool of your feet; because also elsewhere the Spirit says to the Father concerning the Son, You have subjected all things under his feet. If from these things another God and another Christ are inferred, which are recognised in the Creator, let us now seek the Creator. Plainly, I think, we find him, when he says that those were dead in the offences in which they had walked, according to the age of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, who works in the sons of unbelief. But the world here too Marcion cannot interpret as the God of the world. For the made is not like the maker, the thing fashioned like the fashioner, the world like God. Nor will he be called the prince of the power of the air who is the prince of the power of the ages. For never is the president of the higher noted from the lower, though the lower too are reckoned to him. Nor can he be seen as the worker of unbelief, which he himself rather suffers both from the Jews and from the nations. It is enough, then, if these things do not fall upon the Creator. But if there is also one to whom they better befit, surely the apostle knew this the better. Who is he? Without doubt that one who obstructs against the Creator himself the sons of unbelief, having gained possession of this air, as the prophet reports him saying: I will set my throne in the clouds; I will be like the Most High. This will be the devil, whom elsewhere too (if indeed they will so have the apostle read) we shall acknowledge as the god of this age. For thus he has filled the whole world with the lie of his divinity. And plainly, if he had not been, then these things might have looked toward the Creator. But the apostle too had walked in Judaism. Not because he interposed about offences, in which we too all walked, is the Creator on that account to be understood the lord of offences and prince of this air; but because in Judaism he had been one of the sons of unbelief, having the devil as his worker, when he persecuted the church and Christ of the Creator — on which account too, We were, he says, children of wrath, but by nature. Lest, because the Creator called the Jews sons, the heretic argue from this that the Creator is the lord of wrath. For when he says, We were by nature children of wrath, but the Jews are not by nature the sons of the Creator, but by the election of the fathers, he referred the children of wrath to nature, not to the Creator — to sum it up, subjoining, As also the rest, who surely are not the sons of God. It appears that to the common nature of all men are reckoned both offences and the concupiscences of the flesh and unbelief and wrath, the devil nevertheless seizing upon nature, which he too has already infected by the seed of sin brought in. We are, he says, his workmanship, created in Christ. It is one thing to make, another to create; but he gave both to one. Now man is the workmanship of the Creator. The same, then, created in Christ who also made. For as far as concerns substance, he made; as far as concerns grace, he created. Look at the cohering words too. Remember that you were once nations in the flesh, who were called uncircumcision by that which is called circumcision in the flesh, made by hand; that you were at that time without Christ, alienated from the converse of Israel and strangers to their testaments and promise, having no hope, and without God in the world. But without what God were the nations, and without what Christ? Surely him whose was the converse of Israel and the testaments and the promise. But now, he says, in Christ you who were far off are made near in his blood. From whom were they formerly far off? From those whom he names above: from the Christ of the Creator, from the converse of Israel, from the testaments, from the hope of the promise, from God himself. If these things are so, then the nations are now made near in Christ to those from whom they were then far off. But if to the converse of Israel, which is in the religion of God the Creator, and to the testaments — from God himself. If these things are so, then they are now made near, by calling, to those called from afar. They who were far from me have drawn near to my righteousness. For both the righteousness and the peace of the Creator were announced in Christ, as we have often already shown. And so, He himself, he says, is our peace, who made the two one — the Jewish people, namely, and the Gentile. The near and the far, the middle wall of enmity being dissolved, in his flesh. But Marcion took away His, that he might give the enmity to the flesh, as though to a carnal vice, not to a flesh hostile to Christ. Thus, as I said elsewhere, here too, not Marrucinian but Pontic, whose blood you confessed above, here you deny the flesh. If he made void the law of precepts by decrees — surely by fulfilling the law (for now there is no force in, You shall not commit adultery, when it is said, You shall not even look to lust; there is no force in, You shall not kill, when it is said, You shall not even curse) — he cannot make an adversary of the law out of one who assists it. That he might create the two in himself — who had made the same, creating (according to what is above too: We are his workmanship, created in Christ) — into one new man, making peace (if truly new, then truly a man too, not a phantasm; but new and newly — that is, newly born of a virgin by the Spirit of God) — that he might reconcile both to God, even to the God whom both kinds had offended, both the Jewish and the Gentile people, in one body, he says, having slain the enmity in it through the cross. So here too the flesh is the body in Christ, which could suffer the cross. This, then, announcing peace to those near and to those far, having obtained access together to the Father, we are now no longer strangers nor sojourners, but fellow-citizens of the saints, and of the household of God (surely of him from whom we showed above that we were aliens and set far off), built upon the foundation of the apostles. The heretic took away, And of the prophets, forgetting that the Lord set in the church, as apostles, so prophets too. He feared, namely, lest our building in Christ should stand even upon the foundations of the old prophets, since the apostle himself everywhere does not cease to build us up out of the prophets. For whence did he take to call Christ the chief cornerstone, except from the signification of the psalm: The stone which the builders rejected, the same is made into the head of the corner?

Suppose, then, that he came forth into knowledge when he willed, when he was able, when the fatal hour arrived. For perhaps the ascending node stood in his way, or some malefic stars, or a quartile Saturn, or a trine Mars. For the Marcionites are very much astrologers too, and not even blushing at this, that they live by the very stars of the Creator. Here too we must treat of the quality of the revelation: whether he was worthily known, that it may be established whether truly, and so be believed to be the one who shall be established to have been worthily revealed. For things worthy of God will prove God. We define that God is to be known first by nature, then to be recognized by teaching: by nature from works, by teaching from preachings. But to him who has no nature, the instruments of nature are not at hand. Therefore he ought at least to have wrought the revelation of himself by preachings — especially as he had to be revealed against Him who, by works of creation and preaching so many and so great, had nevertheless scarcely filled out the faith of men. How then was he revealed? If by human conjecture, deny that God can be known otherwise than through Himself — challenging not only to the form of the Creator, but also to the condition both of so great a divine greatness and of so small a human mediocrity; lest man be able to seem greater than God, who has, as it were, dragged Him into the public view of recognition by his own forces, though He did not willingly wish to be known — when human mediocrity knows, according to the experiences of every age, more easily to fashion gods for itself than to pursue the true one, whom by nature it already understands. Otherwise, if man will invent a god in the way that Romulus invented Consus and Tatius Cloacina and Hostilius Pavor and Metellus Alburnus and a certain one before this time Antinous, this will be lawful for others too. We know Marcion to have been a shipmaster, not a king or an emperor.

But what goods of the law shall I defend rather than those which the heresy has coveted? — as the definition of retaliation, demanding eye for eye, tooth for tooth, and bruise for bruise. For it does not savour of a licence for mutually exercising injury, but provides for the wholesale restraining of violence; so that, because to a most hardened and faithless people toward God it would seem long, or even incredible, to await defence from God — to be edicted afterward through the prophet, "Vengeance is mine, and I will repay, says the Lord" — meanwhile the committing of injury, by the fear of the requital straightway to be encountered, might be dug up by the roots; and the licence of retribution be a prohibition of provocation, so that, in this way, the wickedness once heated might cease, while the second, being permitted, terrifies the first, and the first, being terrified, even the second is not committed; whereby otherwise too the fear of retaliation is the easier through the same taste of the suffering. Nothing is more bitter than to suffer that very thing which you did to others. And if the law subtracts something from foods and pronounces unclean certain animals which once were blessed, understand it a counsel for the exercising of continence, and acknowledge the reins imposed upon that gullet which, when it ate the bread of angels, desired the cucumbers and melons of the Egyptians. Acknowledge at the same time the provision made for the companions of the gullet, namely lust and luxury, which mostly grow cold by the chastening of the belly. For the people had eaten and drunk and risen up to play. Accordingly, that the ardour for money too might be partly restrained — in so far as it pleads the necessity of sustenance — the ambition for costly foods was subtracted. Finally, that man might be the more easily fashioned to fast for God, being accustomed to few and inglorious viands, and going to hunger for nothing of the more sumptuous things. The Creator is to be reproached, forsooth, that He took foods rather from His own people than from the more ungrateful Marcionites. Let no one reproach also the burdens of sacrifices and the busy scrupulosities of operations and oblations, as though God desired such things properly for Himself, who so manifestly cries out, "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?" and, "Who has required these things at your hands?" But let him perceive that diligence of God whereby He willed to bind to His own religion, by offices of this kind, a people prone to idolatry and transgression — by the very things in which the superstition of the world was carried on — that He might call them away from it, commanding things to be done to Himself, as though desiring them, lest they should sin by making images.

Concerning his end, plainly, I think, they bring in difficulty when challenged, denying that the passion of the cross was proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator, and arguing besides that it is not to be believed that the Creator exposed his son to that kind of death which he himself had cursed. "Cursed," he says, "is everyone that hangs upon a tree." But the sense of this curse I defer, worthy of the sole proclamation of the cross, about which the inquiry now chiefly turns, since in other respects the proof of the facts comes before the discussion of the reason. Concerning the figures I will first instruct you. And surely it was above all fitting that this mystery should be figured in the proclamation — by how much it was incredible, by so much the more bound to be a scandal if it were proclaimed nakedly; and by how much it was magnificent, by so much the more to be overshadowed, so that the difficulty of understanding might seek the grace of God. And so, first of all, Isaac, when, given over by his father for a victim, he himself carried the wood for himself, even then marked out the death of Christ — yielded by the Father to be a victim and bearing the wood of his passion. Joseph too himself figures Christ, and not by this alone (that I may not delay the course): that he suffered persecution from his brothers for the grace of God, just as Christ too from the Jews, his brothers after the flesh, when he is blessed by his father even in these words: "His comeliness is that of a bull, his horns are the horns of a unicorn; with them shall he winnow the nations alike, even to the farthest part of the earth." Surely no rhinoceros was destined as the unicorn, nor a minotaur as the two-horned; but Christ was signified in him — a bull, for his twofold arrangement, to some fierce as a judge, to others mild as a saviour, whose horns would be the extremities of the cross. For even in the cross-beam, which is a part of the cross, the extremities are called horns; while the unicorn is the middle stake of the upright post. By this power of the cross, then, and in this manner horned, he now winnows all the nations through faith, lifting them from earth to heaven; and then he will winnow them by judgement, casting them down from heaven to earth. The same will be also elsewhere a bull, in the same Scripture, when Jacob is spiritually interpreted concerning Simeon and Levi, that is, concerning the scribes and Pharisees — for from them is derived the descent of these men. "Simeon and Levi accomplished iniquity out of their own heresy" — by which, namely, they persecuted Christ. "Into their council let not my soul come, and upon their station let not my inwards lean; for in their indignation they slew men" — that is, the prophets — "and in their concupiscence they hamstrung a bull" — that is, Christ, whom, after the slaying of the prophets, they raged against by fastening his sinews, namely, with nails. Otherwise it is idle, if after men slain he reproaches them with the slaughter of some ox. And now Moses — why, precisely then, when Joshua was fighting against Amalek, did he pray sitting with hands outspread, when in matters so alarming he ought rather to have commended his prayer with knees bowed and hands smiting the breast and face rolling on the ground — unless because there, where the name of the Lord was contending (to contend one day against the devil), the posture of the cross too was necessary, by which Joshua was to carry off the victory? And again, the same Moses — after the likeness of every thing had been forbidden — why did he set forth a brazen serpent placed upon a tree, in the posture of one hanging, for a saving spectacle? Was he not here too intending the power of the Lord's cross, by which the serpent, the devil, was published, and to everyone wounded by the spiritual serpents, yet looking upon it and believing in it, healing of the bites of sins and salvation thence were proclaimed?

Likewise, the faith of the centurion being extolled, it is incredible if he professed that he had found no such faith even in Israel, to whom the faith of Israel did not pertain. But neither thence could it have pertained, still raw to be proved or compared, not to say still none. But why should it not have been lawful for him to use the example of an alien faith? Because, if it were so, he would have said that such faith had never even been in Israel; but in saying that such faith he ought to have found in Israel — he indeed who had come for this, that he might find it, namely the god and the Christ of Israel — he would not have censured it but as the exactor and follower of it.
