But a rival would even have preferred it found such, for the weakening and destroying of which he had rather come, not for the approving. He raised up too the dead son of the widow. No new evidence. This even the prophets of the Creator had put forth; how much more the Son? But so far up to that moment had the Lord Christ brought in no other god, that they all there rendered glory to the Creator, saying, "A great prophet has come forth among us, and God has regarded his people." What god? Surely whose the people was, and from whom the prophets. But if they indeed glorified the Creator, while Christ both hearing and knowing did not correct them — and that in so great an evidence of a dead man raised up, still praying to the Creator — without doubt either he carried about no other god than him whom he suffered to be honoured in his own benefits and powers, or what kind of thing is it that he suffered them so long to err, having come for this, that he might heal their error? But John is scandalized at hearing of the powers of Christ, as of another's. But I will first explain the reason of the scandal, that I may the more easily explode the heretic's scandal. The Lord of powers being now himself, the Word and the Spirit of the Father working on earth and preaching, it was necessary that the portion of the Holy Spirit — which, after the form of a prophetic measure, had wrought in John the preparation of the Lord's ways — should now withdraw from John, reduced, namely, into the Lord, as into its own mass-sum. And so John, now a common man, and now one of the crowd, was scandalized indeed as a man, but not as one hoping for or understanding another Christ, who would neither hope for the same one as teaching or working nothing new. No one will hesitate concerning someone whom, while he knows him not to exist, he neither hopes for nor understands; but John was certain of no god besides the Creator, both as a Jew and as a prophet. Plainly he hesitated, as it were, about one whom, though he knew him to exist, whether he himself were he he knew not. By this fear, then, John too: "Art thou," he says, "he that cometh, or do we look for another?" — simply inquiring whether he himself had come whom he was awaiting. "Art thou he that cometh," that is, who art to come, "or do we look for another?" — that is, is there another whom we look for, if thou art not he whom we look for as to come? For he hoped, as all supposed, that from a likeness of the evidences a prophet too might meanwhile have been sent, from whom another should be, that is, greater — the very Lord, namely, who was awaited as to come. And this then was John's scandal, that he doubted whether he himself had come whom they awaited, whom they ought to have acknowledged also by the proclaimed operations — so that the Lord announced to John that he was to be acknowledged through those same operations. And since these are established to have been proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator, as we have shown at each point, it is perverse enough that by those things he should have announced that a Christ not of the Creator was to be understood, through which he the rather compelled the Christ of the Creator to be acknowledged. Much more perverse, if the Christ who was not John's bears testimony to John, confirming him a prophet — nay, even above as an angel — driving in too what was written concerning him: "Behold, I send my angel before thy face, who shall prepare thy way" — elegantly, toward the former sense of the scandalized John, commemorating the prophecy, that, confirming the forerunner John already to have come, he might extinguish the scruple of that interrogation, "Art thou he that cometh, or do we look for another?" For, the forerunner having now discharged his office, the way of the Lord prepared, he himself was to be understood, to whom the forerunner had ministered — greater indeed than all born of women, but not therefore subject to him who should be lesser in the kingdom of God; as though the kingdom were of one god in which someone modest shall be greater than John, and John, who is greater than all born of women, of another. For whether he speaks, through humility, of someone modest, or of himself, because he was held lesser than John — all, namely, running together into the wilderness to John rather than to Christ ("What did you go out into the wilderness to see?") — equally it both befits the Creator both that John is greater than all born of women, and that Christ, or any modest one, should be greater than John in the kingdom equally of the Creator, and that he who was not scandalized at Christ — which then made John less — should be greater than so great a prophet. We have spoken concerning remission of sins. But the argument of that sinful woman will tend hither: that, when she fastened with kisses the feet of the Lord, inundated them with tears, wiped them with her hair, smeared them with ointment, she handled the truth of a solid body, not an empty phantom; and that the penitence of the sinner deserved pardon according to the Creator, accustomed to prefer it to sacrifice. But also, if the goad of penitence had come by faith, through penitence justified by faith she heard from him, "Thy faith has made thee safe," who through Habakkuk had pronounced, "The just shall live by his faith."

At the hands of the heretic who cuts away, I do not wonder if he withdraws syllables, when he very often subducts whole pages. The apostle, he says, was given grace, last of all, to enlighten all men as to what is the dispensation of the sacrament hidden from the ages in God, who created all things. The heretic snatched away the preposition In, and so makes it read: Hidden from the ages, to God who created all things. But the falsehood flashes out. For the apostle infers, That now there may be made known to the principalities and powers in the super-celestial places, through the church, the manifold wisdom of God. Of what principalities and powers does he speak? If the Creator's, what manner of thing is it that that God wished his wisdom to be shown to the Creator's principalities and powers, but not to himself — when the powers could not have known anything without their own prince? Or if for this reason he did not name God here, as though among them the prince himself too be reckoned, then he would have pronounced the sacrament hidden too from the principalities and powers of him who created all things, reckoning him likewise among them. But if he says it was hidden from them, to that one he ought to have said it was manifest. Therefore it was not hidden from God, but hidden in God the creator of all things, but hidden from his principalities and powers. For who has known the mind of the Lord, or who was his counsellor? Here the heretic, caught, perhaps changed it to say that his God wished to make known to his own powers and principalities the dispensation of his sacrament, of which the God the founder of all things was ignorant. And how was it fitting to allege the ignorance of the Creator — a stranger and severed by long separation — when even the household members of the superior God did not know it? Yet to the Creator too it was to be known as future. Or was it not surely known, what under heaven and on earth, which were his, was to be revealed? Therefore from this is confirmed what we built above. For if the Creator was at some time to know that hidden sacrament of the superior God, and so the scripture ran, Hidden to God who created all things, he ought to have inferred thus: That there may be made known to him the manifold wisdom of God — then also to the powers and principalities of whatever God, with whom the Creator was to know it. So fully is it established that it was subtracted, which even so is safe to its own truth. I wish now too to weave a controversy with you about the apostle's allegories. What forms would he have had in the prophets, as one new? He led captivity captive, he says. With what arms? in what battles? from the laying waste of what nation? from the overthrow of what city? what women, what children, or what petty kings did he, as victor, bind in chains? For when in David Christ is sung as girded with a sword upon his thigh, or in Isaiah as receiving the spoils of Samaria and the strength of Damascus, you truly hammer him out a visible warrior too. Acknowledge, then, both his armour and his warfare to be spiritual, if you have already learned that there is a spiritual captivity, that you may acknowledge this too to be his — or because the apostle took the mention of this captivity too from the prophets, from whom too his commandments. Putting off lying, speak truth, each to his neighbour; and, Be angry and sin not (in the very words by which the psalm would expound his sense), let not the sun go down upon your wrath. Do not partake in the works of darkness. For with the just you shall be just, and with the perverse you shall be perverted; and, Take away evil from your midst; and, Go out from the midst of them; and, Touch not the unclean thing; be separate, you who bear the vessels of the Lord. So too, To be drunk with wine is unto disgrace — that is from the place where those who make the saints drunk are rebuked: And you gave my saints wine to drink; which both Aaron the priest and his sons were forbidden to drink, when they approached the holy things. And to sing to God in psalms and hymns and to teach is his who knew how to accuse before God those who drank wine to timbrels and psalteries. Thus, whose precepts and seeds of precepts or increments I find, his apostle I acknowledge. For the rest, whence does he confirm that women ought to be subject to men? Because the man, he says, is the head of the woman. Tell me, Marcion: from a work of the Creator does your God lend authority to his own law? This now is plainly the lesser thing, since both for his own Christ and for his church he takes a status from there, just as Christ too is the head of the church. Likewise too, when he says, He who loves his own wife loves his own flesh, just as Christ too the church. You see your Christ and your church compared to a work of the Creator. How much honour is given to the flesh in the name of the church! Let no one, he says, hate his own flesh (except plainly Marcion alone), but nourishes and cherishes it, just as Christ too the church. But you alone hate it, taking away from it the resurrection. You ought to hate the church too, because it is likewise loved by Christ. But indeed Christ loved the flesh too, just as the church. No one but loves even the image of his bride; nay, he will both preserve and honour and crown it. The likeness has a partnership of honour with the truth. I shall now labour to prove the same God of the male and of Christ, of the woman and of the church, of the flesh and of the spirit, since the apostle himself adduces — nay, expounds — the sentence of the Creator: For this cause a man shall leave father and mother, and the two shall be in one flesh. This is a great sacrament. It is enough among these things if the Creator's sacraments are great with the apostle, the least with the heretics. But I, he says, speak of Christ and the church. He has an interpretation, not a separation, of the sacrament. He shows the figure of the sacrament to have been furnished beforehand by him whose surely the sacrament was. What seems to Marcion? The Creator surely could not furnish figures beforehand to an unknown God — and even, if known, to an adversary. The superior God ought to have borrowed nothing from the inferior, and that rather unto destruction. Let children too obey their parents. For though Marcion took away, This is the first precept in promise, the law speaks, Honour father and mother; and, Parents, bring up your children in the discipline and correction of the Lord. For you have heard it said to the ancients too, You shall tell these things in the ears of your children, and your children likewise in the ears of their children. Why now do you give me two gods, if the discipline is one? And if there are two, I will follow him who first taught. But if our wrestling is against the world-holders — O how many gods the Creators already are! For why should I not vindicate this too — that one world-holder ought to have been named, if it signified the Creator, whose were those powers which he set before? Further, since above he bids us put on the armour in which we may stand against the machinations of the devil, he now shows that those things are the devil's which he subjoins to the devil — the powers and world-holders of these darknesses, which we too reckon to the devil. Or if the devil is the Creator, who will be the devil with the Creator? Or, as there are two gods, so two devils too, and, in the plural, powers and world-holders? But how is the Creator both devil and God, when the devil is not himself both God and devil? For either both are gods too, if both are now devils; or he who is God here and not devil, just as the devil is not God. The very word devil — I ask of what accusation it can befit the Creator. Perhaps he carried off some plan of the superior God — which the Creator himself suffered from the archangel, and that one lying. For he had not forbidden the taste of that little tree lest they should become gods, but lest they should die of the transgression. Nor did the spiritual wickednesses signify the Creator because he added, In the heavens. For the apostle too knew that spiritual wickednesses had been wrought in the heavens — of the angels that gave offence with the daughters of men. And what manner of thing was it that by ambiguities and through riddles I know not what he should tax the Creator — he who, set already in chains for the liberty of his preaching, was begging from God constancy in manifesting the sacrament by the opening of his mouth, which there he was bidding to be demanded of God, and surely furnishing it for the church?

"Nay," say the Marcionites, "our god, even if not from the beginning, even if not through creation, yet through himself was revealed in Christ Jesus." A book shall be given also concerning Christ, on his whole state. For the matters must be distinguished, that they may be more fully and orderly treated. Meanwhile it will be enough, at the present stage, to meet it thus: to show that Christ Jesus was the bearer of no other god than the Creator — and that in few words. In the fifteenth year of Tiberius, Christ Jesus deigned to flow down from heaven, a saving spirit. Marcion's salvation, who so willed it — in what year of Antoninus the Elder the dog-star breeze breathed out of his Pontus, I have not cared to investigate. But of this it is certain: he is an Antonine heretic, impious under Pius. From Tiberius, however, to Antoninus there are about a hundred and fifteen years and a half, with a half month. They put just so great a span of time between Christ and Marcion. Since, then, under Antoninus Marcion first brought in this god, as we have proved — at once, you who are wise, the thing is plain. The times themselves give the verdict, that what first came forward under Antoninus did not come forward under Tiberius; that is, that the god of the Antonine reign was not of the Tiberian; and so was not revealed by Christ, since it is established that he was first preached by Marcion. To prove that this is established — what remains — I will take from the adversaries themselves. The separation of the Law and the Gospel is the proper and principal work of Marcion; nor will his disciples be able to deny it, since they have it in their chief instrument, by which indeed they are initiated and hardened into this heresy. For these are Marcion's Antitheses, that is, his contrary oppositions, which attempt to set the Gospel at discord with the Law, so that from the diversity of the judgments of the two instruments they may argue a diversity also of gods. Therefore, since that separation of the Law and the Gospel is the very thing that has insinuated another god of the Gospel against the God of the Law, it appears that before that separation the god was not in knowledge who became known from the argument of the separation; and so was not revealed by Christ, who was before the separation, but invented by Marcion, who instituted the separation against the peace of Gospel and Law — that peace which formerly, unhurt and unshaken from the appearing of Christ down to the audacity of Marcion, was preserved by that reasoning which defended no other god of both Law and Gospel than the Creator, against whom, so long a time after, the separation was let loose by the Pontic.

But even in the very dealings of life and of human conduct, at home and abroad, even to the care of vessels, He distinguished all things in every way, so that, with these legal disciplines meeting them everywhere, at no moment might they be void of regard toward God. For what should make man blessed, but his will in the law of the Lord? "And in the law of the Lord will he meditate day and night." Which law no hardness of the Author promulgated, but the reason of supreme kindness, taming rather the hardness of the people and chiselling down to obedience a faith raw with laborious offices — that I may touch nothing of the secret significations of the law, spiritual, namely, and prophetic, and figured in almost all its details. For it is enough at present if it simply bound man to God, so that no one ought to reprobate it, save him to whom it is no pleasure to serve God. Toward this benefit — not burden — of the law, to be aided, the same goodness of God ordained also the prophets, teaching things worthy of God: to take away wickednesses from the soul, to learn to do well, to seek out judgment, to judge for the orphan and justify the widow, to love questions, to flee the contact of the wicked, to send away a wife unhurt, to tear up an unjust writ, to break bread to the hungry and bring into your house him that has no roof, to clothe the naked if you see him, and not to despise the household of your own seed; to restrain the tongue from evil, and the lips, that they speak no guile; to turn aside from evil, and to do good; to seek peace and pursue it; to be angry and sin not, that is, not to persevere in anger or to rage; not to go off into the council of the impious, nor stand in the way of sinners, nor sit in the seat of the pestilent. But where? "Behold how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together as one," meditating day and night in the law of the Lord — because it is good, namely, to trust in the Lord rather than to trust in man, and to hope in the Lord rather than to hope in man. For what is the wage with God for man? "And he shall be as a tree that is planted by the outgoings of the waters, which shall give its fruit in its own time, and its leaf shall not fall, and all things whatsoever he does shall prosper for him." But the innocent and pure of heart, who has not received the name of God in vain and has not sworn to his neighbour in guile, he shall receive blessing from the Lord, and mercy from God his Saviour. "For the eyes of the Lord are upon them that fear Him, that hope in His mercy, to deliver their souls from death" — eternal death, of course — "and to nourish them in famine" — the famine, of course, of eternal life. "For many are the afflictions of the just, and out of them all the Lord will deliver them. Precious is the death of His saints in the sight of the Lord. The Lord keeps all their bones: not one of them shall be broken. The Lord will redeem the souls of His servants." These few things, out of so many writings of the Creator, we have brought in; and nothing, I think, is now wanting to the testimony of the best God, since both His precepts of goodness and His promises sufficiently attest it.

Come now, if you have read in David, "The Lord reigned from a tree," I wait to learn what you understand. Unless perhaps you take it to mean some woodland king of the Jews, and not Christ — who from that time reigned from the wood of the cross, having conquered death. For even if death reigned from Adam unto Christ, why should not Christ be said to have reigned from a tree, who, dead from the wood of the cross, shut out the kingdom of death? Likewise also Isaiah: "Because," he says, "a child is born to us." What new thing, if he does not speak of the Son of God? "And given to us, whose dominion has come upon his own shoulder." What king of all bears the insignia of his power on his shoulder, and not either a diadem on his head or a sceptre in his hand or some mark of his proper robe? But the only new king of the new ages, Christ Jesus, lifted up the power and the loftiness of his new glory upon his shoulder, namely the cross — so that, according to the prophecy above, the Lord might thenceforth reign from a tree. This tree Jeremiah too suggests to you, preaching to the Jews who would say, "Come, let us cast wood upon his bread" — surely upon his body. For so did God in your gospel too reveal it, calling his body bread — so that from this also you may understand that he gave to his body the figure of bread, whose body of old the prophet figured under bread, the Lord himself afterward interpreting this mystery. If you still seek the proclamation of the Lord's cross, the twenty-first psalm can now sufficiently satisfy you, containing the whole passion of Christ, who even then sang his own glory: "They pierced," he says, "my hands and feet" — which is the proper atrocity of the cross. And again, when he implores the Father's help: "Save me," he says, "from the mouth of the lion" — namely of death — "and my lowliness from the horns of the unicorn" — that is, from the tips of the cross, as we showed above. Which cross neither David himself suffered, nor any king of the Jews — lest you should think that the passion of some other is foretold than of him who alone was so signally crucified by the people. Now, even if heretical hardness has spurned and mocked all these interpretations, I will grant it that no cross of Christ was signified by the Creator — because not even from this will it prove that he who was crucified is another. Unless perhaps it should show this end of his foretold by its own god, so that a diversity of passions, and through this of persons too, may be claimed from the diversity of proclamations. But, since not even his Christ has been proclaimed, far less his cross, the prophecy of death alone suffices for my Christ. For from the fact that the manner of his death was not published, it could have come also by the cross — to be then assigned to another, if it had been foretold concerning another. Unless indeed he will not even have the death of my Christ foretold — whereby let him blush the more, if he announces his own Christ dead, whom he denies to have been born, but denies mine mortal, whom he confesses capable of being born. But both the death and the burial and the resurrection of my Christ I wish to show with the single voice of Isaiah, who says, "His burial has been taken from the midst." For he would not have been buried unless dead, nor his burial taken from the midst except by resurrection. In short, he subjoined: "Therefore he shall have many for an inheritance, and shall divide the spoils of many, because his soul was delivered unto death." For the cause of this grace is shown — to be recompensed, namely, for the injury of death. Equally is it shown that he was to obtain these things on account of death — after death, surely, to obtain them through resurrection.

That rich women clung to Christ, who ministered to him out of their faculties, among whom too the wife of the king's procurator — this is from prophecy. For these Isaiah called rich women: "Arise and hear my voice," that he might show them first as disciples, then as workers and ministers: "Daughters in hope, hear my words: in the day of the year remember with labour in hope"; for with labour, by which they followed, and on account of hope, they ministered. Equally, concerning parables, let it suffice once for all to have proved this kind of speech promised by the Creator. But now that pronouncement of his too to the people, "With the ear you shall hear, and shall not hear," gave Christ occasion frequently to inculcate, "He that has ears, let him hear." Not as though, out of diversity, Christ permitted a hearing which the Creator had taken away, but because exhortation followed the threat. First, "With the ear you shall hear, and shall not hear"; then, "He that has ears, let him hear." For they did not hear spontaneously who had ears, but he showed the ears of the heart necessary, with which the Creator had denied they would hear. And therefore through Christ he adds: "See how you hear, and do not hear" — not hearing, namely, with the heart, but with the ear. If you accommodate a worthy sense to the pronouncement, in place of the sense of him who roused them to a hearing, even by saying, "See how you hear," he was threatening those who would not hear. To be sure, the most mild god threatens, since he neither judges nor grows angry! This the underlying sense too proves. "To him who has it shall be given, but from him who has not, even what he thinks he has shall be taken from him." What shall be given? An increase of faith, or of understanding, or salvation itself. What shall be taken? Surely what is given. By whom is it given and taken? If by the Creator it is taken, by him it is also given. If by the god of Marcion it is given, by him it is also taken. By whatever name, however, he threatens a taking-away, it will not belong to that god who knows not how to threaten, because he knows not how to be angry. I marvel, however, when he denies that a lamp is wont to be hidden, who hid himself for so great an age — a greater and more necessary light; when he promises all things from the hidden to the open, who darkens his god even to this point, awaiting, I suppose, the birth of Marcion. We come to the most constant argument of all who bring the Lord's nativity into controversy. "He himself," they say, "attests that he was not born, by saying, 'Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?'" Thus the heretics always either snatch bare and simple voices by conjecture whither they will, or again dissolve conditional and rational ones by the condition of simplicity, as in this place. We on the contrary say, first, that it could not have been announced to him that his mother and his brothers stood outside seeking to see him, if there were no mother to him and no brothers — whom surely he knew who announced them, either formerly known or then and there ascertained, while they desire to see him, or while they themselves send the message. To this our first proposition it is wont to be answered from the opposite side: "What, if it was announced to him for the sake of tempting him?" But this the Scripture does not say, which, in so far as it is wont to signify that something was done out of temptation ("Behold, a doctor of the law rose up tempting him," and concerning the consultation about tribute, "And the Pharisees came to him tempting him"), in so far, where it does not make mention of temptation, it does not admit the interpretation of temptation. And yet, over and above, I demand the reasons of the temptation — for what they tempted him by the naming of mother and brothers. If that they might know whether he had been born or not — when was there a question of this which from that temptation they should discuss? And who would doubt to have been born one whom he saw a man? whom he had heard profess himself the Son of man? whom from the aspect of all human quality he would doubt to believe God or the Son of God? — esteeming him more easily a prophet, even some great one, yet surely born? Even if in the exploration of his nativity he had been to be tempted, any other argument would have suited the temptation than through the mention of those persons whom even one born might not have. Tell me, does the mother survive for all the born? are brothers begotten besides for all the born? Is it not rather lawful to have fathers and sisters, or even no one? But also it is established that censuses were taken under Augustus then in Judea by Sentius Saturninus, among whom they could have inquired his lineage. So in no way did the reason of that temptation stand, and truly his mother and brothers stood outside. It remains also to inspect the sense of one not pronouncing simply, "Who is my mother or brothers?" as toward a denial of his lineage and nativity, but both out of the necessity of the case and from a rational condition. For that persons so near should stand outside, while strangers were fixed within upon his discourse, and besides seeking to call him away from his solemn work — with reason was he indignant. He did not so much abnegate as disavow. And so, when he had premised, "Who is my mother and who are my brothers?" subjoining, "Except those who hear my words and do them," he transferred the names of blood to others, whom he would judge nearer for their faith. But no one transfers a thing except from him who has that which he transfers. If, then, he made his mother and brothers those who were not such, how did he deny those who were? — on the condition, namely, of merits, not out of a denial of his near ones — teaching in himself that he who should prefer father or mother or brothers to the word of God is not a worthy disciple. For the rest, from this he the rather confessed his mother and brothers, in that he was unwilling to acknowledge them. In that he adopted others, he confirmed those whom out of offence he denied — for whom he substituted not truer ones, but worthier. In short, it is nothing great, if he preferred faith to blood, which he did not have.

ON THE EPISTLE TO THE COLOSSIANS. In my prescription against all heresies I am wont to fix a compendium from the testimony of the times, vindicating our rule as prior to all heretical posterity. This now the apostle too will prove, saying, Of the hope laid up in the heavens, which you heard in the word of the truth of the gospel, which has come to you, just as into the whole world too. For if even then the evangelic tradition had spread everywhere, how much more now? Further, if ours is that which has spread everywhere, more than any heretical thing, much less the Antoninian Marcion's, it will be ours, apostolic. But Marcion's, though it have filled the whole world, will not even then be able to defend itself as apostolic. For that will even so be established to be apostolic which first filled the world — namely, with the gospel of that God who sang this too of his preachings: Into all the earth their sound has gone out, and into the ends of the world their words. He says Christ is the image of the invisible God. But we too call the Father of Christ invisible, knowing that the Son was always seen of old, if to any he was seen under the name of God, as his image — lest from this too he split off some difference of a visible and an invisible God, since of old the definition of our God has been, No one shall see God and live. If Christ is not the firstborn of creation, as the Word of the Creator through whom all things were made and without whom nothing was made; if in him were not created all things that are in the heavens and on earth, visible and invisible, whether thrones or dominions or principalities or powers; if all things were not created through him and in him (for these things Marcion ought to have been displeased at) — surely the apostle would not have set it down so nakedly, And he is before all. For how before all, if not before all things? How before all things, if not the firstborn of creation, if not the Word of the Creator? Whence shall he be proved to have been before all, who appeared after all things? Who knows that one to have been prior whom he did not know to be at all? How likewise did he think good that all fullness should dwell in himself? For first, what is this fullness, except out of those things which Marcion took away — created in Christ, in the heavens and on earth, angels and men — except out of those invisible and visible things, except out of thrones and dominions and principalities and powers? Or if our pseudo-apostles and Jewish evangelisers brought these in of their own, and to the fullness of his God, Marcion, who created nothing — for the rest, what manner of thing is it that the rival and destroyer of the Creator should have wished the Creator's fullness to dwell in his own Christ? To whom, in short, does he reconcile all things unto himself, making peace through the blood of his cross, except him whom these same things had offended, against whom they had rebelled by transgression, whose at the last they had been? For they could be conciliated to a stranger, but reconciled to no other than their own. So too us, once alienated and enemies in mind in evil works, he reduces into grace with the Creator, whose offence we had committed, worshipping the creation against the Creator. But if anywhere too he says the church is the body of Christ — as here he says that he fills up the remnants of the tribulations of Christ in his flesh for his body, which is the church — you will not on that account transfer the mention of the body wholly from the substance of the flesh. For above too he says that we are reconciled in his body through death — surely in that body in which he could die, through the flesh he died, not through the church, but plainly for the church, exchanging body for body, the carnal for the spiritual. But when he warns us to beware of subtle speech and philosophy, as of vain seduction which is according to the elements of the world — not speaking of heaven or earth, but of secular letters and tradition, namely of subtle-speaking men and philosophers — it is a long matter, indeed, and of another work, to show that by this sentence all heresies are condemned, because all consist of the resources of subtle speech and the rules of philosophy. But let Marcion acknowledge the chief boundary of his faith from the school of Epicurus, bringing in a dull lord, that he may say he is not to be feared; placing too matter, with God the Creator, from the porch of the Stoics; denying the resurrection of the flesh, on which likewise no philosophy agrees. From whose ingenuities our truth is so far removed, that it both dreads to rouse the wrath of God, and trusts that he brought forth all things out of nothing, and promises that he will restore the same flesh, and does not blush at a Christ born from a virgin's womb — though the philosophers and heretics and the very heathen laugh. For God chose the foolish things of the world to confound the wise — he, without doubt, who out of regard for this his arrangement threatened beforehand that he would destroy the wisdom of the wise. By this simplicity of truth, contrary to subtle speech and philosophy, we can savour nothing perverse. In short, if God makes us alive with Christ, forgiving us our offences, we cannot believe that offences are forgiven by him against whom they were not committed, as one formerly unknown. Come now, when he says, Let no one judge you in food and drink, or in part of a feast-day or a new moon or a sabbath, which is a shadow of things to come, but the body is Christ's — what seems to you, Marcion? Of the law we now do not treat again, except that here too he teaches in what manner it has been excluded, while, namely, it is transferred from the shadow to the body — that is, from figures to the truth, which is Christ. Therefore the shadow too is his whose is the body — that is, both the law is his and Christ. Separate the law to one God and Christ to another, if you can separate any shadow from the body of which it is the shadow. Manifestly Christ is of the law, if he is the body of the shadow. But if he also taxes some who out of angelic visions said that food must be abstained from — Touch not, taste not — wishing to walk in the lowliness of sense, not holding the head — not on that account does he assail the law and Moses, as though out of angelic superstition he had appointed the interdiction of certain foods. For it is established that Moses received the law from God. In short, this discipline — According to the precepts, he says, and doctrine of men — he reckoned upon those who held not the head, that is, him in whom all things are reviewed, brought back to the beginning in Christ — even the indifference of foods. The rest of the precepts — that it may suffice to have already taught elsewhere whence they flowed from the Creator, who, when he preached that the old things would pass, about to make all things new, commanding too, Make for yourselves a new renewal, even then was teaching to put off the old man and put on the new.

To this most ready proof a defence too is necessary for us against the clamours of the other side. For they say that Marcion did not so much innovate the rule by the separation of Law and Gospel as restore it, having been adulterated in time past. O Christ, most patient Lord, who for so many years didst endure the perversion of thy preaching, until, forsooth, Marcion should come to thy aid! For they bring forward also that Peter himself and the rest, pillars of the apostolate, were rebuked by Paul because they did not walk with straight foot toward the truth of the Gospel — by that very Paul, mind you, who, still raw in grace, trembling at last lest he had run or were running in vain, was then for the first time conferring with the apostles who went before him. So if, while still fervent as a neophyte, he thought something in their conduct toward Judaism worthy of rebuke — a passive matter, of course — though he himself afterwards would, by practice, become all things to all men, that he might gain all, to the Jews as a Jew, and to those under the Law as under the Law: do you wish that rebuke, which touched conduct alone — conduct that was to please his accuser afterwards — to be held suspect also of a betrayal of the preaching concerning God? But as to the unity of preaching — as we read above — they had joined right hands, and by that very distribution of office had agreed upon the fellowship of the Gospel, as also elsewhere: "Whether I," he says, "or they, so we preach." But even if he has described that certain false brethren had crept in, who wished to carry over the Galatians to another gospel, he himself shows that the adulteration of the Gospel had no intention of carrying them over to faith in another god and Christ, but of preserving the discipline of the Law; for he detected them, namely, claiming circumcision and observing times and days and months and years of Jewish ceremonies, which they ought to have recognized as already excluded, according to the renewed dispensation of the Creator, who long ago foretold of this very thing through His prophets. As through Isaiah: "The old things have passed away," He says; "behold new things which I now make"; and elsewhere, "And I will arrange a testament, not such as I arranged for your fathers, when I led them out of the land of Egypt." So too through Jeremiah: "Renew for yourselves a new renewal, and be circumcised to your God, and circumcise the foreskins of your heart." This circumcision, then, the apostle now establishing, and this renewal, he was also dissuading those old ceremonies, of which the same Founder of them professed that they should one day cease, through Hosea: "And I will turn away all her joys and her feast days and her new moons and her sabbaths and all her ceremonies." So too through Isaiah: "Your new moons and your sabbaths and the great day I do not endure; your holidays and fasting and feast days my soul hates." But if the Creator long since had rejected all these, and the apostle pronounced them now to be rejected, the very judgment of the apostle, consonant with the decrees of the Creator, proves that no other god was preached by the apostle than He whose decrees he wished now to be acknowledged, branding as false both the apostles and the brethren in this matter, who carried over the Gospel of Christ the Creator from the newness foretold by the Creator to the oldness rejected by the Creator.

But indeed these cuttlefish — under whose figure the law refused that fishy creature too from among foods — when they perceive their own exposure, vomit out from this point the darkness of blasphemy, and so scatter the close-pressed intention of each particular, by tossing about and asserting things that may becloud the shining goodness of the Creator. But even through these murks we will follow their wickedness, and drag into the light the wits of the darkness, which object to the Creator, above all, that fraud and rapine of gold and silver, commanded by Him from the Hebrews against the Egyptians. Come, most unhappy heretic, I appeal to you yourself as arbiter; first take knowledge of both peoples, and so you will judge of the author of the precept. The Egyptians demand back of the Hebrews their vessels of gold and silver. On the contrary, the Hebrews set up counter-claims, alleging that to them too, in the name of the same fathers, out of the same instrument of scripture, the wages of that workhouse-servitude ought to be restored — for the brick-loads carried out, for the cities and villages built. What will you judge, elector of the best god? — that the Hebrews ought to acknowledge fraud, or the Egyptians a compensation? For they say that it was so transacted through legates on both sides, the Egyptians demanding back their vessels, but the Jews claiming back their labours. And yet the Egyptians there renounced the claim of justice as to the vessels. Today, against the Marcionites, the Hebrews allege still more, denying that as compensation it is enough, however much of gold and silver, if the labours of six hundred thousand men through so many years be reckoned even at single coins a day. But which part is greater — of those claiming back vessels, or of those inhabiting villages and cities? Greater therefore the complaint of the Egyptians, or the gratuity of the Hebrews? — so that by the sole judgment of injuries the Hebrews should beat back the Egyptians, free men reduced into a workhouse; so that their scribes should show only their own shoulders, before their benches, mangled with the contumelious atrocity of the lashes? Not by a few platters and cups, of the fewer rich of course in every place, but by the whole faculties of the Egyptians themselves and the contributions of all the common people, He would have pronounced that satisfaction must be made to the Hebrews. Therefore, if the cause of the Hebrews be good, good already is the cause too — that is, the command — of the Creator, who both made the Egyptians, all unknowing, gracious, and discharged His own people, in the strait time of their expedition, with some small solace of a tacit compensation. Plainly He commanded less to be exacted; the Egyptians ought even to have restored their sons to the Hebrews.

It suffices to have run through these matters of Christ's order thus far in the meantime — by which, proved such as he was announced, he ought to be held none other than the one who was so announced; so that now, from this harmony of his affairs and the Creator's Scriptures, faith is to be restored to those too which, owing to diverse opinions, are either brought into doubt or denied. We now further build upon them also the equal points from the Creator's Scriptures, whatever was foresung as to happen after Christ. For the arrangement would not be found discharged, if he had not come, after whom it was to come to pass. Look at all the nations emerging thenceforth from the gulf of human error to the Creator God, to the God Christ, and, if you dare, deny that it was foretold. But at once the Father's promise will meet you in the psalms: "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee. Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession." Nor will you be able to claim him for the son of David rather than for Christ, or claim the ends of the earth as promised rather to David — who reigned within the single nation of the Jews — than to Christ, who has now taken the whole world by the faith of his gospel. So too through Isaiah: "Behold, I have given thee for a covenant of the race, for a light of the nations, to open the eyes of the blind" — surely of the wandering — "to loose from their bonds the bound" — that is, to free from their sins — "and from the prison-cell" — that is, of death — "those sitting in darkness" — namely of ignorance. If these things come to pass through Christ, they will have been foretold of none other than him through whom they come to pass. So too elsewhere: "Behold, I have set him a testimony to the nations, a prince and ruler of nations; nations who know thee not shall call upon thee, and peoples shall flee to thee for refuge." Nor will you interpret these of David, because he premised, "And I will arrange for you an everlasting arrangement, the holy and faithful things of David." And yet rather from this you ought to understand Christ as reckoned from David in fleshly descent, on account of the registration of Mary the virgin. For concerning this promise it is sworn in the psalm to David: "Of the fruit of thy womb will I set upon thy throne." Whose is this womb? David's own? Surely not. For David was not to give birth. But neither his wife's. For he would not have said, "Of the fruit of thy womb," but rather, "Of the fruit of thy wife's womb." But by saying "his womb," it remains that he showed someone of his race, of whose womb the flesh of Christ would be the fruit, which flowered from the womb of Mary. And therefore he named only "the fruit of the womb," as properly of the womb, as of the womb alone, not also of the man; and the womb itself he referred to David, the head of the race and father of the family. For since he could not assign the virgin's womb to a man, he assigned that womb to the father. Thus the new arrangement which is found today in Christ will be that which the Creator then promised, calling "the holy and faithful things of David" the things which were Christ's, because Christ is of David — nay, his very flesh will be the holy and faithful thing of David, now holy by religion and faithful by resurrection. For Nathan too, the prophet, in the first book of Kingdoms, makes a profession to David concerning his seed. "Which shall be," he says, "of his own belly." If you expound this simply of Solomon, you will make me laugh; for it will seem that David gave birth to Solomon. Or is Christ here too signified — the seed of David out of that belly which was of David, that is, of Mary? For because Christ rather was to build the house of God — namely a holy man, in whom, as in a better temple, the Spirit of God should dwell — Christ rather was to be held the Son of God than Solomon the son of David. In short, both an eternal throne and an eternal kingdom suit Christ rather than Solomon, a temporal king. But also from Christ the mercy of God did not depart, whereas to Solomon even the wrath of God came near, after his luxury and idolatry. For God raised up against him Satan, an Idumean enemy. Since, then, none of these things suits Solomon, but only Christ, the reason of our interpretations will be sure — the very outcome of things proving those which appear foretold concerning Christ. And so in him will be the holy and faithful things of David. Him God set a testimony to the nations, not David; a prince and ruler of nations, not David, who ruled over Israel alone. Christ today the nations call upon, who knew him not, and the peoples flee today for refuge to Christ, whom formerly they knew not. That cannot be called future which you see being done.

But who is this who commands both the winds and the sea? Surely a new commander and possessor of the elements, the Creator being already subdued and shut out? It is not so. But the substances acknowledged their author, who had been wont to obey his servants too. Look into Exodus, Marcion; behold the rod of Moses commanding the Red Sea — vaster beyond all the pools of Judea — that, cleft to the bottom and fixed with equal astonishment of the parting on either side, it should let the people across with dry foot by a path through its midst; and again, nature returning at the nod of the same rod, that it should overwhelm the Egyptian army by the concord of the waters — to which work the south winds too gave service. Read that to the exiled family, when it was to be parted, in its crossing, the Jordan was a sword, whose impetus and current Joshua too had plainly taught to stand still as the prophets passed over. What of these? If your Christ is meant, he will not be more powerful than the servants of the Creator. But I should have used these examples alone, had not the proclamation of this marine expedition too preceded Christ. For when he crosses, the psalm is discharged. "The Lord," it says, "upon many waters." When he shakes the waves of the strait, Habakkuk is fulfilled. "Scattering," it says, "the waters by his journey." When at his threats the sea is dashed away, Nahum too is performed. "Threatening," it says, "the sea and drying it up" — surely with the winds, by which it was disquieted. Whence do you wish my Christ to be vindicated — from the examples, or from the prophets of the Creator? Come now, you who think that a soldierly and armed warrior is foretold, not figuratively nor allegorically — one who was to wage a spiritual war against spiritual enemies with spiritual soldiery and spiritual arms, spiritually — when you find in one man a multitude of demons, professing itself a legion, surely a spiritual one, learn too that Christ is to be understood the expugner of spiritual enemies, spiritually armed and spiritually warlike, and so that he himself it is who was to fight with a legion of demons too; so that of this war too the psalm may seem to have pronounced, "The Lord strong, the Lord mighty in war." For when he fought with the last enemy, death, through the trophy of the cross he triumphed. But whose god's son did the legion attest Jesus to be? Without doubt his whose torments and abyss they knew and feared. For neither do they seem to have been able as yet to be ignorant that a power of a new and unknown god was working on earth, because it is not likely that the Creator was ignorant. For if he had once been ignorant of another god above himself, yet now surely he had discovered one acting beneath his own heaven. But what the Lord had discovered would now have become known to the whole household too, in the same world and within the same circuit of heaven in which a foreign divinity was conversing. Inasmuch, then, as the Creator too would have known it, and the substance of it, if it had existed — by so much, because there was none, the demons knew no other than the Christ of their own god. For they do not seek from another what they would remember should be sought by them from the Creator, namely pardon of the abyss of the Creator. In short, they obtained it. By what desert? Because they had lied, because they had made him the son of a fierce god? And what kind of one will he be who helped liars, who suffered defamers? But because they had not lied, because they had known the god of the abyss and their own, so he too confirmed himself the one whom the demons had known, Jesus the judge and the son of the avenging god. Behold something too concerning those littlenesses and infirmities of the Creator in Christ. For I too wish to ascribe ignorance to him. Permit me, against a heretic. He is touched by a woman who flowed with blood, and he knew not by whom. "Who," he says, "touched me?" Even when the disciples make excuse, he persists in the voice of ignorance. "Someone touched me," and this he affirms from argument. "For I felt power gone out from me." What says the heretic? Did he know the person? And why did he speak as one ignorant? To provoke confession, certainly; to prove fear. So too Adam once was sought, as one ignorant, "Adam, where art thou?" You have both the Creator excused along with Christ, and Christ equated with the Creator. But also that, as an adversary of the law — that, because the law removes from the touch of a bleeding woman, therefore he desired not only to admit her touch but even to grant soundness. O a god beneficent not by nature, but by rivalry! But indeed, if we find the woman's faith to have so deserved, when he says, "Thy faith has made thee safe," who are you, to interpret a rivalry of the law in that deed which the Lord himself showed to have been put forth out of the reward of faith? But you wish to constitute this the woman's faith, by which she had despised the law. And to whom is it credible that a woman, conscious as yet of no god, initiated as yet into no new law, should burst into that law by which she was still held? By what faith, in short, did she burst in? believing in what god? despising whom? The Creator? Certainly out of faith she touched. If out of faith in the Creator, who knew no other god, how did she burst into his law? For she burst in, if she burst in, as much out of faith in the Creator. For how shall both agree, both that she burst in, and that out of faith she burst into that on account of which she ought not to have burst in? I will tell. This faith was first that by which she trusted that her own god preferred mercy to sacrifice itself, by which she was certain that he wrought in Christ, by which she so touched him, not as a holy man, nor as a prophet, whom she knew contaminable by reason of human substance, but as the very god, whom she had presumed no filth could pollute. And so she did not rashly interpret the law for herself, signifying that those things were contaminated which were contaminable, not the god, whom she trusted in Christ. But she reconsidered this too, that the ordinary and solemn flux of menstrual or natal blood is taxed in the law, which comes from an office of nature, not from a defect of health. But she was redundant from a defect of health, for whom she knew necessary not the measure of time, but the help of the divine mercy. And so she can seem not to have burst into the law, but to have distinguished it. This will be the faith which had conferred understanding too. "Unless you believe," it says, "you shall not understand." This faith of that woman, who believed only the Creator, Christ approving, answered himself to be the god of that faith which he approved. Nor will I omit that, while his garment is touched — surely a garment put upon a body, not a phantom — a body too was demonstrated; not as though we should now treat of this, but because it conspires to the present question. For if there was no truth of body, surely the phantom, as an empty thing, could not be contaminated. He, then, who cannot be contaminated by reason of the emptiness of substance, how could he have wished to be? As an adversary of the law he was lying, who was not truly polluted.

ON THE EPISTLE TO THE PHILIPPIANS. When he enumerates the variety of preaching — that some, from the confidence of his chains, uttered the word more boldly, others through envy and contention, certain through esteem of the discourse, very many out of love, some out of emulation, now some too out of strife, preached Christ — there was surely here a place too for taxing the very preaching, on the diversity of sentence which made so great a variety even of dispositions. But, setting forth in the diversity the causes only of dispositions, not the rules of the sacraments, he confirms that one Christ nevertheless, and one God of his, was preached, whatever the intent; and therefore, It is nothing to me, he says, whether by occasion or in truth Christ is announced, because one was announced, whether out of occasion or out of the truth of faith. For he referred the mention of truth to the faith of the preaching, not to the rule itself, because the rule indeed was one, but the faith of certain preachers was true, that is, simple, of certain over-learned. Since this is so, it appears that the Christ preached was he who was always announced. For if another, far from the apostle, were brought in, the newness of the thing would have made a diversity. For there would not have been wanting those who would nonetheless interpret the evangelic preaching as of the Christ of the Creator, since even today the greater part in all places is of our sentence than of the heretical. So that here too the apostle would not have been silent about noting and rebuking the diversity. Thus, since the diversity is not even taxed, the newness is not proved. Plainly the Marcionites think that here too the apostle votes for them about the substance of Christ — that there was a phantasm of flesh in Christ — when he says that, being constituted in the form of God, he counted it not robbery to be equal to God, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, not the truth, and in the likeness of man, not in man, and being found in fashion as man, not in substance, that is, not in flesh — as though fashion and likeness and form did not accrue to substance too. But well that elsewhere too he calls Christ the image of the invisible God. Surely, then, here too, in that he sets him in the form of God, will Christ likewise not be truly God, if not truly man too, being constituted in the form of man? For both ways the truth will have to be excluded, if fashion and likeness and form be claimed for a phantasm. But if in form and in image, in which he is the Son of the Father, he is truly God, it is prejudged that in the form and image too of man, in which he is the Son of man, he was found truly man. For he set down found with reason, that is, most certainly man. For what is found is established to be. So too God was found through power, as man through flesh, because he would not have pronounced one subject to death who was not constituted in mortal substance. But more is what he added, And the death of the cross. For he would not have heightened the atrocity by extolling the might of the subjection, had he known it imaginary, by a phantasm — rather frustrated than experienced, nor discharging any might in the passion, but in mockery. But the things which formerly he had reckoned gain, which above too he enumerates — the glory of the flesh, the mark of circumcision, the reckoning of Hebrew race out of a Hebrew, the title of the tribe of Benjamin, the dignity of pure Pharisaism — these now he reckons to himself for loss; not God, but the stupor of the Jews. These he counts but as dung, in comparison with the knowledge of Christ, not in rejection of God the Creator; having a righteousness not now his own, which is of the law, but that which is through him, namely Christ, of God. Therefore, you say, by this distinction the law was not of the God of Christ. Subtly enough. Receive, then, more subtly. For when he says, Not that which is of the law, but that which is through him, he would not have said Through him of another than him whose the law was. Our citizenship, he says, is in the heavens. I recognise the old promise of the Creator to Abraham: And I will make your seed as the stars in heaven. Therefore too star differs from star in glory. But if Christ, coming from the heavens, transfigured the body of our lowliness, conformed to the body of his glory, then this our body shall rise, which is humbled in sufferings, and cast into the earth by the very law of death. For how shall it be transfigured, if it shall be nothing? Or if it is said of those who, found in the flesh at the coming of God, are to be reckoned, what shall they do who first rise? They will have nothing out of which to be transfigured. But, We shall be caught up, he says, together with them in the clouds to meet the Lord. If caught up together with them, surely transfigured too together with them.

For the rest, if anyone preaching a new god wished to exclude the Law of the old god, why does he prescribe nothing concerning the new god, but only concerning the old Law — unless because, the faith in the Creator remaining, His Law alone had to give place? As that psalm too had foresung: "Let us burst their bonds from us, and cast away their yoke from us" — from which, of course, the nations were stirred up and the peoples meditated vain things; the kings of the earth stood by and the magistrates came together as one against the Lord and against His Christ. And surely, if another god were preached by Paul, there would be no dispute whether the Law were to be kept or not — the Law not pertaining, of course, to a new lord and rival of the Law. For the very newness and diversity of the god would have taken away not only the question of an old and alien law, but every mention of it. But this was the whole state of the question: that, since the same God of the Law was preached in Christ, His Law was being derogated. The faith, then, stood always in the Creator and in His Christ; but conduct and discipline wavered. For some disputed about eating things sacrificed to idols, some about the veiling of women, some about marriages or divorces, some too about the hope of resurrection — but no one about God. For if this question too had been disputed, it too would be found in the apostle — and how much more as the principal one. But if after the times of the apostles the truth suffered adulteration concerning the rule of God, then the apostolic tradition suffered nothing in its own time concerning the rule of God; and no other tradition of the apostles is to be recognized than that which is published today among their own churches. But you will find no church of apostolic census which does not Christianize in the Creator. Or if these were corrupted from the beginning, which will be the uncorrupted ones? — those, no doubt, that are adverse to the Creator? Produce, then, some one of yours of apostolic census, and you will have closed the matter. Therefore, since by all means it is established that no other god in the rule of this sacrament existed, from Christ down to Marcion, than the Creator, our proof is now sufficiently fortified, whereby we have shown that the knowledge of the heretic's god began from the separation of Gospel and Law; and the earlier definition is established, that no god is to be believed whom man has composed out of his own senses — unless plainly a prophet, that is, not out of his own senses. But if Marcion can be called such, he ought also to be proved such. There was no need to revise anything. For by this wedge of truth all heresy is thrust out, when Christ is shown to be the bearer of no other god than the Creator.

So in the rest too you reproach Him with contrarieties of precepts, as fickle and unstable, forbidding work on the sabbath and commanding the ark to be carried round for eight days, that is, even on the sabbath, in the storming of the city of Jericho. For you do not look into the law of the sabbath, which forbids human works, not divine. Inasmuch as, "Six days," He says, "shall you labour, and do all your works; but the seventh day is the sabbath of the Lord your God: you shall not do in it any work." What work? Your own, of course. For it is consequent that He should take away on the sabbath those works which He had above enjoined for six days, your own, that is, human and daily ones. But to carry round the ark can be seen as neither a daily work nor a human one, but a rare and most sacred one, and from God's own precept then, surely divine. What this too signified I would expound, were it not long to spread out the figures of all the Creator's arguments, which perhaps you do not even admit. But it is the greater thing if you be convicted out of the plain matters, by the simplicity of the truth, not by curiosity. As even now there is a sure distinction of the sabbath, forbidding human works, not divine. And therefore he who had gone to gather wood on the sabbath was given over to death. For he had done his own work, forbidden by the law. But they who carried round the ark on the sabbaths did it with impunity. For they had administered not their own work, but God's, namely from His own precept.

So neither can you maintain that thrust of yours toward a difference of two Christs — as though the Jewish Christ were destined by the Creator for the people alone, to be gathered out of dispersion, but yours bestowed by the supremely good god for the freeing of the whole human race — since, after all, the Christians of the Creator are found earlier than those of Marcion, all peoples having been called from that time into his kingdom from which "God reigned from a tree," with no Cerdo as yet, far less a Marcion. But you, refuted concerning the calling of the nations, turn now to proselytes. Do you ask who pass over from the nations to the Creator, when the proselytes too, of a diverse and proper condition, are named separately by the prophet? "Behold," says Isaiah, "proselytes through me shall come to thee" — showing that the proselytes too were to come through Christ to God. And the nations — which is what we are — likewise had their own naming, as hoping in Christ. "And in his name," he says, "shall the nations hope." But the proselytes, whom you substitute in the proclamation of the nations, are not wont to hope in the name of Christ, but in the order of Moses, from whom their instruction comes. For the rest, the choosing of the nations arose from the last days. In the same words Isaiah says: "And it shall be in the last days that the mountain of the Lord shall be manifest" — surely the loftiness of God — "and the house of God upon the highest mountains" — surely Christ, the catholic temple of God, in which God is worshipped, set above all eminences of virtues and powers; "and all the nations shall come to it, and many shall go, and shall say, Come, let us ascend into the mountain of the Lord, and into the house of the God of Jacob, and he will announce to us his way, and we will walk in it: for out of Sion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord out of Jerusalem." This way of the new law will be the gospel, and of the new word in Christ, now no longer in Moses. "And he shall judge among the nations" — concerning their error, namely. "And he shall reprove a numerous people" — first of all the Jews themselves and the proselytes. "And they shall beat their swords into ploughshares, and their pikes into pruning-hooks" — that is, the dispositions of injurious minds and hostile tongues and all malice and blasphemy they shall convert into pursuits of modesty and peace. "And nation shall not lift up sword against nation" — surely of discord. "And they shall learn war no more" — that is, to carry out enmities; so that here too you may learn that Christ was not promised mighty in war, but a peace-bringer. Either deny that these things were foretold, when they are seen before your eyes; or that they are fulfilled, when they are read; or, if you deny neither, then they will be fulfilled in him concerning whom they were foretold. For look further at the very entry and course of the calling among the nations, who from the last days approach the Creator God, not at the proselytes, whose choosing is rather from the first days. For indeed the apostles brought in this faith.

He sends the disciples to preach the kingdom of God. Did he even here publish whose? He forbids them to carry anything for food or clothing on the way. Who would have commanded this but he who both feeds the ravens and clothes the flowers of the field, who before granted to the ox too treading out the grain freedom of mouth for the pardon of fodder, in removing it from the work, because the worker is worthy of his hire? Let Marcion delete these, provided the sense be safe. But when he bids the dust be shaken off the feet upon those by whom they had not been received, and commands this too to be done for a testimony — no one testifies what is not destined for judgement; he who bids inhumanity be reduced to a testimony threatens a judge. That no new god was approved by Christ that opinion too of all declared, because some asserted to Herod that Christ Jesus was John, others Elias, others some one of the old prophets. Of whom whichever it had been, surely not for this was he raised up, that after the resurrection he should preach another god. He feeds the people in the wilderness, namely after the former manner. Or if it is not the same majesty, then he is already lesser than the Creator, who not in one day, but in forty years, nor out of the inferior matters of bread and fish, but out of heavenly manna, nor about five, but six hundred thousand men supported. And so far was it majesty, that he willed even a scantiness of food not only to suffice but even to overflow, from the former example. For so too in the time of famine under Elias the scanty and last food of the Sareptan widow, out of the prophet's blessing, had abounded through the whole time of famine. You have the third book of Kingdoms. If you unfold the fourth too, you will find this whole order of Christ about that man of God who, when ten barley loaves had been offered him, bade them be distributed with the people, and his minister, accordingly considering the multitude and the smallness of the food, had answered, "What should I give of this in the sight of a hundred men?" "Give," he says, "and they shall eat, because thus says the Lord, They shall eat and shall leave remnants, according to the word of the Lord." O Christ, old even in the new! These things, then, Peter, who had seen them and had compared them with the former, and had recognized not only things formerly done, but things even then prophesying for the future — when, the Lord inquiring who he seemed to them to be, he answered for all, "Thou art the Christ" — could not but have understood him Christ, none other than the one he had known in the Scriptures, whom he was now recounting in deeds. This he himself too confirms, still patient — nay, even enjoining silence. For if Peter indeed could confess him no other than the Creator's, while he commanded them to tell this to no one, surely he was unwilling that to be divulged which Peter had perceived. "Nay," you say, "because he had not perceived rightly, he was unwilling a lie to be disseminated." But he declared another cause of the silence, that the Son of man must suffer many things, and be reprobated by elders and scribes and priests, and be killed, and after the third day rise again. Which things, since they too are proclaimed concerning the Christ of the Creator — as we shall fulfil in their places — even thus he showed himself to be the very one concerning whom they were proclaimed. Certainly, even if they had not been proclaimed, he brought forth as the cause of the enjoined silence one which should demonstrate not Peter's error, but the necessity of the passions to be undergone. "Whoever," he says, "shall wish to make his soul safe, shall lose it; and whoever shall lose it for my sake, shall make it safe." Certainly the Son of man uttered this opinion. Look, then, you too, with the king of Babylon, into his burning furnace, and you will find there, as it were the Son of man (for he was not yet truly so, namely not yet born of man), even then constituting these issues. He makes safe the souls of the three brothers, who had conspired to lose them for God, but lost those of the Chaldeans, which they had preferred to make safe through idolatry. What is this new teaching, of which the evidences are old? Although the proclamations of martyrdoms too, both as to come and as to bring a reward from God, ran their course. "See," says Isaiah, "how the just man perishes, and no one takes it to heart, and just men are taken away, and no one considers." When more is this done than in the persecution of his saints? Surely not a simple loss, nor a common one by the law of nature, but that signal and warlike-for-faith one, in which he who loses his soul for God saves it — that here too you may acknowledge a judge, who recompenses the evil gain of the soul by its loss, and the good loss of the soul by its salvation. But he exhibits to me a jealous god too, repaying evil with evil. "Whoever," he says, "shall have been confounded at me, I too will be confounded at him." Since the matter of confusion would suit none but my Christ, whose order is the more to be blushed at — so that it lies open even to the revilings of heretics, who harangue with all the bitterness they can about the whole foulness of his nativity and rearing and even the very indignity of his flesh — for the rest, how shall he be liable to confusion who does not admit it? — coagulated not, indeed, in a virgin's womb, yet in a woman's, and even if not of seed, yet by the law of corporeal substance, out of the humour of a woman; not held flesh before its shaping, not called a beast after its figuring, not deliberated through ten months' torment, not poured out to the earth in a sudden shaking of pangs along with the mire of so long a time through the sewer of the body, nor at once auspicating the light with tears and the first wound of his own swaddling, nor much washed, nor medicated with salt and honey, nor first wrapped in the cerements that are already a burial-cloth, nor thence rolled through filth among the bosoms, troublesome to the breasts, long an infant, scarcely a boy, slowly a man — but set forth from heaven, at once grown, at once whole, straightway Christ, only spirit and power and god. For the rest, as not true, who was not seen, so neither to be blushed at for the curse of the cross, of which he lacked the truth, lacking the body. He could not therefore have said, "Whoever shall have been confounded at me." Ours ought to have pronounced this — diminished by the Father a little below the angels, a worm and not a man, the shame of man and the outcast of the people — inasmuch as he so willed it, that by his bruise we should be healed, that by his dishonour our salvation should stand. And with reason he laid himself down for his own man, for his own image and likeness, not another's; that, since man had not blushed to adore stone and wood, with the same constancy, not confounded at Christ, he might make satisfaction to God for the shamelessness of idolatry through the shamelessness of faith. Which of these suits your Christ, Marcion, to the desert of confusion? Plainly you ought to be ashamed that you yourself fashioned him.

ON THE EPISTLE TO PHILEMON. To this epistle alone its brevity was of profit, that it might escape the falsifying hands of Marcion. Yet I wonder that, when he received letters written to one man, he rejected the two to Timothy and the one to Titus, composed about ecclesiastical order. He affected, I think, to interpolate even the number of the epistles. Remember, inspector, that the things which were treated beforehand we have proved of the apostle too in their place, and that whatever was deferred to this work we have discharged — lest either here you think the iteration superfluous, by which we have confirmed the former hope, or there hold the deferment suspect, by which we drew out these very things. If you inspect the whole little work, you will judge neither here a redundance nor there a diffidence.

But how shall antichrist be utterly overthrown, unless room be given for crushing his other inroads too, the defence of prescriptions being relaxed? Let us approach, then, from this point, the very person of his god — or rather his shadow and phantasm, in keeping with his Christ — and let him be examined by that whereby he is preferred to the Creator. And certainly there will be sure rules for examining the goodness of a god. But the first thing is for me to find that goodness and lay hold of it, and so bring it to the rules. For when I look round on the times, it is nowhere — from the beginning of the materials and at the entrance of the causes, with which it ought to have been found, thenceforth doing what it had to do. For already there was death, and the sting of death was sin, and the very malice of the Creator, against which the goodness of another god ought to have come to aid — meeting this first rule of divine goodness, if it should prove itself natural, by aiding at once, as the cause arose. For all things in God must be natural and innate, that they may be eternal, according to His own state, lest they be reckoned things that come upon Him and from outside, and thereby temporal and alien to eternity. So too goodness perennial and continual will be required in God — goodness which, stored up and prepared in the treasuries of natural properties, should anticipate its causes and materials, and take up the very first that arose, not despise and forsake it, if it anticipated it. Lastly, here too I shall ask no less why his goodness did not operate from the beginning, than we asked concerning the god himself, why he was not revealed from the beginning? Why not, indeed, he who had to be revealed through his goodness, if he had existed? It is not lawful that anything be impossible to God — much less that he not perform his own natural functions; which, if they be hindered from running their course, will not be natural. For nature does not even know idleness in itself. By this it is reckoned, if it acts; so neither will he seem to have been unwilling to exercise his goodness, at least under the name of nature. For nature cannot be unwilling toward itself, which so directs itself that, if it cease, it is not. But goodness ceased at some time from work in Marcion's god. Therefore it was not natural goodness, which could at some time have ceased — which is not lawful for natural things. And if it will not be natural, then neither is it to be believed eternal nor equal to God, because it is not eternal, since not natural — which finally establishes for itself no perpetuity, either out of the past or by promise of the future. For both it was not from the beginning, and in the end without doubt it will not be. For it can also not exist at some time, just as it did not exist at some time. Therefore, since it is established that at the beginning the goodness of that god ceased (for he did not set man free from the beginning), and that it ceased by will rather than by weakness, now the will of suppressed goodness will be found to be the end of malignity. For what is so malignant as to be unwilling to do good when you can, as to torment usefulness, as to allow injury? In short, the whole indictment of the Creator will be re-inscribed upon him who, by the delay of his own goodness, abetted the Creator's cruelties. For in whose hand it is that a thing be not done, to him it is reckoned when it is done. Man is condemned to death for the tasting of one little tree, and thence sins go forward with their punishments, and now all perish who know not a single sod of Paradise. And this some better god either knows not, or endures? If it were so that he might thereby be found the better, how much the worse would the Creator be held? — malicious enough even in this counsel, who both wished Him to be loaded, His operations being admitted, and held the world in vexation. What will you judge of such a physician, who should feed the disease by delay of relief and prolong the danger by deferring the remedy, that he might cure more dearly or more famously?
