Such is the sentence to be pronounced upon Marcion's god too: a permitter of evil, a fosterer of injury, a pander of grace, a betrayer of his own kindness, which he did not at once exhibit to its cause — plainly meaning to exhibit it, if good by nature, and not by accession; if best by character, and not by discipline; if a god from eternity, and not from Tiberius — nay, what is truer, from Cerdo and Marcion. Tiberius now, it seems, conferred upon that god this favour, that in his reign divine goodness should be dedicated on earth.

Accordingly, in forbidding the likeness too of all things to be made — of all that are in heaven and in earth and in the waters — He showed the causes also, restraining, namely, the substance of blind idolatry. For He subjoins: "You shall not adore them, neither shall you serve them." But the image of the bronze serpent, afterward commanded to Moses by the Lord, pertained not to the title of idolatry, but to the remedying of those who were infested by serpents. And I am silent about the figure of the remedy. So too the Cherubim and Seraphim of gold, fashioned for the model of the ark — surely a simple ornament, fitted to the mercy-seat, having causes far diverse from the condition of idolatry, on account of which the likeness is forbidden — do not seem to clash with the law of forbidden likenesses, not being detected in that state of likeness on account of which the likeness is forbidden. We have spoken of the rational institution of sacrifices, calling away, namely, those offices from idols to God; which, if again He cast out, saying, "What to me is the multitude of your sacrifices?", He willed this very thing to be understood, that He had not exacted them properly for Himself. "For I will not drink," He says, "the blood of bulls," because elsewhere too He says, "The eternal God will not hunger nor thirst." For even if He had regard to the oblations of Abel, and smelled the holocausts of Noah with pleasure — what gladness is there either in the entrails of a wether or in the reek of burning victims? But the simple mind, fearing God, of those who offered the things they had from God, both of food and of sweet odour, was reckoned to grace with God — not He requiring the things that were done, but that on account of which they were done, namely for the honour of God. If a client should offer to a rich man or a king who desires nothing some little gift of the meanest kind, will the quantity and quality of the gift bring the rich man and king into contempt, or will the title of the office delight him? But if a client offer him gifts of his own accord, or even commanded, in their due order, and observe the solemnities of the king, yet not out of fidelity, nor with a pure heart, nor full in his other obediences too, is it not consequent that that king or rich man should cry out, "What to me is the multitude of your gifts? I am full of them. And your solemnities and feast days and your sabbaths" — calling those "yours" which they had now made their own, not God's, having celebrated them according to their own caprice, not according to the religion of God: by this He demonstrated a refusal conditional therefore and rational of the things He had prescribed to be administered.

You have the work of the apostles too foretold. "How seasonable the feet of those who evangelize peace, who evangelize good things" — not war nor evils. The psalm too answered: "Into all the earth their sound has gone out, and to the ends of the earth their voices" — namely of those carrying about the law gone forth from Sion and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem, so that what is written might come to pass: "All who are far from my justice have drawn near to my justice and truth." When the apostles girt themselves for this business, they renounced the elders and rulers and priests of the Jews. "Was it not above all," he says, "as preachers of another god?" And yet of the very same whose Scripture they were at that moment fulfilling. "Depart, depart," cries Isaiah, "go out from thence, and touch not the unclean thing" — blasphemy, namely, against Christ. "Go out from the midst of it" — namely of the synagogue; "be separated, you who carry the vessels of the Lord." For now, according to the things written above, the Lord had revealed his Holy One by his arm — that is, by his power, Christ — in the sight of the nations, that all the nations and the ends of the earth might see the salvation that was from God. So too, turning aside from Judaism itself, when they exchanged the bonds and burdens of the law for the liberty of the gospel, they were carrying out the psalm: "Let us burst their chains and cast off from us their yoke" — certainly after the nations were in tumult and the peoples meditated vain things; "the kings of the earth stood up, and the princes were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." What did the apostles suffer thereafter? "Every iniquity," you say, "of persecutions" — from the men of the Creator, namely, as adversaries of him whom they preached. And why does the Creator, if he was an adversary of Christ, not only foretell that his apostles should suffer this, but even reproach it? For he would neither foretell the order of another god, of whom he was ignorant, as you would have it, nor would he reproach what he himself had procured. "See how the just man perishes, and no one lays it to heart, and just men are taken away, and no one regards it. For from the face of injustice the just man has been taken away." Who, but Christ? "Come," they say, "let us take away the just man, because he is unprofitable to us." Premising this, then, and subjoining accordingly that Christ too suffered, he prophesied that his just ones equally would suffer the same — both the apostles and thereafter all the faithful — marked, namely, with that sign concerning which Ezekiel: "The Lord says to me, Pass through the midst of the gate, in the midst of Jerusalem, and set the sign Tau on the foreheads of the men." For this is the letter Tau of the Greeks, but ours, T — the figure of the cross, which he foreshowed to be in the future on our foreheads, in the true and catholic Jerusalem, in which the brothers of Christ — namely the sons of God — were to render glory to God the Father, as the twenty-first psalm sings in the person of Christ himself to the Father: "I will declare thy name to my brothers, in the midst of the Church I will sing a hymn to thee." For what was to be done today in his name and spirit, he rightly proclaimed would be done by himself. And a little below: "From thee is my praise in the great Church." And in the sixty-seventh: "In the churches bless the Lord God"; so that equally might concur the prophecy of Malachi: "My will is not in you, says the Lord, and your sacrifices I will not accept; for from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is glorified among the nations, and in every place a sacrifice is offered to my name, even a clean sacrifice" — namely the rendering of glory, and blessing, and praise, and hymns. All which, since they are found in you too — both the sealing of foreheads, and the mysteries of the churches, and the cleanness of the sacrifices — you ought now to burst out and say that the Spirit of the Creator prophesied to your Christ.

For this too you ought to have blushed at most of all, that you allow him to be seen with Moses and Elias on the retirement of the mountain, whose destroyer he had come. This, namely, that voice from heaven willed to be understood, "This is my beloved Son, hear him" — that is, no longer Moses and Elias. Therefore the voice alone sufficed, without the showing of Moses and Elias. For by defining whom they should hear, he would have forbidden any others to be heard. Or perhaps did he permit Isaiah and Jeremiah and the rest, whom he did not show, to be heard, if he forbade those whom he showed? Now even if their presence was necessary, surely they would not be shown in colloquy, which is a sign of familiarity, nor in a fellowship of brightness, which is an example of esteem and grace, but in some foulness, which is an argument of destruction — nay, in the darkness of the Creator, for the dispelling of which he had been sent — far removed too from the brightness of Christ, who was to separate even their voices and letters from his gospel. Thus he demonstrates them aliens while he has them with him. Thus he teaches that they are to be left whom he joins to himself. Thus he destroys those whom he builds up out of his own rays. What would the Christ of those men do? I believe, according to the perversity, he would have revealed them such as Marcion's Christ ought to have been, or any others with him than his own prophets. But what is so the Christ of the Creator's as to show his own preachers with himself? to be seen with those to whom in revelations he had been seen? to speak with those who had spoken him? to share his glory with those by whom he was named the Lord of glory? — with his own chief men, of whom the one was once the informer of the people, the other one day the reformer, the one the initiator of the old testament, the other the consummator of the new. And so Peter too, with reason acknowledging the comradeship of his own Christ by the individuality of his presence, suggests counsel: "It is good for us to be here" (good plainly where Moses, namely, and Elias are), and, "Let us make here three tabernacles, one for thee, and one for Moses, and one for Elias"; but not knowing what he said. How not knowing? Either through simple error, or by that reason by which we defend, in the cause of the new prophecy, that ecstasy — that is, a being out of one's mind — befits grace? For a man set in the spirit, especially when he beholds the glory of God, or when God speaks through him, must of necessity fall from his senses, overshadowed, namely, by the divine power — concerning which there is a question between us and the psychics. Meanwhile it is easy to prove the ecstasy of Peter. For how would he have known Moses and Elias, except in the spirit? (for the people could not have had their images or statues and likenesses, the law forbidding) — except that he had seen them in the spirit? And so what he had said in the spirit, not set in his senses, he could not know. For the rest, if he so knows not as one erring — in that he thought Christ to belong to them — then it is now established that above too, when Peter was interrogated by Christ whom they esteemed him to be, he said, of the Creator's, "Thou art the Christ"; because, if he had then acknowledged him to be of another god, here too he would not have erred. But if here too he therefore erred because above too, then you are certain that on that day too no new divinity was revealed by Christ, and that Peter had not yet erred, Christ hitherto revealing nothing of the kind, and that Christ was so long not to be reckoned of another than the Creator, whose whole order he here too expressed. Three of the learners he takes as witnesses of the coming vision and voice. And this is the Creator's. "In three witnesses," it says, "shall every word stand." He retires into the mountain. I acknowledge the form of the place. For the former people too the Creator had initiated at the mountain both by vision and by his voice. It behoved that upon that platform the new testament should be sealed where the old had been written, under the same circuit too of the cloud, which no one will doubt to be massed out of the Creator's air. Unless he had led even his own clouds thither, because he too had broken his way through the Creator's heaven; or else he used the Creator's cloud-cover by leave. And so neither now was the cloud mute, but the wonted voice from heaven, and the Father's new testimony over the Son, as in the first psalm: "Thou art my Son, this day have I begotten thee." Concerning whom also through Isaiah: "Who fearing God shall hear the voice of his Son?" And so, now representing him, "This is my Son" — surely it is understood, "whom I promised." For if he promised at some time, and afterward says, "This is he," it is the part of one exhibiting to use a voice in the demonstration of the promise who at some time promised, not of one to whom it can be answered, "Who indeed art thou who sayest, This is my Son, concerning whom thou hast no more premised than that thou hast revealed thyself, which thou wast before?" Hear him therefore whom he had from the beginning declared was to be heard in the name of a prophet, since he was to be esteemed a prophet too by the people. "A prophet," says Moses, "shall God raise up to you from your sons," namely according to carnal descent, "as me; him shall you hear. But everyone who shall not hear him, his soul shall be exterminated from his people." So too Isaiah: "Who among you fearing shall hear the voice of his Son?" — which the Father himself too was to commend. For "establishing," it says, "the words of his Son," by saying, namely, "This is my beloved Son, hear him." And so, even if a transference of hearing has been made from Moses and Elias to Christ, yet not as from another god, nor to another Christ, but from the Creator to his Christ, according to the decession of the old and the succession of the new testament. "Not a legate," says Isaiah, "nor a messenger, but he himself, God, shall save them" — he himself now preaching and fulfilling the law and the prophets. The Father, then, handed over new disciples to the Son, Moses and Elias being first shown with him in the prerogative of brightness, and so dismissed, as already discharged both in office and in honour — that this very thing might be confirmed against Marcion, that there is a fellowship even of Christ's brightness with Moses and Elias. But the whole bearing of that vision we have also with Habakkuk, where the spirit, sometimes in the person of the apostles: "Lord, I have heard thy hearing, and was afraid." What rather than that of the heavenly voice: "This is my beloved Son, hear him"? "I considered thy works, and was astonished." When more than when, the brightness of him being seen, Peter knew not what he said? "In the midst of two living creatures thou shalt be known" — Moses and Elias. Concerning whom Zechariah too saw in the figure of two olives and two olive-branches. For these are they of whom it was said to him, "Two sons of fatness stand by the Lord of the whole earth." And again the same Habakkuk: "A power covered the heavens" — surely with that cloud-cover; "and his splendour shall be as the light" — surely by which his garment too shone. And if we be reminded of the promise of Moses, here it will be found discharged. For when Moses had desired the sight of the Lord, saying, "If, then, I have found grace before thee, manifest thyself to me, that knowing I may see thee" — desiring that sight in which he was to act a man, which the prophet knew — for the rest, concerning the face of God he had already heard, "No man shall see me and live." "And this word too which thou hast said I will do for thee." And again Moses: "Show me thy glory." And the Lord likewise of the future: "I will go before in my glory," and the rest. And at the last: "And then thou shalt see my hinder parts." Not loins nor calves, but the glory which he had desired, to be revealed in later times. In which face, face to face visible, he had promised himself to him, saying to Aaron too, "And if there be a prophet among you, in a vision I will be known to him, and in a vision I will speak to him, not as to Moses: mouth to mouth I will speak to him in appearance" (surely of a man, which he was to bear), "not in a riddle." For even though Marcion was unwilling that he should be shown speaking with the Lord, but standing, yet even standing he stood mouth to mouth and face to face with him, "with him," it says, not outside him, into his glory, not to say in his sight. From which glory, illumined no otherwise, he departed from Christ than he was wont from the Creator — and so then to smite the eyes of the sons of Israel, just as now those of the blinded Marcion, who did not see that this argument too works against himself.

I hold out to him another rule: that as all things in God ought to be natural, so they ought to be rational. I demand a reason of his goodness, since nothing else may be held good which is not rationally good — much less may goodness itself be detected as irrational. More easily will an evil to which some measure of reason has been present be held for good, than that a good deserted by reason be not judged for evil. I deny the goodness of Marcion's god to be rational, on this first ground: that it went forth for the salvation of an alien man. I know they will say that this is precisely the principal and perfect goodness, when, without any debt of kinship, it is poured out upon strangers, voluntary and free — according to which we too are bidden to love even our enemies, and on this score now strangers. Since, then, he did not look upon man from the beginning — a stranger from the beginning — by his ceasing he prejudged that he had nothing to do with the stranger. For the rest, the discipline of loving the stranger or the enemy was preceded by the precept of loving the neighbour as yourself; which, though it be from the Law of the Creator, you too must except, as not destroyed by Christ but rather built up. For the more you love your neighbour, the more you are bidden to love your enemy and the stranger. The exaction of the goodness not owed is an enhancement of the owed. But the owed precedes the not-owed, as the principal, as the worthier, with its handmaid and companion — that is, the not-owed. The first reason of goodness, then, being to be exhibited toward one's own out of justice, and the second toward another out of the overflow of justice above the Scribes and Pharisees — what sort of thing is it that the second reason should be referred to him to whom the first is lacking, who has no man of his own, and thereby is also of scant goodness? Further, the scant goodness, which had nothing of its own, how has it overflowed upon another's? Exhibit the principal reason, and then claim the consequent. No thing without order can be claimed as rational — so far is it from this, that reason itself should in anything lose order. Let now the reason of goodness begin even from the second degree, namely toward the stranger; not even that second degree of his will stand by reason, being in another way destroyed. For then will even the second goodness toward the stranger be held rational, if it operate without injury to him whose the thing is. Whatever goodness, the first justice makes rational. So too in the principal degree it will be rational, when it is exhibited toward one's own, if it be just. So too toward the stranger it will be able to seem rational, if it be not unjust. But for the rest, what sort of goodness is that which stands by injury, and indeed for a stranger? For perhaps for a member of one's household injurious goodness might to some extent be held rational. But for a stranger, to whom not even honest goodness was lawfully owed — by what reason shall a goodness so unjust be defended as rational? For what is more unjust, what more iniquitous and dishonest, than so to benefit another's slave that he is snatched from his master, claimed for another, suborned against his master's life — and indeed, what is more unworthy, while still in his master's very house, living still off his stores, trembling still under his lashes? Such an abettor would be condemned even in the world, not to say a kidnapper. Not otherwise is Marcion's god, breaking into another's world, snatching man from God, the son from the father, the pupil from the trainer, the servant from the lord — to make him impious to God, irreligious to his father, ungrateful to his trainer, worthless to his lord. I ask you, if rational goodness makes a man such as irrational goodness would make him —? I should think none more impudent than one who is baptized in another god's water to another god, stretched out to another god under another's heaven, prostrated to another god on another's earth, who performs over another's bread thanksgivings to another god, who out of another's goods works in the name of almsgiving and love on account of another god. What god is this, so good that by him man is made evil, so propitious that he makes another god — and that one the man's own lord — angry?

But if you will have Him understood as fickle even about persons — when He sometimes reprobates the approved, or improvident when He sometimes approves the reprobate, as though He either condemned His own past judgments or were ignorant of those to come — yet nothing so suits a good judge as both to reject and to accept according to present deserts. Saul is accepted, but while not yet a despiser of the prophet Samuel. Solomon is rejected, but when already possessed by strange women and made over to the idols of the Moabites and Sidonians. What should the Creator do, that He might not be reproached by the Marcionites? Should He pre-condemn men still acting well, on account of future sins? But it was not of a good god to pre-condemn those not yet deserving it. Accordingly, should He not refuse those now sinning, on account of their former well-doings? But it was not of a just judge to remit crimes, their former good deeds being now rescinded. Or what man is there without sin, that God should always accept him whom He could never refuse? Or who again is without some good work, that God should always refuse him whom He could never accept? Exhibit good always, and you will not be refused; exhibit evil always, and you will never be accepted. For the rest, if the same man, as in either case according to the times, is in either case discharged by God both good and judge, who turns His sentences not from fickleness or improvidence, but by a most weighty and most provident censure dispenses the merits of each time.

Now, since with the Jews you deny that their Christ has come, recognize also their own end, which they were foretold to bring upon themselves after Christ, on account of the impiety by which they both despised and slew him. For first, from the day on which, according to Isaiah, "man cast away his abominations of gold and silver, which they had made to adore vain and noxious things" — that is, from the time when the human race, the truth made clear through Christ, cast away its idols. See whether what follows has been discharged: "For the Lord of Sabaoth has taken away from Judea and from Jerusalem, among the rest, both the prophet and the wise architect" — namely the Holy Spirit, who builds the Church, namely the temple and house and city of God. For thenceforth the grace of God ceased among them, and it was commanded to the clouds that they should not rain rain upon the vineyard Sorek — that is, the heavenly benefits, that they should not come forth to the house of Israel. For it had brought forth thorns, of which it had crowned the Lord, and not justice, but a clamour, by which it had extorted him to the cross. And thus, the dews of the spiritual gifts being withdrawn, the law and the prophets reached only to John. Then, when, with such perseverance of fury, the name of the Lord too was blasphemed through them — as it is written: "Because of you my name is blasphemed among the nations" (for from them began the infamy) — and in the intervening time, from Tiberius to Vespasian, they had not understood repentance, their land was made desolate, their cities burned up, their region devoured before their own eyes by strangers, the daughter of Sion forsaken and like a watchtower in a vineyard or a hut in a cucumber-field — from that time, namely, when Israel did not know the Lord, and the people did not understand him, but forsook him, and provoked to indignation the Holy One of Israel. So too the conditional threat of the sword: "If you will not, and will not hearken to me, the sword shall devour you" — proved that it was Christ whom by not hearing they perished. He who also, in the fifty-ninth psalm, demands their dispersion from the Father: "Scatter them in thy power." Who again, through Isaiah, declaiming against their burning up, says, "Because of me these things have come upon you; you shall sleep in anguish." Quite idly, if they did not suffer these things on account of him who had pronounced that they would suffer on his account, but on account of the Christ of another god. And yet, I say, you say that the Christ of another god was driven to the cross by the virtues and powers of the Creator, as by rivals. But behold, he is shown defended by the Creator — and "the worst men were given for his burial," namely those who had asserted that it was stolen away, "and the rich for his death," namely those who had both bought the betrayal from Judas and the false testimony of the stolen corpse from the soldiers. Therefore, either these things did not befall the Jews on account of him — but you are refuted, since both the sense of the Scriptures and the outcome of events and the order of the times conspire — or, if they befell on account of him, the Creator could not have avenged any but his own Christ, intending rather to reward Judas, if they had slain the adversary of his Lord. Certainly, if the Christ of the Creator has not yet come, on whose account these things are proclaimed as about to be suffered, then when he comes they will suffer them. And where then will be the daughter of Sion to be forsaken, which today is nowhere? Where the cities to be burned, which already lie in heaps? Where the dispersion of the nation, which is already in exile? Restore the state of Judea which the Christ of the Creator may find, and then contend that another came. But truly, what kind of thing is it that, by means of his own heaven, he admitted one whom he was to slay in his own land — the more honourable and glorious region of his kingdom being violated, his very court and citadel trodden under foot? Or did he rather affect this? Plainly a jealous god — yet he conquered. Blush, you who believe in a conquered god. What will you hope from one who could not protect himself? For either he was overpowered through weakness by the virtues and men of the Creator, or through malice, that he might only fasten upon them so great a guilt by his endurance.

I take upon myself the person of Israel. Let the Christ of Marcion stand and cry out: "O unbelieving generation, how long shall I be with you? how long shall I bear with you?" Straightway he ought to hear from me: "Whoever thou art, thou newcomer, first publish who thou art, and from whom thou comest, and what right thou hast in us. Hitherto with thee all is the Creator's. Plainly if thou comest from him, and for him thou actest, we admit the reproach. But if from another, say, I pray, what hast thou ever committed to us of thine own, which we ought to have believed, that thou shouldst reproach unbelief — thou who hast never even revealed thyself to us? How long since didst thou begin to act among us, that thou shouldst complain of the time? In what didst thou bear with us, that thou shouldst impute patience? An ass from Aesop's well, thou comest only now, and already criest out." I take up also the person of the disciples, on whom he leapt: "O unbelieving nation, how long shall I be with you, how long shall I bear with you?" This outburst of his I should most justly strike back, surely in this manner: "Whoever thou art, thou newcomer, first publish who thou art, from whom thou comest, what right thou hast in us. Hitherto, I think, thou art the Creator's, and therefore we have followed thee, recognizing in thee all that is his. But if thou comest from him, we admit the reproach. But if for another thou actest, I pray thee, say, what hast thou ever committed to us, at least of thine own, which we ought already to have believed, that thou shouldst reproach unbelief — thou who dost not even hitherto publish thine author? How long since didst thou begin to act among us, that thou shouldst oppose the time too? In what didst thou bear with us, that thou shouldst boast patience too? An ass from Aesop's well, thou hast only now appeared here, and already criest out." Who would not so have beaten back the injustice of the reproach, if he had believed him to belong to one who ought not yet to complain? Save that not even that other would have leapt upon them, had he not, long since dwelling among them in the law, in the prophets, in powers and benefits, ever found them unbelieving. But behold, Christ loves the little ones, teaching that such ought they to be who always wish to be greater. But the Creator sent bears upon the boys, avenging Elisha the prophet, who had suffered insults from them. A shameless enough Antithesis, when it commits things so diverse — little ones and boys, an age yet innocent and one already capable of judgement, which could insult, not to say blaspheme. By which, then, as just god, he spared not even impious boys, exacting honour for the greater age, and surely the more from the lesser; but by which, as good, he so loves the little ones that in Egypt he did good to the midwives, who protected the Hebrew births endangered by the edict of Pharaoh. Thus this affection too of Christ is with the Creator. Even now, the god of Marcion, who opposes marriage, how can he seem a lover of little ones, whose whole cause is marriage? He who hates the seed must of necessity execrate the fruit too. Nay, that one is to be held more savage than the king of Egypt. For Pharaoh did not suffer the infants to be reared, this one not even to be born — taking life from them even of ten months in the womb. But how much more credible that the affection toward little ones be reckoned to him who, in blessing marriage for the propagation of the human race, blessed and promised the very fruit of marriage, of which infancy is the first part. The Creator represents a plague of fire at Elias' demand upon that false prophet. I acknowledge the severity of a judge. On the contrary, the disciples destining the same animadversion against Christ upon that little village of the Samaritans. Let the heretic acknowledge too that this gentleness of Christ was promised by the same most severe judge. "He shall not contend," it says, "nor shall his voice be heard in the street: the bruised reed he shall not break, and the smoking flax he shall not quench." Such a one, surely, was much more not about to burn men. For then too to Elias, "Not in fire," says the Lord, "but in a mild spirit." But why does the most humane god refuse him who offers himself so inseparable a companion to him? If because he had said proudly or out of hypocrisy, "I will follow thee wherever thou goest," then either pride or hypocrisy he acted as a judge in judging it to be refused. And surely he condemned whom he refused, namely not about to follow unto salvation. For as he calls to salvation whom he does not refuse, or even whom he calls spontaneously, so to perdition he condemns whom he refuses. But to that man pleading the burial of his father, when he answers, "Let the dead bury their dead, but go thou and announce the kingdom of God," he manifestly confirmed both laws of the Creator: both that in Leviticus, forbidding the priests to be present even at the last rites of parents ("Over every dead soul," it says, "the priest shall not enter, and over his own father he shall not be defiled"), and that of consecration in Numbers; for there too he who vows himself to God bids, among the rest, that he enter not over any dead soul, not even over a father's or mother's or brother's. But I think he was destining for both consecration and priesthood him whom he had imbued with preaching the kingdom of God. Or if it is not so, he must be pronounced impious enough who, with no reason of law intervening, commanded the burials of parents to be despised by their sons. But when he forbids that third one, preparing first to bid farewell to his own, to look back, he follows out the sect of the Creator. This too that other one had been unwilling to have done by those whom he had freed from Sodom.

But God, as eternal and rational, so, I suppose, is also perfect in all things. "For you shall be perfect, as your Father who is in heaven." Exhibit, then, his perfect goodness too. Even though concerning its imperfection it is sufficiently established — goodness which is found neither natural nor rational — now it shall be convicted by another reasoning too: no longer imperfect, nay, even defective, scant and exhausted, less than the number of its own materials, not exhibited in all. For not all are saved, but fewer than all, both the Jews and the Christians of the Creator. But with the greater part perishing, how is that goodness defended as perfect which is, for the greater part, a ceaser — to a few something, to the greater number nothing — yielding to perdition, a partner in destruction? But if more are not to be saved, it will now be not goodness, but a more perfect malice. For just as the operation of goodness is what makes men saved, so the operation of malignity is what does not make them saved. But not making more saved, while making few, it will be more perfect in not helping than in helping. You cannot refer to the Creator too a goodness toward all and a defect. For Him whom you hold a judge, you show, if at all, to be understood as a dispenser of goodness, not a profligate squanderer — which you claim for your god. So far do you prefer him to the Creator by this goodness alone, that, if he professes it alone and whole, it ought to have been wanting to none. But I will not now charge Marcion's god with imperfection of goodness from the greater part of those who perish. It is enough that the very ones whom he saves, found to be of an imperfect salvation, show his goodness to be imperfect — saved, namely, only as to the soul, lost as to the flesh, which with him does not rise again. Whence this halving of salvation, except from a defect of goodness? What belonged to perfect goodness but to bring back the whole man into salvation — the whole man condemned by the Creator, the whole man chosen by the best god? As far as I know, with him the flesh too is baptized, and the flesh is taken away from marriages, and the flesh is treated cruelly in the confession of his name. But even if sins are reckoned to the flesh, the guilt of the soul goes before, and the leadership of the fault is rather to be ascribed to the soul, to which the flesh meets only in the name of a servant. The flesh, finally, when destitute of the soul, sins only so far. So in this too the goodness is unjust and thereby imperfect, leaving the more innocent substance to destruction — a substance that sins by compliance, not by choice; whose truth, even if Christ did not put on, as your heresy thought, yet he deigned to undergo its image. By the very fact that he counterfeited it, he owed it that he owed it something. But what else is man than flesh, since the name of man was assigned by the Author to the bodily material, not the animate? "And God made man," it says, "of the slime of the earth" — not the soul; for the soul is from the breath: "and man became a living soul." What man? Surely he who was of the slime. "And God placed the man in Paradise" — the one he formed, not the one he breathed; the one who is now flesh, not the one who is soul. So if it is thus, with what face will you contend for a perfect title of goodness, which has now failed not from a special partition of the man to be freed, but from the general property? If the grace be full, and the mercy solid, which is salutary to the soul alone, this life confers more, in which we enjoy the man whole and entire. For the rest, to rise again in part will be to be mulcted, not freed. There was this too belonging to perfect goodness, that man, set free into the faith of the best god, should at once be exempted from the dwelling and dominion of the cruel god. But as it is, O Marcionite, you both run a fever, and the pain of your flesh breeds for you the rest of the thorns and thistles, and you are exposed not only to the Creator's lightnings or wars and plagues and other strokes, but even to His scorpions. In what do you suppose yourself freed from His kingdom, when His flies still trample you? If you are rescued from the future, why not from the present too, that you may be perfectly freed? Other is our condition with the Author, with the Judge, with the offended sovereign of the race. You only put forward a good god. But you cannot show him perfectly good, by whom you are not perfectly freed.

So too you wrongly interpret repentance in Him, as though accordingly out of fickleness or improvidence — nay, now out of the recollection of a sin — He repents; since indeed He said, "It repents me that I made Saul king," prescribing, namely, that repentance savours of the confession of some evil work or error. But not always. For the confession of repentance comes to pass even in good deeds, unto the upbraiding and reproach of him who has shown himself ungrateful for a benefit; as also then it is announced by the Creator concerning the person of Saul, who was to be honoured — He who had not sinned when He took Saul into the kingdom and increased him with the Holy Spirit; for, being still the best — "such as," it says, "there was not among the sons of Israel" — He had most worthily accepted him. Yet neither had He been ignorant that it would so turn out. For no one will endure you ascribing improvidence to Him whom, not denying Him God, you confess also provident. For this divinity is His own and established. But Saul's evil deed, as I said, He burdened with the profession of His repentance — which, since the sin is absent in the case of Saul's acceptance, it is consequent to understand as upbraiding rather than criminating. "Behold," you say, "I observe it as criminating in the case of the Ninevites, the scripture of Jonah saying, And the Lord repented of the malice which He had said He would do to them, and did it not." As also Jonah himself to the Lord: "Therefore I made haste to flee away to Tarshish, because I knew that you are merciful and pitying, patient and of much mercy, and repenting of malices." Well, then, that he set forth first the title of the best God — most patient, namely, toward the evil, and most abounding in mercy and pity toward those who acknowledge and bewail their sins, such as the Ninevites then were. For if He is best who is such, you ought first to have yielded this point — that there does not suit such a one, that is, the best, even a meeting with malice. And because Marcion too maintains that the good tree may not produce evil fruits either, yet named malice, which the best does not admit — is there not some interpretation underlying for the understanding of those malices too which may have run even unto the best? But it underlies. We say, finally, that "malice" is now signified, not that which is reduced to the nature of the Creator, as of an evil one, but that which is reduced to His power, as of a judge; according to which He should pronounce, "I am he who creates evils," and, "Behold, I send upon you evils" — not sinful, but avenging, the infamy of which we have sufficiently washed away as suiting a judge. But just as, although they be called evils, they are not reproached in a judge, nor on this their own name show the judge to be evil, so too this malice will now have to be understood which, reckoned out of those judicial evils, suits the judge together with them. For with the Greeks too "malices" are sometimes put for vexations and hurts, not for malignities, as also in this article. And so, if the Creator repented of that malice, namely of a creature to be reprobated and to be vindicated upon for sin, yet here too no criminal admission will be reckoned to the Creator, who had worthily and deservedly decreed that a most iniquitous city should be abolished. So what He had justly destined, not destining ill, He had destined out of justice, not out of malice; but the punishment itself He named "malice" out of the evil and deserving of the very suffering of it. "Therefore," you will say, "if you excuse the malice under the name of justice — because He had justly destined destruction upon the Ninevites — even so He is to be blamed, who exercised a repentance of a justice surely not to be repented of." Nay, neither of justice, I say, will God repent; and it remains now to acknowledge what the repentance of God is. For not if a man repents, mostly out of the recollection of a sin, and sometimes out of the thanklessness of some good work, is therefore God so too. For in so far as God neither admits evil nor condemns good, in so far neither is there a place of repentance of good or evil with Him. For this too the same scripture determines for you, Samuel saying to Saul: "The Lord has cut away the kingdom of Israel from your hand this day, and will give it to your neighbour, better than you; and Israel shall be rent in two parts, and shall not turn nor do repentance, because He is not as a man, to repent." This definition, then, in all cases sets up another form of divine repentance, which is to be reckoned neither out of improvidence nor out of fickleness nor out of any condemnation of a good or evil work, as the human is. What then will be the manner of divine repentance? It already shines forth, if you refer it not to human conditions. For nothing else will be understood than a simple turning of a former sentence, which may be admitted even without reprehension of him — even in man, much more in God, whose every sentence is free of fault. For even in the Greek sound the name of "repentance" is composed not of the confession of a sin, but of a change of mind, which with God we have shown to be governed for the meeting of varying matters.

"Nay," you say, "I hope from him what he himself does for the testimony of the difference: the kingdom of God of an eternal and heavenly possession." But your Christ promises to the Jews the former state, by the restitution of their land, and, after the course of life is run, refreshment in the bosom of Abraham among the dead. A most good god, if he gives back when appeased what he had also taken away when angered! O your god, who both wounds and heals, makes evils and works peace! O god merciful even to the underworld! But concerning the bosom of Abraham in its place. As for the restitution of Judea — which the Jews themselves too, led by names of places and regions, hope for just as it is described — how an allegorical interpretation may spiritually suit it to Christ and to the Church and to its state and fruit, it would be long to pursue, and it is treated in another work, which we entitle Concerning the Hope of the Faithful; and for the present it is even idle here, because the question is not of an earthly but of a heavenly promise. For we too confess that a kingdom is promised to us on earth — but before heaven, only in another state: namely, after the resurrection, for a thousand years, in the city of divine workmanship, Jerusalem brought down from heaven, which the apostle too designates as our mother on high; and, pronouncing our citizenship — that is, our municipality — to be in the heavens, he assigns it surely to some heavenly city. This city Ezekiel too knew, and the apostle John saw. And the word of the new prophecy, which is with our faith, testifies — so that it even foretold that the effigy of the city would be present to view before its actual representation, for a sign. In short, it was lately discharged in the eastern expedition. For it is established, by heathen witnesses too, that in Judea, for forty days, in the early hours of the morning, a city hung from heaven, the whole fabric of its walls vanishing with the advance of the day, and at other times nothing near at hand. This city we say is provided by God for the receiving of the saints at the resurrection and for their refreshing with an abundance of all good things — spiritual, surely — in compensation for those which in the world we either despised or lost. Since indeed it is both just and worthy of God that there too his servants should exult where they were also afflicted in his name. This is the rationale of the heavenly kingdom; after whose thousand years — within which space is enclosed the resurrection of the saints, who rise sooner or later according to their merits — then, the destruction of the world and the conflagration of judgement being accomplished, we shall be changed in a moment into the angelic substance, namely by that putting-on of incorruption over us, and shall be translated into the heavenly kingdom; concerning which the matter is now thus handled, as though it were not proclaimed with the Creator, and on this account proves the Christ of another god, by whom first and alone it was revealed. Learn, then, henceforth, that it was both proclaimed by the Creator and is to be believed, even without proclamation, with the Creator. What does it seem to you, when the seed of Abraham, after the first promise by which it is promised to the likeness of the sand, is destined also to the pattern of the stars — are not these the auspices both of an earthly and of a heavenly arrangement? When Isaac, blessing his son Jacob, says, "May God give thee of the dew of heaven and of the fatness of the earth" — are these not examples of a twofold indulgence? In short, here too the structure of the blessing itself is to be noticed. For concerning Jacob — who is the figure of the later and preferred people, that is, of us — the first promise is of the dew of heaven, the second of earthly fatness. For we are first invited to heavenly things, when we are torn from the world, and so afterward are found about to obtain earthly things too. And your gospel also has it: "Seek first the kingdom of God, and these things shall be added to you." But to Esau he promises an earthly blessing, and subjoins a heavenly one out of the fatness of the earth, saying, "Thy dwelling shall be also of the dew of heaven." For the arrangement of the Jews is in Esau — of sons elder by birth and later by affection — first imbued with earthly goods through the law, afterward led to heavenly things through the gospel by believing. But when Jacob dreams of a ladder fixed firm in the earth up to heaven, with some angels ascending and others descending, and the Lord leaning above — rashly, if at all, shall we interpret that by this ladder is shown a way to heaven, by which some arrive, from which others fall — established by the Lord's judgement. But why, when he awoke and was first struck with the awe of the place, did he turn to the interpretation of the dream? For when he had said, "How terrible is this place!" he says, "It is nothing else but the house of God, and this is the gate of heaven." For he had seen Christ the Lord, the temple of God and the gate, the same through whom heaven is entered. And surely he would not have named "the gate of heaven" if heaven is not entered with the Creator. But there is a gate too, which both receives and leads through, paved already by Christ. Of which Amos says: "Who builds his ascent into heaven" — surely not for himself alone, but for his own too, who will be with him. "For thou shalt put them about thee," he says, "as the ornament of a bride." Thus, tending through that ascent to the heavenly kingdoms, the Spirit marvels, saying, "They fly as those who are kites, as the clouds fly, and as the young of doves" — to me, namely, simply as doves. For we shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, according to the apostle (that son of man, namely, coming in the clouds, according to Daniel), and so we shall ever be with the Lord — in so far as we shall be both on earth and in heaven; who, on account of the ungrateful of either promise, calls the very elements to witness: "Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth." And for my part, even if no hand of heavenly hope were held out to me by Scripture so often, I should have prejudice enough of this promise too, from the fact that I already hold the earthly grace; I should expect something from heaven also, from the God of heaven as well as of earth; thus I should believe that Christ, promising loftier things, belongs to him who had promised humbler ones too — who had also made trials of greater things by small ones, who had reserved the proclamation of this kingdom (unheard-of, if at all) for Christ alone, so that by his servants earthly glory should be announced, but the heavenly by God himself. But you argue from this too another Christ, because he announces a new kingdom. First you must bring forward some example of his indulgence, lest with reason I doubt the credit of so great a promise, which you say is to be hoped for; nay, before all things, that you should prove some heaven of his whom you preach to promise heavenly things. But as it is, you call to a supper and do not show the house; you allege a kingdom and do not point out the palace. Or is it because your Christ promises a heavenly kingdom while having no heaven — just as he furnished forth a man too while having no flesh? O the all-phantom! O the sleight even of so great a promise!

He chooses too another seventy apostles over and above the twelve. For to what end twelve, after just so many springs in Elim, if not also seventy after just so many palm-trees? The diversity of cases, not of powers, made most of the Antitheses. But he who did not regard the diversity of cases, easily esteemed it one of powers. The Creator brings out the departure of the sons of Israel from Egypt, stuffed and packed with those spoils of golden and silver vessels and garments besides the burdens of their dough; but Christ prescribed that the disciples should not carry even a staff on the way. For the former were being advanced into the wilderness, but these were sent into cities. Consider the bringing-forward of the cases, and you will understand one and the same power which arranged the expedition of its own according to penury and plenty — cutting short, as it was to abound through the cities, just as it had provided furnishing for one about to journey through the wilderness. He forbade them also to carry shoes. For he it was under whom the people, even in the wilderness through so many years, had not worn out its shoes. "Salute no one," he says, "on the way." O Christ the destroyer of the prophets, from whom he received even this! Elisha, when he sent his servant Gehazi on the way to the son of the Shunammite, to be raised from death, I think thus commanded him: "Gird thy loins and take my staff in thy hand and go: whomever thou meetest on the way, do not bless him" — that is, do not salute him — "and whoever blesses thee, do not answer him" — that is, do not salute him back. For what is the blessing on the ways but a mutual salutation from meeting? So too the Lord, that into whatever house they should enter, they should say peace to it. The example is the same. For this too Elisha commanded — that, when he had entered to the Shunammite, he should say to her, "Peace to thy husband, peace to thy son." These will rather be our Antitheses, which compare, not which separate Christ. But "the worker is worthy of his hire" — who could more have pronounced this than a god a judge? — for this very thing is to judge, to make the worker worthy of his hire. No retribution stands without judgement. Even now here the law of the Creator is sealed, who judges even the working oxen worthy workers of their hire. "An ox," it says, "treading out, thou shalt not bind the mouth." Who so generous toward men but he who is so toward cattle too? But if Christ too pronounces the workers worthy of their hire, he excused that precept of the Creator about the golden and silver vessels of the Egyptians to be carried off. For those who had worked villas and cities for the Egyptians, surely workers worthy of their hire, were not equipped for fraud, but for the compensation of a hire which otherwise they could not have exacted from their masters. The kingdom of God, neither new nor unheard-of, he thus too confirmed, while he bids it be announced to have drawn near. For what at some time had been far off, that can be said to have drawn near. But if it had never before existed before it drew near, neither could that be said to have drawn near which had never been far off. Everything that is new and unknown is sudden. Everything that is sudden, when it is announced, then for the first time, bringing in its appearance, then for the first time receives its time. For the rest, it could not have delayed before, so long as it was not announced, nor have drawn near from the time it began to be announced. He even adds, that to those who had not received them they should say, "Know, however, that the kingdom of God has drawn near." If he commands this not for the sake of threatening too, he commands it most vainly. For what is it to them if the kingdom draw near, except because it draws near with judgement? — unto the salvation, namely, of those who shall have received its announcement. How, if a threat can be without execution, have you a god an executor in the threatener and a judge in both? So too he bids the dust be shaken off upon them, for a testification, even what cleaves to their land — far less anything of the remaining communion. For if inhumanity and inhospitality are to bring back from him no vengeance, to what purpose does he prefix a testification, surely portending threats? Now, since the Creator too in Deuteronomy forbids the Ammonites and Moabites to be received into the church, because they had inhumanly and inhospitably defrauded of supplies the people departing from Egypt, then it will be established that the interdict of communion flowed thence into Christ, where he has the form, "Whoever despises you, despises me." This too the Creator to Moses: "They have not despised thee, but me." For Moses is as much an apostle as the prophets too are apostles. The authority of either office will have to be matched, from one and the same lord of apostles and of prophets. Who now will give power to tread upon serpents and scorpions? Whether the lord of all animals, or the god not even of one lizard? But well that the Creator promised this power even to little boys through Isaiah — to thrust their hand into the den of asps and into the bed of the young of asps, and not at all be hurt. And surely we know (saving the simplicity of the Scripture — for not even could the beasts themselves harm where faith was) that figuratively scorpions and serpents portend spiritual things of wickedness, of which their very prince too is reckoned under the name of serpent and dragon and of each most eminent beast with the Creator, who granted this power to his former Christ, as the ninetieth psalm to him: "Upon the asp and the basilisk thou shalt tread, and thou shalt trample the lion and the dragon." As also Isaiah: "In that day the Lord God shall bring on a sword, holy, great, and strong" — namely his Christ — "upon that dragon, the great and crooked serpent, and he shall slay him in that day." But when the same says, "It shall be called a clean way and a holy way, and the unclean shall not pass there, nor shall there be there an unclean way; but those who shall be dispersed shall go in it, and shall not err, and there shall no longer be a lion there, nor shall any of the worst beasts go up upon it, nor shall it be found there" — since the way demonstrates faith, through which we come to God, even then to the same way, that is, to faith, he promises this evacuation and subjection of the beasts. In short, you may find too the times of the promise to agree, if you read what goes before: "Be strong, you hands let down, and you knees dissolved: then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall hear: then the lame shall leap as a hart, and the tongue of the dumb shall be clear." Therefore where he published the benefits of medicines, then too he subjected both scorpions and serpents to his holy ones — he, namely, who had received this power, that he might furnish it to others too, first from the Father, and exhibited it according to the order of the proclamation.

As concerns the question of goodness, by these lines we have brought it down that it is by no means made equal to a god — being neither inborn nor rational nor perfect, but even dishonest and unjust and now unworthy of the very name of goodness; so that, in so far as it suits a god, in so far it is fitting that he be not a god who is preferred even because of such goodness — and not because of such goodness merely, but even because of it alone. For now it is fit that this too be examined: whether God is to be reckoned of goodness alone, the other appendages being denied — the senses and affections, which the Marcionites indeed drive away from their god into the Creator, but which we both acknowledge in the Creator as worthy of a god. And from this too we shall deny him a god in whom not all things that are worthy of a god are established. If he affected to entitle, under the name of Christ, some god out of the school of Epicurus — to the end that, being blessed and incorruptible, he should offer molestation neither to himself nor to another (for chewing over this maxim Marcion removed from him severities and judicial powers) — he ought either to have conceived a god altogether immobile and stupefied (and what has he to do with Christ, troublesome both to the Jews by his teaching and to himself by his sense?), or else to have acknowledged him capable of the other motions too (and what has he to do with Epicurus, necessary neither to himself nor to the Christians?). For lo, by this very fact, that he who was formerly quiet, who took no care for the knowledge of himself by any work in the meantime, after so great an age felt a concern for the salvation of man — by will, of course — was he not then shakeable by a new will, so that he seems liable to the other motions too? But what will is there without the goad of desire? Who will wish what he will not desire? But care too will attach to will. For who will wish anything and desire it, and not care for it? Therefore, since he both willed and desired the salvation of man, he has now made business both for himself and for others — Epicurus unwilling, Marcion his counsellor. For he set up an adversary to himself in that very thing against which he both willed and desired and cared — whether sin or death — first of all the very arbiter and lord of these, man's Creator. Further, nothing will run its course without rivalry which will not be without an adversary. In short, willing and desiring and caring to free man, by this very fact he is now a rival even of Him from whom he frees him, to free him against Him, of course; and of those things from which he frees him, to free him into others. Accordingly, into that which he rivals there must of necessity meet the officials of his rivalry: anger, discord, hatred, disdain, indignation, gall, unwillingness, offence. If all these stand by rivalry, but rivalry is procured by freeing man, but the freeing of man is an operation of goodness, that goodness will not be able to subsist without its own endowments — that is, without the senses and affections through which it is administered against the Creator — lest in this way too it be prescribed as irrational, if it lack both the senses and the due affections. These things we shall defend much more fully in the cause of the Creator, in which they are also reproached.

Now then, that I may dispatch all things of this kind, I will press on to interpret and clear the other littlenesses and weaknesses and incongruities, as you reckon them. God cries out, "Adam, where are you?" — being ignorant, forsooth, where he was; and, alleging the shame of nakedness, He asks whether he had tasted of the tree — being uncertain, forsooth. Nay, neither uncertain of the deed nor ignorant of the place. For indeed it behoved that the man, lurking in the consciousness of his sin, being summoned, should come forth into the sight of the Lord, not by the mere outcry of his name, but with some impeaching now of the deed admitted. For it is not in the simple manner, that is, in an interrogatory tone, that we are to read, "Where are you, Adam?", but in one impressed and dashed in and imputative: "Adam, where are you?" — that is, you are in perdition, that is, you are no longer here; so that the voice may be the issue both of one rebuking and of one grieving. For the rest, would some portion of Paradise have escaped the eyes of Him who grasps the whole world in His hand like a nest, whose throne is heaven and the earth His footstool, so that Adam was anywhere too hidden from Him to be seen, before being summoned, as taking of the forbidden fruit? The watcher of your vineyard or garden is not hidden from by the wolf or the little thief. God, I think, more keen-eyed from the higher places, cannot let anything below pass Him by. Foolish you, who turn so great an argument of divine majesty and human instruction to a sneer. God asked as though uncertain, that here too, proving man free of arbitration in the matter of either denial or confession, He might give him room of his own accord to confess the sin, and on this score to be relieved. As of Cain He inquires where his brother is — as though He had not already heard the blood of Abel crying out from the earth; but that he too might have the power, out of the same power of arbitration, of his own accord to deny the sin, and on this score to be aggravated; and so that examples might be laid up for us of sins rather to be confessed than denied; that even then the evangelical doctrine might be initiated, "By your mouth you shall be justified, and by your mouth you shall be condemned." For even though Adam, by reason of the state of the law, was given over to death, yet hope is saved for him, the Lord saying, "Behold, Adam is become as one of us" — concerning, namely, the future acceptance of man into divinity. Finally, what follows? "And now, lest at any time he stretch out his hand and take of the tree of life and live for ever." For by interposing "and now," a word of present time, He showed that He had made a delay of life temporal and unto the present. And therefore He did not curse Adam himself and Eve, as candidates of restitution, as relieved by confession. But Cain He both cursed, and forbade — though desirous to atone for his sin by death — to die for the present, as one burdened, beyond his deed, also by the denial of it. This will be the ignorance of our God, which was therefore feigned, lest the sinning man should be ignorant what he ought to do. But descending to Sodom and Gomorrah, He says, "I will see whether they are consummated according to the cry that comes to me; but if not, that I may know." And here, forsooth, uncertain out of ignorance and desirous to know? Or is this sound of the pronouncement necessary, expressing not a doubting but a threatening sense, under the pretext of an inquiry? But if you mock the descent of God too, as though He could not otherwise have completed the judgment unless He had descended, see that you do not equally batter your own god. For he too descended, that he might effect what he willed.

Who shall be invoked as Lord of heaven who is not first shown to be its maker? "For I give thanks," he says, "and confess to thee, Lord of heaven, that what was hidden from the wise and prudent thou hast revealed to babes." What things are these? and whose? and by whom hidden? and by whom revealed? If hidden by the god of Marcion and revealed, who had sent forth absolutely nothing before in which anything could have been hidden — no prophecies, no parables, no visions, no arguments at all of things or words or names overshadowed through allegories and figures or the mists of riddles, but had hidden his very magnitude, which he was now most of all revealing through Christ — unjustly enough. For what had the wise and prudent delinquished, that god should be hidden from them, to the knowing of whom their wisdom and prudence had not sufficed? No way being given by him through any proclamation of works, or any footprints, by which the wise and prudent might be led on. Although too even if they had delinquished in something toward an unknown god — suppose now a known one — yet they ought not to have experienced him a jealous one, who is brought in as unlike the Creator. Therefore if he had neither sent forth materials in which to have hidden anything, nor had had guilty parties from whom to hide it, nor ought to have hidden it, even if he had had them — then neither will he himself be the revealer, who was not the hider; thus neither the Lord of heaven nor the Father of Christ, but he in whom all these things suit. For he both hid, the instrument of prophetic obscurity being sent before, whose understanding faith should deserve ("Unless you believe, you shall not understand"), and had as guilty the wise and prudent, who from his works so many and so great did not seek out an intelligible god, or philosophized perversely concerning him, and supplied wits to the heretics, and lastly is jealous. In short, of old he harangued through Isaiah what Christ rejoices at: "I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and the prudence of the prudent I will hide." As also elsewhere he signifies both to have hidden and to be about to reveal: "And I will give them hidden treasures, the invisible I will open to them." And again: "Who else shall scatter the signs of ventriloquists and the divinations from the heart, turning back the wise and infatuating their thoughts?" But if he designated his own Christ too the illuminator of the nations — "I have set thee for a light of the nations," which we interpret in the name of the babes, namely those once small in sense and infants in imprudence, but now too small through the humility of faith — surely we shall the more easily believe that the same one revealed too to the babes through Christ who both formerly hid and through Christ promised the revelation. Or if the god of Marcion has laid open those things which had formerly been hidden by the Creator, then now he has done business for the Creator, expounding his things. "But for destruction," you say, "that he might traduce them." Then he ought to have traduced them to those from whom the Creator hid them — the wise and prudent. For if he did it out of benignity, acknowledgement was to be furnished to those to whom it had been denied, not to babes, to whom the Creator had begrudged nothing. And yet hitherto, I think, we prove that rather a building-up of the law and the prophets is found in Christ than a destruction. He says all things were handed over to him by the Father. You might believe it if Christ is the Creator's, whose all things are, because the Creator handed over all things to a Son not lesser than himself — the things he founded through him, namely through his Word. But if that newcomer is meant, what are the "all things" which were handed over to him by the Father? Which are the Creator's? Therefore good are the things which the Father handed to the Son, and the Creator now good, whose all things are good, and that other now not good, who invaded another's goods, that he might hand them to a Son, teaching to abstain from another's. Certainly a most beggarly one, who had not whence to enrich even his Son but out of another's. Or if nothing of the Creator's was handed to him by the Father, how does he claim the Creator's man for himself? Or if the man alone was handed to him, "all things" is not the man. But the Scripture declares a handing over of all things made to the Son. But even if you interpret "all things" of the kinds of men, that is, of all the nations, even to have handed these over to the Son is the Creator's: "I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance, and the ends of the earth for thy possession." Or if that other too has some things of his own, all of which he handed to the Son, equally with the man of the Creator, show some one out of all for credence, for an example, lest I as deservedly not believe that all things are his of whom I see nothing, as deservedly believe even the things I do not see to be his whose are all the things I do see. "But no one knows who the Father is, save the Son, and who the Son is, save the Father, and to whomever the Son shall reveal him." And so Christ preached an unknown god. For hence too the other heretics are propped, opposing the Creator as known to all, both to Israel by familiarity and to the nations by nature. And how does he himself attest that he was not known even to Israel? "But Israel has not known me, and the people has not understood me"; nor to the nations: "For behold, of the nations," he says, "there is no one." Wherefore he reckoned them a drop of a bucket, and Zion he left as a watch-tower in a vineyard. See, then, whether it be a confirmation of the prophetic voice reproaching the merely human ignorance, which was up to the Son. For therefore he subjoined that the Father is known by him to whom the Son shall have revealed him, since he himself was the one who, set by the Father, was announced as the illumination of the nations — of God, namely, the nations to be illumined, even Israel — surely through a fuller acknowledgement of God. Thus the arguments will not avail for the faith of another god which can suit the Creator, because those which do not suit the Creator, these will be able to avail for the faith of another god. If you inspect what follows too — "Blessed are the eyes which see what you see: for I say to you, that prophets did not see what you see" — they descend from the higher sense, so that no one, as was fitting, had known God, since not even the prophets had seen what was being seen under Christ. For if Christ were not mine, he would not have placed mention of the prophets in this passage. For what wonder if they had not seen the things of an unknown god, and one revealed after so long an age? But what would have been the happiness of those who then saw what others could not with reason have seen, if they had not obtained the representation of those things which they had never proclaimed — except that those who could equally have seen the things of their own god, which they had even proclaimed, yet had not seen them? But this will be the happiness of others who saw what others had only proclaimed. In short, we will show — and have already shown — that the things were seen in Christ which had been proclaimed, yet hidden even from the prophets themselves, that they might be hidden too from the wise and prudent of the world. In the gospel of truth a doctor of the law, assailing the Lord, "What doing," he says, "shall I obtain eternal life?" In the heretical one, only "life" is set, without mention of "eternal," so that the doctor may seem to have consulted about that life which is promised in the law by the Creator as long-lasting, and the Lord therefore to have given him an answer according to the law, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart and with thy whole soul and with all thy strength," because it was about the law of life he was inquiring. But the doctor of the law surely knew by what manner he could obtain the legal life, so that he would not have asked about that whose rules he even taught. But because the dead too were now being raised by Christ, roused to the hope of eternal life through the examples of return, lest he should demand something more of observance, loftier in hope, he therefore consulted about the obtaining of eternal life. And so the Lord, as himself neither another, nor bringing in any new precept other than that which principally makes for all salvation and either life, sets the very head of the law against him — of loving in all ways the Lord his God. In short, if the doctor too consulted about long-lasting life, and Christ answered, which is with the Creator, not about eternal, which is with the god of Marcion, how does he obtain the eternal? Surely not in the same way as the long-lasting too. For according to a difference of rewards, a distance of works too must be believed. Therefore not out of love of your god will the Marcionite obtain eternal life, as the lover of the Creator the long-lasting. But what kind of thing is it that he should not the more be loved who promises the eternal, if he is to be loved who promises the long-lasting? Therefore both lives will belong to the same one, since the same discipline is to be caught at for either life. What the Creator teaches, that it needs Christ too to be loved that he may furnish — that objection too intervening here, by which the greater ought the more easily to be believed with him with whom the lesser go before, than with him for whom no lesser things prepared any faith concerning the greater. Let it now be his concern whether our people added "eternal." This is enough for me, that that Christ, the inviter to eternal, not to long, life, consulted about the long, which he was destroying, exhorted a man rather to the eternal, which he was bringing in. What, I ask you, would the Christ of the Creator have done, if he who had built up a man toward loving the Creator were not the Creator's? I believe he would have denied the Creator to be loved.

But here it is enough to show the god most perverse in the very heralding of his solitary goodness, by which they will not ascribe to him those motions of mind which they blame in the Creator. For if he neither rivals nor is angry nor condemns nor vexes — inasmuch as he furnishes not even a judge — I do not find how the system of disciplines can stand for him, and that the fuller one. For what sort of thing is it that he should set up precepts which he will not enforce, that he should forbid sins which he will not avenge, since he will not judge — being, of course, a stranger to all the senses of severity and animadversion? For why does he forbid a thing to be committed which he does not punish when committed — when it had been far more right not to have forbidden what he was not going to punish, than not to punish what he had forbidden? Nay, he ought even outright to have permitted it, being about to forbid it to no purpose, as not about to punish it. For even now what is forbidden without vengeance is tacitly permitted. And surely he forbids nothing to be committed except what he does not love to be done. Most stupid, then, is he who is not offended by a deed which he does not love to be done — since offence is the companion of a thwarted will. Or if he is offended, he ought to be angry; if he is angry, he ought to avenge. For vengeance too is the fruit of anger, and anger the debt of offence, and offence, as I said, the companion of a thwarted will. But he does not avenge; therefore he is not offended. But he is not offended; therefore neither is his will hurt, when that is done which he was unwilling should be done — and so the sin now happens according to his will, since that does not happen against his will which does not hurt his will. Or if this shall be of divine power or goodness — to be unwilling indeed that a thing be done, and to forbid it being done, yet not to be moved if it be done — we say that he has now been moved who was unwilling, and that he is to no purpose unmoved at the deed who was moved at the not-doing, since he was unwilling that it be done. For in being unwilling he forbade. Did he not also judge by being unwilling that it be done, and therefore by forbidding? For he judged that it ought not to be done, and pronounced that it ought to be forbidden. Therefore he too now judges. If it is unworthy of God to judge — or if it is worthy of God to judge only so far as merely to be unwilling and to forbid, but not also to punish the deed — yet nothing is so unworthy of God as not to follow up what he was unwilling and forbade to be committed: first, because to any verdict and law of his he owes vengeance, for authority and the necessity of obedience; secondly, because it must of necessity be a rival, that which he was unwilling should be committed and by being unwilling forbade. But to spare evil is more unworthy of God than to chastise it — and that of a best god, who is not otherwise fully good unless a rival of evil, so as to exercise love of the good by hatred of the evil, and to fulfil the guardianship of the good by the storming of the evil.

But God even swears. Perhaps by Marcion's god? Nay, He says — much more vainly — by Himself. What would He have wished to do, if there were no other god in His consciousness, than this very thing, while swearing, that there is altogether no other besides Himself? Do you then catch Him perjuring Himself, or swearing in vain? But He cannot be seen to have perjured Himself who knew not another to exist, as you say. For what He knows, that swearing truly He did not forswear. But neither did He swear in vain that no other god exists. For then would He swear in vain, if there were none who believed in other gods — then, indeed, the worshippers of images, but now also the heretics. He swears, therefore, by Himself, that, even to a swearing God, you may believe there is altogether no other god. That God should do this, you too, Marcion, compelled Him. For even then you were foreseen. Accordingly, if He also swears in His promises or threats, wringing out a faith hard in the beginnings, it is nothing unworthy of God to make one believe God by what He does. Little enough, even then, is the god in his very fierceness, when, made savage against the people for the consecration of the calf, He demands of His own servant Moses, "Let me alone, and in my indignation I will destroy them in anger, and I will make you into a great nation." Whence you are wont to affirm Moses better than his god, the deprecator, nay even the forbidder, of the anger. "For you shall not do this," he says, "or expend me too together with them." Pitiable you too, with the people, who do not acknowledge Christ, figured in the person of Moses — the deprecator of the Father and the offerer of his own soul for the people's salvation. But it is enough if the people was even properly given to Moses for the present. What a servant could ask of his Lord, that the Lord asked of Himself. For to this end He said to His servant, "Let me alone, and I will destroy them," that the other, by asking and offering himself, should not let Him; and so you might learn how much is permitted to a faithful one and a prophet with God.

When in a certain place he had prayed to that higher Father, with eyes shameless enough and rash looking up to the heaven of the Creator — by whom, so harsh and savage, he could have been struck with hail and lightning, just as Jerusalem too could be fastened down by him — one of the disciples accosting him, "Lord," he says, "teach us to pray, as John too taught his disciples" — namely because he esteemed that another god should be prayed to otherwise. He who had presumed this, let him first prove another god published by Christ. For no one would have wished to know how to pray before he had learned whom he should pray to. Therefore if he had learned, prove it. If nowhere yet do you prove it, know that he asked of him a form of prayer toward the Creator, to whom the disciples of John too prayed.
