But because John too had brought in some new order of prayer, therefore his disciple had not without reason presumed that this too should be demanded of Christ — that they too, after the proper institution of their own master, should pray, not another, but otherwise, to God; accordingly neither would Christ have conferred the knowledge of prayer on a disciple before that of the god himself. Thus he himself too taught prayer toward him whom the disciple hitherto had known. In short, recognize what god the sense of the prayer savours. To whom shall I say, "Father"? to him who did not make me at all, from whom I draw no origin, or to him who by making and instructing me begat me? From whom shall I ask the Holy Spirit? from whom not even the worldly spirit is furnished, or from whom even the angels are made spirits, whose spirit too in the beginning was borne over the waters? Whose kingdom shall I wish to come — whom I never heard king of glory, or in whose hand are even the hearts of kings? Who shall give me daily bread? — he who founds me not even a millet-grain, or he who furnished even from heaven the daily bread of angels to his people? Who shall remit my delinquencies? — he who by not judging them does not retain them, or he who, if he shall not remit them, will retain them, that he may judge? Who shall not suffer us to be led into temptation? — whom shall the tempter be able not to fear, or he who from the beginning pre-condemned the tempting angel? In this order, he who supplicates another god and not the Creator does not pray him, but defames him. Accordingly, from whom shall I ask, that I may receive? with whom seek, that I may find? at whom knock, that it may be opened to me? Who has it to give to the asker, save he whose all things are, whose even I am who ask? But what have I lost with that other god, that with him I should seek and find? If wisdom and prudence, the Creator hid these. With him, then, shall I seek? If salvation and life, these too with the Creator? Nothing shall be sought elsewhere to be found than where it lay hidden to appear. So neither shall I knock elsewhere than whence I have departed. In short, if to receive and to find and to be admitted is the fruit of labour and instance to him who asked and sought and knocked, understand that these things are commanded and promised by the Creator. For that best god, coming spontaneously to furnish to a man not his own, would have indicted no labour nor instance on him. For he would now be no longer best, if he did not spontaneously give to one not asking, and furnish finding to one not seeking, and open to one not knocking. But the Creator could indict these things through Christ, that, because by delinquency man had offended his god, he should labour and by instance of asking receive, and by seeking find, and by knocking enter in. So too the foregoing likeness makes the nocturnal asker of bread a friend, not a stranger, and one knocking at a friend's, not a stranger's. But a friend, even if he has offended, is rather the Creator's man than the god of Marcion's. And so he knocks at him to whom he had a right, whose door he knew, whom he knew to have loaves, lying now with his infants, whom he had willed to be born. Even that he is knocked at late is the Creator's time. His too is the late, whose is the age and the setting of the age. But at a new god no one would have knocked late, only just as he was dawning. It is the Creator who both shut the door once to the nations, which was once knocked at by the Jews; he both rises and gives, and, even if now not as to a friend, yet not as to a stranger man, but, as he says, as to a troublesome one. But so newly a god could suffer no one to be troublesome to him. Acknowledge therefore the Father too whom you even call Creator. He it is who knows what his sons ask. For to those asking bread from heaven he gave manna, and to those desiring flesh he sent forth the quail; not a serpent for a fish, nor a scorpion for an egg. But it will belong to him not to give evil for good whose both are. For the rest, the god of Marcion, not having a scorpion, could not say that he would not give what he did not have; but he who, having a scorpion too, does not give. And so the Holy Spirit too will be given by him with whom the not-holy too is. When he had cast out a deaf demon (that in this species of cure too he might meet Isaiah), said to cast out demons in Beelzebub, "If I," he says, "in Beelzebub cast out demons, in whom do your sons cast them out?" — by this voice what does he portend rather than that he casts out in him in whom their sons too do? In the power, namely, of the Creator. For if you think it is to be taken thus, "If I in Beelzebub, in whom your sons?" as though he were censuring them as casting out in Beelzebub, the former sense will resist you, that Satan cannot be divided against himself. So far neither did they cast out in Beelzebub, but, as we have said, in the power of the Creator, which, that he might make understood, he subjoins: "But if I in the finger of God expel demons, then has the kingdom of God drawn near unto you?" For with Pharaoh those sorcerers, employed against Moses, called the power of the Creator the finger of God. The finger of God is this, that it should signify even what is small, yet most strong. This too Christ showing — a reminder, not an obliterator, namely, of his own antiquities — called the power of God the finger of God, to be understood of none other than him with whom this had been so named. Therefore his kingdom too had drawn near whose power too was called a finger. With reason, then, he applied to the parable of that strong armed man, whom another stronger overpowered — the prince of demons, whom he had above called Beelzebub and Satan — signifying him overpowered by the finger of God, not the Creator subdued by another god. For the rest, how should his kingdom still stand within its boundaries and laws and offices, whom, though with the world entire, that stronger god of Marcion could even thus have seemed to overcome, if the Marcionites too did not even die according to his law, flowing down into the earth, often taught even by a scorpion that the Creator is not overcome? A woman out of the crowd cried out, "Blessed the womb that bore him, and the breasts that nourished him." And the Lord, "Nay, blessed are they who hear the word of God and do it." For before too he had thus rejected his mother or brothers, while he prefers the hearers and obeyers of God. For neither here did a mother stand by him. So far had he not before denied him born. When he hears this again, again accordingly he transferred the felicity from the womb and breasts of his mother to the disciples — from her from whom he would not have transferred it if he had her not.

But he plainly judges evil by being unwilling, and condemns it by forbidding; yet he dismisses it by not avenging, and absolves it by not punishing. O god, betrayer of the truth! a circumventer of his own verdict! He fears to condemn what he condemns, fears to hate what he does not love; he allows the deed which he does not allow to be done, and would rather show what he does not wish than approve it. This will be an imaginary goodness, a phantasm of discipline, and the precepts themselves perfunctory, the sins secure. Hear, O sinners — and whoever are not yet such, that you may be able to be! — a better god has been found, who is neither offended nor angry nor avenges, for whom no fire is kindled in Gehenna, for whom no gnashing of teeth shudders in the outer darkness: he is only good. In short, he forbids sinning — but by letters alone. It is in you, if you will, to subscribe him your obedience, that you may seem to have paid honour to a god; for fear he does not want. And to such a point do the Marcionites parade it, that they fear their god not at all. "But the evil one," they say, "shall be feared; the good one shall be loved." Fool, do you deny that he must be feared whom you call lord — when this name belongs to a power that must also be feared? But how will you love, unless you fear not to love? Plainly he is not your father, in whom should meet both love for piety's sake and fear for power's sake; nor a legitimate lord, that you should love him for his humanity and fear him for his discipline. So, finally, are kidnappers loved, but not also feared. For nothing will be feared except just and ordinary dominion; but even an adulterous one can be loved — for it stands by solicitation, not by authority, by flattery, not by power. And what, in fine, is more flattering than not to follow up sins? Come, then, you who fear not God as good — why do you not boil over into every lust, the highest fruit of life, as far as I know, for all who fear not God? Why do you not frequent the so solemn pleasures of the raging circus and the savaging amphitheatre and the wantoning stage? Why do you not, in persecutions too, the moment the censer is offered, gain your life by denial? God forbid, you say; God forbid. Then you already fear sin, and by fearing you have proved that He is feared who forbids sin. It is another matter if, by that same perversity of your god whom you fear not, you observe him — by which he too forbids what he does not avenge. Vainer still is it when, asked, "What will become of every sinner in that day?", they answer that he will be cast away, as it were from his eyes. Is not this too transacted by judgment? For he is judged to be cast away — and surely by a judgment of condemnation; unless indeed the sinner be cast away into salvation, that this too may suit the best god. And what will it be to be cast away, but to lose that which he would have obtained had he not been cast away — that is, salvation? Therefore he will be cast away to the detriment of salvation; and this cannot be decreed except by one who is angered and offended and an executor of the deed — that is, a judge.

Now then, that I may dispatch the rest also in a summary, whatever things you yet gather, as little and weak and unworthy, toward the destruction of the Creator, I will propound by a plain and sure reasoning: that God could not have entered into intercourse with men unless He had taken on both human senses and human affections, through which He might temper, by His own humility, the force of His majesty — surely intolerable to human mediocrity — things unworthy of Himself indeed, but necessary for man, and so already worthy of God, because nothing is so worthy of God as the salvation of man. Of this I would treat at greater length, if I were dealing with the heathen — although even with heretics the engagement stands not much different. Inasmuch as you yourselves have now believed that God too was diversified into a figure and into the rest of the order of human condition, you will surely not require to be persuaded any longer that God conformed Himself to humanity, but you are convicted out of your own faith. For if a god — and indeed a loftier one — laid low the summit of his majesty in so great a humility as even to subject himself to death, and the death of the cross, why do you not think that some littlenesses suited our God too, yet more tolerable than the Jewish contumelies and gibbets and sepulchres? Or are these the littlenesses which ought from this very point to prejudge that Christ, exposed to human sufferings, is of that god to whom human things are reproached by you? For we even profess that Christ always acted in the name of God the Father; that He from the beginning held intercourse, He held converse with the patriarchs and prophets — the Son of the Creator, His Word, whom by putting Him forth from Himself He made His Son, and thenceforth set Him over His every disposition and will, diminishing Him a little beneath the angels, as it is written in David; by which diminution He was disposed by the Father even unto these things which you reprehend as human, learning even from the beginning, even from then, man, what He was to be in the end. He it is who descends, He who asks, He who demands, He who swears. For the rest, that the Father was seen of none even the common gospel will attest, Christ saying, "No one has known the Father but the Son." For He Himself had pronounced even in the Old Testament, "No man shall see God and live," determining the Father invisible, in whose authority and name He Himself was the God who was seen, namely the Son of God. But with us too Christ is received in the person of Christ, because in this manner also He is ours. Therefore whatever things you demand as worthy of God will be held in the Father, invisible and inaccessible and placid and (so to speak) the God of the philosophers. But whatever things you reprehend as unworthy will be reckoned to the Son, both seen and heard and met with, the arbiter of the Father and His minister, mingling in Himself man and God — in mighty works God, in littlenesses man — that He may confer upon man so much as He detracts from God. The whole, finally, that with you is the disgrace of my God, is the sacrament of man's salvation. God held converse, that man might be taught to do divine things. God dealt on equal terms with man, that man might be able to deal on equal terms with God. God was found little, that man might be made greatest. You who disdain such a God — I know not whether out of faith you believe in a crucified God. How great, then, is your perversity toward each order of the Creator? You designate Him a judge, and reproach the judge's severity, suited to the deserts of the causes, as fierceness. You demand a best god, and depreciate his leniency, suited to kindness, conducted more lowly to the capacity of human mediocrity, as littleness. Neither the great pleases you, nor the moderate; neither the judge, nor the friend. But what if now these same things be detected in your own god too? That he too is a judge we have already shown in his own little book; and from being a judge, of necessity severe; and from being severe, so also fierce — if indeed fierce.

Elsewhere I prefer to purge the things which the Marcionites reprehend in the Creator. For here it suffices if these are found in Christ. Behold, unequal himself, inconstant, light, teaching one thing, doing another; he bids give to everyone that asks, and himself gives no sign to those who ask. For so great an age he hid his light from men, and denies that a lamp is to be hidden away, but confirms that it is to be set forth upon a candlestick, that it may shine for all. He forbids to curse back, much more surely to curse, and drives in a "Woe" upon the Pharisees and doctors of the law. Who is so like my god's Christ as his own? Often already we have fixed it that he could in no way be noted a destroyer of the law if he had promulgated another god. And therefore then too the Pharisee, who had called him to dinner, debated within himself why he had not first washed before he reclined, according to the law — since he carried about the god of the law. But Jesus even interpreted the law for him, saying that they cleansed the outside of the cup and platter, but their own inward parts were full of rapine and iniquity — to signify that the cleanness of vessels was to be understood, with God, of men; because the Pharisee too had debated within himself about the man, not about the unwashed cup. Therefore, "You wash the outside," he says, "of the cup," that is, the flesh, "but your inward parts you cleanse not," that is, the soul; adding, "Is it not he who made the outside" — that is, the flesh — "who made the inward parts too" — that is, the soul? By which saying he openly demonstrated that the cleanness of the outer and inner man pertains to the same God, whose both are, who prefers mercy not only to the washing of the man, but even to sacrifice. For he subjoins, "Give what you have as alms, and all things shall be clean to you." But if another god too could have commanded mercy — yet not before he was known. And here too it appears that they were rebuked not concerning a god, but concerning his discipline, by whom both figuratively the cleansing of the vessels and manifestly the works of mercies were enjoined upon them. So too he chides those who tithe their little herbs but pass over the calling and the love of God. Of what god the calling and love, if not of him whose rue and mint too, after the form of the law, they offered out of tithes? For the whole of the reproach was this, that they cared for the modest things, surely toward him to whom they did not exhibit the greater things — to him who says, "Thou shalt love the Lord thy God with thy whole heart, and with thy whole soul, and with all thy strength," who called thee out of Egypt. For the rest, neither would the time have allowed that Christ should demand so precocious — nay, so unripe a love as yet — for a new and recent god, not to say one not yet made manifest. When he accuses too those who catch at the chief places and the honour of salutations, he administers the sect of the Creator, who calls such princes rulers of the Sodomites, who forbids even trust in superiors — nay, pronounces altogether most wretched the man who has hope in man. But if for this reason anyone affects a princedom, that he may glory in the offices of others, since he forbade offices of this kind of hoping and trusting in man, the same rebuked too the affecters of princedoms. He inveighs too against the doctors of the law themselves, that they loaded others with unbearable burdens, which they themselves dared not attempt even with a finger — not censuring the burdens of the law as if its detester. For how a detester, who, while he was most of all accusing those who passed over the more weighty things of the law — alms and the calling and the love of God — did not even hold these heavy, far less the tithes of rue and the cleanness of platters? For the rest, he would rather have judged them to be excused if they could not bear unbearable things. But what burdens does he tax? Those which they themselves heaped up out of their own, teaching precepts, the doctrines of men, for the cause of their own conveniences, joining house to house, that they might carry off what was their neighbours', crying down the people, loving gifts, following after retribution, plundering the things judged for the poor, that there might be to them the widow for spoil and the orphan for prey. Concerning whom the same Isaiah: "Woe to those who are strong in Jerusalem"; and again: "Those who demand of you, lord it over you." Who more than the doctors of the law? These, if they displeased Christ too, displeased as his own. For of an alien law he would not at all have assailed the doctors. But why do they hear a "Woe" too because they built monuments to the prophets slain by their fathers — they rather worthy of praise, who by that work of piety testified that they did not consent to the deeds of their fathers — if he were not a jealous one, such as the Marcionites arraign him, exacting the delinquencies of the fathers from the sons even to the fourth nativity? But what key had the doctors of the law except the interpretation of the law? to the understanding of which neither did they themselves approach, not believing, namely (for "Unless you believe, you shall not understand"), nor did they admit others, teaching rather precepts and the doctrines of men. He, then, who rebuked those who neither entered themselves nor furnished entry to others — is he to be held a disparager of the law or a fautor? If a disparager, then the closers of the law too ought to have pleased him; if a fautor, then he is no longer the rival of the law either. But all these things he drove in to blacken the Creator, as savage, toward whom delinquents should have a "Woe." And who would not rather fear to provoke a savage one by falling away from him? So much the more, then, he taught one to be deserved well of whom he drove in as one to be feared. So it behoved the Christ of the Creator.

But what end awaits that cast-away one? "He will be seized," they say, "by the Creator's fire." Has he then no element of his own, provided even for this case, by which he may at least relegate his sinners without cruelty, rather than give them up to the Creator? What then does the Creator do? He will prepare for them, I believe, a more sulphurous Gehenna — as for his blasphemers, of course; unless perchance God the jealous one should spare the deserters of his rival. O god in every way perverse, everywhere irrational, in all things vain, and so a god who is no one! — whose state, whose condition, whose nature, whose any order I see not standing fast; nor now even the very sacrament of faith in him. For to what end is baptism too exacted with him? If it is the remission of sins, how will he seem to remit sins who will not seem to retain them? For he would retain them, if he judged. If it is the absolution of death, how would he absolve from death who has not bound to death? For he would have bound, if he had condemned from the beginning. If it is the regeneration of man, how does he regenerate who has not generated? For repetition does not belong to him by whom a thing was not done even once. If it is the obtaining of the Holy Spirit, how will he bestow the spirit who did not first confer the soul? For the soul will somehow suffice in place of the spirit. He seals, then, a man never unsealed with him; he washes a man never defiled with him; and in this whole sacrament of salvation he plunges a flesh that is excluded from salvation. Not even a countryman will water ground that will bring back no fruit — unless he be as vain as Marcion's god. Accordingly, why does he lay so great a burden, or glory, of holiness upon a flesh most weak or most unworthy? But what shall I say of the vanity of the discipline, by which he sanctifies a holy substance? Why does he either burden a weak one or adorn an unworthy one? Why does he not requite with salvation that which he burdens or adorns? Why does he defraud the wage of the work, not repaying salvation to the flesh? Why does he suffer even the honour of holiness to die in it?

Now too, concerning the littlenesses and malignities and the rest of the marks, I in turn will make Antitheses to rival Marcion's. If my God was ignorant that there was another above Him, your god too altogether knew not that there was another beneath him. For what that dark Heraclitus said — "the same way up and down." Finally, if he had not been ignorant, he would have met it even from the beginning. Sin and death, and the very author of sin, the devil, and every evil which my God suffered to exist, this yours too suffered to exist, who suffered it to exist. Our God changed His sentences — accordingly so did yours too. For he who so late regarded the human race changed that sentence by which for so great an age he regarded it not. It repented our God of evil in some matter — but yours too. For in that he at length turned his mind to man's salvation, he made a repentance, due to an evil deed, of his former dissembling. Further, the neglect of human salvation will be reckoned an evil deed, not amended save by repentance with your god. Our God commanded a fraud — but of gold and silver. But by how much man is more precious than gold and silver, by so much is your god the more fraudulent, who snatches man from his Lord and Maker. Our God demands eye for eye — but yours too, by forbidding the requital, does the rather an iterable injury. For who will not strike again, being not struck back? Our God knew not whom He accepted. Therefore neither did yours. He would not have accepted Judas the traitor, if he had foreknown. If you say the Creator lied somewhere, far greater is the lie in your Christ, whose body was not true. The fierceness of my God consumed many. Your god too, those whom he does not save, surely disposes unto destruction. My God commanded someone to be slain. Yours willed himself to be slain, no less a homicide against himself than against him by whom he willed to be slain. But that his god slew many I will prove to Marcion. For he made a homicide, surely to perish, unless indeed the people did no wrong against Christ. But ready virtue loves the truth with few words. Many words will be necessary to a lie.

With reason, therefore, the hypocrisy of the Pharisees did not please him — those, namely, who loved God with their lips, not with their heart. "Beware," he says to the disciples, "of the leaven of the Pharisees, which is hypocrisy" — not the preaching of the Creator. The Son hates those contumacious toward the Father; he does not wish his own to be such toward him, not toward another, toward whom hypocrisy might be committed, of which the example should be guarded against by the disciples. Thus he forbids the example of the Pharisees. He was forbidding it to be committed against him against whom the Pharisees committed it. Therefore, since he had taxed their hypocrisy — concealing the hidden things of the heart, namely, and overshadowing the secrets of unbelief with superficial offices, which, having the key of acknowledgement, neither entered itself nor suffered others — therefore he adds, "But nothing is covered which shall not be laid open, and nothing hidden which shall not be discerned"; lest anyone esteem that he intends the revelation and re-acknowledgement of a god formerly unknown and hidden, when he subjoins even the things which they muttered or treated among themselves — namely, saying about himself, "This man does not expel demons but in Beelzebub" — as about to proceed into the open, and to be in the mouth of men, from the promulgation of the gospel. Thereupon, turning to the disciples, "But I say to you, my friends," he says, "be not terrified by those who can only kill you, and after this have no further power over you." But to these Isaiah will be foretelling: "See how the just is taken away, and no one notices." "But I will show you whom you should fear: Fear him who, after he has killed, has power to send into Gehenna" — surely signifying the Creator: "Therefore, I say to you, fear him." And in this passage it would suffice me, if he whom he bids be feared he forbids to be offended, and whom he forbids to be offended he bids be deserved well of, and he who commands these things is his own to whom by fearing and not offending and deserving well of he procures it. But I have also to take from what follows. For "I say to you, everyone who shall confess in me before men, I too will confess in him before God." But those who shall confess in Christ shall have to be killed before men, surely about to suffer nothing more after the killing by them. These, then, will be those whom above he forewarns not to fear that they only be killed; therefore premising that the killing is not to be feared, that he might subjoin that the confession is to be sustained: "And everyone who shall deny me before men shall be denied before God" — by him, surely, who was to confess one confessing him. For if he shall confess the confessor, he himself it is who will also deny the denier. Now, if the confessor is one who has nothing to fear after the killing, the denier will be one who has to fear even after death. And so, since that which is to be feared after death is the Creator's — namely the penalty of Gehenna — then the denier too is the Creator's. But if the denier, then the confessor too, who after the killing is to suffer nothing from man, but plainly something from God if he denied. And thus Christ is the Creator's, who shows that his deniers ought to fear the Gehenna of the Creator. After the deterring of denial, therefore, follows too the admonition of a blasphemy to be dreaded: "He who shall speak against the Son of man, it shall be remitted to him, but he who shall speak against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be remitted to him." But if now both the remission and the retention of delinquency savour of a god a judge, his will be the Holy Spirit not to be blasphemed — not about to remit blasphemy, namely — just as above not to be denied — about to kill even into Gehenna, namely. But if Christ averts blasphemy too from the Creator, how he has come as his adversary I do not know. Or if by these things too he blackens his severity — not about to remit blasphemy and about to kill even into Gehenna — it remains that that diverse god's spirit too may be blasphemed with impunity, and that Christ may be denied, and that there be no difference about his worship or contempt; and, just as from contempt no penalty, so from worship no reward is to be hoped. Those brought before powers he forbids to think for the interrogation about an answer. "For the Holy Spirit," he says, "shall teach you in that very hour what you ought to speak." If an evidence of this kind is the Creator's, his too will be the precept whose the example went before. Balaam the prophet in Numbers, summoned by king Balak to curse Israel, with which he was entering battle, while he was being filled with the spirit, pronounced not the malediction to which he had come, but the benediction which the spirit suggested to him in that very hour — having professed before, among the king's messengers, and presently before the king himself, that he would pronounce what God should put in his mouth. These are the new doctrines of the new Christ, which of old the servants of the Creator initiated. Behold, a plainly diverse example of Moses and of Christ. Moses spontaneously intervenes among quarrelling brothers and rebukes the injurious one: "Why dost thou strike thy neighbour?" And he is rejected by him: "Who set thee a master or a judge over us?" But Christ, when he was asked by a certain man to settle between him and his brother concerning the dividing of an inheritance, denied his service, and that indeed to so honest a cause. Already then my Moses is better than your Christ, studying the peace of brothers, meeting injury. But indeed the Christ of a best and not a judging god says, "Who set me a judge over you?" He could find no other voice of excuse but that one with which a wicked man and impious brother had shaken off the asserter of probity and piety. In short, he approved the evil voice by using it, and the evil deed, by the declining of composing peace between brothers. Or did he perhaps take it ill that Moses had been put to flight by that saying, and therefore in the like cause of the brothers debating willed to have confounded them by the recollection of the same saying? Plainly so. For he himself it was then who had been in Moses, who had heard such things — the Spirit, namely, of the Creator. I think I have already sufficiently elsewhere shown that the glory of riches is condemned by our god, who pulls the very magnates down from their throne and lifts up the poor from the dung-heap. From him, then, will be the parable of the rich man flattering himself on the produce of his fields, to whom God says, "Fool, this night they shall demand back thy soul; but the things thou hast prepared, whose shall they be?" So too, in short, the king who gloried among the Persians over the storehouses and granaries of his delights heard ill through Isaiah.

With him the flesh is not baptized, unless it be virgin, unless widow, unless celibate, unless it has purchased baptism by divorce — as though even eunuchs were not born of marriage. Without doubt this institution will stand from the condemnation of wedlock. Let us see whether justly — not as though we meant to destroy the felicity of holiness, like certain Nicolaitans, champions of lust and luxury, but as men who have known holiness without the condemnation of marriage, and follow and prefer it — not as good to evil, but as better to good. For we do not cast away marriages, but lay them down; nor do we prescribe holiness, but persuade it, preserving both the good and the better by pursuing them according to each one's strength; defending wedlock outright then, finally, when it is enemy-wise accused under the name of foulness, to the destruction of the Creator, who accordingly blessed wedlock for the honesty of the thing toward the increase of the human race, just as He blessed the whole of creation for whole and good uses. Nor are foods therefore to be condemned because, more elaborately sought after, they go over into gluttony; nor will clothing therefore be accused because, more costly procured, it swells into ostentation. So neither will the matter of marriage therefore be spat upon because, more intemperately spread abroad, it burns into luxury. There is much difference between the cause and the fault, between the state and the excess. So in things of this kind it is not the institution but the going-out-of-bounds that is to be condemned, according to the censure of the Founder Himself, whose it is to say both "Increase and multiply" and "You shall not commit adultery, and you shall not covet your neighbour's wife" — punishing with death both the incestuous and the sacrilegious and the monstrous madness of lusts against males and against cattle. But even if a measure is now set for marrying — which indeed among us spiritual reason, on the authority of the Paraclete, defends, prescribing one marriage in the faith — it will belong to the same One to fix a measure who had at some time spread the measure abroad; the same will gather who scattered; the same will cut the wood who planted; the same will reap the harvest who sowed; the same will say, "It remains that even they who have wives be as though they had none," whose also formerly was "Increase and multiply" — the same the end whose also the beginning. Yet the wood is not cut as if to be accused, nor the harvest mown as if to be condemned, but as obeying its own time. So too the matter of wedlock admits the axe and the sickle of holiness not as an evil, but as ripe to be discharged, as reserved for holiness itself, to which by cutting it would yield a harvest. Whence I will now say that Marcion's god, when he condemns marriage as evil and as a business of unchastity, acts against the very holiness which he seems to study. For he erases its material; since, if there shall be no marriages, there is no holiness. For the testimony of abstinence falls empty, when licence is taken away, since certain things are proved only by their opposites. As virtue is perfected in weakness, so abstinence from marrying is recognized in the faculty of marrying. Who, in fine, shall be called abstinent, when that from which he must abstain is taken away? What temperance of the gullet in famine? What repudiation of ambition in want? What curbing of lust in castration? Now indeed, to suppress wholly the sowing of the human race — I know not whether even this suits the best god. For how will he wish man saved whom he forbids to be born, taking away that from which man is born? How will he have him in whom to mark his goodness, whom he suffers not to be? How does he love one whose origin he loves not? He fears, perhaps, an overflow of offspring, lest he labour to free more, lest he make many heretics, lest he have nobler Marcionites born of Marcionites. There will be no fiercer hardness than Pharaoh's, the slayer of newborns. For Pharaoh takes away souls; this god does not give them. The one takes away from life; the other does not admit to life. With both there is no difference from murder: under either, man is killed — under the one already born, under the other to be born. You would be welcome, O heretic god, if you had gone over to the dispensation of the Creator, who mingled male and female; for surely your own Marcion too was born of marriage. Enough of this concerning Marcion's god, whom both the definitions of the one divinity and the conditions of His states confirm to be altogether non-existent. But the whole course of this little work tends to this very thing. Accordingly, if to anyone we seem to have done too little, let him hope it reserved for its own time — as also the examination of those very Scriptures which Marcion uses.

For the rest, I would have cut down close at hand even Marcion's Antitheses themselves, had the defence of the Creator — as good as also judge — needed a more laborious destruction of them, according to the examples of either part suiting God, as we have shown. But if both parts, of goodness and of justice, make up a worthy plenitude of the divinity of the all-powerful One, in summary fashion meanwhile I can have beaten back the Antitheses, eager to discern, out of the qualities whether of dispositions or of laws or of virtues, and so to alienate Christ from the Creator, as the best from the judge, and the mild from the fierce, and the salutary from the destructive. For they rather conjoin those whom they set in those diversities which suit God. For so far was the substance one and the same to the divinities, good and severe; and by the same examples and in like arguments, that He willed to show His goodness in those in which He had sent severity before; since neither was the temporal diversity a wonder, if God was afterward milder for things subdued, who before was more austere for things untamed. So through the Antitheses it can the more easily be shown that the order of the Creator was reformed by Christ rather than beaten back, and rather restored than excluded — especially since you sever your god from every more bitter motion, and so, of course, from rivalry with the Creator. For if it be so, how do the Antitheses demonstrate him a rival of the Creator's several kinds? I will therefore acknowledge in this too, through them, my God a zealous God, who with His own right took beforehand care of His matters — too shrubby in the beginnings — with a good, as a rational, rivalry of maturity; whose Antitheses even His own world will acknowledge out of the contrarieties of the elements, yet modulated by the highest reason. Wherefore, most inconsiderate Marcion, you ought to have shown one god of light and another of darkness, that you might the more easily persuade of one god of goodness and another of severity. For the rest, the Antithesis will belong to Him whose it is in the world also.

Who would not wish us to take care for the soul about food and for the body about clothing, but he who provided these things for man beforehand, and who, furnishing them thence, with reason forbids care of them as a rival of his own liberality? — who both fitted the very substance of the soul as superior to food, and figured the very matter of the body as superior to a tunic; whose ravens too neither sow nor reap nor lay up in storehouses, and yet are fed by him; whose lilies and grass neither weave nor spin, and yet are clothed by him; whose Solomon too, most glorious, yet was adorned with no flowerlet more elaborate. For the rest, nothing is so abrupt as that one should furnish, and another bid the furnishing to be securely managed — and that indeed a disparager of him. In short, whether as a disparager of the Creator he will not have it thought of such frivolities, about which neither ravens nor lilies labour, subjected spontaneously, namely, by reason of their worthlessness — will presently appear. Meanwhile, why does he accuse them of small faith, that is, of what faith? Of that which they could not yet exhibit perfect to a god whom they were as yet, at the moment of his being revealed, just learning? or of that which by this very title they owed to the Creator — to believe, namely, that he furnishes these things spontaneously to the human race, and not to be anxious about them? For also, when he subjoins, "For these things do the nations of the world seek" — not believing, namely, in a god the founder and supplier of all — whom he wished not to be like the Gentiles, those he reproached of small faith toward the same god toward whom he marked the Gentiles unbelieving. For the rest, when he adds too, "But your Father knows that you have need of these things," first I will ask whom Christ wishes to be understood as Father. If he demonstrates their Creator, he confirms him good too, who knows what his sons need; but if that other god, how does he know food and clothing to be necessary to man, of whom he furnished none? For if he had known, he would have furnished. For the rest, if he knows what is necessary to man, and yet did not furnish, it was either from malignity or from infirmity that he did not furnish. But by professing these things necessary to man, surely he confirmed them good. For nothing evil is necessary. And he will now no longer be a depreciator of the works and indulgences of the Creator — so that I may discharge what I deferred above. Now if another both foresaw and furnishes the things which he knows necessary to man, how does he himself promise them? Or is he good out of another's goods? "For seek," he says, "the kingdom of God, and these things shall be added to you." Surely by himself. But if by himself, what kind of one is he who shall furnish another's goods? If by the Creator, whose they are too, who is it that promises another's? If they accrue to the kingdom, to be restored in the second degree, his is the second degree whose is the first too, his food and clothing whose the kingdom too is. Thus the whole promise is the Creator's — the state of the parables, the levelling of the likenesses, if they look to no other than him to whom they have through all things matched. We are servants, for we have for lord the god. We ought to gird our loins, that is, to be expedited from the impediments of an entangled and complicated life. Likewise to have lamps burning, that is, minds kindled from faith and shining with the works of truth, and so to await the lord, that is, Christ. Returning whence? If from a wedding, it is the Creator's, whose the wedding is; if not the Creator's, neither would Marcion himself, invited to the wedding, have gone, regarding his god as a detester of weddings. The parable, then, would have failed in the person of the lord, if there were not one to whom weddings suit. In the following parable too he errs enough who arranges that thief, whose hour if the householder knew, he would not suffer his house to be undermined, into the person of the Creator. For how can the Creator seem a thief, lord of the whole man? No one steals or undermines his own goods, but rather he who descends into another's, and estranges the man from his lord. Now since he demonstrates the devil to us as the thief — whose hour too, had man known in the beginning, he would never have been undermined by him — therefore he bids that we be prepared, because at what hour we do not think the Son of man shall come, not as though he himself were a thief, but as the judge, namely, of those who shall not have prepared themselves, nor guarded against the thief. Therefore, if he himself is the Son of man, I hold the judge, and in the judge I defend the Creator; but if in the name of Son of man in this place he shows the Christ of the Creator, that he may portend him a thief whose coming we know not when — you have above the prescription that no one is a thief of his own goods, with that too safe, that in so far as he drives in the Creator to be feared, in so far doing his business he is the Creator's. And so, to Peter asking whether he had told the parable against them or against all, against them and against all who should preside over the churches he sets forth a likeness of stewards, of whom he who shall well have treated his fellow-servants, the lord being absent, shall, on his return, be set over all his goods; but he who shall act otherwise, the lord returning on the day he thought not, at the hour he knew not — namely that Son of man, the Christ of the Creator, not a thief, but a judge — shall be set apart, and his part shall be placed with the unbelievers. Accordingly, then, either here too he opposes a lord a judge and catechizes them toward him, or, if a best god, then he affirms even him a judge, though the heretic be unwilling. For they attempt to temper this sense, when it is claimed for his god. As though it were a thing of tranquillity and mildness only to set apart and to place his part with the unbelievers — as if he were not summoned, so as to be restored to his own state. As if this very thing were not done by judgement. Folly! What will be the issue of the set-apart? Surely the loss of salvation? — seeing that they shall be set apart from those who shall obtain salvation. What, then, the state of the unbelievers? Surely condemnation? Or if the set-apart and the unbelievers shall suffer nothing, equally on the other side the retained and the faithful shall obtain nothing. But if the retained and the faithful shall obtain salvation, the set-apart and the unbelievers must of necessity lose it on the other side. This will be judgement, which he who intends is the Creator's. What other shall I understand cutting the servants with few or many stripes, and according as each has committed against them, so exacting too of them, but a god a recompenser? Whom does it befit me to obey but a remunerator? Your Christ proclaims, "I have come to send fire upon the earth." That best one, lord of no Gehenna, who a little before had coerced the disciples, lest they should demand fire upon a most inhuman little village — when this one burnt up Sodom and Gomorrah with a fiery storm, when it was sung, "Fire shall go forth before him and shall consume his enemies," when too through Hosea he threatened, "I will send fire upon the cities of Judea," or through Isaiah, "A fire is kindled out of my indignation." Let him not lie. If he is not he who sent forth his voice even from the burning bush, let it be his to see what fire he contends is to be understood. Even if it is a figure, by this very thing, that he takes arguments for his sense from my element, he is mine who uses my things. His will be the likeness of the fire whose is the truth too. He himself will better interpret the quality of that fire, adding, "Do you think I have come to send peace upon the earth? No, I say to you, but separation." Indeed "a sword" is written. But Marcion emends it; as though separation too were not the work of a sword. Therefore he intends a fire too of subversion, who has denied peace. As the battle, such too the burning. As the sword, such too the flame, neither suiting the lord. In short, "There shall be divided," he says, "father against son, and son against father, and mother against daughter, and daughter against mother, and daughter-in-law against mother-in-law, and mother-in-law against daughter-in-law." If this battle among parents was sung in the very words by the trumpet of the prophet, I fear lest Micah foretold it to the Christ of Marcion. And therefore he pronounced them hypocrites, who indeed approved the face of heaven and earth, but did not discern that time, namely, in which, fulfilling all the things which had been foretold concerning him, and teaching not otherwise, he ought to have been acknowledged. For the rest, who could know the times of him for whom he had nothing by which he might prove them? With reason he reproaches too that they did not judge what is just out of themselves. Of old he commands this through Zechariah: "Judge a just judgement and one of peace"; through Jeremiah: "Do judgement and justice"; through Isaiah: "Judge the orphan and justify the widow" — imputing too to the vineyard Sorek that it had made not judgement but an outcry. He, then, who had taught them to do it by precept, demanded that they do it also by their own choice. He who had sown the precept urged also its overflow. But indeed how absurd that he should command to judge justly who was destroying the just god a judge! For even the judge who sends into prison nor brings out thence until even the last farthing be paid, in the person of the Creator they discuss under the name of disparagement. To which I must of necessity meet at the same step. For as often as the severity of the Creator is opposed, so often is Christ his to whom by fear he compels obedience.

The question again about a cure made on the sabbath, how did he discuss it? "Does not each of you on the sabbaths loose his ass or ox from the stall and lead it to drink?" Therefore, working according to the condition of the law, he confirmed the law, did not dissolve it — the law that bids no work be done except what shall be done for every soul; how much rather for a human one? Everywhere I am acknowledged to demand the congruence of the parables. "The kingdom of God," he says, "is like to a grain of mustard, which a man took and sowed in his garden." Who is to be understood in the person of the man? Surely Christ, because, though Marcion's, he is called the Son of man, who received from the Father the seed of the kingdom, namely the word of the gospel, and sowed it in his garden, surely in the world, say now in man. But since he said "in his garden," and yet the world is not his, nor man, but the Creator's, then he who sowed in his own is shown to be the Creator. Or if, to escape this snare, they shall turn the person of the man from Christ to the man receiving the seed of the kingdom and sowing it in the garden of his heart, not even this matter will suit any but the Creator. For what kind of thing is it that the kingdom of a most gentle god should be that which even the heat of judgement follows with a tearful austerity? But concerning the following likeness I fear, perhaps, lest it portend further the kingdom of God. For he compared it to leaven, not to unleavened bread, which is more familiar to the Creator. This conjecture too suits those who beg for arguments. And so I too will drive out vanity with vanity, saying that the leavening too suits the kingdom of the Creator, because after it the oven or furnace of Gehenna follows. How often besides does he show himself a judge, and in the judge the Creator? As often surely as he casts out and condemns by rejecting. As here too, "When the householder," he says, "shall have risen and shut the door" — surely for cutting off the iniquitous. To whom, knocking, he will answer, "I know not whence you are," and again, to those enumerating that they had eaten and drunk before him and that he had taught in their streets, he will add, "Depart from me, all you workers of iniquity: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth." Where? outside, namely, where they shall be shut out, the door shut by him. Therefore there will be punishment whence comes the exclusion unto punishment, when they shall see the just entering into the kingdom of God, but themselves detained outside. By whom? If by the Creator, who then will be within receiving the just into the kingdom? The good god. What, then, is there for the Creator to do there, to detain outside unto punishment those whom his adversary shut out, to be received by himself, if at all, the more to his adversary's spite? But that other too, about to shut out the iniquitous, must surely either know that the Creator will detain them unto punishment, or not know. Therefore either they will be detained against his will, and he who detains is lesser than the other, yielding to him unwillingly; or, if he wills it so to be done, he himself judged it should so be done, and the author of the Creator's infamy will not himself be better than the Creator. If these things stand by no reasoning — that one be believed to punish, another to free — then to one will belong both the judgement and the kingdom, and, while both belong to one, he who also judges is the Creator's.

To a dinner or to a supper what kind of men does he bid be invited? Such as he had shown through Isaiah: "Break thy bread to the hungry, and the beggars, and those who are without a roof, bring into thy house" — those, namely, who could not requite the return of this humanity. If Christ forbids this to be caught at, promising it again at the resurrection, it is the Creator's form, who is not pleased with those who love gifts, who follow after retribution. The parable too of the inviter — to which party it the rather meets, weigh. "A certain man made a supper and invited many." Surely the preparation of the supper figures the fullness of eternal life. I say, first, that strangers and those connected by no right are not wont to be invited to a supper; certainly the domestic and familiar are more readily wont. It is the Creator's, then, to have invited those to whom belonged the invited — both through Adam, as men, and through the fathers, as Jews — not his to whom they belonged neither by nature nor by prerogative. Next, if he who prepared the supper sends to the guests, even thus the supper is the Creator's, who sent to admonish the guests, already invited before through the fathers, but to be admonished through the prophets — not he who sent no one to admonish, nor who did anything beforehand toward inviting, but himself descended suddenly, just as he became known, already inviting, just as he invited, already forcing them into the banquet, making the same hour of supping and of inviting to supper. The invited excuse themselves. If by another god, with reason, because suddenly invited; if not with reason, then not suddenly. But if not suddenly invited, then by the Creator, by whom of old; whose vocation, in short, they had declined, first saying to Aaron, "Make us gods to go before us"; and thereafter hearing with the ear and not hearing, namely the vocation of God, who most pertinently to this parable through Jeremiah, "Hear," he says, "my voice, and I will be to you a lord and you to me a people, and you shall walk in all my ways, whatsoever I shall command you." Behold the invitation of God. "And they heard not," it says, "and turned not their ear." Behold the refusal of the people. "But they went away in the things which they desired in their evil heart. I bought a field, and I bought you a yoke of oxen, and I married a wife." And further he drives in: "And I sent to you all my servants the prophets." This will be the Holy Spirit, the admonisher of the guests, by day and before light. "And my people heard not, and inclined not their ears, and hardened their neck." This, when it had been reported to the householder, then moved (well that he is moved too, for Marcion denies his god is moved, so this too is mine), he bids a gathering be made from the streets and lanes of the city. Let us see whether in that sense by which again through Jeremiah: "Have I become a wilderness to the house of Israel? or a land left untilled?" — that is, "Have I not those whom I may choose, or whence I may choose? since my people said, We come not to thee." And so he sent to call others from the same city still. Then, the place abounding, he commanded a gathering too from the ways and hedges, that is, us now from the foreign nations — by that emulation, namely, by which in Deuteronomy: "I will turn my face away from them, and I will show what shall be to them in the last things" — that is, others to possess their place — "because they are a perverse generation, sons in whom there is no faith. They have provoked me to emulation with a no-god, and have moved me to anger with their idols; and I too will provoke them to emulation with a no-nation, with a foolish nation I will move them to anger" — namely with us, whose hope the Jews bear, of which the Lord denies they shall taste, Zion being forsaken, like a watch-tower in a vineyard and a hut in a cucumber-field, after they refused even the last invitation in Christ. What out of this order, to be recounted according to the arrangement and proclamations of the Creator, can suit him who has neither the order nor the arrangement for the conspiration of the parable, who did his whole work at once? Or what will be his first vocation, and what the admonition in the second act? — to invite both parties at once, from the city, from the hedges, against the mirror of the parable. Nor can he now judge as disdainful those whom he never before invited, whom he most of all accosts at the moment. Or if he judges them, as for the future, about to despise the vocation, then for the future too he portends a gathering in their place from the nations. Plainly for this he is to come a second time, to preach to the nations. And if he is to come — yet, I think, not as if to invite the guests still, but already to place them. Meanwhile, you who interpret the vocation of this supper into a heavenly banquet of spiritual fullness and joyfulness, remember that the earthly promises too of wine and oil and corn and the very city are equally figured by the Creator as spiritual.

Who seeks the lost sheep and the lost drachma but he who lost it? Who lost it but he who had it? Who had it but he whose it was? If, then, the man is the thing of no other than the Creator, he had him whose he was, he lost what he had, he sought what he lost, he found who sought, he exulted who found. Thus the argument of either parable is void in regard to him whose neither the sheep nor the drachma is, that is, man. For neither did he lose, because he did not have; nor seek, because he did not lose; nor find, because he did not seek; nor exult, because he did not find. And so it is his to exult over the penitence of a sinner — that is, over the recovery of the lost — who professed of old that he preferred the penitence of the sinner to his death.

Whom two masters one cannot serve, because the one must of necessity be offended and the other defended, he himself declares, setting forth God and mammon. Then, whom he would have mammon understood to be, if you have no interpreter, you can learn from himself. For admonishing us, concerning worldly things, to provide for ourselves the supports of friendships, after the example of that servant who, removed from his office, relieves his master's debtors by diminishing their bonds, for a help to himself, "And I," he says, "say to you, make for yourselves friends out of the mammon of injustice" — out of money, namely, like that servant. For we all know money to be the author and lord of all the world's injustice. Seeing the cupidity of the Pharisees enslaved to it, he loosed off this opinion: "You cannot serve God and mammon." In short, the Pharisees, greedy of money, derided him, because they understood, namely, mammon said of money. Lest anyone esteem that in mammon the Creator is to be understood, and that Christ called them back from the servitude of the Creator — what? rather from this learn one god shown by Christ. For he named two masters, God and mammon, the Creator and money. In short, "You cannot serve God" — surely him whom they seemed to serve — "and mammon" — to whom they were rather destined. But if he were himself acting as another, he would have demonstrated not two masters but three. For the Creator too is a master, because he is a god, and surely the more a master than mammon, and the more to be regarded, as the more a master. For what kind of thing is it that he who had called mammon a master, and had joined it with God, should be silent about their true master, that is, the Creator? Or did he by being silent concede that he is to be served, if he denied only that himself and mammon could be served? Thus, when he sets one god — about to name the Creator too, if he himself were another — he named the Creator, whom without another god he did not set as master. And so this too will shine out, how it was said, "If in unjust mammon you have not been faithful, what is true who will entrust to you?" — in money, namely, unjustly, not in the Creator, whom even Marcion makes just. "And if in another's you have not been found faithful, mine who will give to you?" For what is unjust ought to be alien to the servants of God. But how was the Creator alien to the Pharisees, the proper god of the Jewish nation? If, then, these things fall not upon the Creator but upon mammon, "Who will believe to you what is truer?" and "Who will give you what is mine?" cannot have been said as by another concerning the grace of another god. For then he would seem to have so said, if, marking them unbelievers toward the Creator, not toward mammon, he had through the mention of the Creator made distinctions of another god, not about to commit his own truth to the unbelievers of the Creator. How then can he be seen as another, if he be not set forth for this, that he be separated from the matter in hand? But if the Pharisees too, justifying themselves before men, were placing the hope of reward in man, he rebuked them in that sense in which the prophet Jeremiah too: "Wretched the man who has hope in man." If he adds too, "But God knows your hearts," he was commemorating the force of that god who pronounced himself a lamp, searching the reins and hearts. If he touches pride, "What is exalted among men is detestable to God," he sets Isaiah before the eyes: "For the day of the Lord of Sabaoth is upon every contumelious and proud one, upon every lofty and exalted one, and they shall be humbled." I can now gather why for so great an age the god of Marcion was in hiding. He was waiting, I suppose, until he should learn all these things from the Creator. He learned, then, up to the times of John, and so thereafter proceeded to announce the kingdom of God, saying, "The law and the prophets unto John, from whom the kingdom of God is announced." As though we too do not acknowledge a certain boundary, John, set between the old and the new, at whom Judaism should cease and from whom Christianity should begin — yet not so that the settling of the law and the prophets and the initiation of the gospel, in which is the kingdom of God, Christ himself, should have been made by another power. For even if we have proved both that the old things were proclaimed to pass and the new to succeed by the Creator, if John is shown to be the forerunner and preparer of the ways of the Lord about to bring on the gospel and promulgate the kingdom of God — even from this, that John came, he himself will be the Christ who was to follow John as forerunner; and if the old things ceased and the new began, John intervening, it will be no wonder that this is from the arrangement of the Creator — so that it may be the more proved whence soever than from the setting of the law and prophets at John, and from there the rising of the kingdom of God. Let heaven and earth pass, then, sooner, just as the law and the prophets, than one apex of the words of the Lord. For "the word," says Isaiah, "of our God abides for ever." For since in Isaiah even then Christ — the Word, namely, and the Spirit of the Creator — had proclaimed John, the voice of one crying in the wilderness, "Prepare the way of the Lord" — for this, that he should come that the order of the law and prophets should thenceforth cease, through fulfilment, not through destruction, and that the kingdom of God should be announced by Christ — therefore he subjoined that the elements should sooner pass than his words, confirming this too, that what he had said of John had not passed away.

But Christ forbids divorce, saying, "He who shall dismiss his wife and shall marry another, commits adultery; he who shall marry one dismissed by a husband, is equally an adulterer." That even thus he may forbid divorce, he makes the marriage of a repudiated woman unlawful. But Moses permits repudiation in Deuteronomy: "If anyone take a wife and dwell with her, and it come to pass that she find no grace with him, because something unseemly is found in her, he shall write a bill of repudiation and shall give it into her hand, and shall dismiss her from his house." You see a diversity of law and gospel, of Moses and Christ? Plainly. For you have not received that other gospel too, of the same truth and the same Christ, in which, forbidding divorce, he solves the proper question of it: "Moses, for the hardness of your heart, commanded to give a bill of repudiation; but from the beginning it was not so" — because, namely, he who made male and female had said, "They shall be two in one flesh: what therefore God has joined, let not man put asunder." For by this answer he both protected the constitution of Moses, as his own, and directed the institution of the Creator, as Christ his own. But inasmuch as you must be refuted from those things which you have received, so I will meet you as though my Christ. Does not he too, while he forbids divorce, yet, bearing as Father him who joined male and female, rather excuse than destroy the constitution of Moses? But behold, suppose this Christ of yours be teaching contrary to Moses and the Creator, so that, if I shall not show it not contrary, he is mine. For I say that he now made a prohibition of divorce conditionally — if anyone for this reason dismiss his wife, that he may marry another. "He who shall dismiss," he says, "his wife, and shall marry another, has committed adultery; and he who shall marry one dismissed by a husband, is equally an adulterer" — one dismissed, surely, from the same cause from which it is not lawful to be dismissed, that another may be married; for he who marries one unlawfully dismissed, as though undismissed, is an adulterer. For the marriage abides which has not been rightly dissolved; the marriage abiding, to marry is adultery. Thus if he conditionally forbade dismissing a wife, he did not forbid it altogether; and what he did not forbid altogether, he permitted in other cases, where the cause ceases on account of which he forbade it. He even teaches nothing contrary to Moses, whose precept he somewhere preserves — not yet, I say, confirms. Or if you altogether deny that divorce is permitted by Christ, how do you yourself dissolve marriages, neither joining male and female, nor admitting those elsewhere joined to the sacrament of baptism and the eucharist, unless they have conspired between themselves against the fruit of marriage, as against the Creator himself? Certainly, what does a husband do with you, if his wife shall commit adultery? Shall he keep her? But not even your apostle suffers the members of Christ to be joined to a harlot. And so justice of divorce has even Christ as its asserter. From this point too Moses is confirmed by him, forbidding repudiation under the same title under which Christ does, if something unseemly be found in the woman. For also in the gospel of Matthew, "He who shall dismiss," he says, "his wife, except for the cause of adultery, makes her commit adultery." He too is equally reckoned an adulterer who shall marry one dismissed by a husband. For the rest, save for the cause of adultery, not even the Creator puts asunder what he himself joined — Moses elsewhere constituting that he who by violence had made a marriage cannot dismiss his wife for all time. But if a marriage compelled by violence shall stand, how much more a voluntary one out of agreement? — just as by the authority of prophecy too, "The wife of thy youth thou shalt not dismiss." You have therefore Christ spontaneously entering everywhere upon the footsteps of the Creator, both in permitting repudiation and in forbidding it. You have him too, however he wishes to lie hid, the foreseer of marriages, which he wishes neither to be separated by forbidding repudiation, nor to be held with a stain by then permitting divorce. Blush, who do not join those whom your Christ too joined. Blush, who put asunder without that desert by which your Christ too willed it put asunder. Now I must also show whence the Lord deduced this opinion, or whither he directed it. For so it will more fully be established that he did not look toward the destroying of Moses through a sudden proposal interposed concerning repudiation — because it was not suddenly interposed, having its root from the same mention of John. For John, censuring Herod because, against the law, he had married the wife of his deceased brother, who had a daughter by her (the law not permitting this otherwise — nay, even commanding it — except when a brother had died childless, that seed should be raised up to him by his own brother and from his rib), had been cast into prison, and afterward also slain by the same Herod. Mention being made, then, of John, and surely of the issue of his end, the Lord shot the figure of unlawful marriages and of adultery against Herod, pronouncing him too an adulterer who should marry one dismissed by her husband — the more to load the impiety of Herod, who had married one dismissed from her husband no less by death than by repudiation, and that while a brother had a daughter by her, and even on that account unlawfully, by the instinct of lust, not of law, and therefore had slain too the prophet, the asserter of the law. This to have discussed will profit me also toward the following argument of the rich man grieving in the underworld and the poor man resting in the bosom of Abraham. For that too, as to the surface of the Scripture, is suddenly set forth; as to the intention of the sense, this too coheres to the mention of John ill treated and of Herod ill married, deforming the issue of each — Herod's torments and John's refreshings — so that Herod might now hear, "They have there Moses and the prophets, let them hear them." But Marcion forces it elsewhere — namely, that he may determine that both rewards of the Creator, whether of torment or of refreshment, are placed in the underworld for those who shall have obeyed the law and the prophets, but may define that the bosom and harbour of Christ and his god is heavenly. We will answer to these things, the very Scripture refuting his eyes, which distinguishes the bosom of Abraham from the underworld for the poor man. For one thing, as I think, is the underworld, another too the bosom of Abraham. For he says that a great deep intervenes between those regions and prohibits passage from either side. But neither would the rich man have lifted up his eyes, and that from afar, but into the higher region, and from the distance of a height, through that immense interval of loftiness and of depth. Whence it appears to any wise man, who has at some time heard of the Elysian fields, that there is some local determination, which has been called the bosom of Abraham, for receiving the souls of his sons, even from the nations — of him, namely, the father of many nations to be reckoned into the census of Abraham, and out of the same faith by which Abraham too believed God, under no yoke of the law nor in the sign of circumcision. This region, then, I call the bosom of Abraham, though not heavenly, yet loftier than the underworld, which shall meanwhile furnish refreshment to the souls of the just, until the consummation of things discharge the resurrection of all with the fullness of reward — then to appear by the heavenly promise, which Marcion claims for his own, as though not promulgated by the Creator. To which Christ builds his ascent into heaven, according to Amos, surely for his own, where is also the eternal place, of which Isaiah: "Who shall announce to you the eternal place," save, namely, Christ, walking in justice, speaking the right way, holding in hatred injustice and iniquity? But if an eternal place is promised, and an ascent into heaven is built by the Creator, promising too that the seed of Abraham should be as the stars of heaven, surely on account of a heavenly promise — that promise being safe, why should it not admit that the bosom of Abraham be called some temporal receptacle of faithful souls, in which already the image of the future is delineated, and a certain white preview of either judgement is foreseen? — admonishing you heretics too, while you are in life, that Moses and the prophets preach one god the Creator, and one Christ his, and that either judgement, of penalty and of eternal salvation, is placed with the one god who kills and makes alive. "Nay," he says, "the decree of our god from heaven bade not Moses and the prophets be heard, but Christ: hear him." With reason. For then the apostles had already sufficiently heard Moses and the prophets, who had followed Christ by believing Moses and the prophets. For neither would Peter have received to say, "Thou art the Christ," before he had heard and believed Moses and the prophets, by whom alone as yet Christ was announced. This faith of theirs, then, had deserved that it should be confirmed even by the heavenly voice, bidding him be heard whom they had acknowledged evangelizing peace, evangelizing good things, announcing the eternal place, building for them his ascent into heaven. But in the underworld it is said of those: "They have there Moses and the prophets, let them hear them" — those who did not believe, or who did not so at all believe, that after death there are torments of the pride of riches and of the glory of delights, announced by Moses and the prophets, but decreed by that god who deposes magnates from thrones, and lifts up the needy from dung-heaps. Thus, since on either side the diversity of the pronouncement suits the Creator, no distance of divinities is to be established, but of the very matters.

Turning in the same place to the disciples, he says "Woe" to the author of scandals — that it would have been better for him if he had not been born, or if a millstone fastened to his neck he had been thrown into the deep, than that he should scandalize one of those little ones, namely his disciples. Estimate what kind of punishment he threatens him. For no other shall avenge the scandal of his disciples. Acknowledge, therefore, both a judge, and one pronouncing with that affection concerning the care of his own with which the Creator too of old: "He who touches you touches as it were the pupil of my eye." The same sense is of the same one. He bids a sinning brother be corrected; and he who shall not do this surely delinquishes, either out of hatred wishing his brother to persevere in his delinquency, or out of acceptance of persons sparing him — having Leviticus: "Thou shalt not hate thy brother in thy mind; with a traducing thou shalt traduce thy neighbour" — surely thy brother too — "and thou shalt not take a delinquency on account of him." Nor is it wonderful if he so teaches who forbids you to despise even your brother's cattle, if you find them straying on the way, but to lead them back to your brother — far less the man himself to himself. But he bids you also give pardon to a brother delinquent against you, even seven times. Plainly little. For it is more with the Creator, who set no measure, pronouncing infinitely, "Be not mindful of thy brother's malice"; nor does he command that it be furnished to one asking, but even to one not asking. For he wishes the offence not to be forgiven but to be forgotten. Of how great interpretation the law of lepers is, touching the species of that very defect and the inspection of the high priest, is for us to know, for Marcion to oppose the tediousness of the law, that here too he may affirm Christ its rival, anticipating the solemnities of the law even in the cure of the ten lepers, whom, bidden only to go to show themselves to the priests, he cleansed on the way, without touch now and without a word, by a silent power and by his will alone — as though it were necessary, Christ being once announced the remedier of languors and defects and proved by his effects, that the qualities of the cures should be discussed, or that the Creator in Christ should be provoked to the law; if he did anything otherwise than the law distinguished, he himself perfected it, since surely the Lord works otherwise through himself or through his Son, otherwise through the prophets his servants — especially the evidences of his power and might, which, as clearer and stronger, since proper, it is right should differ from the vicarious. But of this kind things have already been said elsewhere in the former evidence. Now, even though he premised that there were then many lepers in Israel in the days of Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed but Naaman the Syrian — surely the number too will not make for a difference of gods, toward the destruction of the Creator remedying one, and the preference of him who cleansed ten. For who will doubt that more could have been cured by him who had cured one, than by that one ten who had never before one? But by this pronouncement most of all he strikes the diffidence or pride of Israel, that, when there were many lepers there, and a prophet was not wanting, even when an evidence was put forth, no one ran to the god working in the prophets. Therefore, since he himself was the authentic pontiff of God the Father, he inspected them according to the secret of the law, signifying that Christ is the true discerner and disposer of human stains. But also what was in the manifest of the law he commanded, "Go, show yourselves to the priests." Why, if he was about to cleanse them before? Or as a mocker of the law, that, the cured being on the way, he might show that the law with its very priests was nothing? And let it surely be his concern, if to anyone Christ shall seem so opinionated. Nay, worthier things are to be interpreted, and juster as to faith. Therefore were they remedied, in that, bidden according to the law to go to the priests, they had obeyed; for it is not credible that observers of the law should have deserved medicine from a destroyer of the law. But why to the former leper did he command no such thing? Because neither did Elisha to Naaman the Syrian; and yet not on that account was he not the Creator's. I have answered enough; but he who has believed understands also something deeper. Learn, then, the causes too. The thing was being done in the regions of Samaria, whence too was meanwhile one of the lepers. But Samaria had revolted from Israel, having that schism out of the nine tribes, which, torn away through the prophet Ahijah, Jeroboam had placed at Samaria. But also otherwise the Samaritans were always self-pleasing concerning the mountains and wells of their fathers — as in the gospel of John that Samaritan woman in colloquy with the Lord at the well: "Art thou greater?" and the rest; and again: "Our fathers adored in this mountain, and you say that at Jerusalem one ought to adore." Therefore he who through Amos too had said "Woe" to those who trust in the mountain of Samaria, deigning now of set purpose to restore even her, bids them show themselves to the priests — surely who were nowhere but where the temple too was — subjecting the Samaritan to the Jew, since salvation is of the Jews, although both were Israelites and Samaritans. For the whole promise was Christ to the tribe of Judah; that they might know that at Jerusalem were both the priests and the temple and the mother of religion and the fountain, not the well, of salvation. And therefore, as he saw that they acknowledged the law to be discharged at Jerusalem, he remedied them, now to be justified out of faith without the order of the law. Whence too that one of the ten, loosed, mindful of the divine grace, the Samaritan whom he wonders at, he does not bid offer the gift out of the law, because he had already offered enough, rendering glory to God — this too at the Lord's wish, that the law might be interpreted. And yet to what god did the Samaritan render grace, when not even the Israelite had as yet learned of another god? To what other than him to whom all formerly remedied by Christ had? And therefore, "Thy faith has made thee safe," he heard, because he had understood that he ought to make a true oblation, namely the act of thanksgiving, to the omnipotent God, at the true temple and to his true high priest, Christ.
