But neither can the Pharisees seem to have consulted the Lord about the kingdom of another god, when it would come, so long as no god other than Christ had been published, nor he to have answered about another's kingdom than about whose he was consulted. "The kingdom of God comes not with observation," he says, "nor do they say, Behold here, behold there: for behold, the kingdom of God is within you." Who will not so interpret it: "Within you is," that is, in your hand, in your power, if you hear, if you do the precept of God? But if the kingdom of God is in the precept, then set against it, according to our antitheses, Moses, and it is one opinion. "The precept," he says, "is not lofty, nor far from thee. It is not in heaven, that thou shouldst say, Who shall ascend into heaven and bring it down to us, and we shall hear it and do it? Nor is it beyond the sea, that thou shouldst say, Who shall cross over and take it for us, and we shall hear it and do it? The word is near thee, in thy mouth, and in thy heart, and in thy hands to do it." This will be, "Not here, nor there; for behold, the kingdom of God is within you." And lest heretical audacity argue that the Lord answered them about the kingdom of the Creator, concerning which he was consulted, not about his own, the sequel resists. For saying that the Son of man must first suffer many things and be reprobated, before his coming, in which the kingdom too shall be substantially revealed, he showed his own the kingdom too concerning which he had answered, which was awaiting his passions and reprobations. But being about to be reprobated, and afterward acknowledged and assumed and exalted, he plucked the very word "reprobated" thence where, in the riddle of the stone, either revelation of him was sung with David — the first refusable, the second honourable. "The stone," it says, "which the builders reprobated, the same is made into the head of the corner. By the Lord was this done." For it is idle, if we have believed God to have proclaimed concerning the contumely or glory, namely, of someone, that he should not portend him whom he had portended both in the figure of a stone and of a rock and of a mountain. But if he speaks of his own coming, why does he compare it to the days of Noah and of Lot, foul and atrocious — a god gentle and mild? Why does he admonish to remember the wife of Lot, who contemned the precept of the Creator not with impunity, if he does not come with judgement to avenge his own precepts? Even if he avenges as that one, if he judges me, he ought not to have formed me by the evidences of him whom he destroys, lest that one seem to form me. But if here too he speaks not of his own coming, but of the Jews' Christ, let us await even now lest he proclaim anything of his own, believing meanwhile him to be the one whom in every place he proclaims.

For commanding too the perseverance and instance of praying, he sets forth the parable of the judge compelled to hear the widow by the instance and perseverance of her interpellations. Therefore he shows that a god a judge is to be prayed, not himself, if he himself is not the judge. But he subjoined that God would make the vengeance of his elect. If, then, he himself shall be the judge who is also the avenger, he has therefore proved the Creator the better god, whom he shows the avenger of his elect crying to him day and night. And yet, when he brings in the temple of the Creator, and describes two adoring with diverse mind — the Pharisee in pride, the publican in humility — and therefore the one reprobated, the other justified to have gone down — surely, by teaching by what discipline he is to be prayed, he constitutes him also to be prayed here from whom they were to bring back that discipline of praying, whether the reprobatrix of pride or the justificatrix of humility. Of another god I find with Christ neither temple nor worshippers nor judgement, but the Creator's. Him he bids be adored in humility, as the lifter-up of the lowly, not in pride, as the destroyer of the proud. What other to be adored has he shown me? by what discipline? by what hope? None, I think. For even the prayer which he taught we have proved to suit the Creator. It is another matter if he, as a best and spontaneously good god, does not even wish to be adored. But "Who is good, except one God only?" he says. Not as though out of two gods he had shown one to be best, but that one only is best, the only god, who is so the one best, because the only god. And surely best, who rains upon the just and unjust, and makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, sustaining and nourishing and helping even the Marcionites. In short, asked by a certain man, "Good master, what doing shall I possess eternal life?" he inquired about the precepts of the Creator, whether he knew them, that is, did them — to attest that everlasting life is acquired by the precepts of the Creator; and when that man had affirmed that he had observed from his youth all the more principal things, "One thing," he says, "is wanting to thee: all things whatsoever thou hast, sell, and give to the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven, and come, follow me." Come now, Marcion, and all you fellow-sufferers and co-hateful ones of his, you heretics, what will you dare to say? Did Christ rescind the prior precepts, of not killing, of not committing adultery, of not stealing, of not testifying false, of loving father and mother? or did he both keep them and add what was lacking? Although this precept too of largesse to the needy is everywhere diffused in the law and the prophets, so that that most glorious observer of the precepts was traduced as about to hold his money far dearer. So this too is safe in the gospel: "I came not to dissolve the law and the prophets, but rather to fulfil." At the same time he freed too the rest from doubt, manifesting that the name both of God and of "good" is one, and eternal life, and treasure in heaven, and himself — whose precepts by supplying he both preserved and increased — to be recognized in this place too according to Micah, who says, "If it has been announced to thee, man, what is good, or what does the Lord require of thee, but to do judgement, to love mercy, and to be prepared to follow the Lord thy God?" For Christ too, a man, announcing what is good, the knowledge of the law, "The precepts," he says, "thou knowest." To do judgement: "Sell," he says, "what thou hast." To love mercy: "And give," he says, "to the needy." To be prepared to go with the Lord: "And come," he says, "follow me." So distinguished was the Jewish nation from the beginning by tribes and peoples and families and houses, that no one could easily be ignorant of his lineage, even from the recent Augustan censuses, then perhaps still pending. But the Jesus of Marcion (and one would not doubt born who appeared a man) surely, in that he was not born, could have had no public knowledge of his lineage, but was to be reckoned some one of those who in whatever way were held unknown. When, therefore, the blind man heard him passing by, why did he cry out, "Jesus, son of David, have mercy on me," unless because he was not rashly reckoned the son of David — that is, of the family of David — through his mother and brothers, who at some time, surely out of knowledge, had been announced to him? But those going before rebuked the blind man, that he should be silent — with reason, namely because he was crying out, not because he lied about the son of David. Or teach that those rebuking knew that Jesus was not the son of David, that on that account they may be believed to have enjoined silence on the blind man. But even if you should teach it, he would more easily presume them to be ignorant than that the Lord could have sustained a false proclamation about himself. But the Lord was patient. Yet not a confirmer of error — nay, even a detector of it — so that he would not have first cleared up this blindness of that man, lest he should further esteem Jesus the son of David. And yet, lest you should defame his patience, and affix to him any reason of dissimulation, and deny him the son of David — most manifestly he confirmed the blind man's proclamation both by the very reward of the medicine and by the testimony of his faith. "Thy faith," he says, "has made thee safe." What would you have the blind man have believed? That Jesus had come down from that god toward the casting-down of the Creator, toward the destruction of the law and the prophets? not that he was the one who was destined from the root of Jesse and from the fruit of the loins of David, the remunerator of the blind too? But not yet, I think, were the blind then such as Marcion is, that this should have been the faith of that blind man, by which he believed in the voice of "Jesus, son of David." He who both knew this of himself and willed himself to be known by all, gave the man's faith — even though better-eyed, even though sharer of the true light — an outer vision too, that we too might learn both the rule and at once the reward of faith. He who wishes to see Jesus the son of David, let him believe through the registration of the virgin. He who shall not so believe, shall not hear from him, "Thy faith has made thee safe," and so shall remain blind, rushing into the antithesis, the antithesis itself too rushing. For so the blind is wont to lead the blind. For if at some time the blind, in the recovery of Zion, had offended David, resisting that he should be admitted (into a figure of the people, accordingly blind, not about to admit one day Christ the son of David), therefore Christ on the contrary aided the blind man, that from this he might show himself not to be the son of David — that out of a diversity of mind he was good to the blind, whom that one had bidden be cut down. And why indeed did he say he had furnished it to a depraved faith? Nay, this too the son of David, the antithesis to be beaten back out of his own. For they too who had offended David were blind; but now a man of the same flesh had offered himself a suppliant to the son of David. Therefore, to him making satisfaction in a manner, the son of David, appeased, restored his sight, with the testimony of the faith by which he had believed this very thing, that the son of David was to be entreated by him. And yet David, I think, the audacity of men had offended, not their ill health.

There follows too the salvation of the house of Zacchaeus. By what desert? Had he too believed that Christ had come from Marcion? And yet there was still in the ears of all that voice of the blind man, "Have mercy on me, Jesus, son of David," and "All the people rendered praises to God" — not Marcion's, but David's. Truly Zacchaeus, even though a foreigner, perhaps yet, breathed upon by some knowledge of the Scriptures out of Jewish commerce — but it is more even if, ignorant of Isaiah, he had fulfilled his precepts. "Break," it says, "thy bread to the hungry, and those not having a roof bring into thy house." This he was doing most of all, received in his house feeding the Lord. "And if thou see one naked, cover him." This he was promising most of all, offering half his substance to all works of mercy, loosing the obligations of more violent contracts and dismissing the afflicted into release, and dissipating every unjust bond, by saying, "And if I have taken anything from anyone by calumny, I restore fourfold." And so the Lord, "Today," he says, "is salvation to this house," testified that those things were salutary which the prophet of the Creator had enjoined. But when he says, "For the Son of man has come to save what perished," I no longer contend that he has come to save what had perished, whose it had been and to whom it had perished which he had come to save; but I direct to the step of another question. That it is about man there is no doubt. He, since he consists of two substances, of body and soul, it must be inquired of what species of substance they seem to have perished. If of body, then the body had perished, the soul not. What had perished, the Son of man makes safe: the flesh therefore too has salvation. If of soul it had perished, the perdition of the soul is destined for salvation: the flesh, which did not perish, is safe. If the whole man had perished out of either substance, the whole man must of necessity be made safe, and the opinion of the heretics, denying the salvation of the flesh, is dashed. Now too the Christ of the Creator is confirmed, who according to the Creator promised the salvation of the whole man. The parable too of the servants, who are judged according to the reckoning of the lord's money lent at interest, shows God a judge, even from the part of severity, not only honouring but also taking away what one seems to have had. Or if here too he shall fashion the Creator austere, taking up what he laid not down and reaping what he sowed not, here too that one instructs me whose money he teaches me to lend at interest.

Christ knew whence the baptism of John was. And why did he ask as one ignorant? He knew the Pharisees would not answer him. And why did he ask in vain? Was it that out of their own mouth he might judge them, or out of their heart? Refer, then, these things too to the excuse of the Creator, and to the comparison with Christ, and consider now what was to follow, if the Pharisees had reported anything to the interrogation. Suppose they had reported the baptism of John to be human — they would straightway have been crushed with stones. Some Marcion would arise against Marcion, who should say, "O best god, O god diverse from the examples of the Creator! Knowing men would go headlong, he set them himself upon the precipice." For so too concerning the Creator it is treated in the law of the tree. But the baptism of John was from heaven. "And why then," says Christ, "did you not believe him?" Therefore he who had willed John to be believed, about to rebuke that they had not believed him, was his whose sacrament John administered. Certainly to those unwilling to report what they thought, when he too opposes a reciprocal, "And I do not tell you in what power I do these things," he rendered evil for evil. "Render the things that are Caesar's to Caesar, and the things that are God's to God." What will be God's? Those which are like Caesar's denarius — namely his image and likeness. Man, therefore, he bids be rendered to the Creator, in whose image and likeness and name and matter he was expressed. Let the god of Marcion seek himself a coinage; Christ bids the denarius of man be rendered to his own Caesar, not to an alien — unless of necessity, since he has no denarius of his own. A just and worthy prescription is it, in every question, that the sense of the answer ought to pertain to the proposal of the interrogation. For the rest, to answer one thing to one who consults about another is the part of a madman. So much the more let it be far from Christ which befits not even a man. The Sadducees, deniers of the resurrection, having a question about it, had proposed to the Lord, out of the law, the matter of the woman who, seven brothers dying in order, had married them according to the legal precept — of which man's wife she should be reckoned at the resurrection. This was the matter of the question, this the substance of the consultation. To this Christ must of necessity have answered. He feared no one, that he should seem to have declined the questions, or, by occasion of them, to have shown beneath the surface what he did not otherwise teach openly. He answered, then, that the sons of this age marry. You see how pertinently to the cause. Because it was asked about the age to come, in which he was to determine that no one marries, he prebuilt here that one marries and is given in marriage where there is also dying. But those whom God shall have deemed worthy of the possession of that age and of the resurrection from the dead, neither marry nor are given in marriage, because neither are they about to die any longer, since they are made like the angels, made sons of God and of the resurrection. Since, then, the sense of the answer is to be directed to nothing else than to the proposal of the interrogation, if by this sense the answer solves the proposal of the interrogation, the answer of the Lord savours of nothing else than that by which the question is solved. You have both the times of marriages permitted and denied, not out of their own proper question, but out of the question of the resurrection. You have both the confirmation of the resurrection itself, and the whole of what the Sadducees were inquiring — not interrogating about another god, nor seeking about the proper right of marriages. But if you make Christ answer to those things about which he was not consulted, you deny that he could answer to those about which he was interrogated, caught, namely, by the wisdom of the Sadducees. Over and above now, and after the prescription, I will treat against the cohering argumentations. For they have run in reading the text of the Scripture thus woven together: "But whom God has deemed worthy of that age." To "that age" they join "of god," that they may make another god of that age; when it ought to be read thus: "But whom God has deemed worthy" — so that, a distinction being made here after "God," "of that age" may pertain to what follows, that is, "whom God has deemed worthy of the possession and resurrection of that age." For it was consulted not about God, but about the state of that age — whose wife she would be after the resurrection in that age. So too the answer about the very marriages they subvert, so that, "The sons of this age marry and are given in marriage," may be said of the men of the Creator permitting marriages, but that he, those whom the god of that age — another, namely — has deemed worthy of the resurrection, that now these too do not marry, because they are not the sons of this age; when, consulted about the marriages of that age, he had not denied those of this age, about which he was consulted. And so those who received the very force both of the voice and of the pronouncement and of the distinction, perceived nothing else than what pertained to the matter of the consultation. And indeed the scribes, "Master," they say, "thou hast spoken well." For he had confirmed the resurrection, by publishing its form against the opinion of the Sadducees. In short, he did not refuse the testimony of those who had presumed that he had so answered. But if the scribes esteemed Christ the son of David, while David himself calls him lord, what is this to Christ? He was not blunting the error of the scribes, but procuring honour to Christ from David, whom he confirmed lord of David rather than son — which would not suit a destroyer of the Creator. But on our part how congruent the interpretation! For he who of old had been invoked by that blind man as the son of David — what he then kept silent, not having the scribes present, now spontaneously, of set purpose, before them, he brought forth, that he might show himself, whom the blind man, according to the doctrine of the scribes, had proclaimed only the son of David, to be also his lord — the faith indeed of the blind man being rewarded, by which he had believed him the son of David, but the tradition of the scribes being beaten back, by which they did not know him as lord too. Whatever should look to the glory of Christ the Creator's, thus no other would protect than the Christ of the Creator.

It has been established concerning the propriety of names, that it is owing to him who first both announced his own Christ to men and renamed Jesus. It will be established therefore too concerning the shamelessness of him who says that many shall come in his name, which is not his, if Christ and Jesus is not the Creator's, to whom the propriety of the names pertains; and besides forbids them to be received, of whom he himself too is the equal, as one who comes likewise in another's name, if it were not his to forestall the disciples against the lie of a name, who through the propriety of the name possessed the truth of it. They will come, in short, those saying, "I am Christ." You will receive them, who have received a like one. For this one too came in his own name. What now, since he too will come, the lord of the names, the Christ and Jesus of the Creator? Will you reject him? And how iniquitous, how unjust and unworthy of a best god, that you should not receive him coming in his own name, who received another in his name! Let us see too what signs he imposes on the times. Wars, I suppose, and kingdom upon kingdom, and nation upon nation, and pestilence, and famines, and earthquakes, and terrors, and prodigies from heaven — all which suit a severe and atrocious god. When he adds too that these things must come to pass, what does he exhibit himself? a destroyer or an approver of the Creator? Whose arrangements he confirms must be fulfilled — which, as a best god, he would rather have taken away than constituted, both so sad and so atrocious, if they had not been his own. But before these things he foretells too that persecutions and passions shall come upon them, surely unto martyrdom and unto salvation. Receive it proclaimed in Zechariah: "The Lord almighty," it says, "shall protect them, and they shall consume them and shall stone them with sling-stones, and shall drink their blood like wine, and shall fill the bowls as of an altar; and the Lord shall save them in that day, like sheep, his people, because holy stones are rolled." And lest you think these things are proclaimed of the passions which awaited them at the hands of the foreigners under the name of so many wars, regard the species. No one in the proclamation of wars to be waged with legitimate arms enumerates stoning, more familiar to popular assemblies and an unarmed tumult. No one in war measures such floods of blood by the capacity of bowls, or equates it to the bloodying of a single altar. No one calls sheep those who in war, armed and themselves fighting out of the same fierceness, fall — but those who, in their own propriety and patience, are slaughtered rather giving up themselves than avenging. In short, "Because holy stones," it says, "are rolled," not because soldiers fight. For stones are also the foundations upon which we are built, built up, according to Paul, upon the foundation of the apostles, who, holy stones set against the offence of all, were rolled. Here too, then, the same one forbids to think what ought to be answered before tribunals, who both suggested to Balaam what he had not thought — nay, contrary to what he had thought — and to Moses, pleading slowness of tongue, promised a mouth. And he demonstrated through Isaiah wisdom itself, which no one should resist: "This one shall say, I am God's, and shall cry out in the name of Jacob, and another shall be inscribed in the name of Israel." For what is wiser and more incontradictible than a simple and outstretched confession in the name of a martyr prevailing with God — which is the interpretation of Israel? Nor is it wonderful if he restrained forethought, who himself too received from the Father the seasonable supply of pronouncing: "The Lord gives me the tongue of discipline, when I ought to bring forth a word" — unless Marcion brings in a Christ not subject to the Father. From the near ones too persecutions, and surely a blasphemy of the name out of hatred, having been proclaimed, I need not again show. But "by endurance," he says, "you shall make safe your souls" — concerning which surely the psalm, "The endurance," it says, "of the just shall not perish unto the end." Because elsewhere too, "Honourable is the death of the just" — out of endurance without doubt, because Zechariah too: "But there shall be a crown for those who have endured." But lest you dare to argue that the apostles were harassed by the Jews as heralds of another god, remember that the prophets too suffered the same from the Jews, yet were apostles of no other god than the Creator. But, the time of the destruction being shown thereafter — when Jerusalem had begun to be walled about with armies — he narrates the signs of the last end, prodigies of sun and moon and stars, and on earth distresses of the nations astounded as it were by the sound of a fluctuating sea, in expectation of the evils impending over the world. That the very powers of the heavens too should be shaken, hear Joel: "And I will give prodigies in heaven, and on earth blood and fire and the vapour of smoke: the sun shall be turned into darkness and the moon into blood, before the great and illustrious day of the Lord come." You have Habakkuk too: "The earth shall be burst by the rivers, they shall see thee, and the peoples shall be in travail: thou shalt scatter the waters with thy step; the abyss gave its sound, the loftiness of its fear was lifted up: the sun and the moon stood in their order, into light thy lightnings shall go, into brightness the lightning of thy shield: in thy threatening thou shalt diminish the earth, and in thy indignation thou shalt put down the nations." They agree, I think, both the Lord's pronouncements and the prophets', concerning the shakings of the world and the orb of the elements and the nations. After these things, what does the Lord say? "And then they shall see the Son of man coming from the heavens with very great power." "But when these things shall begin to come to pass, you shall lift yourselves up and raise your heads, because your redemption has drawn near" — namely in the time of the kingdom, concerning which the very parable will be subjoined: "So you too, when you shall see all these things come to pass, know that the kingdom of God has drawn near." This will be the great and illustrious day of the Lord, of the Son of man coming from the heavens, according to Daniel: "Behold, with the clouds of heaven as it were the Son of man coming," and the rest. "And there was given to him royal power" — which in the parable he had gone out to ask, having left money with his servants, that it might be lent at interest; "and all the nations" — which the Father had promised him in the psalm: "Ask of me, and I will give thee the nations for thine inheritance"; "and all glory serving him, and his power eternal, which shall not be taken away, and his kingdom, which shall not be corrupted" — because they shall neither die in it, nor marry, but shall be as the angels. Concerning the same coming of the Son of man and its fruit, in Habakkuk: "Thou wentest forth unto the salvation of thy people, to save thy Christs" — about to lift themselves up, namely, and raise their heads in the time of the kingdom, redeemed. Therefore, since these things which are of the promises agree accordingly, just as those which are of the shakings, out of the consonance of the prophetic and dominical pronouncements, you will be able here to interstructure no distinction, so as to refer the shakings indeed to the Creator, the god of savagery namely — which the best god ought neither to permit, far less to await — but to ascribe the promises to the best god, which the Creator, ignorant of that one, would not have prophesied. Or if he prophesied his own, not distant from the promises of Christ, he will be equal in liberality to the best god, nor will more seem to be promised by your Christ than by my Son of man. The very course of the gospel Scripture, from the interrogation of the disciples even to the parable of the fig-tree, you will find by the context of the sense so to cleave to the Son of man on this side and that, that it compacts into him both the sad and the joyful, both the shakings and the promises, nor can you separate from him the one part. For one coming of the Son of man being constituted between two issues, of shakings and of promises, it is of necessity that to the one Son of man pertain both the incommodities of the nations and the vows of the saints — who is so placed in the midst that he is common to both issues, about to conclude the one by his coming, that is, the incommodities of the nations, to begin the other, that is, the vows of the saints — so that, whether you concede the coming of the Son of man to be my Christ's, by which you assign to him the impending evils which precede his coming, you are compelled to ascribe to him too the goods which arise from his coming; or whether you prefer it to be yours, by which you ascribe to him the goods which arise from his coming, you are compelled to reckon to him too the evils which precede his coming. For the evils cohere to the coming of the Son of man by preceding it, as much as the goods by following it. Seek, then, which of the two Christs you will constitute in the person of the one Son of man, into whom either arrangement is referred. Either you have given me the Creator best, or your god harsh by nature. In sum, consider the example of the very parable. "Look at the fig-tree and all the trees: when they have brought forth fruit, men understand that summer has drawn near; so you too, when you see these things come to pass, know that the kingdom of God is at hand." For if the fruitings of the little trees give a sign of the summer time, by preceding it, accordingly the conflictings of the world prenote a sign of the kingdom, by preceding it. But every sign belongs to him whose is the thing of which it is the sign, and to every thing a sign is imposed by him whose the thing is. Thus if the conflictings are signs of the kingdom, just as the fruitings of summer, then the kingdom too is the Creator's, whose are reckoned the conflictings which are signs of the kingdom. He had premised that these things, so atrocious, so dreadful, must come to pass — a best god — certainly proclaimed by the prophets and the law; so far did he not destroy the law and the prophets, since he confirms that the things they had proclaimed must be perfected. He drives in still further that heaven and earth shall not pass until all things be accomplished. What are these? If they are the Creator's, with reason the elements shall sustain the order of their lord to be discharged; if they are the best god's, I know not whether heaven and earth would sustain the things a rival has appointed to be perfected. If the Creator shall suffer this, he is not a jealous god. Let heaven and earth pass, then, come now. For so their lord has destined, while his word abides for ever. For so too Isaiah foretold. Let the disciples too be admonished, lest at any time their hearts be weighed down with surfeit and drunkenness and worldly cares, and that day come suddenly upon them as a snare — surely upon those who have forgotten God out of the fullness and thought of the world. It will be an admonition of Moses. So far will he free from the snare of that day who brought in this admonition of old. There were other places too at Jerusalem for teaching, and others outside Jerusalem for retiring. But by day he taught in the temple, as one who through Hosea had foretold, "In my temple they found me, and there it was disputed with them." But at night he retired into the olive-grove. For so Zechariah had demonstrated: "And his feet shall stand upon the mount of olives." There were hours too suited to the audience. At dawn it was to be assembled, who, when he had said through Isaiah, "The Lord gives me the tongue of discipline," added, "He has set an ear to me in the morning to hear." If this is to dissolve the prophecies, what will it be to fulfil them?

Accordingly he knew too when he ought to suffer, whose passion the law figures. For out of so many Jewish feasts he chose the day of the passover. For into this mystery Moses had pronounced, "It is the passover of the Lord." Therefore too he showed his affection: "With desire I have desired to eat this passover with you before I suffer." O destroyer of the law, who had desired even to keep the passover! Did the Jewish mutton-flesh delight him, forsooth? Or was he not the one who, about to be led like a sheep to the slaughter, and like a sheep before the shearer, so not about to open his mouth, desired to fulfil the figure of his own salutary blood? He could have been betrayed too by any stranger — that I might not say that in this too the psalm is discharged: "He who eats bread with me shall lift up his heel against me." He could have been betrayed too without a price. For what need of the labours of a betrayer about him who, offending the people openly, could no more have been betrayed than assailed? But this would have suited another Christ, not one who fulfilled the prophecies. For it is written: "Because they sold the just." For both the quantity and the issue of the price, afterward, Judas repenting, recalled and given for the purchase of the potter's field — as is contained in the gospel of Matthew — Jeremiah foresang: "And they took thirty pieces of silver, the price of him appraised or honoured, and gave them for the potter's field." Professing therefore that with desire he had desired to eat the passover as his own (for it is unworthy that God should desire anything alien), he took bread and distributed it to the disciples, and made it his body, by saying "This is my body," that is, the figure of my body. But it would not have been a figure, were it not the body of a truth. For the rest, an empty thing, which is a phantom, could not take a figure. Or if for this reason he fashioned bread for himself a body, because he lacked the truth of a body, then he ought to have delivered bread for us. It made for the vanity of Marcion, that bread should be crucified. But why does he call bread his body, and not rather a pumpkin, which Marcion had in place of a heart? Not understanding that this was an old figure of the body of Christ, who says through Jeremiah, "Against me they have devised a device, saying, Come, let us cast wood upon his bread" — namely the cross upon his body. And so the illuminator of antiquities sufficiently declared what he then willed to have signified by bread, calling bread his body. So too, in the mention of the cup, constituting the testament sealed with his blood, he confirmed the substance of the body. For of no body can there be blood but of flesh. For even if some quality of body not fleshy be opposed to us, surely it will not have blood unless fleshly. Thus the proof of the body will stand from the testimony of the flesh, the proof of the flesh from the testimony of the blood. But that you may recognize the old figure too of blood in wine, Isaiah will be at hand: "Who," he says, "is he that comes from Edom? the redness of his garments from Bozrah? so comely in a violent robe with strength? Why are thy garments red, and thy raiment as of one who treads a full winepress?" For the prophetic spirit, as it were already contemplating the Lord coming to his passion, clothed namely in flesh, as suffering in it, designates the bloody state of the flesh in the redness of the garments, of the flesh trodden and pressed out by the force of the passion as in a winepress, because thence men come down as it were bloody from the redness of the wine. Much more manifestly Genesis, in the blessing of Judah, of whose tribe the registration of the flesh of Christ was to proceed, even then delineated Christ in Judah: "He shall wash," it says, "his robe in wine, and his garment in the blood of the grape" — showing his robe and garment to be the flesh, and the wine the blood. So too now he consecrated his blood in wine, who then figured wine in blood.

"Woe," he says, "to him through whom the Son of man is betrayed." Therefore now the "Woe" is established to be understood an outcry of imprecation and threatening, and to be reckoned to one angered and offended; unless Judas was to bring back so great a crime with impunity. Or if with impunity, the "Woe" is idle; if not with impunity, then surely he is to be punished by him against whom he admitted the crime of betrayal. Now if knowingly he suffered the man whom he had himself enrolled into his company to rush into so great a crime, do not now bring up again concerning the Creator, in the matter of Adam, the things which are retorted upon your god too — that either he was ignorant, who out of providence did not stand in the way of one about to sin, or could not stand in the way, if he was ignorant, or would not, if he both knew and could, and so is to be judged malicious, who suffered his own man to perish out of a delinquency. I persuade you, then, to acknowledge rather in this one too the Creator, than to make a best god equal to him against your own opinion. For both, in destining Peter, who had spoken something presumptuously, rather to denial, he showed you a jealous god. He ought too to be betrayed by a kiss, the prophetic Christ, namely — as the son of him who was loved by the people with the lips. Brought into the assembly, he is interrogated whether he were the Christ. Concerning what Christ would the Jews have inquired but their own? Why then did he not, even then, betray another to them? "That he might be able to suffer," you say. That is, that that best one might plunge those still ignorant into crime. And yet, even if he had said it, he would have been about to suffer. "For if I tell you," he says, "you do not believe." But, not about to believe, they would have persevered in his slaying. And why should he not the rather have been about to suffer, if he had been of another god, and through this had manifested himself the adversary of the Creator? Therefore not that he might suffer did he then too forbear to show himself another, but because they were desiring to wring a confession out of his mouth — yet, even confessing, not about to believe, who ought to have acknowledged him from his works fulfilling the Scriptures — therefore it was his to hide himself from those to whom acknowledgement was spontaneously due. And yet, still reaching out his hand to them, "Henceforth," he says, "shall the Son of man be sitting at the right hand of the power of God." For he was suggesting himself, out of the prophecy of Daniel, the Son of man, and, out of the psalm of David, the one sitting at the right hand of God. And so, illumined out of that saying and the comparison of Scripture as to whom he wished himself to be understood, "Then art thou the Son of God?" they say. Of what god, but whom alone they had known? Of what god, but whom they remembered in the psalm to have said to his Son, "Sit at my right hand"? But he answered, "You say it" — as though "not I." And yet he confirmed that he was that which they had said, while they again interrogate. But whence will you prove that they pronounced it interrogatively and not themselves confirmingly, "Then art thou the Son of God?" So that, because obliquely he had shown himself to be understood through the Scriptures as the Son of God, they so perceived, "Then art thou the Son of God?" which thou wilt not openly say; equally so he too, "You say it," answered confirmingly, and so was his pronouncement, that they persevered in that which the pronouncement savoured.

For having led him to Pilate, they began to charge that he called himself Christ a king, without doubt the Son of God, about to sit at the right hand of God. For otherwise they would have weighed him with another title, uncertain whether he had called himself the Son of God, had he not pronounced "You say it" thus, that he was that which they said. To Pilate too, interrogating, "Art thou Christ?" likewise, "Thou sayest," lest for fear of his power he should seem to have answered more. The Lord was set, therefore, in judgement. "And he set in judgement his people." "The Lord himself shall come into judgement with the elders and the rulers of the people," according to Isaiah. And thereafter he fulfilled every writing of his own passion. "There the nations were in tumult, and the peoples meditated vain things. The kings of the earth stood up, and the rulers were gathered together against the Lord and against his Christ." The nations, the Romans who were with Pilate; the peoples, the tribes of Israel; the kings, in Herod; the rulers, in the chief priests. For also sent to Herod as it were a gift by Pilate, he gave faith to the voices of Hosea. For of Christ he had prophesied: "And bound they shall lead him as a gift to the king." In short, Herod was delighted at the sight of Jesus, but heard no voice from him. For "as a lamb before the shearer, so he opened not his mouth" — because the Lord had given him the tongue of discipline, that he might know how he ought to bring forth a word — that tongue, namely, which in the psalm he then proved glued to his throat, by not speaking. And Barabbas indeed, most guilty, is granted his life as if a good man, but Christ, most just, is demanded for death as a homicide. But also two criminals are fastened about him, that he might be reckoned among the iniquitous, namely. His clothing plainly, divided by the soldiers, part assigned by lot — Marcion took away, regarding the prophecy of the psalm: "They divided my garments among them, and upon my vesture they cast lots." Take away therefore the cross itself. Yet the same psalm is not silent about it: "They pierced my hands and my feet." The whole issue in him is read. "Dogs surrounded me, the synagogue of the malicious encompassed me: all who looked at me mocked me with the nose: they spoke with the lips, and shook their heads: he hoped in God, let him free him." To what end now is the testimony of the garments? Have the booty of your falsity; the whole psalm is the garments of Christ. But behold, the elements too are shaken. For their Lord was suffering. For the rest, had it been the adversary that was hurt, the heaven would have flourished with its lights, the sun would the rather have insulted with its rays, the day the rather would have stood, gladly beholding Marcion's Christ hanging on the gibbet. These arguments too would have suited me, even had they not been foretold. "The heaven," says Isaiah, "I will clothe with darkness." This will be the day of which also Amos: "And it shall be in that day, says the Lord, the sun shall set at noon" (you have too the signification of the sixth hour), "and it shall be darkened upon the earth." The veil of the temple too was rent, by the eruption of the angel, forsaking the daughter of Zion, as a watch-tower in a vineyard and a hut in a cucumber-field. O how far he persevered, even in the thirtieth psalm, to render Christ himself! He cries out to the Father, that even dying with his last voice he might fulfil the prophets. With this saying he expired. Who? The spirit himself, or the flesh the spirit? But the spirit could not expire itself. He is one who expires, another who is expired. If the spirit is expired, it must of necessity be expired by another. But if it had been spirit alone, it would rather have been said to have departed than to have expired. Who then expires the spirit but the flesh, which both breathes while it has it, and so, when it loses it, expires it? In short, if there was no flesh, but a phantom of flesh, and the phantom was of spirit, but the spirit expired itself and by expiring departed, without doubt the phantom departed when the spirit, which was a phantom, departed, and the phantom appeared nowhere along with the spirit. Nothing therefore remained on the tree, nothing hung even after the expiration, nothing was demanded of Pilate, nothing taken down from the gibbet, nothing wrapped in linen, nothing laid in a new tomb. And yet not nothing. What, then, was that? If a phantom, then Christ was still in it. If Christ had departed, then he had taken away the phantom. It remains for heretical shamelessness to say that a phantom of the phantom remained there. But if Joseph too knew it to be a body which he handled with all piety — that Joseph who had not consented with the Jews in their crime? "Blessed the man who has not gone away in the counsel of the impious, and in the way of sinners has not stood, and in the seat of pestilence has not sat."

It behoved that the Lord's burier too be prophesied, and even then deservedly be blessed, if not even the office of those women be passed over by prophecy, who before light came together to the sepulchre with a preparation of spices. For concerning this through Hosea: "That they may seek my face," it says, "before light they shall watch toward me, saying, Let us go and turn back to the Lord, because he himself has snatched away and will heal us, has struck and will have mercy upon us, he will heal us after two days, on the third day we shall rise again." Who would not believe these things rolled in the reconsideration of those women, between the grief of the present destitution, by which they seemed to themselves stricken by the Lord, and the hope of the resurrection itself, by which they rightly esteem they are restored? But the body not being found, his burial had been taken away from the midst, according to Isaiah. But also two angels appeared there. For with about so many attendants the word of God was wont to be employed, consisting in two witnesses. The women too returning from the sepulchre, and from that vision of angels, Isaiah foresaw: "Women," he says, "coming from a sight, come" — to announce, namely, the resurrection of the Lord. But well that the disbelief of the disciples persevered, that even to the end our defence might stand — that Christ Jesus published himself to the disciples as no other than the prophets'. For when two of them were journeying, and the Lord had joined himself to them, not appearing as himself, even dissembling out of consciousness of the thing done, "But we thought," they say, "that he himself was the redeemer of Israel" — surely their own Christ, that is, the Creator's. So far had he published himself no other to them. For the rest, they would not have esteemed him the Creator's; and when he was esteemed the Creator's, he would not have sustained this esteem of himself, if he were not he who is esteemed. Or else he himself will be the author of error and the prevaricator of truth, against the title of a best god. But neither after the resurrection did he show himself to them any other than the one they had said was esteemed by them. Plainly he inveighed against them: "O foolish and slow of heart in not believing all things which he spoke to you." Which things he spoke, prove him to be not of another god, but of the same god. For the same things the angels too to the women: "Remember what he spoke to you in Galilee, saying, that the Son of man must be betrayed and crucified and on the third day rise again." And why must he, except because thus it was written by God the Creator? Therefore he rebuked them as scandalized only by the passion, and as doubtful about the faith of the resurrection announced to them by the women — through which they had not believed him to be the one whom they had esteemed. And so, what they had esteemed, wishing it to be believed, he confirmed himself to be the one they had esteemed — namely the Christ of the Creator, the redeemer of Israel. But concerning the truth of the body, what can be clearer? — when, while they hesitated lest it be a phantom — nay, believing it a phantom — "Why are you troubled?" he says, "and why do thoughts rise in your hearts? See my hands and feet, that it is I myself; because a spirit has not bones, as you see me to have." And Marcion was unwilling, I believe of set purpose, to erase certain things contrary to him from his gospel, that out of those which he could have erased and did not, he might either be denied to have erased those which he erased, or be said to have erased them with reason. Nor does he spare any but those which he subverts by interpreting otherwise no less than by deleting. He wishes therefore "A spirit has not bones, as you see me to have" to be so said that "as you see me to have" be referred to the spirit — "as you see me to have," that is, not having bones, just as a spirit too. And what is the reason of that tortuousness? — when he could have pronounced simply, "Because a spirit has not bones, as you see me not to have." But why does he offer to their inspection his hands and feet, which members consist of bones, if he had no bones? Why does he add, "And know that it is I," whom, namely, they had formerly known to be corporeal? Or if he was a phantom utterly, why did he rebuke them for believing him a phantom? And yet, while they still did not believe, on that account he desired food, that he might show himself to have teeth too. We have fulfilled, as I think, our undertaking. We have exhibited Jesus Christ, by the doctrines, opinions, affections, senses, powers, passions, even by the resurrection of the prophets, no other than the Creator's — since, sending too his apostles to preach to all nations, he commanded the fulfilment of the psalm, "Into all the earth their sound shall go out, and to the ends of the earth their voices." I pity thee, Marcion; in vain hast thou laboured. For Christ Jesus in thy gospel is mine.
